solution: Solution: Given, $f(x)=\frac{a^{x}+a^{-x}}{2}$ Then, $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=\frac{a^{x+y}+a^{-(x+y)}}{2} +\frac{a^{x-y}+a^{-(x-y)}}{2}$ $=\frac{a^{x}\cdot a^{y}+a^{-x}\cdot a^{-y}+a^{x}\cdot a^{-y}+a^{-x} a^{y}}{2}$ $=\frac{a^{x}(a^{y}+a^{-y})+a^{-x}(a^{y}+a^{-y})}{2}$ $=\frac{(a^{x}+a^{-x})(a^{y}+a^{-y})}{2}$ $=2\cdot\frac{a^{x}+a^{-x}}{2}\cdot\frac{a^{y}+a^{-y}}{2}=2 f(x) f(y)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\because (x^2+5x+5)^{x+5}=1$ For an integer power to equal $1$ , the possibilities are: the exponent is $0$ with a nonzero base, the base is $1$ , or the base is $-1$ with an even exponent. Case I $x+5=0$ $\Rightarrow \; x=-5$ Here the base is $5 \ne 0$ , so $x=-5$ is valid. Case II $x^2+5x+5=1$ $\Rightarrow \; x^2+5x+4=0$ $\Rightarrow \; (x+1)(x+4)=0$ $\Rightarrow \; x=-1,-4$ Both are valid. Case III $x^2+5x+5=-1$ and $x+5$ is even. $\Rightarrow \; x^2+5x+6=0$ $\Rightarrow \; (x+2)(x+3)=0$ $\Rightarrow \; x=-2,-3$ For $x=-2$ , the exponent is $3$ , which is odd, so it is not valid. For $x=-3$ , the exponent is $2$ , which is even, so $x=-3$ is valid. Thus the integer solutions are $x=-5,-4,-3,-1$ . Hence the number of integers satisfying the equation is $4$ . © examsnet.com

Option (a), (c) and (d) are multiple of 3 . $\Rightarrow \; \; a \neq 1214$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $e^{4 t}-10 e^{3 t}+29 e^{2 t}-22 e^{t}+4=0$ ...(i) Let $e^{t}=x$ and roots of (1) be $t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, t_{4}$ $\therefore x^{4}-10 x^{3}+29 x^{2}-22 x+4=0$ Then, roots are $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}$ product of roots $x_{1} \cdot x_{2} \cdot x_{3} \cdot x_{4}=4$ $\Rightarrow e^{t_1}\cdot e^{t_2}\cdot e^{t_3} e^{t_4}=4$ $\Rightarrow e^{t_{1}+t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}}=4$ $t_{1}+t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}=\log_{e}\;4=\log_{e}\;2^{2}=2\log_{e}\;2$ Sum of roots $=2\log_{e}\;2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{x^{4}}{(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{x^{4}}{x^{2} - 3x + 2}$ is an improper  fraction. $\therefore \frac{x^{4}}{(x-1)(x-2)} = x^{3} + 3x + 7 + \frac{15x - 14}{(x-1)(x-2)}$ $= x^{2} + 3x + 7 + \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x-2}$ On comparing with given equation, $\frac{x^{4}}{(x-1)(x-2)} = f(x) + \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x-2}$ , we have $f(x) = x^{2} + 3x + 7$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+1 .2}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+2 .3}\right)+\dots +\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+n(n+1)}\right)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2-1}{1+1 .2}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3-2}{1+2 .3}\right)+\dots +\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{n+1-n}{1+n(n+1)}\right)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}(2)-\tan^{-1}(1)+\tan^{-1}(3)-\tan^{-1}(2)+\dots +\tan^{-1}(n+1)-\tan^{-1}(n)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}(n+1)-\tan^{-1}(1)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{n+1-1}{1+(n+1) .1}\right)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{n}{n+2}\right)=\tan^{-1}(x)$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{n}{n+2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: △ABC, $a=3, b=4$ and, $A=\frac{3}{4}$ $\therefore \cos A = \sqrt{1-\sin^{2} A} = \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ But $\cos A = \frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4} = \frac{4^{2}+c^{2}-3^{2}}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot c}$ $\Rightarrow 2 \sqrt{7} c = 7 + c^{2}$ $\Rightarrow c^{2} - 2 \sqrt{7} c + 7 = 0$ $\Rightarrow (c - \sqrt{7})^{2} = 0$ $\therefore c = \sqrt{7}$ Now, $\cos B = \frac{c^{2}+a^{2}-b^{2}}{2 a c}$ $\Rightarrow \cos B = \frac{7+9-16}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot \sqrt{7}} = 0$ $\Rightarrow B = 90^{\circ}$ $\therefore \angle CBA = 90^{\circ}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $A=75^{\circ}, B=45^{\circ}$ , then $C=180^{\circ}-(75^{\circ}+45^{\circ})=60^{\circ}$ $\because \frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{C}{\sin C}=2R$ where R is circum  radius $\Rightarrow a=2R\sin A, b=2R\sin B, c=2R\sin C$ Then, $b+c\sqrt{2}=2R(\sin B+\sqrt{2}\sin C)$ $=2R(\sin 45^{\circ}+\sqrt{2}\sin 60^{\circ})$ $=2R\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=2R\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $=2\cdot 2R\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $=2\cdot\left(2R\sin 75^{\circ}\right)$ $=2\left(2R\sin A\right)$ $=2a$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In $\Delta ABC$ $a=2 R \sin A=4 R \sin \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{A}{2}$ $b=2 R \sin B=4 R \sin \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2}$ $r=4 R \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}$ $r_{1}=4 R \sin \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}$ $r_{2}=4 R \cos \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}$ $r_{3}=4 R \cos \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}$ Now, $a b - r_{1} r_{2}=16 R^{2} \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2} \left(1-\cos^{2} \frac{C}{2}\right)$ $=16 R^{2} \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{B}{2} \sin^{2} \frac{C}{2}$ $\therefore \frac{a b - r_{1} r_{2}}{r_{3}}=4 R \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}=r$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $p = \hat{i} + a \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ $q = \hat{j} + a \hat{k}$ $\Rightarrow r = a \hat{i} + \hat{k}$ Volume of parallelopiped $= [pqr]$ $= p \cdot (q \times r)$ $V = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & a \\ a & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$ $\Rightarrow V = a^{3} - a + 1$ Differentiating V with respect to a $\frac{dV}{da} = 3 a^{2} - 1$ Again, differentiating w.r.t. a $\frac{d^{2} V}{d a^{2}} = 6 a$ For stationary points $\frac{dV}{da} = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3 a^{2} - 1 = 0$ or $a^{2} = \frac{1}{3} \text{ or } a = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ At, $a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\frac{d^{2} V}{d a^{2}} = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} > 0$ ∴ Volume is minimum at $a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $a = \frac{3}{2} \hat{k}, b = \frac{2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}}{2}$ $a + b = \frac{3}{2} \hat{k} + \frac{\hat{2i+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}}}{2} = \hat{i}+\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ $a - b = \frac{3}{2} \hat{k} - \frac{2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}}{2} = -\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Let θ be the angle between $(a+b)$ and $(a-b)$ then $\cos \theta = \frac{(a+b) \cdot (a-b)}{\lvert a+b \rvert \lvert a-b \rvert}$ $= \frac{1(-1)+1(-1)+1(2)}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}} \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2^{2}}} = 0$ ∴ θ = 90° © examsnet.com

Solution: $a=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $b=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ $c=7\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$ Then, $a+b=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ and $b+c=8\hat{i}+12\hat{j}+16\hat{k}$ $=4(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$ Area of parallelogram $=\frac{1}{2}\left|(a+b)\times(b+c)\right|$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left|2(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})\times4(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})\right|$ $=\frac{8}{2}\left|(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})\times(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})\right|$ $=4\left|\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\right|=4\left|\hat{i}+\hat{2j}-\hat{k}\right|$ $=4\sqrt{1+4+1}=4\sqrt{6}$ sq units © examsnet.com

Solution: $a=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}, b=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}, c=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $a \cdot a = 4+1+9 = 14$ $a \cdot b = b \cdot a = 2+3-3 = 2$ $a \cdot c = c \cdot a = 6-1-6 = -1$ $b \cdot c = c \cdot b = 3-3+2 = 2$ $c \cdot c = 9+1+4 = 14$ $\text{Now,}\begin{vmatrix} a \cdot a & a \cdot b & a \cdot c \\ b \cdot a & b \cdot b & b \cdot c \\ c \cdot a & c \cdot b & c \cdot c \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 14 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 11 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 14 \end{vmatrix}$ $= 14(154-4) - 2(28+2) - 1(4+11)$ $= 2100 - 60 - 15$ $= 2025$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\left|a\right|=2,\left|b\right|=3$ $\because (a+t b) \perp (a-t b)$ $\Rightarrow (a+t b) \cdot (a-t b)=0$ $\Rightarrow a \cdot a - t(a \cdot b) + t(b \cdot a) - t^{2}(b \cdot b)=0$ $\Rightarrow \left|a\right|^{2} - t^{2} \left|b\right|^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow t^{2} = \frac{\left|a\right|^{2}}{\left|b\right|^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow t = \frac{\left|a\right|}{\left|b\right|} = \frac{2}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Sample space of a dice $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ Let $E=$ getting even number $\Rightarrow E=\{2,4,6\}$ $P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ If dice is thrown three times Let $X=$ success, then X x = 0 x = 1 x = 2 x = 3 $P(X=x)$ ${}^3C_0\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$ ${}^3C_1\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$ ${}^3C_2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$ ${}^3C_3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$ Probability of getting at least 2 successes $=P(X \ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)$ $={}^3C_2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3+{}^3C_3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, coordinate $(x, y)=(2\sqrt{2},-3\sqrt{2})$ Let new coordinates be $(x', y').$ Then, $x'=x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta$ and $y'=-x \sin \theta + y \cos \theta$ Here, $\theta = 45^{\circ}$ $\therefore x'=2\sqrt{2} \cos 45^{\circ} + (-3\sqrt{2}) \sin 45^{\circ}$ $=2\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 3\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 2-3 = -1$ and $y'=-2\sqrt{2} \sin 45^{\circ} + (-3\sqrt{2}) \cos 45^{\circ}$ $=-2\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 3\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = -2-3 = -5$ New coordinate is $(-1,-5).$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int\limits_{2}^{4} (|x-2|+|x-3|) d x$ $\because x - a = \begin{cases} x - a, & x \ge a \\ -(x - a), & x < a \end{cases}$ $\therefore I = \int\limits_{2}^{4} |x-2| d x + \int\limits_{2}^{3} |x-3| d x + \int\limits_{3}^{4} |x-3| d x$ $= \int\limits_{2}^{4} (x-2) d x - \int\limits_{2}^{3} (x-3) d x + \int\limits_{3}^{4} (x-3) d x$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x \right)_{2}^{4} - \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 3x \right)_{2}^{3} + \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 3x \right)_{3}^{4}$ $= \left[ \left( \frac{16}{2} - 8 \right) - \left( \frac{4}{2} - 4 \right) \right] - \left[ \left( \frac{9}{2} - 9 \right) - \left( \frac{4}{2} - 6 \right) \right] + \left[ \left( \frac{16}{2} - 12 \right) - \left( \frac{9}{2} - 9 \right) \right]$ $= \left| \left[ 0 - (-2) \right] - \left[ \left( \frac{-9}{2} \right) - (-4) \right] + \left[ (-4) - \left( -\frac{9}{2} \right) \right] \right|$ $= \left| 2 + \frac{9}{2} - 4 - 4 + \frac{9}{2} \right| = \left[ 2 + 9 - 8 \right] = 3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Series equivalent inductance, $L_{eq}=8\,\mathrm{H}$ Parallel equivalent inductance, $L_{\text{eq}_2}=1.5\,\mathrm{H}=\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{H}$ Let two inductors used here be $L_1$ and $L_2$ , then $L_{\text{eq}_1}($ series $) = L_1 + L_2$ $\therefore L_{\text{eq}_1}=L_1+L_2=8$ ...(i) and $\frac{1}{L_{\text{eq}_1}}$ (parallel) $= \frac{1}{L_1} + \frac{1}{L_2}$ $\Rightarrow L_{\text{eq}_2}=\frac{L_1 L_2}{L_2+L_1}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{2}=\frac{L_1(8-L_1)}{8}$ $\Rightarrow 12=8L_1-L_1^2$ $\Rightarrow L_1^2-8L_1+12=0$ $\Rightarrow L_1^2-6L_1-2L_1+12=0$ $\Rightarrow L_1(L_1-6)-2(L_1-6)=0$ $\therefore L_1=2\,\mathrm{H}$ or $6\,\mathrm{H}$ and $L_2=(8-2)$ or $(8-6)$ $=6\,\mathrm{H}$ or $2\,\mathrm{H}$ ∴ Difference between inductances is $(L_1-L_2)$ or $(L_2-L_1)=6-2$ = 4H © examsnet.com

Solution: According to Gibb's free energy, $\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S$ Reaction is non spontancous i.e. $\Delta G > 0$ at $298\,\text{K}$ . As the temperature increases from $298\,\text{K}$ to $350\,\text{K}$ . The reaction becomes spontaneous i.e. $\Delta G < 0$ . $\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S$ $\Delta G < 0$ When $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are +ve then, $\Delta G$ will be positive till $\Delta H > T \Delta S$ . When the temperature is increased further $\Delta H$ becomes less than $T \Delta S$ i.e. $\Delta H < T \Delta S$ and $\Delta G$ becomes $-\text{v e.}$ Thus, reaction becomes spontancous. © examsnet.com

Solution: The unbalanced redox reaction is $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} + \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + \mathrm{CO}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ (i) Balanced C atoms $\mathrm{MnO}_{\overset{+7}{4}} + \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} + \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ Oxidation state of Mn decreases from $+7$ to $+2$ . To balance the increase or decrease in oxidation number, multiply Mn  containing species with 2 and C containing species with $5.$ $2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 5 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 10 \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ (ii) Balance $\text{'O'}$ atoms by adding 8 water molecules to the product side. $2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 5 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 10 \mathrm{CO}_{2} + 8 \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ (iii) Balance 'H' atoms by adding $16 \mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions to the reactant side. $2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 5 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} + 16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 10 \mathrm{CO}_{2} + 8 \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ Hence, $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} \Rightarrow 5, \mathrm{H}^{+}=16$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\lim\limits_{x \to 1} \frac{(1-x)(1-x^{2}) \cdots (1-x^{2n})}{\left\{ (1-x)(1-x^{2}) \cdots (1-x^{n}) \right\}^{2}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 1} \frac{(x-1)(x^{2}-1) \cdots (x^{2n}-1)}{\left\{ (x-1)(x^{2}-1) \cdots (x^{n}-1) \right\}^{2}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 1} \frac{(x-1)(x^{2}-1) \cdots (x^{2n}-1)}{\left\{ \frac{x-1}{x-1} \cdot \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \cdots \frac{x^{n}-1}{x-1} \right\}^{2} \cdot (x-1)^{2n}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 1} \frac{ \frac{x-1}{x-1} \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \cdots \frac{x^{2n}-1}{x-1} }{ \left\{ \frac{x-1}{x-1} \cdot \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \cdots \frac{x^{n}-1}{x-1} \right\}^{2} }$ $= \frac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots 2n}{\left\{ 1 \cdot 2 \cdots n \right\}^{2}}$ $= \frac{(2n)!}{(n!)^{2}} = \frac{(2n)!}{n! n!}$ $= {}^{2n}C_{n}$ $\left[ \because \lim\limits_{x \to a} \frac{x^{n} - a^{n}}{x - a} n a^{n-1} \right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=\frac{\log_e (1+x^{2} \tan x)}{\sin x^{3}}. x \neq 0$ $f$ is continuous at $x=0$ , then $f(0)= LHL = RHL$ $RHL =\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\log_e (1+h^{2} \tan h)}{\sin h^{3}}$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\log_e (1+h^{2} \tan h)}{h^{3} \cdot \left(\frac{\sin h^{3}}{h^{3}}\right)}$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\log_e (1+h^{2} \tan h)}{h^{3}}$ $\left[\because\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=1\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\log_e \left(1+h^{3} \frac{\tan h}{h}\right)}{h^{3}}$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\log_e (1+h^{3})}{h^{3}}$ $\left(\because\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\tan h}{h}=1\right)$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{1}{1+h^{3}}(3h^{2})}{3h^{2}}$ [L-Hospital] $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{1+h^{3}}=1$ $\therefore f(0)=1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $x=\sec\theta-\cos\theta$ , then $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\sec\theta\tan\theta+\sin\theta=\tan\theta(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)$ $y=\sec^{n}\theta-\cos^{n}\theta$ , then $\frac{dy}{d\theta}=n\sec^{n-1}\theta\sec\theta\tan\theta+n\cos^{n-1}\theta\sin\theta$ $=n\tan\theta(\sec^{n}\theta+\cos^{n}\theta)$ $\therefore\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}}$ $=\frac{n\tan\theta(\sec^{n}\theta+\cos^{n}\theta)}{\tan\theta(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)}$ $=\frac{n(\sec^{n}\theta+\cos^{n}\theta)}{\sec\theta+\cos\theta}$ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=\frac{n^{2}(\sec^{n}\theta+\cos^{n}\theta)^{2}}{(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}}$ $=\frac{n^{2}\{(\sec^{n}\theta-\cos^{n}\theta)^{2}+4\}}{(\sec\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}+4}$ $=\frac{n^{2}(y^{2}+4)}{x^{2}+4}$ $\Rightarrow(x^{2}+4)\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=n^{2}(y^{2}+4)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y =\log_{\cot x}\tan x-\log_{\tan x}\cot x+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ $=\frac{\log_e\tan x}{\log_e\cot x}-\frac{\log_e\cot x}{\log_e\tan x}+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ $=\frac{\log_e\tan x}{\log_e\left(\frac{1}{\tan x}\right)}-\frac{\log_e\left(\frac{1}{\tan x}\right)}{\log_e(\tan x)}+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ $=\frac{\log_e\tan x}{-\log_e\tan x}+\frac{\log_e\tan x}{\log_e\tan x}+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ $=-1+1+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ Now, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)^2}\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{4x}{4-x^2}\right)$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(4-x^2)^2}{(4-x^2)^2+16x^2}\left[\frac{(4-x^2)4+(4x)(2x)}{(4-x^2)^2}\right]$ $=\frac{(4-x^2)^2}{16+x^4+8x^2}\left[\frac{16-4x^2+8x^2}{(4-x^2)^2}\right]$ $=\frac{16+4x^2}{(x^2+4)^2}=\frac{4(x^2+4)}{(x^2+4)^2}$ $=\frac{4}{x^2+4}$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4}{4+x^2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\int \cos(\log x) \,dx$ $= f(x)\{\cos(g(x))+\sin(h(x))\}$ $I=\int\limits_{II}\underset{I}{\cos(\log x)dx}$ { using by-part method of integration} $=\cos(\log x) \cdot x + \int \frac{\sin(\log x)}{x} \cdot x \,dx$ $=\cos(\log x) \cdot x + \int \sin(\log x) \,dx$ $=\cos(\log x) \cdot x$ $+\left[\sin(\log x) \cdot x - \int \frac{\cos(\log x)}{x} \cdot x \,dx\right]$ $I = x \cdot \cos(\log x) + x - \sin(\log x) - I$ $2I = x (\cos(\log x) + \sin(\log x))$ $\Rightarrow I = \frac{x}{2} (\cos(\log x) + \sin(\log x))$ $\therefore f(x)=\frac{x}{2} \Rightarrow f'(x)=\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int \frac{\sec x}{\sqrt{\sin(2x+\theta)+\sin \theta}} dx = I$ (say) $I = \int \frac{\sec x}{\sqrt{\sin 2x \cos \theta + \cos 2x \sin \theta + \sin \theta}} dx$ $I = \int \frac{\sec x}{\sqrt{\sin 2x \cos \theta + (\cos 2x+1) \sin \theta}} dx$ $= \int \frac{\sec x}{\sqrt{2 \cos x (\sin x \cos \theta + \cos x \sin \theta)}} dx$ $[\because \cos 2x+1=2 \cos^2 x]$ $= \int \frac{\sec x}{\sqrt{2 \cos^2 x \cos \theta (\tan x + \tan \theta)}} dx$ $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \cos \theta}} \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\sqrt{\tan x + \tan \theta}} dx$ Let $\tan x + \tan \theta = u$ $\Rightarrow \sec^2 x dx = du$ $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \cos \theta}} \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \cos \theta}} \cdot 2 \cdot \sqrt{u} + c$ $= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\cos \theta}} \cdot \sqrt{\tan x + \tan \theta} + c$ $= \sqrt{\frac{2(\tan x + \tan \theta)}{\cos \theta}} + c$ $= \sqrt{2(\tan x + \tan \theta) \sec \theta} + c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $A=\{x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5}\}$ Mean $= \frac{\sum x_{i}}{5} = 2 \Rightarrow \sum\limits_{i=1}^{j} x_{i} = 10$ Variance, $\frac{1}{5-1} \left[ \sum x_{i}^{2} - \frac{\left(\sum x_{1}\right)^{2}}{5} \right] = 4$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4} \left[ \sum x_{i}^{2} - \frac{(10)^{2}}{5} \right] = 4$ $\Rightarrow \sum x_{i}^{2} - 20 = 16$ $\Rightarrow \sum x_{i}^{2} = 36$ $B=\{y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3} y_{4}, y_{5}\}$ , Mean $= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{5} \frac{y_{1}}{5} = 4$ $\Rightarrow \sum y_{i} = 20$ Variance, $\frac{1}{5-1} \left[ \sum y_{i}^{2} - \frac{\left(\sum y_{i}\right)^{2}}{5} \right] = 5$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4} \left[ \sum y_{i}^{2} - \frac{(20)^{2}}{5} \right] = 5$ $\Rightarrow \sum y_{i}^{2} - 80 = 20$ $\Rightarrow \sum y_{i}^{2} = 100$ Now, $A \cup B = \{y_{1}, y_{2}, \dots, y_{5}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots, x_{5}\}$ , $= \{a_{i} ; i=1,2, \dots, 10\}$ $\text{Variance} = \frac{1}{10-1} \left[ \sum a_{i}^{2} - \frac{\left(\sum a_{i}\right)^{2}}{10} \right]$ $= \frac{1}{9} \left[ (x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\dots+x_{5}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}+\dots+y_{5}^{2}) - \frac{1}{10} \{ x_{1}+\dots+x_{5}+y_{1}+\dots+y_{5} \}^{2} \right]$ $= \frac{1}{9} \left[ \sum x_{i}^{2} + \sum y_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{10} \{ \sum x_{i} + \sum y_{1} \}^{2} \right]$ $= \frac{1}{9} \left[ 36+100 - \frac{1}{10} (10+20)^{2} \right]$ $= \frac{46}{9} \sim 5.11$ © examsnet.com

(i) and (ii), we obtain $a=a,\; 2h=6\Rightarrow h=3$ , $b=b$ , $2g=-10\Rightarrow g=-5$ $2f=10\Rightarrow f=5,\; c=-6$ $\begin{vmatrix} a & h & g \\ h & b & f \\ g & f & c \end{vmatrix}=0$ $\Rightarrow \begin{vmatrix} a & 3 & -5 \\ 3 & b & 5 \\ -5 & 5 & -6 \end{vmatrix}=0$ $\Rightarrow a(-6b-25)-3(-18+25-5(15-5b)=0$ $\Rightarrow 25a+25b+6ab+96=0$ ...(iii) Since, lines are perpendicular $\Rightarrow a+b=0$ or $a=-b$ ...(iv) Use Eq. (iv) in Eq. (iii), $25(a-a)+6a(-a)+96=0$ $\Rightarrow 6a^{2}=96\Rightarrow a^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow a=\pm 4$ $\Rightarrow \left|a\right|=4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given curve, $3x^{2}-y^{2}-2x+4y=0$ ...(i) Chord passes through $(1,-2)$ cut the given curve at $P$ and $Q$ Let slope of line $PQ$ is $m.$ Then, equation of line is $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ $\Rightarrow y+2=m(x-1)$ $\Rightarrow y+2=mx-m$ $\frac{mx-y}{2+m}=1$ ...(ii) Use Eq. (i) as follows, $3x^{2}-y^{2}-2x\left(\frac{mx-y}{2+m}\right)+4y\left(\frac{mx-y}{2+m}\right)=0$ $\Rightarrow 3(2+m)x^{2}-(2+m)y^{2}$ $-2x(mx-y)+4y(mx-y)=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}(6+3m-2m)$ $-y^{2}(2+m+4)+xy(4m+2)=0$ ...(iii) General equation of curve is $ax^{2}+2hxy+by^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ ...(iv) Compare Eqs. (iii) and (iv). $a=6+m,\ b=-6-m$ This gives, $a+b=0$ ⇒ Angle subtended by these two lines at origin is $90^{\circ}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation, $15 x^{2}+31 x y+14 y^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow 15 x^{2}+10 x y+21 x y+14 y^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow 5 x(3 x+2 y)+7 y(3 x+2 y)=0$ $\Rightarrow (3 x+2 y)(5 x+7 y)=0$ ∴  Two lines have following equation $3 x+2 y=0$ ...(i) $5 x+7 y=0$ ...(ii) Perpendicular distance from $(2,3)$ to the line $3 x+2 y=0$ is given as $\left| \frac{3(2)+2(3)}{\sqrt{9+4}} \right| = \frac{12}{\sqrt{13}}$ Perpendicular distance from $(2,3)$ on line $5 x+7 y=0$ is given as $\left| \frac{5(2)+7(3)}{\sqrt{25+49}} \right| = \frac{31}{\sqrt{74}}$ Given, $p_{1}>p_{2}$ $\Rightarrow p_{1}=\frac{31}{\sqrt{74}}$ and $p_{2}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{13}}$ $\Rightarrow p_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{74}-p_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{13}$ $= \frac{(31)^{2}}{74}+\frac{1}{74}-\frac{(12)^{2}}{13}+\frac{1}{13}$ $= \frac{962}{74}-\frac{143}{13} = \frac{1924}{962} = 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $(x_{1}, y_{1})$ and $(x_{2}, y_{2})$ be end point of diameter of circle, then equation of circle be $(x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})+(y-y_{1})(y-y_{2})=0$ ...(i) Given, equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-2 x-6 y+6=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-2 x+1+y^{2}-6 y+5=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)^{2}+(y-1)(y-5)=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)(x-1)+(y-1)(y-5)=0$ ...(ii) Compare Eqs. (i) and (ii), we obtain end points of    diameter be  (1,1)   and  (1,5). Now, we have to find radius of circle having    centre at (2,1) and one of its chord having end   point (1,1)   and (1,5) From given circle, $x^{2}+y^{2} =r^{2}$ $x=\sqrt{(2-1)^{2}+(1-3)^{2}} =\sqrt{5}$ $y=\sqrt{(1-1)^{2}+(3-1)^{2}} =\sqrt{4}$ $\Rightarrow r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}=5+4 =9$ $\Rightarrow r =3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-14x+2y+25=0$ $\Rightarrow (x^{2}-14x+49)+(y^{2}+2y+1)$ $-49-1+25=0$ $(x-7)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=25=5^{2}$ ⇒ Radius of circle $=5$ Centre of circle $=(7,-1)$ Distance between origin and centre $=\sqrt{(7)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$ $\therefore OP=5\sqrt{2}$ and $PA=5$ Now, $\sin \theta = \frac{AP}{OP} = \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \theta = 45^{\circ}$ Similarly, $\sin \alpha = \frac{PR}{OP} = \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha = 45^{\circ}$ $\therefore \theta + \alpha = 90^{\circ}$ Thus, angle between two tangent drawn from origin to given circle is 90°. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, planes are $2x - y + z = 6$ and $x + y + 2z = 3$ General equation of plane is $ax + by + cz = d$ Normal vector of plane is $a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$ . For plane $2x - y + z = 6$ $n_1 = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ For plane $x + y + 2z = 3$ $n_2 = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ Angle between $n_1$ and $n_2$ is given as, $\cos \theta = \frac{\left| n_1 \cdot n_2 \right|}{\left| n_1 \right| \left| n_2 \right|}$ $= \frac{(2-1+2)}{\sqrt{4+1+1} \sqrt{1+1+4}}$ $= \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ $\cos \theta = \cos \frac{\pi}{3}$ ∴ Angle between given planes is $\frac{\pi}{3}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $L=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{\sqrt{1-\cos 2(x-1)}}{x-1}$ $=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{\sqrt{2 \sin^{2}(x-1)}}{x-1}$ $[\because 1-\cos 2\theta = 2 \sin^{2} \theta]$ $=\sqrt{2} \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{|\sin(x-1)|}{x-1}$ $\left[\frac{0}{0}\right]$ form $=\sqrt{2} \lim\limits_{(x-1) \rightarrow 0} \frac{|\sin(x-1)|}{x-1}$ $=\sqrt{2} \lim\limits_{z \rightarrow 1} \frac{|\sin z|}{z}$ [Let $x-1=z$ ] $RHL = \sqrt{2} \lim\limits_{z \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{\sin z}{z} = \sqrt{2}$ $LHL = \sqrt{2} \lim\limits_{z \rightarrow 0^{-}} -\frac{\sin z}{z} = -\sqrt{2}$ $\because RHL \neq LHL$ ∴  Limit does not exist. © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=\begin{cases} \sin x, & x \leq 0 \\ x^{2}+a, & 0 < x < 1 \\ b x+3, & 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ -3, & x > 3 \end{cases}$ Given that, $f(x)$ is continuous on $R$ . Then, $f(x)$ is continuous at $n=0,3$ $\Rightarrow f(0)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x)$ Now, $f(0)=\sin 0=0$ $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}(x^{2}+a)$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}(h^{2}+a)=a$ $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}(\sin x)$ $=\lim\limits_{h \rightarrow 0}\sin (0-h)=0$ $\Rightarrow a=0$ Again, we must have $f(3)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 3^{+}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 3^{-}}f(x)$ Now, $f(3)=b(3)+3=3 b+3$ $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 3^{+}}f(x)=-3$ $\Rightarrow 3 b+3=-3 \Rightarrow b=-2$ Then, $a+b=0-2=-2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y = \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{a \cos x - b \sin x}{b \cos x + a \sin x} \right)$ $= \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{ \frac{a}{b-\tan x} }{ 1 + \frac{a}{b} \tan x } \right)$ [Take $b \cos x$ common  from numerator and denominator] $= \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{ \tan \theta - \tan x }{ 1 + \tan \theta \tan x } \right)$ $\left[ \text{Let } \frac{a}{b} = \tan \theta \right]$ $= \tan^{-1}( \tan( \theta - x ) ) = \theta - x$ $y = \tan^{-1} \frac{a}{b} - x$ $\left[ \because \frac{a}{b} = \tan \theta \right]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = 0 - 1 = -1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $8 f(x)+6 f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)=x+5$ ...(i) $y=x^{2} f(x)$ Replace $x$ by $\frac{1}{x}$ in Eq. (i), we obtain $8 f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+6 f(x)=\frac{1}{x}+5$ ...(ii) Solve Eqs. (i) and (ii) for $f(x)$ and $f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$ Multiply by 8 in Eq. (i) and by 6 in Eq. (ii) and subtract, we get $64 f(x)-36 f(x)=8 x-\frac{6}{x}+10$ $\Rightarrow 28 f(x)=8 x-\frac{6}{x}+10$ Now, $28 x^{2} f(x)=8 x^{3}-6 x+10 x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 28 y=8 x^{3}-6 x+10 x^{2}$ Differentiating it, $28 \frac{d y}{d x}=24 x^{2}-6+20 x$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{24 x^{2}-6+20 x}{28}$ $\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{x=-1}$ $=\frac{24(-1)^{2}-6+20(-1)}{28}$ $=-\frac{1}{14}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y=\frac{1}{4} \log \left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} x$ $y=\frac{1}{4} \log (1+x)-\frac{1}{4} \log (1-x)$ $-\frac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} x$ Then, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+x)}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{(1-x)}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}=\frac{1}{4}\left\{\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}+\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\right\}$ $-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ $=\frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}-1)+\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}+1)}{(\sqrt{2}+1)(\sqrt{2}-1)}\right]-\frac{1}{3}$ $=\frac{1}{4}\left\{\frac{2-\sqrt{2}+2+\sqrt{2}}{2-1}\right\}-\frac{1}{3}$ $=-\frac{1}{4}\left\{\frac{4}{1}\right\}-\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}$ $\therefore \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}=\frac{2}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x) =\sin x \sin 2 x \cdot \sin 3 x$ $=\frac{(2 \sin x \sin 2 x) \sin 3 x}{2}$ $=\frac{1}{2}\{\cos x-\cos 3 x\} \sin 3 x$ $=\frac{1}{2}[\cos x \sin 3 x-\cos 3 x \sin 3 x]$ $=\frac{2}{4} \cos x \sin 3 x-\frac{2}{4} \cos 3 x \sin 3 x$ $=\frac{1}{4}[\sin 4 x+\sin 2 x]-\frac{1}{4} \sin 6 x$ $f'(x) =\cos 4 x+\frac{1}{2} \cos 2 x-\frac{3}{2} \cos 6 x$ $f''(x) =-4 \sin 4 x-\sin 2 x+9 \sin 6 x$ $a =-4, b=4, c=-1$ , $d=2 e=9, k=6$ $(a+c+e)-(b+d+k)$ $=4-12=-8$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ Then, $\frac{dT}{dl}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{g}}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{l}}$ $=\frac{T}{\sqrt{l}}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{l}}$ $\left[\because T=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{g}}\cdot\sqrt{l}\right]$ $\frac{dT}{dl}=\frac{T}{2l}\Rightarrow\frac{dT}{T}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{dl}{l}$ Given, $\frac{dl}{l}\times 100=1\Rightarrow\frac{dl}{l}=\frac{1}{100}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{dT}{T}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{100}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{dT}{T}\times 100$ $=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{100}\times 100$ $=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\%$ ∴  Change in its time period $T$ is $0.5\%$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $x^{4}-x^{2}-2x+5=f(x)$ (say) Then, $f'(x)=4x^{3}-2x-2$ Equate $f'(x)=0 \Rightarrow 4x^{3}-2x-2=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x^{3}-x-1=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x(x^{2}-1)+(x-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x(x-1)(x+1)+(x-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)[2x(x+1)+1]=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)(2x^{2}+2x+1)=0$ $\Rightarrow x-1=0$ and $2x^{2}+2x+1=0$ $\Rightarrow x=1$ and $x=\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4-8}}{4}$ (Imaginary) $\Rightarrow x=1$ and $x=\frac{-1 \pm 1i}{2}$ $f''(x)=12x^{2}-2$ $\frac{f''(x)}{x=1}=10>0$ $\Rightarrow f(x)$ is minimum at $x=1$ Now, $f(1)=(1)^{4}-(1)^{2}-2+5=3$ ∴ Absolute minimum value is 3 © examsnet.com

Solution: Given curve, $2 y^{3}=a x^{2}+x^{3}$ and $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=61$ Let $A(a, a)$ be the point. Differentiate Eq. (i) w.r.t $x$ we get $6 y^{2} \frac{dy}{dx}=2 a x+3 x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax}{3y^{2}}+\frac{x^{2}}{2y^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(a,a)}=\frac{a^{2}}{3a^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2a^{2}}$ $=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{6}$ Now, slope of line at $(a, a)=\frac{5}{6}$ Equation of line is $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ $\Rightarrow y-a=\frac{5}{6}(x-a)$ or $6y-5x=a$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{\frac{a}{6}}-\frac{x}{\frac{a}{5}}=1$ or $\frac{x}{-\frac{a}{5}}+\frac{y}{\frac{a}{6}}=1$ Compare with intercept form of line $\frac{x}{\alpha}+\frac{y}{\beta}=1$ Gives $\alpha=-\frac{a}{5}, \beta=\frac{a}{6}$ Given, $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=61$ $\Rightarrow \frac{a^{2}}{25}+\frac{a^{2}}{36}=61$ $\Rightarrow \frac{36a^{2}+25a^{2}}{25 \times 36}=61$ $\Rightarrow \frac{61 a^{2}}{25 \times 36}=61$ $\Rightarrow \frac{61 a^{2}}{25 \times 36}=61$ $\Rightarrow a^{2}=25 \times 36=900$ $\Rightarrow a=\sqrt{900}$ $\Rightarrow \lvert a \rvert=30$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ and $x = a(\theta - \sin\theta), y = a(1 - \cos\theta)$ Differentiate it, w.r.t. ' $\theta$ ' $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = a(1 - \cos\theta) . \frac{dy}{d\theta} = a(\sin\theta)$ Then, $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{a \sin\theta}{a(1 - \cos\theta)} = \frac{\sin\theta}{1 - \cos\theta}$ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}} = \frac{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}}$ $= \frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{3}$ ∴ Slope of tangent $= \sqrt{3}$ Length of subtangent $= \frac{(y)_{\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}}}{m}$ $= \frac{a\left(1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}\right)}{\sqrt{3}}$ $= \frac{a\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}}$ ...(i) Length of subnormal $= (y)_{\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}} . m = a\left(1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}\right) . \sqrt{3}$ $= a\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right) \sqrt{3} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}$ ...(ii) Sum of Eqs. (i) and (ii), $\frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}} + \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $= \frac{\sqrt{3} a}{6} + \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2}$ $= \frac{\sqrt{3} a + 3\sqrt{3} a}{6}$ $= \frac{4\sqrt{3} a}{6}$ $= \frac{2\sqrt{3} a}{3} = \frac{2a}{\sqrt{3}}$ ∴ Sum of length of subtangent and sub-normal is $\frac{2a}{\sqrt{3}}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $I = \int \frac{\sqrt{1-x^{4}}}{x^{7}} \, dx$ Let $x^{2} = u$ , then $2x \, dx = du$ $I = \int \frac{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}{2 u^{4}} \, du$ $= \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}{u^{4}} \, du$ Let $u = \sin v$ , then $du = \cos v \, dv$ $I = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\cos^{2} v}{\sin^{4} v} \, dv$ $= \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{1}{\cos^{2} v \tan^{4} v} \, dv$ $= \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\sec^{2} v}{\tan^{4} v} \, dv$ Let $\tan v = w$ , then $\sec^{2} v \, dv = dw$ $I = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{dw}{w^{4}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{w^{-3}}{-3} \right)$ $= -\frac{1}{6 w^{3}} + C$ $= -\frac{1}{6 \tan^{3} v}$ $= -\frac{(\sqrt{1-u^{2}})^{3}}{6 u^{3}}$ $= -\frac{1}{6} \frac{(1-x^{4})^{3/2}}{x^{6}} + C$ $\therefore I = -\frac{1}{6} \frac{(1-x^{4})^{3/2}}{x^{6}} + C$ Now, $I = f(x) (1-x^{4})^{n/2} + C$ on Comparing, we obtain $f(x) = -\frac{1}{6 x^{6}}$ and $n = 3$ $\therefore (f(x))^{n} = \left( -\frac{1}{6 x^{6}} \right)^{3} = -\frac{1}{216 x^{18}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $I = \int \frac{dx}{\cos^4 x + \sin^4 x}$ $= \int \frac{\sec^4 x}{1 + \tan^4 x} dx$ $= \int \frac{\sec^2 x (1+\tan^2 x)}{1+\tan^4 x} dx$ Let $\tan x = t$ , then $\sec^2 x \, dx = dt$ $I = \int \frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4} dt$ $= \int \frac{1 + \frac{1}{t^2}}{t^2 + \frac{1}{t^2}} dt$ $= \int \frac{1 + \frac{1}{t^2}}{\left(t - \frac{1}{t}\right)^2 + 2} dt$ Let $t - \frac{1}{t} = u$ , then $\left(1 + \frac{1}{t^2}\right) dt = du$ $I = \int \frac{du}{u^2+2} = \int \frac{du}{u^2 + (\sqrt{2})^2}$ $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + C$ $I = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{t - \frac{1}{t}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + C$ $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{t^2-1}{\sqrt{2} \, t} \right) + C$ $I = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{\tan^2 x - 1}{\sqrt{2} \tan x} \right) + C$ $\therefore g(x) = \frac{\tan^2 x - 1}{\sqrt{2} \tan x}$ $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\tan x - \cot x)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, efficiencies $\eta_{1}=\eta_{2}=\eta_{3}=\eta$ and temperature, $T_{1}>T_{2}>T_{3}>T_{4}$ As we know that, in case of Carnot engine, Efficiency $(\eta)=1-\frac{T_{\mathrm{sink}}}{T_{\mathrm{source}}}$ $\therefore \eta_{1}=\eta=1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}$ $\Rightarrow T_{2}=( 1 -\eta) T_{1}$ ...(i) Similarly, $T_{3}=( 1 -\eta) T_{2}$ ...(ii) $T_{4}=( 1-\eta) T_{3}$ ...(iii) Now, by using Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get $(T_{1}^{2} \cdot T_{4})^{1/3} = \left[ \left( \frac{T_{2}}{1-\eta} \right)^{2} \cdot (1-\eta) T_{3} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ \frac{T_{2}^{2}}{1-\eta} \cdot T_{3} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ \left( \frac{T_{2}^{2}}{1-\eta} \right) (1-\eta) T_{2} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ T_{2}^{3} \right]^{1/3}$ $= T_{2}$ Again, by using Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get $(T_{1} \cdot T_{3}^{2})^{1/3}$ $= \left[ \left( \frac{T_{2}}{1-\eta} \right) \left[ (1-\eta) T_{3} \right]^{2} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ T_{2} (1-\eta) T_{3}^{2} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ \frac{T_{3}}{1-\eta} (1-\eta) T_{3}^{2} \right]^{1/3}$ $= \left[ T_{3}^{3} \right]^{1/3} = T_{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\cos \alpha +3 \cos 3\beta +5 \cos 5\gamma =0$ ...(i) $\sin \alpha +3 \sin 3\beta +5 \sin 5\gamma =0$ ...(ii) $\cos 3\alpha +27 \cos 9\beta +125 \cos 15\gamma$ $= (\lambda^{2}-4) \cos (\alpha +3\beta +5\gamma)$ ...(iii) To find, $\lambda =$ ? Let $a=\cos \alpha +i \sin \alpha$ $b=3(\cos 3\beta +i \sin 3\beta)$ $c=5(\cos 5\gamma +i \sin 5\gamma)$ Consider, $a+b+c =(\cos \alpha +i \sin \alpha)$ $+3(\cos 3\beta +i \sin 3\beta)$ $+5(\cos 5\gamma +i \sin 5\gamma)$ $=(\cos \alpha +3 \cos 3\beta +5 \cos 5\gamma)$ $+ i(\sin \alpha +3 \sin 3\beta +5 \sin 5\gamma) =0$ $\because a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}=3 a b c$ , if $a+b+c=0$ $(\cos \alpha +i \sin \alpha)^{3}+\{3(\cos 3\beta +i \sin 3\beta)\}^{3}$ $+\{5(\cos 5\gamma +i \sin 5\gamma)\}^{3}$ $=3(\cos \alpha +i \sin \alpha)\{3(\cos 3\beta +i \sin 3\beta)\}$ $\{5(\cos 5\gamma +i \sin 5\gamma)\}$ $=[\cos 3\alpha +i \sin 3\alpha)+\{27(\cos 9\beta +i \sin 9\beta)\}$ $+\{25(\cos 15\gamma +i \sin 15\gamma)\}$ $=45(\cos \alpha +i \sin \alpha)(\cos 3\beta +i \sin 3\beta)$ $(\cos 5\gamma +i \sin 5\gamma)$ $\therefore \lambda^{2}-4 =45$ $\Rightarrow \lambda^{2} =49$ $\Rightarrow \lambda = \pm 7$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation $x^{4}-3x^{2}+6x-12=0$ ...(i) On comparing with $ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+dx+e=0$ $a=1,\ b=0,\ c=-3,\ d=6,\ e=-12$ Since $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are the zeroes of the polynomial equation, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=\frac{-b}{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\delta,\ \alpha+\delta+\gamma=-\beta$ and $\alpha+\beta+\delta=-\gamma,\ \delta+\beta+\gamma=-\alpha$ Also, $\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=\frac{-d}{a}=-6$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=\frac{e}{a}=-12$ Now consider, $\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\alpha+\delta+\gamma}{\beta^{2}}+\frac{\alpha+\beta+\delta}{\gamma^{2}}+\frac{\delta+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha^{2}}$ $=\frac{-\delta}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{-\beta}{\beta^{2}}+\frac{-\gamma}{\gamma^{2}}+\frac{-\alpha}{\alpha^{2}}$ $=-\frac{1}{\delta}-\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{\gamma}-\frac{1}{\alpha}$ $=-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\gamma\delta+\alpha\beta\delta+\beta\gamma\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{\sum\alpha\beta\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{-6}{-12}\right)$ $=-\frac{1}{2}$ Hence the value of the given expression is $-\frac{1}{2}$ , which corresponds to option (1). © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation $x^{2}+p x+q=0$ ...(i) On comparing with $a x^{2}+b x+c=0$ $a=1, b=p, c=q$ Let $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of Eq. (i) and given that $\alpha=\beta^{2}$ $\therefore \alpha+\beta=\frac{-b}{a}=-p$ and $\alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a}=q$ $\Rightarrow \beta^{2}+\beta=-p$ and $\beta^{2} \cdot \beta=q$ and $\beta^{3}=q$ ...(ii) and $\beta=(q)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ On taking cube both sides $(\beta^{2}+\beta)^{3}=(-p)^{3}$ $\Rightarrow \beta^{6}+\beta^{3}+3\beta^{3}(\beta^{2}+\beta)=-p^{3}$ $\Rightarrow q^{2}+q+3q(-p)=-p^{3}$ [using Eq. (ii)] $\Rightarrow q^{2}+q-3pq=-p^{3}$ $\Rightarrow -p^{3}+3pq=q^{2}+q$ $\Rightarrow p(3q-p^{2})=q(q+1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\tan 70^{\circ} - \tan 20^{\circ} = a \cdot \tan 50^{\circ}$ $\frac{\sin 70^{\circ}}{\cos 70^{\circ}} - \frac{\sin 20^{\circ}}{\cos 20^{\circ}} = \frac{a \sin 50^{\circ}}{\cos 50^{\circ}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\sin 70^{\circ} \cdot \cos 20^{\circ} - \sin 20^{\circ} \cdot \cos 70^{\circ}}{\cos 70^{\circ} \cos 20^{\circ}} = \frac{a \sin 50^{\circ}}{\cos 50^{\circ}}$ $[\because \sin(A-B) = \sin A \cos B - \sin B \cos A]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\sin(70^{\circ} - 20^{\circ})}{\cos 70^{\circ} \cdot \cos 20^{\circ}} = \frac{a \sin 50^{\circ}}{\cos 50^{\circ}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2 \sin 50^{\circ}}{2 \cos 70 \cdot \cos 20^{\circ}} = \frac{a \sin 50^{\circ}}{\cos 50^{\circ}}$ $\Rightarrow a\{ 2 \cos 70^{\circ} \cos 20^{\circ} \} = 2 \cos 50^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow a\{ \cos 90^{\circ} + \cos 50^{\circ} \} = 2 \cos 50^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow a\{ \cos 50^{\circ} \} = 2 \cos 50^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow a=2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\sin^{2} 5^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 10^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 15^{\circ}+\dots+\sin^{2} 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \sin^{2} 5^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 10^{\circ}+\dots+\sin^{2} 45^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 50^{\circ}$ $+\dots+\sin^{2} 80^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 85^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \{\sin(90-85^{\circ})\}^{2}+\{\sin(90-80)\}^{2}+\dots$ $+\{\sin(90-50)\}^{2}+\sin^{2} 45^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 50^{\circ}+\dots$ $+\sin^{2} 80^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 89^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{2} 85^{\circ}+\cos^{2} 80^{\circ}+\dots$ $+\cos^{2} 50^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 45^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 50^{\circ}$ $+\dots+\sin^{2} 80^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 85^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow (\sin^{2} 85^{\circ}+\cos^{2} 85^{\circ})$ $+(\sin^{2} 80^{\circ}+\cos^{2} 80^{\circ})$ $+\dots+(\sin^{2} 50^{\circ}+\cos^{2} 50^{\circ})+\sin^{2} 45^{\circ}+\sin^{2} 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow 1+1+\dots 1+\frac{1}{2}+1=9\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $5 \tan^{2}\alpha + \frac{9}{\tan^{2}\alpha} + 4 \sec^{2}\alpha$ $=5 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9^{2}\alpha + 4(1+\tan^{2}\alpha)$ $[\because \sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x]$ $=9 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9 \cot^{2}\alpha + 4$ Since, we know that $\text{AM} \geq \text{GM}$ $\frac{9 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9 \cot^{2}\alpha}{2} \geq \sqrt{9 \tan^{2}\alpha \cdot 9 \cot^{2}\alpha}$ $9 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9 \cot^{2}\alpha \geq 9 \cdot 2 \cdot \tan\alpha \cdot \cot\alpha$ $9 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9 \cot^{2}\alpha > 18$ $\therefore 9 \tan^{2}\alpha + 9 \cot^{2}\alpha + 4 \geq 18 + 4 = 22$ ∴ Hence, minimum values  = 22 © examsnet.com

Solution: $\sin x + \sqrt{3} \cos x = \sqrt{2}$ $\Rightarrow \sin x = \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3} \cos x$ On squaring both sides, $\sin^2 x = 2 + 3 \cos^2 x - 2 \sqrt{6} \cos x$ $\Rightarrow 1 - \cos^2 x = 2 + 3 \cos^2 x - 2 \sqrt{6} \cos x$ $\Rightarrow 4 \cos^2 x - 2 \sqrt{6} \cos x + 1 = 0$ $\Rightarrow \cos x = \frac{2 \sqrt{6} \pm \sqrt{24-16}}{2 \times 4}$ $= \frac{2 \sqrt{6} + 2 \sqrt{2}}{8}$ $\Rightarrow \cos x = \frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4} = \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \pm \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ $\Rightarrow x = 2n\pi + \frac{\pi}{6} \pm \frac{\pi}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) - \sec^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{b}\right)$ $= \sec^{-1} b - \sec^{-1} a$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{x}\right) - \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{x}\right)$ $= \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{b}\right) - \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{-1}\left\{ \frac{a b}{x^{2}} + \sqrt{1-\frac{a^{2}}{x^{2}}} \cdot \sqrt{1-\frac{b^{2}}{x^{2}}} \right\}$ $= \cos^{-1}\left\{ \frac{1}{a b} + \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{b^{2}}} \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{a^{2}}} \right\}$ $[\because \cos^{-1} x - \cos^{-1} y = \cos^{-1}\left\{ x y + \sqrt{1-x^{2}} \sqrt{1-y^{2}} \right\}]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{a b}{x^{2}} + \frac{\sqrt{(x^{2}-a^{2})(x^{2}-b^{2})}}{x^{2}}$ $= \frac{1}{a b} + \frac{\sqrt{(b^{2}-1)(a^{2}-1)}}{a b}$ $\Rightarrow a^{2} b^{2} + a b \sqrt{(x^{2}-a^{2})(x^{2}-b^{2})}$ $= x^{2} + x^{2} \sqrt{(a^{2}-1)(b^{2}-1)}$ $\Rightarrow a b \sqrt{(x^{2}-a^{2})(x^{2}-b^{2})} - x^{2} \sqrt{(a^{2}-1)(b^{2}-1)} = x^{2} - a^{2} b^{2}$ $x^{2} - a^{2} b^{2}$ in RHS $x^{2}$ has the minimum value zero because $a^{2} b^{2}$ is always positive and $x^{2} - a^{2} b^{2} = 0$ is positive. If $\Rightarrow x^{2} = a^{2} b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x = a b$ $a b$ © examsnet.com

Let $R$ be the circumradius and $s$ be semi-perimeter and $\Delta$ be the area of $\Delta ABC$ $[\because \frac{\sin A}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{b c}}$ , $\frac{\sin B}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{a c}}$ , $\frac{\sin C}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{a b}}]$ and $\left[ r_1 = \frac{\Delta}{s-a}, r_2 = \frac{\Delta}{s-b}, r_3 = \frac{\Delta}{s-c} \right]$ and $\left[ \Delta = \frac{abc}{4R} \Rightarrow 4R \Delta = abc \right]$ $\frac{16 R s \Delta \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}}{s-c} = \frac{(4 R \Delta)(4 s)}{s-c} \sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{b c}} \sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{a c}} \sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{a b}}$ $= \frac{(a b c)(4 s)}{s-c} \frac{(s-c) \sqrt{ s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) }}{a b c}$ $= 4 \Delta s$ $= \frac{4 s \Delta^{3}}{\Delta^{2}} = \frac{4 s \Delta^{3}}{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ $= 4 \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s-a} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s-b} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s-c}$ $= 4 r_{1} r_{2} r_{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $|\mathbf{a}| = |\mathbf{b}| = |\mathbf{c}| = 1$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0 = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}$ and the acute angle between $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$ To find $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}|$ Given that, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}) = 0$ ⇒ The angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $( \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} )$ is $\frac{\pi}{2} .$ Now, $| \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c} | = | \mathbf{a} \times ( \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} ) |$ $= | \mathbf{a} | | \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} | \sin 90^{\circ}$ ...(i) $| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} |^{2} = | \mathbf{b} |^{2} + | \mathbf{c} |^{2} - 2 \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}$ $= 1 + 1 - 2 \left( | \mathbf{b} | | \mathbf{c} | \cos \frac{\pi}{3} \right)$ $= 2 - 2 \left( 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \right)$ $| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} |^{2} = 1 \Rightarrow | \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} | = 1$ From Eq. (i), we get $| \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c} | = 1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Since, we know that the equation of plane passing through a point $A$ and perpendicular to vector $\mathbf{n}$ is $(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0$ where, a is the position vector of point and $n$ is the normal vector. Given, $A=(2,1-3)$ , $\mathbf{n} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ $\Rightarrow \mathbf{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ $\therefore (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \{ (x-2)\hat{i} + (y-1)\hat{j} + (z+3)\hat{k} \} \cdot \{ 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} \} = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3(x-2) - (y-1) + 2(z+3) = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3x - 6 - y + 1 + 2z + 6 = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3x - y + 2z + 1 = 0$ $\because \left(\frac{1}{3}, 3, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ and $\left(1,5,\frac{1}{2}\right)$ satisfies the above equation. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $n=10$ , $\sum x_{i}=60$ $\sum x_i^2 = 1000$ $\because \underset{(x)}{\text{Mean}} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n} = \frac{60}{10} = 6$ Variance $= \frac{\sum (x_i - \overline{x})^2}{n}$ $= \frac{\sum x_i^2 + \sum \overline{x}^2 - 2 \overline{x} \sum x_i}{n}$ $= \frac{1000}{10} + \frac{36-10}{10} - \frac{2 \times 6 \times 60}{10}$ $=100+36-72$ $=64$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $A$ be the event that aeroplane-I hit the target correctly and $B$ be the event that aeroplane-II hit the target correctly. $\Rightarrow P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.2$ $\therefore P(A')=1-P(A)=1-0.3=0.7$ where $A'$ , first misses the target $P(B')=1-P(B)=1-0.2=0.8$ $B'$ , second misses the target. Let $X$ be the event that target is hit by plane-II $\therefore P(X)=P(A') P(B)$ $+P(A') P(B') P(A') P(B)$ $+P(A') P(B') P(A') P(B') P(A')P(B)+.....$ $= 0.7 \times 0.2+0.7 \times 0.8 \times 0.7 \times 0.2$ $+0.7 \times 0.8 \times 0.7 \times 0.8 \times 0.7 \times 0.2+....$ $= 0.14[1+(0.56)+(0.56)^{2}+....]$ $= 0.14\left[\frac{1}{1-0.56}\right]$ $=0.14 \times \frac{1}{0.44}=0.32$ $[\because 1+0.56+(0.56)^{2}+....$ forms an infinite GP whose sum $=\frac{a}{1-r}$ where $a$ is first term and $r$ is common ratio] $\therefore P(X)=0.32$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $A$ be the event of getting a road contract and $B$ be the event of getting a building contract. $\therefore P(A) = \frac{2}{9}, P(B) = \frac{5}{9}$ $P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{6}$ $\therefore P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ $= \frac{2}{9} + \frac{5}{9} - \frac{1}{6}$ $= \frac{7}{9} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{14-3}{18}$ $= \frac{11}{18}$ $\therefore P((A \cup B)') = 1 - P(A \cup B)$ $= 1 - \frac{11}{18} = \frac{7}{18}$ Hence, the probability to get neither of these two contracts is $\frac{7}{18}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $P(A)=\frac{1}{3}, P(B)=\frac{1}{4}, P(A \cup B)=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore P(A^{C})=1-P(A)$ $=1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}$ $P(A) P(B)=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{12}$ and $P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cup B)$ $=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{12}$ $\Rightarrow A$ and $B$ are independent. $P(A / B)=\frac{P(A \cup B)}{P(B)}=\frac{\frac{1}{12}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{3}$ $P(A^{C} \cup B)=P(B)-P(A \cup B)$ $=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6}$ $P(A \cup B^{C})=P(A) \cdot P(B^{C})$ $=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}$ $\therefore P(A^{C} \cup B)=\frac{1}{3}$ is incorrect among above options. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Mean of Poisson distribution $=\frac{1}{3}$ For a Poisson distribution, the mean is equal to the parameter. Hence, the parameter is $\frac{1}{3}$ . $\therefore P(X=1)=\frac{e^{-1/3}(1/3)^{1}}{1!} = e^{-1/3}(1/3)$ $P(X=2)=\frac{e^{-1/3}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}{2!}$ $\therefore P(X=1): P(X=4)$ $=\frac{e^{-1/3}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}{\frac{e^{-1/3}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}{2!}}$ $=\frac{2}{\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{6}{1}=6:1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $P(X=x)=K(x+1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{x}$ To find, $P(X=0)$ Since sum of all the probabilities in a probability distribution is $1.$ $\therefore P(X=0)+P(X=1)$ $+P(X=2)+\dots=1$ $\Rightarrow K(0+1)\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{0}+K(1+1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{1}$ $+K(2+1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{2}+\dots=1$ $\Rightarrow K+2K\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)+3K\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{2}+\dots=1$ $\Rightarrow K\left[1+2\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)+3\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{2}+\dots\right]=1$ Let $r=\frac{1}{5}$ $K\left[1+2r+3r^{2}+\dots\right]=1$ $\Rightarrow K(1-r)^{-2}=1$ $\Rightarrow K\left(1-\frac{1}{5}\right)^{-2}=1$ $\therefore P(X=0)=\frac{16}{25}(0+1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{0}=\frac{16}{25}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Statement I The length of common chord of the circles $x^{2}+y^{2}+a x+b y+c=0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}+b x+a y+c=0$ equals $\frac{\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-8c}}{2}$ Let the circles $c_{1}$ be the center of $x^{2}+y^{2}+a x+b y+c=0$ ...(i) and $c_{2}$ be the center of $x^{2}+y^{2}+b x+a y+c=0$ ...(ii) $\therefore c_{1} =\left(\frac{-a}{2}, \frac{-b}{2}\right)$ and $c_{2} =\left(\frac{-b}{2}, \frac{-a}{2}\right)$ $r_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}}{4}+\frac{b^{2}}{4}-c}$ $\Rightarrow r_{1} =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-4c}$ $r_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{b^{2}}{4}+\frac{a^{2}}{4}-c}$ $\Rightarrow r_{2} =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-4c}$ ∵  Radius of both circles is same. $c_{1}c_{2}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{-a}{2}+\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{-b}{2}+\frac{a}{2}\right)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{4}}$ $\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=\frac{a-b}{\sqrt{2}}$ Let $AB$ be common chord and $M$ is its mid-point. $\therefore C_{1}M=\frac{c_{1}c_{2}}{2}=\frac{a-b}{2\sqrt{2}}$ $\because A c_{1} M$ forms a right angle triangle. $\therefore AM =\sqrt{r_{1}^{2}-(c_{1}M)^{2}}$ $= \sqrt{\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-4c}{4}-\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-2ab}{8}}$ $= \frac{\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-8c}}{2\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore AB =2 AM=\frac{\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-8c}}{\sqrt{2}}$ ⇒ Statement- 1 is false. We know that if two circles intersect at two distinct points, then their  radical axis is their common chord. ⇒ Statement-2 is true. © examsnet.com

Solution: $\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\tan x+4\tan 2x-3\tan 3x}{x^{2}\tan x}$ $=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left[\frac{\tan x+4\left(\frac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^{2}x}\right)-\left(\frac{3\tan x-\tan^{3}x}{1-3\tan^{2}x}\right)}{x^{2}\tan x}\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left[\frac{\tan x\left\{1+\frac{8}{1-\tan^{2}x}-\frac{9-3\tan^{2}x}{1-3\tan^{2}x}\right\}}{x^{2}\tan x}\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left[\frac{(1-\tan^{2}x)(1-3\tan^{2}x)+8(1-3\tan^{2}x)-(9-3\tan^{2}x)(1-\tan^{2}x)}{x^{2}(1-\tan^{2}x)(1-3\tan^{2}x)}\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left[\frac{-16\tan^{2}x}{x^{2}(1-\tan^{2}x)(1-3\tan^{2}x)}\right]$ $=-16\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left(\frac{\tan x}{x}\right)^{2}\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{1}{(1-\tan^{2}x)(1-3\tan^{2}x)}$ $=-16(1)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1\cdot 1}=-16$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{8}{x^{8}}\left[1-\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)-\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)\right.$ $+\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)\cdot\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)$ $=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{8}{x^{8}}\left\{1\left(1-\cos\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)-\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)^{2}\cdot\left(1-\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)\right)\right\}$ $=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{8}{x^{8}}\left\{\left(1-\cos\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)\left(1-\cos\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)\right)\right\}$ $\left[\because (1-\cos\theta)=2\sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{8}{x^{8}}\left\{\left(2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)\right)\left(2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{8}\right)\right)\right\}$ $=32\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^{8}}\left(\frac{\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)}{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\right)\times\frac{x^{4}}{16}\times\left(\frac{\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{8}\right)}{\frac{x^{2}}{8}}\right)^{2}\times\frac{x^{4}}{64}$ $\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{32x^{8}}{16\times64x^{8}}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{x^{2}}{4}}{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{x^{2}}{8}}{\frac{x^{2}}{8}}\right)^{2}$ $=\frac{1}{32}\cdot 1\cdot 1$ $=\frac{1}{32}$ $\left\{\because\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1\right\}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\because y=\log_{y} x$ To find, $\frac{dy}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{\log_{e} x}{\log_{e} y}$ $\Rightarrow y \log y = \log x$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , $y = \frac{d}{dx} \log y + \log y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx} \log x$ $\Rightarrow y \cdot \frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} + \log y \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x}$ $\Rightarrow (1 + \log y) \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x(1+\log y)}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $x=a[\cos \theta+\log (\tan \theta/ 2)]$ and $y=a \sin \theta$ $\therefore \frac{dx}{d\theta}=a\left[-\sin \theta+\frac{1}{\tan (\theta/ 2)} \cdot \sec ^{2} \theta/ 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\right]$ $[\because \frac{d}{dx} \tan x=\sec ^{2} x$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \cos x=-\sin x$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \log x=\frac{1}{x}]$ $=a \left[-\sin \theta+\frac{1}{2 \sin \theta/ 2 \cdot \cos \theta/ 2}\right]$ $=a\left[-\sin \theta+\frac{1}{\sin \theta}\right]$ $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=a\left[\frac{1-\sin ^{2} \theta}{\sin \theta}\right]=\frac{a \cos ^{2} \theta}{\sin \theta}$ ...(i) and $y =a \sin \theta$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{d\theta}=a \cos \theta$ ...(ii) Eq. (ii) divide by Eq. (i) $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a \cos \theta}{\frac{a \cos ^{2} \theta}{\sin \theta}}$ $=\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}=\tan \theta$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=\log_{x^{2}}(\log x)$ $\therefore f'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\log_{x^{2}}(\log x)$ $=\frac{d}{dx}\left\{\frac{\log(\log x)}{\log(x^{2})}\right\}$ $[\because \frac{d}{dx}\frac{u}{v}=\frac{vu'-uv'}{v^{2}}, \frac{d}{dx}\log x=\frac{1}{x}$ and $\log_{a}b=\frac{\log_{e}b}{\log_{e}a}]$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\log x \cdot \frac{1}{\log x} \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \log(\log x) \cdot \frac{1}{x}}{(\log x)^{2}}\right\}$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{x}\frac{1-\log(\log x)}{(\log x)^{2}}\right]$ At, $x=e$ $f'(e)=\frac{1}{2e(\log_{c}e)^{2}}(1-\log_{e}(\log_{e}e))$ $f'(e)=\frac{1}{2e\cdot (1)^{2}}(1-0)=\frac{1}{2e}=(2e)^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, curves are : $x^{2}+y^{2}=4 x$ ...(i) and $x^{2}+y^{2}=8$ ...(ii) $\because \frac{d y}{d x}$ is the slope of tangent drawn to curve. Slope of the tangent drawn to curve (i) is $m_{1}=\frac{d y}{d x}$ [ from curve (i)] On differentiating Eq. (i) w.r.t. $x$ $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+y^{2})=\frac{d}{dx}(4 x)$ $\Rightarrow 2 x+2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=4$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{4-2 x}{2 y}$ $\therefore m_{1}|_{(2,2)}=\frac{4-2 \times 2}{2 \times 2}=0$ On differentiating Eq. (ii) w.r.t. $x$ , $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+y^{2}) =\frac{d}{dx}(8)$ $\Rightarrow 2 x+2 y \frac{d y}{d x} =0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x} =\frac{-2 x}{2 y}=\frac{-x}{y}$ $\therefore m_{2}|_{(2,2)}=\frac{-2}{2}=-1$ $\tan \theta =\left|\frac{m_{2}-m_{1}}{1+m_{1}\cdot m_{2}}\right| =\left|\frac{-1-0}{1+0}\right|=1$ $\Rightarrow \theta =\tan^{-1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\because \theta =\sin^{-1}(a)$ [Given] $\Rightarrow \sin^{-1}(a) =\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow a =\sin \frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow a =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given curve, $y=x^{2}-3x+2$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-3$ Which represents the slope of tangent drawn to the curve. $m_{1}=2x-3$ ...(i) Given line, $y=x$ ...(ii) On comparing with $y=mx+c$ Slope of line (ii), $m_{2}=1$ ∴ Tangent to the curve is perpendicular to line (ii). $\therefore m_{1}\cdot m_{2}=-1$ $\Rightarrow m_{1}\cdot 1=-1$ $\Rightarrow m_{1}=-1$ $\Rightarrow 2x-3=-1$ $\Rightarrow 2x=2$ $\Rightarrow x=1$ $\Rightarrow y=(1)^{2}-3\times 1+2$ $\Rightarrow y=0$ ∴ Point of tangent drawn $=(1,0)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, the perimeter of circular sector $=60\text{m}$ Let radius be $r \;\text{m}$ . Length of arc $AB = l$ ∴ perimeter $(p) = 1 + 2r$ $\Rightarrow l = p - 2r$ ∵ Area $= \frac{1}{2} l r$ $\Rightarrow A = \frac{(p-2r)r}{2} = \frac{pr-2r^{2}}{2}$ For $A$ to be maximum, $\frac{dA}{dr} = 0$ $\frac{d}{dr} \left( \frac{pr-2r^{2}}{2} \right) = 0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{p-4r}{2} = 0$ $\Rightarrow p = 4r$ $\Rightarrow 60 = 4r$ $\Rightarrow r = 15\,\text{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=a x^{3}+b x^{2}+26 x-24 \dots$ (i) on $[2,4]$ $\because f(x)$ satisfies the Role's theorem $\Rightarrow f(2)=f(4)$ $\Rightarrow a(2)^{3}+b(2^{2})+26(2)-24$ $=a(4)^{3}+b(4)^{2}+26(4)-24$ $\Rightarrow 8a+4b+28=64a+16b+80$ $\Rightarrow 56a+12b+52=0$ $\Rightarrow 14a+3b+13=0$ ...(ii) On differentiating Eq. (i) w.r.t. $x$ $f'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(a x^{3}+b x^{2}+26 x-24)$ $f'(x)=3 a x^{2}+2 b x+26$ At, $x=3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $f'\left(3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=3a\left(3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2}+2b\left(3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)+26$ $0=3a\left(9+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\right)+6b+\frac{2b}{\sqrt{3}}+26$ $\Rightarrow (28+6\sqrt{3})a+\left(\frac{6\sqrt{3}+2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)b+26=0$ $(28a+6b+26)+(18a+2b)\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ ...(iii) $=0+0\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $28a+6b+26=0$ On comparing rational and irrational part, $18a+2b=0$ and $54a+6b=0$ and $\therefore 28a-54a+26=0$ $6b=-54a$ and $\Rightarrow -26a+26=0$ $\Rightarrow a=1$ $b=\frac{-54 \times 1}{6} \Rightarrow b=-9$ $\therefore ab=-9$ $∴a b =-9$ © examsnet.com

Solution: To find $k$ Given, $\int \cos^{k}(x) \sin(x) dx = \frac{-1}{4} \cos^{4}(x) + C$ Let $I = \int \cos^{k}(x) \sin(x) dx$ Let $\cos x = t$ $\Rightarrow -\sin x dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \sin x dx = -dt$ $\therefore I = -\int t^{k} dt$ $I = \frac{-t^{k+1}}{k+1} + C$ $I = \frac{-\cos^{k+1} x}{k+1} + C$ $= \frac{-1}{4} \cos^{4}(x) + C$ $\Rightarrow k+1=4 \Rightarrow k=3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f'(x)=\tan^{2}x+\cot^{2}x$ $\therefore f(x)=\int(\tan^{2}x+\cot^{2}x)\,dx$ $=\int\left(\frac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}+\frac{\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x}\right)dx$ $=\int\frac{\sin^{4}x+\cos^{4}x}{\sin^{2}x\cdot\cos^{2}x}\,dx$ $=\int\frac{(\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x)^{2}-2\sin^{2}x\cdot\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x\cdot\cos^{2}x}\,dx$ $=\int\frac{1}{\sin^{2}x\cdot\cos^{2}x}\,dx-\int2\,dx$ $=\int\frac{\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x\cdot\cos^{2}x}\,dx-2x+C$ $=\int\sec^{2}x\,dx+\int\csc^{2}x\,dx-2x+C$ $f(x)=\tan x-\cot x-2x+C$ $\because f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=0$ $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\cot\frac{\pi}{4}-2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+C=0$ $1-1-\frac{\pi}{2}+C=0\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\therefore f(x)=\tan x-\cot x-2x+\frac{\pi}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I=\int\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{\sqrt{\sin 2 x}} .d x$ $I=\int\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{\sqrt{1+2\sin x .\cos x-1}} d x$ $I=\int\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{\sqrt{(\cos x+\sin x)^2-1}} d x$ Let $\sin x+\cos x=t$ $\Rightarrow \cos x-\sin x=\frac{dt}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow -(\sin x-\cos x) d x = d t$ $\Rightarrow (\sin x-\cos x) d x = -d t$ $\therefore I=-\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2-1}}$ $\left[\because \int\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} d x = \log \left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|+C \right]$ $=-\log \left|t+\sqrt{t^2-1}\right|$ $=-\log \left|\sin x+\cos x+\sqrt{(\sin x+\cos x)^2}-1\right|+C$ $I=-\log \left|\sin x+\cos x+\sqrt{\sin 2 x}\right|+C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I=\int\limits_{2/e}^{1/e} \frac{1}{x(\log x)^{1/3}} dx$ Let $\log x=t$ ∴ Upper limit $t=\log\frac{1}{e}=-1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x} dx = dt$ lower limit $t=\log\frac{2}{e}$ $=\log 2 - \log e = \log 2 - 1$ $\therefore I=\int\limits_{\log 2-1}^{-1}\frac{dt}{t^{1/3}}$ $=\left.\frac{t^{-1/3+1}}{-1/3+1}\right|_{\log 2-1}^{-1}$ $=\frac{3}{2}\left((-1)^{2/3}-(\log 2-1)^{2/3}\right)$ $I=\frac{3}{2}\left[1-(\log 2-1)^{2/3}\right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: (c) Given, differential equation $(1+x^{2}) \; \frac{dy}{dx} \;\; =e^{m(\tan^{-1} x)}-y, y(0)=1$ $\; \frac{dy}{dx} \;\; =\; \frac{e^{m \tan^{-1} x}}{1+x^{2}}-\; \frac{y}{1+x^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \; \frac{dy}{dx}+y\left(\; \frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\right)=\; \frac{e^{m \tan^{-1} x}}{1+x^{2}} \;\;\; \cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (i)$ On comparing with Bernoulli's equation $\; \frac{dy}{dx}+P y=Q$ $\Rightarrow \;\; P=\; \frac{1}{1+x^{2}},$ $Q=\; \frac{e^{m \tan^{-1} x}}{1+x^{2}}$ $\therefore \;\; I F=e^{\int P dx}=e^{\int\; \frac{1}{1+x^{2}} dx}=e^{\tan^{-1} x}$ Solution $y$ Eq. (i), we get $y \cdot I F=\int Q \cdot I F dx+C$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y \cdot e^{\tan^{-1} x}=\int\; \frac{e^{m \tan^{-1} x}}{1+x^{2}} \cdot e^{\tan^{-1} x} dx+C$ $\; \text{ Put } \; \tan^{-1} x=t$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \; \frac{1}{1+x^{2}} dx=dt$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y \cdot e^{\tan^{-1} x}=\int e^{m t} \cdot e^{t} dt+C$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y \cdot e^{\tan^{-1} x} \;\; =\; \frac{e^{(m+1) t}}{m+1}+C$ $\;\; =\; \frac{e^{(m+1) \tan^{-1} x}}{m+1}+C$ $\because \;\; y \;\; =1, \; \text{ when, } \; x=0$ $1 \cdot e^{0} \;\; =\; \frac{e^{(m+1) \cdot 0}}{m+1}+C$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \;\; =\; \frac{1}{m+1}+C$ $C \;\; =1-\; \frac{1}{m+1}=\; \frac{m}{m+1}$ $\therefore \;\; y e^{\tan^{-1} x} \;\; =\; \frac{e^{(m+1) \tan^{-1} x}}{m+1}+\; \frac{m}{m+1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of cylinder, $m = 12\;\mathrm{kg}$ Initial velocity, $u = 20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ Coefficient of friction, $\mu = 0.5$ We know that, the retardation produced by friction $a = -\mu g$ $= -0.5 \times 10$ $= -5\;\mathrm{m/s}^2$ [using, $g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s}^2$ ] Let $S$ be the distance travelled by cylinder to stop. Solution: Given, mass of body $=M$ Height above the sand floor $=h$ Distance penetrated into sand $=x$ Let $v$ be the velocity with which body strikes the surface. Then, by equation of motion, we get $v^{2}=u^{2}+2 g h \Rightarrow v^{2}=2 g h$ ...(i) $[\because$ Initial velocity at highest point, $u=0]$ With this velocity $v$ , when body passes through the sand floor it comes to rest after travelling a distance $x$ . Let $F$ be the resisting force acting on body. Then, net downward force will be $F_{\text{net}}=Mg-F$ By work-energy theorem, work done by all forces is equal to change in $\text{KE}$ , which gives $W = \Delta K$ $F_{\text{net}} \times x = K_f - K_i$ $(Mg-F) x = 0 - \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}$ $[\because \text{ Final KE, } K_f = 0]$ $(Mg-F) x = -\frac{1}{2} M v^{2}$ ...(ii) Substituting the value from Eq. (i) in Eq. (ii), we get $\Rightarrow Mg x - F x = -\frac{1}{2} M (2 g h)$ $\Rightarrow Mg x - F x = -Mg h$ $\Rightarrow F x = Mg x + Mg h$ $\Rightarrow F = Mg \left( \frac{x+h}{x} \right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of disc, $M=4\text{ kg}$ Radius of disc, $R=0.4\text{ m}$ Initial angular velocity of disc, $\omega_{1}=30\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ Mass of point-masses, $m=0.25\text{ kg}$ Now, moment of inertia of disc, $I_{3}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ Moment of inertia of disc and two point mass system, $I_{2}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+2mR^{2}$ Let $\omega_{2}$ be the final angular velocity. According to conservation of angular momentum, $I_{1}\omega_{1}=I_{2}\omega_{2}\Rightarrow\omega_{2}=\frac{I_{1}\omega_{1}}{I_{2}}$ Substituting the values, we get $\omega_{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}(30)}{\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+2mR^{2}}$ $=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\times4\times(0.4)^{2}\times30}{\frac{1}{2}\times4\times(0.4)^{2}+2\times0.25\times(0.4)^{2}}$ $\omega_{2}=24\text{ rad/s}$ Hence, the final angular velocity of system is $24\text{ rad/s}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of body $=M$ Radius $=R$ Angle of inclination $=\theta$ Height of inclined surface $=h$ Also, $\beta = \frac{I_{CM}}{MR^{2}}$ Using, the acceleration produced in body rolling down the inclined plane $a = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1+\frac{I_{CM}}{MR^{2}}} = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1+\beta}$ By using equation of motion, $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ where $u = 0$ (initial velocity) $t =$ time taken to reach at bottom. $s = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{g \sin\theta}{(1+\beta)} t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow t^{2} = \frac{2 s (1+\beta)}{g \sin\theta}$ But, from the diagram, $\frac{h}{s} = \sin\theta$ $\Rightarrow s = \frac{h}{\sin\theta}$ Substituting the value of $s$ , we get $t = \sqrt{\frac{2 h (1+\beta)}{g \sin^{2}\theta}}$ $= \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \sqrt{\frac{2 h (1+\beta)}{g}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For SHM, we know that, Maximum acceleration, $|a_{\max}| = \omega^{2} A$ Maximum velocity, $|v_{\max}| = \omega A$ where, $\omega = \frac{\text{angular velocity}}{\text{frequency}}$ $A =$ amplitude ∴ According to question, the ratio is $\frac{|a_{\max}|}{|v_{\max}|} = \frac{\omega^{2} A}{\omega A} = \omega$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, length of pendulum, $l=0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ Speed at lowest point, $v_{1}=6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ Angle made by string with vertical, $\theta=60^{\circ}$ In $\Delta OBC,\ \frac{OC}{OB}=\cos\theta=\cos 60^{\circ}$ $\frac{l-h}{l}=\cos 60^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow h =l(1-\cos 60^{\circ})$ $\Rightarrow h =0.5\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ Using law of conservation of mechanical energy, we get $K_{i}+U_{i}=K_{f}+U_{f}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m v_{1}^{2}+0=\frac{1}{2} m v_{2}^{2}+m g h$ [Taking initial potential energy at ground is equal to zero.] $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m v_{2}^{2} =\frac{1}{2} m v_{1}^{2}-m g h$ $\Rightarrow v_{2}^{2} =v_{1}^{2}-2 g h$ Substituting the values, we get $v_{2} =\sqrt{(6)^{2}-2\times10\times0.25}$ $=\sqrt{31}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ Hence, the final velocity at an angle $60^{\circ}$ is $\sqrt{31}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, radius of Earth and Mars are $6400 \text{km}$ and $3200 \text{km}$ , respectively. Mass of Earth $=10$ (Mass of Mars) $M_e = 10 M_m$ We know that, acceleration due to gravity at surface of a planet is $g = \frac{GM}{R^2},$ where, $M =$ mass of planet and $R =$ radius of planet. Taking the ratio of acceleration due to gravity of Mars to Earth, $\frac{g_m}{g_e} = \frac{ \frac{GM_m}{R_m^2} }{ \frac{GM_e}{R_e^2} }$ $= \frac{M_m}{M_e} \times \left( \frac{R_e}{R_m} \right)^2$ By substituting the values, we get $\frac{g_m}{g_e} = \frac{1}{10} \times \left( \frac{6400}{3200} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{10} \times 4$ $\Rightarrow g_m = \frac{2}{5} g_e$ Given, the weight on earth's surface, $w_e = m g_e = 200 \text{N}$ ∴ Weight on the Mars surface, $w_m = m g_m = \frac{2}{5} (m g_e)$ $= \frac{2}{5} \times 200 \text{N} = 80 \text{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, gravitational field intensity, $\mathbf{I} = (5\hat{i}+12\hat{j})\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ Mass of object, $m=3\,\mathrm{kg}$ We know that, change in potential energy from to $P(8\,\mathrm{m},-2\,\mathrm{m})$ is given by $\Delta U = m \Delta V = m \int\limits_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)} \mathbf{I} \cdot d\mathbf{r}$ $=3 \int\limits_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)} (5\hat{i}+12\hat{j}) \cdot (dx\,\hat{i}+dy\,\hat{j})$ $=3\left[5x+12y\right]_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)}$ $\Delta U = 3[40-24] = 48\,\mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, Mass of particle $=m$ Restoring force, $\mathbf{F} = (-k \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{F}_0) N$ $= -k \left(x - \frac{\mathbf{F}_0}{k}\right) = -k y$ $\left[\text{Take, } x - \frac{\mathbf{F}_0}{k} = y\right]$ Which is SHM. We know that, at the mean position, $y = 0$ $x - \frac{\mathbf{F}_0}{k} = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{\mathbf{F}_0}{k}$ $\therefore F = m a \Rightarrow m a = -k y$ $m(-\omega^{2} y) = -k y \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ Frequency of SHM, $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let radius of big drop $=R$ Radius of small drop $=T$ Number of small drops, $n=1000$ In this process, the volume remains same $V_{f}=V_{i}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}=n\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow R^{3}=1000 r^{3} \Rightarrow R=10r$ ...(i) Initial surface area, $A_{1}=n 4 \pi r^{2}$ Final surface area, $A_{2}=4 \pi R^{2}$ Now, increase in surface area, $\Delta A=A_{2}-A_{1}=4 \pi [R^{2}-n r^{2}]$ We know that, surface energy, $SE = TA$ [where, $T=$ surface tension of liquid $]$ According to question. $\frac{SE_{f}}{SE_{i}}=\frac{TA_{2}}{TA_{1}}=\frac{4 \pi R^{2}}{n(4 \pi r^{2})}$ $=\frac{R^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}$ [From Eq. (i)] $=\frac{(10 r)^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}=\frac{100 r^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}=\frac{1}{10}$ or $1:10$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, the ratio of amplitudes of two interfering waves is $4:3$ i.e., $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\frac{4}{3}$ We know that, intensity of wave is proportional to square of amplitude. $\therefore \frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\frac{A_{max}}{A_{min}}\right)^{2}$ , where maximum and minimum amplitudes are $A_{max} = A_{1}+A_{2}$ and $A_{min} = A_{1}-A_{2}$ Substituting the values, we get $\frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}$ Multiplying and dividing by $A_{2}^{2}$ in RHS, we get. $\frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left( \frac{ \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} + 1 }{ \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} - 1 } \right)^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{ \frac{4}{3} + 1 }{ \frac{4}{3} - 1 } \right)^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{7}{1} \right)^{2} = \frac{49}{1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Consider two dipoles are placed at two points $A$ and $B$ in opposite direction. Therefore, $E_{1}=E_{2}$ $\frac{2 k p}{x^{3}} = \frac{2 k (27 p)}{(24-x)^{3}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x} = \frac{3}{24-x}$ $24-x = 3x \Rightarrow 24 = 4x$ $\Rightarrow x = 6 \text{ cm}$ from point A © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, two capacitors of same capacities $C$ . In series, equivalent capacitance is given by $\frac{1}{C_S}=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}=\frac{2}{C}$ $C_S = \frac{C}{2}$ In parallel, equivalent capacitance is given by $C_P = C_1 + C_2 = C + C = 2C$ Ratio $= \frac{C_P}{C_S} = \frac{2C}{\left(\frac{C}{2}\right)} = \frac{4}{1}$ $\Rightarrow C_P: C_S = 4:1$ Hence, Assertion is true. In parallel, $C_P > C$ In series, $C_S < C$ So, in parallel, capacity is increased but in series, capacity is decreased. Hence, Reason is also true, but it is not the correct explanation of  Assertion. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Electric field $E_{0}=500\ \mathrm{V}\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}$ $E = (E_{0} \cos\theta \hat{i} + E_{0} \sin\theta \hat{j})\ \mathrm{V}\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}$ $OA=3\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $OB=5\ \mathrm{m}$ Now, displacement vector. $\vec{AB} = d\vec{r} = (3 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j})\ \mathrm{m}$ We know that, potential difference, $\Delta V = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$ i.e. $V_{B} - V_{A}$ $= (E_{0} \cos\theta \hat{i} + E_{0} \sin\theta \hat{j})(3 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j})$ Substituting the values, we get $V_{B} - V_{A} = -500(\cos 30^{\circ} \hat{i} + \sin 30^{\circ} \hat{j})(3 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j})$ $= -500(3 \cos 30^{\circ} + 5 \sin 30^{\circ})$ $= -500\left[ \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{5}{2} \right]\ \mathrm{V}$ $\therefore V_{B} - V_{A} = -250(3\sqrt{3} + 5)\ \mathrm{V}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, for a moving coil galvanometer, Effective area, $A = 4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{m}^2$ Magnetic field, $B = 5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Wb\,m}^{-2}$ Angle of deflection, $\phi = 0.2 \text{ rad}$ Electric current, $l = 5 \mathrm{mA} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{A}$ By using the relation, $N A B I = C \phi$ [where, C =  torsional constant] $\Rightarrow C = \frac{N A B I}{\phi}$ By substituting the values, we get $C = \frac{4 \times 10^{-2} \times 5 \times 10^{-2} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}{0.2}$ $= 5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{Nm\,rad}^{-1}$ Current sensitivity $S_i = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{0.2}{5 \times 10^{-3}} \text{ rad/A} = 40 \text{ rad A}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Side of square frame, $a = 1\,\mathrm{m}$ Electric current $= I$ For square, Let $r$ be the distance of centre $O$ from all sides, $r = \frac{a}{2}$ Since, all sides of square produces equal field in the same direction. Using, $B = 4\left[ \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}(\sin 45^{\circ}+\sin 45^{\circ}) \right]$ $\Rightarrow B = \frac{4 \mu_0 I}{4 \pi \left(\frac{a}{2}\right)} \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)$ $\Rightarrow B = \frac{2 \mu_0 I}{\pi a} \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow B = \frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_0 I}{\pi a}$ ...(i) For circle, Let $R$ be the radius of circular coil. Then, $2 \pi R = 4 a$ $\Rightarrow R = \frac{4 a}{2 \pi} = \frac{2 a}{\pi}$ Using the expression for magnetic field at centre of circular coil, $B' = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}$ $\Rightarrow B' = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \left( \frac{2 a}{\pi} \right)} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi I}{4 a}$ ...(ii) From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{B}{B'} = \frac{ \frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_0 I}{\pi a} }{ \frac{\mu_0 \pi I}{4 a} } = \frac{8\sqrt{2}}{\pi^2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\text{PQ}$ arm is moving with constant speed $v$ perpendicular to the magnetic field $B$ . (ii)] $f'(x)=4 f(x)$ ∴ $f'(6)=4 f(6)=4 \times 3=12$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f'(x)=\sqrt{2 x^{2}-1}$ $y=f(x^{3})$ Differentiation w.r.t. $x$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=f'(x^{3}) \cdot 3 x^{2}$ [Using chain rule] ∴ $\frac{dy}{dx}\big|_{x=1}=f'(1^{3})3(1)^{2}$ $=f'(1) \cdot 3$ $=\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-1} \cdot 3$ $[\because f'(x)=\sqrt{2 x^{2}-1}]$ $=\sqrt{2-1} \cdot 3=\sqrt{1} \cdot 3$ $=3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y=x(\log x)^{2}$ For maximum value $\frac{dy}{dx}=x\left(2\log x \cdot \frac{1}{x}\right)+(\log x)^{2}$ $=2\log x+(\log x)^{2}$ Now, put $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $2\log x+(\log x)^{2}=0$ $(\log x)[\log x+2]=0$ $\log x=0 | \log x+2=0$ $x=1$ | $\log x=-2$ & $x=e^{-2}$ Using second order derivative lest. Again differentiating $y$ w.I.t. $x$ $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=2x+2\log x \cdot \frac{1}{x}$ $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\big|_{x=1}=2>0$ ∴ $x=1$ is point of minima $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\big|_{x=e^{-2}} =\frac{2}{e^{-2}}+2\cdot \log e^{-2} \cdot \frac{1}{e^{-2}}$ $=\frac{1}{e^{-2}}(2-4)=-\frac{2}{e^{-2}}<0$ ∴ $x=e^{-2}$ is point of maxima. ∴ $y_{\max}=e^{-2}(\log e^{-2})^{2}$ $=e^{-2}(-2)^{2}=4e^{-2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Elipse, $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ ...(i) To find Equation of tangent and normal at point $\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ We have to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ . Slope of tangent $=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}=m_{T}$ Now, differentiating Eq. (i) w.r.t. $x$ $\frac{2x}{a^{2}}+\frac{2y}{b^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2x}{a^{2}\times\frac{2y}{b^{2}}}=-\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$ ∴ $m_{T}=-\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\frac{\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}}\right)=-\frac{b}{a}$ and $m_{N}=-\frac{1}{m_{T}}=\frac{a}{b}$ Equation of tangent $\left(y-\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=-\frac{b}{a}\left(x-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ ...(ii) Equation of normal $\left(y-\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=\frac{a}{b\left(x-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}$ ...(iii) To find Area of triangle made by tangent, normal and X-axis.We have to find points on X-axis cut by tangent and normal, i.e B and C For B Put $y=0$ in Eq. (ii) $\Rightarrow -\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{b}{a}\left(x-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}=x\frac{-a}{\sqrt{2}}(x=\sqrt{2}a)$ ∴ B is $(\sqrt{2}a,0)$ For C Put $y=0$ in Eq. (iii) $\Rightarrow -\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{a}{b}\left(x-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{-b^{2}}{\sqrt{2a}}+\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}=x$ $\Rightarrow \frac{a^{2}-b^{2}}{\sqrt{2}a}=x$ Area of $\Delta ABC=\frac{1}{2}\times$ Base × Height $=\frac{1}{2}\times BC\times AM$ $=\frac{1}{2}\times\left[\sqrt{2}a-\left(\frac{a^{2}-b^{2}}{\sqrt{2a}}\right)\right]\times\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2a^{2}-a^{2}+b^{2}}{\sqrt{2}a}\right)\cdot\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}$ $=\frac{b}{4a}(a^{2}+b^{2})$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=x^{a} \log x$ and $f(0)=0$ ∵ Rolle's theorem is applicable in $[0,1]$ ⇒ It is continuous in closed interval $[0,1]$ and It is differentiable in $(a, b)$ and $f(0)=f(1)$ , ∵ $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$ $\because \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}} f(x)=f(0)$ $\Rightarrow \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}} x^{a} \log x = 0$ $\Rightarrow \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{\log x}{x^{-4}} = 0$ [∵ It is $-\frac{\infty}{\infty}$ indeterminate form] Using L' hospital rule $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{\frac{1}{x}}{-a x^{-a-1}} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}} -\frac{x^{a}}{a} = 0$ ∵ It is possible when $a>0 \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}(x)}}{1+x^{2}}\left[(\sec^{-1}\sqrt{1+x^{2}})^{2}\right]$ $+\left[\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)\right] dx$ $(x>0)$ Let us take $\tan^{-1} x = \theta \Rightarrow x = \tan \theta$ $\frac{1}{1+x^{2}} dx = d\theta$ $I=\int e^{\theta}\left[(\sec^{-1}(\sqrt{1+\tan^{2}\theta}))^{2} +\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}\right) \right] d\theta$ $=\int e^{\theta}\{(\sec^{-1}\sec\theta)^{2}+(\cos^{-1}\cos 2\theta)\} d\theta$ $\left[\because \cos 2\theta = \frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}\right]$ $=\int e^{\theta}\{\theta^{2}+2\theta\} d\theta$ $[\because \sec^{-1}\sec\theta = \theta$ and $\cos^{-1}\cos 2\theta = 2\theta]$ $\left[\because \int e^{x}(f(x)+f'(x)\right] dx = e^{x}f(x)+c]$ So, $I=e^{\theta} \cdot \theta^{2}+c$ $I=e^{\tan^{-1} x} \cdot (\tan^{-1} x)^{2}+c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int \sqrt[3]{x} \left(1+\sqrt[3]{x^{4}}\right)^{\frac{1}{7}} \, dx = A\left(1+\sqrt[3]{x^{4}}\right)^{B}+C$ Let us assume $I = \int \sqrt[3]{x} \left(1+\sqrt[3]{x^{4}}\right)^{\frac{1}{7}} \, dx = \int x^{\frac{1}{3}} \left(1+x^{\frac{4}{3}}\right)^{\frac{1}{7}} \, dx$ Let $1+x^{\frac{4}{3}}=t$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} x^{\frac{4}{3}-1} dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} x^{\frac{1}{3}} dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow x^{\frac{1}{3}} dx = \frac{3}{4} dt$ ∴ $I = \int (t)^{\frac{1}{7}} \cdot \frac{3}{4} \, dt = \frac{3}{4} \int (t)^{\frac{1}{7}} \, dt$ $= \frac{3}{4} \left[ \frac{(t)^{\frac{1}{7}+1}}{\frac{1}{7}+1} \right] + c = \frac{3}{4} \frac{(1+x^{4/3})^{\frac{8}{7}}}{\frac{8}{7}} + c$ $= \frac{21}{32} (1+\sqrt[3]{x^{4}})^{\frac{8}{7}} + c$ ∴ $A = \frac{21}{32}$ and $B = \frac{8}{7}$ ∴ $AB = \frac{21}{32} \times \frac{8}{7} = \frac{3}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int \frac{\sqrt{2} \sin x}{\sin \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)} \, dx$ $\text{Let } x + \frac{\pi}{4} = t$ $\Rightarrow x = t - \frac{\pi}{4}$ $dx = dt$ $\int \frac{\sqrt{2} \sin \left(t - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\sin t} \, dt$ $= \int \frac{\sqrt{2} \left( \sin t \cos \frac{\pi}{4} - \cos t \sin \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}{\sin t} \, dt$ $= \int \frac{\sqrt{2} \left( \frac{\sin t}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\cos t}{\sqrt{2}} \right)}{\sin t} \, dt$ $= \int \frac{\sin t - \cos t}{\sin t} \, dt = \int (1 - \cot t) \, dt$ $= t - \ln |\sin t| + c$ $= x + \frac{\pi}{4} - \ln \left|\sin \left( x + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)\right| + c$ $= x - \log \left|\sin \left( x + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)\right| + c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ Let $I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ ...(i) $\because \int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x) d x = \int\limits_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x) d x$ $\Rightarrow I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \tan (\pi-x)}{\sec (\pi-x)+\tan (\pi-x)} d x$ $I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x)(-\tan x)}{-\sec x-\tan x} d x$ $I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ ...(ii) Adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $2 I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \tan x+(\pi-x) \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ $2 I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\pi \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}{\frac{1}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \frac{\sin x}{1+\sin x} \times \frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x} \right) d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin^{2} x} d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x - \sin^{2} x}{\cos^{2} x} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2} x} - \frac{\sin^{2} x}{\cos^{2} x} \right) d x$ $\frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \sec x \tan x - \tan^{2} x \right) d x$ $\frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left\{ \sec x \tan x - (\sec^{2} x - 1) \right\} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \sec x \tan x - \sec^{2} x + 1 \right) d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \sec x - \tan x + x \right]_{0}^{\pi}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left\{ (\sec \pi - \tan \pi + \pi) - \frac{\pi}{2} \right\}$ $\left\{ \sec 0^{\circ} - \tan 0^{\circ} + 0 \right\}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left\{ (-1-0+\pi) - (1-0+0) \right\}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} (\pi-1-1) = \frac{\pi}{2} (\pi-2)$ $I = \frac{\pi (\pi-2)}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int\limits_{a}^{b} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x-a)(b-x)}}$ $\int\limits_{a}^{b} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{-x^{2}+(a+b)x-ab}}$ $= \int\limits_{a}^{b} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{-(x^{2}-(a+b)x+ab)}}$ $= \int\limits_{a}^{b} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{-\left[x^{2}+\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2}+ab-\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-(a+b)x}}$ $= \int\limits_{a}^{b} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(x-\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2}}}$ $[\because b > a]$ ∴ $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}} = \sin^{-1} \frac{x}{a} + C$ $= \left| \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{x - \frac{a+b}{2}}{\frac{b-a}{2}} \right) \right|_{a}^{b}$ $= \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{b - \frac{a+b}{2}}{\frac{b-a}{2}} \right) - \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{a - \frac{a+b}{2}}{\frac{b-a}{2}} \right)$ $= \sin^{-1}(+1) - \sin^{-1}(-1) = +\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} = +\pi$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x+y}$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x} \cdot e^{y}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{e^{y}}=e^{x} dx$ $e^{-y} dy=e^{x} dx$ Integrating both sides, $\int e^{-y} dy=\int e^{x} dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{e^{-y}}{-1}=e^{x}+c$ $\Rightarrow e^{x}+e^{-y}+c=0$ $\Rightarrow e^{x}+e^{-y}=-c$ $\Rightarrow e^{x}+e^{-y}=c$ when $c=-c$ $\Rightarrow v_{av}=\frac{2 v_{1} v_{2}}{v_{1}+v_{2}}$ By substituting the values, we get $v_{av}=\frac{2 \times 18 \times 36}{18+36}$ $=\frac{2 \times 36 \times 18}{54}=\frac{72}{3} \text{m/s}$ © examsnet.com
