Solution: Given that, initial speed of car, $v_i=v$ Final speed of car when it stops, $v_f=0$ Distance travelled $=s$ Retarding force $=F$ By Newton's law of motion, $F = m a = m \left( \frac{v_i^2 - v_i^2}{2 s} \right)$ ...(i) $\begin{bmatrix} \text{using relation} \\ a = \frac{v_f^2 - v_i^2}{2 s} \end{bmatrix}$ $= \frac{m (-v^2)}{2 s}$ $F = \frac{-m v^2}{2 s}$ When, retarding force, $F' = 3 F$ Let $s'=$ New distance travelled. Similarly, from Eq. (i) we can write $3 F = \frac{-m v^2}{2 s'}$ ...(ii) Substituting value of F from Eq. (i) into Eq. (ii), we get $3 \left( \frac{-m v^2}{2 s} \right) = \frac{-m v^2}{2 s^2}$ ⇒ $s' = \frac{s}{3}$ Hence, the body will stop by travelling distance $\frac{s}{3}$ , when retarding force is $3 F$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of rod $=m$ Length of rod, $L=21$ Initial and final angular velocities are 0 and $\omega$ respectively, Time taken $=t$ We know that, torque acting on body having moment of inertia $(I)$ and angular acceleration $(\alpha)$ is $\tau = l \alpha$ where, $I = \frac{1}{12} ML^{2} = \frac{1}{12} m(2)^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{3} m l^{2}$ and $\alpha = \frac{\omega_{f} - \omega_{i}}{t} = \frac{\omega - 0}{t} = \frac{\omega}{t}$ Now, substituting the values, we get $\tau = \frac{1}{3} m l^{2} \frac{\omega}{t}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, moment of inertia, $I=10 \text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^{2}$ Initial angular velocity, $\omega_{0}=50 \text{ rad} / \text{s}$ Final angular velocity, $\omega=0$ Time taken to stop wheel, $t=10 \text{ s}$ We know that, work done by torque = change of rotational KE $W=\Delta \text{KE}=K_f - K_i$ $W=\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} - \frac{1}{2} I \omega_{a}^{2}$ $W=0-\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (50)^{2}$ = -12500 J So, amount of work done to bring the flywheel to rest is $12500 \text{ J}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, two particles P and Q describes SHM of same amplitude $a$ and frequency $f$ . Let equation of motion of two particles are $x_{1}=a \sin \omega t$ and $x_{2}=a \sin (\omega t + \phi)$ where, $\phi$ be the phase difference. ∴ Path difference, $x_{2}-x_{1}=a \sin (\omega t + \phi) - a \sin \omega t$ $x_{2}-x_{1}=2 a \sin \left( \frac{\omega t + \phi - \omega t}{2} \right) \cos \left( \frac{\omega t + \phi + \omega t}{2} \right)$ [Using identity $\sin A - \sin B = 2 \sin \left( \frac{A-B}{2} \right) \cdot \cos \left( \frac{A+B}{2} \right) ]$ ∴ $x_{2}-x_{1}=2 a \sin \left( \frac{\phi}{2} \right) \cos \left( \omega + \frac{\phi}{2} \right)$ The distance $x_{2}-x_{1}$ will be maximum when $\cos \left( \omega t + \frac{\phi}{2} \right) = 1$ ∴ Maximum distance $x_{2}-x_{1} = \sqrt{2} a$ $= 2 a \sin \frac{\phi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \frac{\phi}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \frac{\phi}{2} = \sin 45^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\phi}{2} = 45^{\circ}$ Phase difference, $\phi = 90^{\circ} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, equation of a particle executing Simple harmonic motion is $x=A \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ Now, velocity of particle, $v=\frac{dx}{dt}$ $v=\frac{d}{dt}\left[A \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]$ $=-A\omega \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ $v$ is maximum when $\sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1$ $\sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin \frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow t=\frac{\pi}{4\omega}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of satellite, $m=500\ \mathrm{kg}$ Radius of orbit, $r=4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$ Now, the satellite is revolving in equatorial plane so, its time period will be equal to time period of  rotation of earth i.e., $T=24\ \mathrm{h}$ . ∴ Angular velocity of satellite, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ Now, angular momentum, $L = m \omega r^{2} = m \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right) r^{2}$ $= 500 \times \left(\frac{2\pi}{24 \times 3600}\right) \times (4 \times 10^{7})^{2}$ $= 0.58 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, angle of laticude, $\lambda = 45^{\circ}$ We know that, the expression of gravity at latitude angle is $g_{\lambda} = g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} \lambda$ The weight of man of mass $m$ at this point $w = m g_{\lambda} = m(g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ})$ According to question, man feels weightlessness ∴ w = 0 $m(g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ}) = 0$ But $m \neq 0$ , then $g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\frac{2q}{R}}$ Now, using time period, (duration of day) $= T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R}{2g}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{2R}{g}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, weight of load, $w=10\ \mathrm{kg}$ -wt $F=w=10 \times 10\ \mathrm{N}=100\ \mathrm{N}$ Elongation in wire, $\Delta l=1.5\ \mathrm{mm}=1.5 \times 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{m}$ Length of wire, $l=8\ \mathrm{m}$ We know that, elastic potential energy stored in wire, $U=\frac{1}{2} F \Delta l=\frac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}=0.075\ \mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, force on small piston, $F_1=F$ Diameter of small piston, $d_1=8\,\text{cm}$ Mass of vehicle placed on large piston (lift), $M=1400\,\text{kg}$ Diameter of large piston, $d_2=24\,\text{cm}$ By using Pascal's law, Equal pressure will be  transmitted from small piston to lift $p=\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_2}{A},$ $\Rightarrow\frac{F}{\frac{\pi d_4^2}{4}}=\frac{Mg}{\frac{\pi d_2^2}{4}}$ $F=M a\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^2=1400\times10\times\left(\frac{8}{24}\right)^2$ = 1556 N = 1600 N © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, for first condition, Initial temperature, $T_{1}=52.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Final temperature, $T_{v}=47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Average temperature, $T_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{T_{1}+T_{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{525+47.5}{2}=50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ For second condition, Initial temperature, $T_{1}=47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Final temperature, $T_{2}=42.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Average temperature, $T_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{T_{1}+T_{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{47.5+42.5}{2}=45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Let $T_{0}$ be the temperature of surroundings. Now, using expression of rate of cooling, $R=\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta}=-K(T_{\mathrm{av}}-T_{0})$ Substituting the values in above equation from $1^{\text{st}}$ and 2nd conditions, we get $\frac{T_{1}-T_{2}}{t_{1}}=-K(T_{\mathrm{av}}-T_{0})$ $\frac{52.5-47.5}{5}=-K(50-T_{0})$ ...(i) Similarly, $\frac{47,5-42.5}{7.5}=-K(45-T_{0})$ ...(ii) Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{\frac{52.5-47.5}{5}}{\frac{47.5-42.5}{7.5}}=\frac{-K(50-T_{0})}{-K(45-T_{0})}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{5}{5} \times \frac{7.5}{5} = \frac{50-T_{0}}{45-T_{0}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{2} = \frac{50-T_{0}}{45-T_{0}}$ $T_{0}=35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Hence, the temperature of surroundings is $35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, two plates are having same surface area (A). Let $K_{1},K_{2}$ and $t_{1}, t_{2}$ be their conductivities and thickness respectively, According to question, $\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}}=\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{2}{3}$ ...(i) Since, the rate of flow of heat through both plates be same, then $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}=\frac{K_{1} A \Delta T_{1}}{t_{1}}=\frac{K_{2} A \Delta T_{2}}{t_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}} \times \frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}} \times (T_{1}-T)=(T-T_{2})$ [where T be the temperature of common surface] $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} (10-T)=(T-0)$ T = 5°C © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, heat released, $\Delta Q = -30 \mathrm{J}$ Work done on the gas, $\Delta W = -18 \mathrm{J}$ Change in internal energy $=\Delta U$ Initial internal cnergy, $U_i = 60 \mathrm{J}$ Let final internal energy, $U_f = U$ By using first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta W + \Delta U$ Substituting the values, we get $-30 = -18 + (U_f - U_i)$ $-30+18=U-60$ $\Rightarrow U=48 \mathrm{J}$ Hence, the final internal energy of gas is $48 \mathrm{J}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: For Oxygen, Molar mass, $M_1=32$ Heat capacity ratio at constant pressure to that at constant volume, $\gamma_1=\frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}=\frac{7}{5}$ [for diatomic gas] Speed of sound, $v_1=460\ \mathrm{m/s}$ For Helium, Molar mass, $M_2=4$ Heat capacity ratio $\left(\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}}\right)$ , $\gamma_2=\frac{5}{3}$ [for monoatomic gas] Let speed of sound $=v_2$ Using the expression of speed of sound in an ideal gas at certain temperature $(T)$ is $v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$ ∴ $v_1=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_1 RT}{M_1}}$ ...(i) and $v_2=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_2 RT}{M_2}}$ ...(ii) Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{v_1}{v_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_1 RT}{M_1}}\times\sqrt{\frac{M_2}{\gamma_2 RT}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_1}{\gamma_2}\times\frac{M_2}{M_1}}$ Substituting the values, we get $\frac{460}{v_2}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}\times\frac{4}{32}\times\frac{3}{5}}$ $\Rightarrow v_2=1420\ \mathrm{m/s}$ Hence, speed of sound in helium gas at the same temperature is $1420\ \mathrm{m/s}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: (c) Given, refractive index of lens, $\mu=1.5$ Radius of curved face, $R_{1}=12\,\text{cm}$ Radius of plane face, $R_{2}=\infty$ Now, using the expression of focal length. $\frac{1}{f}=\mu-1\left[\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right]$ Substituting the values, we get $\frac{1}{f}=(1.5-1)\left[\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right]$ $\frac{1}{f}=0.5\times\frac{1}{12}$ $\Rightarrow f=\frac{12}{0.5}\,\text{cm}=24\,\text{cm}$ Hence, the focal length of given plano-convex lens is $24\,\text{cm}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, the point charges are placed on vertices of a square as shown in figure. Let $r$ be the distance of $O$ from the each comer. In $\triangle ABC,\ AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}$ $(2r)^{2}=a^{2}+a^{2}=2a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow r=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ $r=\frac{2.8}{\sqrt{2}}\ \mathrm{m}$ $(\because a=2.8\ \mathrm{m})$ Now, using expression of electric potential at a point due to point charge $V=\frac{Kq}{r}$ Now, total electric potential at O due to all the four charges $q_{1}, q_{2} q_{3}$ and $q_{4}$ $V_{0}=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}+V_{4}$ $V_{0}=\frac{Kq_{1}}{r}+\frac{Kq_{2}}{r}+\frac{Kq_{1}}{r}+\frac{Kq_{4}}{r}$ $V_{0}=\frac{K}{r}[q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+q_{4}]$ Substituting the values, we get $V_{e}=\frac{9 \times 10^{9} \times \sqrt{2}}{2.8}(20+40-34+16) \times 10^{-9}$ $=190.89\ \mathrm{V}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, magnetic moment, $M=2\ \mathrm{JT}^{-1}$ Magnetic field, $B=0.1\ \mathrm{T}$ Since, magnetic moment is aligned in the direction of magnetic field, i.e. initial angle, $\theta_1=0^{\circ}$ When magnet is normal, then final angle, $\theta_2=90^{\circ}$ Using relation for work done, $W=-MB(\cos\theta_2-\cos\theta_1)$ Substituting the values, we get $W=-2\times0.1(\cos90^{\circ}-\cos0^{\circ})$ $=-2\times0.1(0-1)=0.2\ \mathrm{J}$ Hence, $0.2\ \mathrm{J}$ work will be done to rotate a magnet from $0^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$ angle with in magnetic field. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, the length of wire $=L$ Current passing through ring $=I$ Let R be the radius of ring. Then, $2\pi R=L$ $R=\frac{L}{2\pi}$ ...(i) Consider an element of ring AB which subtends an angle $\Delta\theta$ at the centre O, such that, $AB=\Delta l=R\Delta\theta$ ...(ii) If T be the tension at point P as shown in figure, We know that, force acting on element AB in uniform magnetic field. $F=IB\Delta l$ ...(ii) (radially outward) By resolving tension into sine and cosine components $T\cos\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}$ is acting equal and opposite. So, it is cancelled. But sum of sine component is equal and opposite to F. ∴ At equilibrium, we get $2T\sin\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}=F$ As $\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}$ is very small angle, so, $\sin\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}=\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}$ By substituting the values, we get $2T\frac{\Delta\theta}{2}=IB\Delta l$ $\Rightarrow T\Delta\theta=1BR\Delta\theta$ T = IBR ...(iv) Using Eqs. (i) and (iv), we get $T=\frac{IBL}{2\pi}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, emf of batrery, $E=6\ \mathrm{V}$ Resistance, $R=12\ \Omega$ Inductance, $L=2\ \mathrm{H}$ We know that, the instantaneous current in the circuit containing $R$ and $L$ in series with battery of emf $E$ is $I=I_{0}\left(1-e^{\frac{-z}{2}t}\right)$ where, maximum current at steady state $I_{0}=\frac{E}{R}$ ∴ $I=\frac{E}{R}\left(1-e^{\frac{-R}{t}}\right)$ Now, the rate of increase of current. $\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{E}{R}\left[0-\frac{-R}{L}e^{\frac{-R}{2}t}\right]=\frac{E}{L}e^{\frac{-R}{L}t}$ At $(t=0)$ initial condition, $\frac{dl}{dt}\big|_{t=0}=\frac{E}{L}e^{0}=\frac{E}{L}=\frac{6}{2}=3\ \mathrm{A}/\mathrm{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, wavelength, $\lambda=800 \text{ nm}$ speed of light, $c=3 \times 10^{8} \text{m/s}$ Then, frequency, $f=\frac{c}{\lambda}$ Substituting the values, we get Source frequency, $f=\frac{3 \times 10^{4}}{800 \times 10^{-9}} \text{ Hz}$ $=375 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ It is said in the question that only $1\%$ of source frequency is available as signal bandwidth. ∴ Total available signal bandwidth $=1\%$ of $375 \times 10^{14}$ $=\frac{1}{100} \times 3.75 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}=3.75 \times 10^{12} \text{ Hz}$ Given that, the frequency bandwidth of one signal $=6 \text{ MHz}=6 \times 10^{6} \text{ Hz}$ Hence, the number of channels $=\frac{\text{Total available signal bandwidth}}{\text{Bandwidth of one signal}}$ $=\frac{3.75 \times 10^{12}}{6 \times 10^{6}}=\frac{1}{16} \times 10^{7}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Molecular orbital configuration of $\mathrm{O}_2 = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{z}^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1} \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{1}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic Bond order $= \frac{10-6}{2}=2$ $\mathrm{O}_2^{+} = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{z}^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2} \pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic Bond order $= \frac{10-5}{2}=2.5$ $\mathrm{C}_2 = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{2} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2}$ ⇒ Diamagnetic Bond order $= \frac{8-4}{2}=2$ $\mathrm{C}_2^{+} = \sigma l s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{+} 2s^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{1}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic $\mathrm{NO} = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{z}^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2} \pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic Bond order $= \frac{10-5}{2}=2.5$ $\mathrm{NO}^{+} = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{z}^{2} \pi 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2}$ ⇒ Diamagnetic Bond order $= \frac{10-4}{2}=3$ $\mathrm{N}_2 = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2} \pi 2p_{z}^{2}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic Bond order $= \frac{10-4}{2}=3$ $\mathrm{N}_2^{+} = \sigma 1s^{2} \sigma^{*} 1s^{2} \sigma 2s^{2} \sigma^{*} 2s^{2} \sigma 2p_{x}^{2} \pi 2p_{y}^{2} \sigma 2p_{z}^{1}$ ⇒ Paramagnetic Bond order $= \frac{9-4}{2}=2.5$ Bond order increase from $\mathrm{NO}$ to $\mathrm{NO}^{+}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the event A and B $A=$ fair coin tossed $B=$ biased coin tossed $E=$ first time head second time tail $P(A)=\frac{m}{n}, P(B)=\frac{n-m}{n}$ $P(E/A)=\frac{1}{4}, P(E/B)=\frac{2}{9}$ Required probability $P(A/E)=\frac{P(A) \times P(E/A)}{P(A) \times P(E/A)+P(B) \times P(E/B)}$ $=\frac{\frac{m}{n} \times \frac{1}{4}}{\frac{m}{n} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{n-m}{n}\left(\frac{2}{9}\right)}$ $=\frac{9m}{9m+8n-8m}=\frac{9m}{8n+m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $P(A)=\frac{1}{3}, P(B)=\frac{2}{7}$ $P(A \mid B') = \frac{P(A \cap B')}{P(B')} = \frac{P(A)-P(A \cap B)}{1-P(B)}$ $= \frac{P(A)-P(A) P(B)}{1-P(B)}$ $[ \because A$ and B are independent events] $= \frac{ \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{7} }{ 1 - \frac{2}{7} } = \frac{7-2}{3(7-2)} = \frac{1}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Consider the events $A=$ Probability that prime number occur $B=$ Probability that prime number does not occur $E=$ prime number occur when man reports 25 prime number from 1 to 100 ∴ $P(A)=\frac{25}{100}=\frac{1}{4}$ $P(B)=\frac{75}{100}=\frac{3}{4}$ $P(E/A)=\frac{7}{10}, P(E/B)=\frac{3}{10}$ Required probability $P(A/E)=\frac{ \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{7}{10} }{ \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{7}{10} + \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{10} }=\frac{7}{16}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the coordinate of vertices of $\triangle OAB$ $O=(0,0) A=(x, 0)$ and $B=(0, y)$ $(h, k)$ is centroid of $\triangle OAB$ . ∴ $h=\frac{x}{3}$ and $k=\frac{y}{3}$ $x=3 h$ and $y=3 k$ $x=3 h$ and $y=3 k$ Given, $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ $x^{2}+y^{2}=9(h^{2}+k^{2})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{16}{9}=h^{2}+k^{2}$ ∴ Locus of centroid of $\triangle OAB$ is $x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{16}{9}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation, $x^{2}+2\sqrt{3}xy-y^{2}=8$ Since, the axes are rotated through an angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ . ∴ $(x,y)$ replaced by $\left( x \cos\frac{\pi}{3} - y \sin\frac{\pi}{3}, x \sin\frac{\pi}{3} + y \cos\frac{\pi}{3} \right)$ i.e. $\left( \frac{x-\sqrt{3}y}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}x+y}{2} \right)$ in the given equation. ∴ $\left(\frac{x-\sqrt{3}y}{2}\right)^{2}+2\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{x-\sqrt{3}y}{2}\right)$ $\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}x+y}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}x+y}{2}\right)^{2}=8$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}(x^{2}-2\sqrt{3}xy+3y^{2}+6x^{2}-4\sqrt{3}xy-6y^{2}-3x^{2}-2\sqrt{3}x-y^{2})=8$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}(4x^{2}-8\sqrt{3}xy-4y^{2})=8$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-2\sqrt{3}xy-y^{2}=8$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given line, $2x+3y=6$ Slope of line $=-\frac{2}{3}$ Equation of lines passing through origin and form an isosceles right angle triangle with the given line ∴ Each angle be $45^{\circ}$ ∴ Equation of line passing through origin and making an angle $45^{\circ}$ with the line $2x+3y=6$ is $\frac{y}{x}=\frac{-\frac{2}{3}+\tan 45^{\circ}}{1+\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) \tan 45^{\circ}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}=\frac{-\frac{2}{3}+1}{1+\frac{2}{3}}$ or $\frac{y}{x}=\frac{-\frac{2}{3}-1}{1-\frac{2}{3}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{5}$ or $\frac{v}{x}=\frac{-5}{1}$ $\Rightarrow 5y=x$ or $y+5x=0$ $\Rightarrow x-5y=0$ or $5x+y=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the point $P(h, k)$ lie on the linc $3x+5y=15$ Distance from coordinate axes are equal from P. ∴ $|h|=|k|$ $\Rightarrow h = \pm k$ Point P line of $3x+5y=15$ $3h+5k=15$ $\Rightarrow 3h+5h=15$ $\Rightarrow h = \frac{15}{8}$ $\Rightarrow k = \frac{15}{8}$ Put $k = -h$ , $3h-5h=15=h=\frac{-15}{2}, k=\frac{15}{2}$ $\left(\frac{15}{8}, \frac{15}{8}\right)$ lie in first quadrant and $\left(\frac{-15}{2}, \frac{15}{2}\right)$ ∴ P lies in the first or in second quadrant. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given line, $x^{2}+2 x y-35 y^{2}-4 x+44 y-2=0$ $\Rightarrow (x+7y-6)(x-5y+2)=0$ $x+7y-6=0$ and $x-5y+2=0$ and $5x+\lambda y-8=0$ are concurrent. ∴ $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 7 & -6 \\ 1 & -5 & 2 \\ 5 & \lambda & -8 \end{vmatrix}$ $1(40-2\lambda)-7(-8-10)-6(1\lambda+25)=0$ $\Rightarrow 40-2\lambda+126-6\lambda-150=0$ $\Rightarrow 8\lambda=16$ ⇒ λ = 2 © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation, $2x^{2}+kxy-6y^{2}+3x+y+1=0$ is a pair of straight line. ∴ $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & \frac{k}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{k}{2} & -6 & \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 1 \end{vmatrix}=0$ ⇒ $\begin{vmatrix} 4 & k & 3 \\ k & -12 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}=0$ $\Rightarrow 4(-24-1)-k(2k-3)+3(k+36)=0$ $\Rightarrow -100-2k^{2}+3k+3k+108=0$ $\Rightarrow 2k^{2}-6k-8=0$ $\Rightarrow k^{2}-3k-4=0$ $\Rightarrow (k-4)(k+1)=0, \therefore k=4$ $\{\because k>0\}$ ∴ Equation of line is $\Rightarrow 2x^{2}+4xy-6y^{2}+3x+y+1=0$ $\Rightarrow (2x-2y+1)(x+3y+1)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x-2y+1=0$ and $x+3y+1=0$ Solving equation, we get $x=\frac{-5}{8}, y=\frac{-1}{8}$ ∴ Intersection point $\left(\frac{-5}{8}, \frac{-1}{8}\right)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, equation of pair of straight line $2 x^{2}+a x y+3 y^{2}=0$ and $2 x^{2}+b x y-3 y^{2}=0$ Let the slope of line $m$ and $m_{1}$ of the equation $2 x^{2}+a x y+3 y^{2}=0$ ∴ $m+m_{1}=\frac{-a}{3}$ and $m m_{1}=\frac{2}{3}$ Slope of the other line is $m$ and $m_{2}$ . Then, $m+m_{2}=\frac{b}{3}$ and $m m_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}$ Given, $m_{1} m_{2}=-1$ ...(i) ∴ $\frac{m m_{1}}{m m_{2}}=-1$ $\Rightarrow m_{1}=-m_{2}$ $\Rightarrow m_{1}+m_{2}=0$ ...(ii) From Eqs.(i) and (ii), we get $m_{1}=1$ and $m,=-1$ $\therefore m=\frac{2}{3}$ $m+m_{1}=-\frac{a}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}+1=-\frac{a}{3}$ $\Rightarrow a=-5$ and $\Rightarrow b=-1$ $a=-5$ $b=-1$ ∴ $a=-5 \ \& \ b=1$ and $a=-4 \ \& \ b=-1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given circle, $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+4y-4=0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}+4x-6y-3=0$ Equation of common chord of circle is $S_{1}-S_{2}=0$ ∴ $(x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+4y-4)$ $-(x^{2}+y^{2}+4x-6y-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow -6x+10y-1=0$ $\Rightarrow 6x-10y+1=0$ Perpendicular distance from the point $(1,2)$ to the line $6x-10y+1=0$ is $\left| \frac{6-20+1}{\sqrt{6^{2}+10^{2}}} \right|$ $=\frac{13}{\sqrt{136}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $2x - y + 3 = 0$ and $4x + ky + 3 = 0$ are conjugate with respect to ellipse $5x^{2} + 6y^{2} - 15 = 0$ We know that $a_{1}x + b_{1}y + c_{1} = 0$ and $a_{2}x + b_{2}y + c_{2} = 0$ are conjugate with $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b} = 1$ Then, $a^{2}a_{1}a_{2} + b^{2}b_{1}b_{2} = c_{1}c_{2}$ ∴ Here, $a_{1} = 2, b_{1} = -1, c_{1} = 3$ $a_{2} = 4, b_{2} = k_{,}, c_{2} = 3$ $a^{2} = \frac{15}{5}, b^{2} = \frac{15}{6}$ ∴ $\frac{15}{5}(2)(4) - \left(\frac{15}{6}\right)(k) = 9$ $\Rightarrow k = 6$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $e = \frac{5}{3}$ and $2 a e = 10$ $\Rightarrow 2 a \left( \frac{5}{3} \right) = 10$ $\Rightarrow a = 3$ $(a e)^2 = a^2 + b^2$ $\Rightarrow (5)^2 = 3^2 + b^2$ $\Rightarrow b^2 = 25 - 9 = 16$ ∴ Equation of hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1$ $\Rightarrow 16 x^2 - 9 y^2 = 144$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, orthocentre and circumcentre of triangle are $(3,-4,2)$ and $(2,1,3)$ respectively We know that centroid of triangle is divide orthocentre and circumcentre in the ratio $2: 1$ . ∴ Centroid of triangle is $\left(\frac{3+2(2)}{3}, \frac{-4+2(1)}{3}, \frac{2+2(3)}{3}\right)$ i.e., $\left(\frac{7}{3}, \frac{-2}{3}, \frac{8}{3}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Here, line AB in line dimensions makes an  angle $45^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$ with positive X-axis and Y-axis respectively and acuts angle $\theta$ with positive Z-axis. ∴ $\cos^{2}45^{\circ}+\cos^{2}120^{\circ}+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ $\Rightarrow \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ $\Rightarrow\cos^{2}\theta=1-\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)$ $\cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\frac{1}{2}$ ⇒ θ = 60° © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}+\frac{z}{c}=1$ which is unit distance from the origin cuts the coordinates axes at A, B and C. ∴ $1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}=1$ Coordinate of vertices of $\triangle ABC$ is $A(a, 0,0), B(0, b, 0), C(0,0, c)$ ∵ Centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is $\left(\frac{a}{3}, \frac{b}{3}, \frac{c}{3}\right)$ Now, $\left(\frac{a}{3}, \frac{b}{3}, \frac{c}{3}\right)$ satisfied the equation $\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}+\frac{1}{z^{2}}=k$ ∴ $\frac{9}{a^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}+\frac{9}{c^{2}}=k$ $9\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right)=k$ $\left[\because \frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}=1\right]$ ∴ k = 9 © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $f(x)=\lfloor x \rfloor^{2}-\lfloor x^{2} \rfloor$ $\lim\limits_{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\lfloor 0-h \rfloor^{2}-\lfloor (0-h)^{2} \rfloor$ $=(-1)^{2}-0=1$ $\lim\limits_{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim\limits_{h\to 0}(0+h)^{2}-\lfloor (0+h)^{2} \rfloor$ $=0-0=0$ ∵ $f(x)$ is discontinuous of $x=0$ Now, $\lim\limits_{x\to 1}f(x)=\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\lfloor 1-h \rfloor^{2}-\lfloor (1-h)^{2} \rfloor$ $=1-1=0$ ∵ $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$ . ∴ $f(x)$ is discontinuous at all integer except 1. © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $y=\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}}$ $\Rightarrow y=\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{2 \sin^{2} \frac{x}{2}}{2 \cos^{2} \frac{x}{2}}}=\tan^{-1}\left(\tan \frac{x}{2}\right)$ $y=\frac{x}{2}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2}=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{Let } u=\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2x^{2}-1}\right)$ and $v=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ Put $x=\cos\theta$ ∴ $u=\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2\cos^{2}\theta-1}\right)$ and $v=\sqrt{1-\cos^{2}\theta}$ $\Rightarrow u=\sec^{-1}(\sec 2\theta)$ and $v=\sin\theta$ $\Rightarrow u=2\theta$ and $v=\sin\theta$ $\frac{du}{d\theta}=2$ and $\frac{dv}{d\theta}=\cos\theta$ $\Rightarrow \frac{du}{dv} = \frac{ \frac{du}{d\theta} }{ \frac{dv}{d\theta} } = \frac{2}{\cos\theta}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{du}{dv} = \frac{2}{x}$ $[\because \cos\theta = x]$ At $x=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \left( \frac{du}{dv} \right)_{x=\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}} = 4$ © examsnet.com
Solution: We have, $f(x)=x^{3}-6 x^{2}-12 x-3$ $f'(x)=3 x^{2}-12 x-12$ $f''(x)=6 x-12$ $\Rightarrow f''(2)=12-12=0$ Here, $f''(x)=0$ at $x=2$ ∴ $x=2$ is a point of inflection. © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $f(x)=\sqrt{x^{2}-x}, x \in[1,4]$ $\Rightarrow f(1)=\sqrt{1-1}=0$ $f(4)=\sqrt{16-4}=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow f'(c)=\frac{2c-1}{2\sqrt{c^{2}-r}}$ By Lagrange's mean value theorem $f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ $\frac{2c-1}{2\sqrt{c^{2}-c}}=\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}-0}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2c-1}{2\sqrt{c^{2}-c}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sqrt{3}(2c-1)=4\sqrt{c^{2}-c}$ $\Rightarrow 3(2c-1)^{2}=16c^{2}-16c$ $\Rightarrow 3(4c^{2}-4c+1)=16c^{2}-16c$ $\Rightarrow 12c^{2}-12c+3=16c^{2}-16c$ $\Rightarrow 4c^{2}-4c-3=0$ $(2c-3)(2c+1)=0$ $\Rightarrow c=\frac{3}{2} \in(1,4)$ ∴ $c=\frac{3}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y=5x-2x^{3}$ $\frac{d y}{d x}=5-6x^{2}$ ∴ $m=5-6x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{d m}{d t}=(-12x)\frac{d x}{d t}$ $\left(\frac{d m}{d t}\right)_{x=3}=-12(3)\times 2=-72$ $\left[\because\frac{d x}{d t}=2\right]$ ⇒ Rate of change of slope at $x=3$ is $-72$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given curve, $b y^{2}=(x+a)^{3}$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get $2 b y \frac{dy}{dx}=3(x+a)^{2}$ Length of subnormal $= y \frac{dy}{dx} = y \left( \frac{3(x+a)^{2}}{2 b y} \right)$ Given, P( Subnormal length $)=$ (subtangent length $)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow P \left( y \frac{dy}{dx} \right) = q \left( y \frac{dx}{dy} \right)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{P}{q} = y \left( \frac{dx}{dy} \right)^{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{P}{9} = y \left( \frac{2 b y}{3(x+a)^{2}} \right)^3 = \frac{8 y^{4}}{27} \frac{b^{3}}{((x+a)^{3}]^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{P}{q} = \frac{8b}{27} \left( \frac{b y^{2}}{(x+a)^{3}} \right)^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{P}{q} = \frac{8b}{27}$ $[\because b y^{2} = (x+a)^{3}]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 2x + 2y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-x}{y}$ Tangent is parallel to $X$ -axis. ∴ $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{-x}{y} = 0 ; \therefore x = 0$ Putting the value of $x$ in $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 0 + y^{2} = a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow y = a, y \geq 0$ ∴ The point on the curve is $(0, a)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{Let } I = \int 3^{x} f'(x)+f(x) \log 3) dx$ $I = \int 3^{x} f'(x) dx + \int 3^{x} f(x) \log 3 dx$ $I = 3^{x} \int f'(x) dx - \int \left( \frac{d(3^{x})}{dx} \int f'(x) dx \right) dx + \int 3^{x} f(x) \log 3 dx$ $I = 3^{x} f(x) - \int (3^{x} f(x) \log 3) dx + \int 3^{x} f(x) \log 3 dx$ $I = 3^{x} f(x) + c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int \frac{x+\sin x}{1+\cos x} dx$ $I = \frac{1}{2} \int x \sec^2(x/2) dx + \int \tan(x/2) dx$ $I = x \int \frac{1}{2} \sec^2(x/2) dx - \int \left( \frac{dx}{dx} \int \frac{1}{2} \sec^2(x/2) dx \right) dx + \int \tan(x/2) dx$ $\Rightarrow I = x \tan(x/2) - \int \tan(x/2) dx + \int \tan(x/2) dx + c$ $I = x \tan(x/2) + c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $\int \frac{3\cos x-2\sin x}{4\sin x+5\cos x} \, dx$ $= A(5\cos x+4\sin x)+Bx+c$ On differentiating both sides, we get $\frac{3\cos x-2\sin x}{4\sin x+5\cos x}=\frac{A(-5\sin x+4\cos x)}{4\sin x+5\cos x}+B$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3\cos x-2\sin x}{4\sin x+5\cos x}$ $=\frac{-5A\sin x+4A\cos x+4B\sin x+5B\cos x}{4\sin x+5\cos x}$ $\Rightarrow 3\cos x-2\sin x=(4B-5A)\sin x+(5B+4A)\cos x$ Equating the coefficient of $\cos x$ and $\sin x$ , we get $5B+4A=3$ and $5A-4B=2$ Solving, we get $A=\frac{22}{41}$ and $B=\frac{7}{41}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int \frac{x-1}{(x-2)(x-3)} d x$ $I = \int \left( \frac{2}{x-3} - \frac{1}{x-2} \right) d x$ $I = \int \frac{2}{x-3} d x - \int \frac{d x}{x-2}$ $I = 2 \log (x-3) - \log (x-2) + c$ $I = \log (x-3)^2 - \log (x-2) + c$ $I = \log \left( \frac{(x-3)^2}{x-2} \right) + c$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} x\{\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)\}\,dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)[\sin^{2}(\sin(\pi-x)]+\cos^{2}(\cos(\pi-x))\,dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $2I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $\left[\because\int\limits_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx=2\int\limits_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx\right]$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[\sin^{2}\left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right)+\cos^{2}\left(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right)\right]\,dx$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^{2}(\cos x)+\cos^{2}(\sin x)\,dx$ $2l=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} 2\,dx$ $\Rightarrow I=\pi\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}$ $[I]=\left[\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}\right]=4\;\;\;\;$ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}\because \pi^2 & \in (9,10) \\ \frac{\pi^2}{2} & \in (4.5,5) \end{array}\right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $u$ and $\theta$ be the velocity of projection and angle of projection, respechively. Given that, horizontal component of velocity. $u_{x}=u \cos \theta=3\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ Equation of projectile motion is given by $y=12x-\frac{3}{4}x^{2}$ ...(i) We know, General equation of projectile motion, $y=x \tan \theta-\frac{g x^{2}}{2 u^{2} \cos^{2} \theta}$ ...(ii) Comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get tanθ = 12 $\Rightarrow \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}=12$ $\sin \theta=12 \cos \theta$ Multiplying on both side by $(u)$ $u \sin \theta=12(u \cos \theta)=12 \times 3$ i.e. $u \sin \theta=36\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ Now, using the expression of range. $R=\frac{u^{2} \sin 2\theta}{g}$ $R=\frac{2 u^{2} \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}$ $R=\frac{2(u \sin \theta)(u \cos \theta)}{g}$ [Using identity $\sin 2\theta=2 \sin \theta \cos \theta$ ] Substituting the values, we get $R=\frac{2 \times 36 \times 3}{10}$ = 21.6 m © examsnet.com

Since, the graph is completing one cycle in $8\ \mathrm{s}$ , hence time period, $T=8\ \mathrm{s}$ Using expression of change of momentum. $\Delta n=\int\limits_{n}^{8} F\,dt=\int\limits_{n}^{8} -2 \cos \omega t\,dt$ [from Eq. Solution: Given that, mass of body, $m=2\text{ kg}$ Two forces $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ each of magnitude $1\text{ N}$ are acting on the body by making an angle $\theta=60^{\circ}$ with each other, then magnitude of resultant force by addition of two vectors is Net force, $F=\sqrt{F_{1}^{2}+F_{2}^{2}+2 F_{1} F_{2} \cos 60^{\circ}}$ Substituting the values, we get $F=\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}+2(1)(1) \times \frac{1}{2}}$ $=\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$ By Newton's second law of motion, $F=m a$ ∴ Acceleration of body, $a=F m = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{m} / \text{s}^{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of shell $=m$ Mass of Lst part, $m_{1}=\frac{m}{6}$ Then, mass of 2nd part, $m_{2}=m-\frac{m}{6}=\frac{5m}{6}$ Velocity of lst part, $v_{1}=0$ Velocity of shell $=v$ Let velocity of $2\text{nd}$ part $=v_{2}$ By using law of conservation of linear momentum, Initial linear momentum = final linear momentum. $m v = m_{1} v_{1} + m_{2} v_{2}$ Substituting the values, we get $m v = \frac{m}{6} \times 0 + \frac{5m}{6} \times v_{2}$ $\Rightarrow v_{2} = \frac{6}{5} v$ Hence, the velocity of $2\text{nd}$ part is $\frac{6}{5} v$ in the same direction as that of shell. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of oxygen, $m_{0}=16\ \mathrm{amu}$ Mass of carbon, $m_{c}=12\ \mathrm{amu}$ Distance between them, $r=11\,\text{\AA}$ Let $x$ be the distance of centre of mass from carbon atom By using expression of centre of mass for two particle system, $X_{com}=\frac{m_{1} x_{t}+m_{2} x_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}$ Assuming centre of mass at orgin, we get $X_{COM}=0=\frac{m_{C}(-x)+m_{O}(r-x)}{m_{c}+m_{O}}$ $m_{c} x=m_{o}(r-x)$ $m_{c} x+m_{0} x=m_{0} r$ $x=\frac{m_{o}}{m_{c}+m_{o}} r$ By substituting the values, we get $x=\frac{16}{16+12} \times (1.1) \text{\AA} =0.63 \text{\AA}$ Hence, position of centre of mass is $0.63 \text{\AA}$ from carbon atom. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, mass of body, $m=4.9\ \mathrm{kg}$ Time period of oscillation of spring. $T=0.5\ \mathrm{s}$ Acceleration due to gravity, $g=10\ \mathrm{m/s}^2$ and $\pi^{2}=10$ We know that, time period of spring $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ By squaring on both sides, $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}\;\frac{m}{k}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{m}{k}=\frac{T^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}$ $=\frac{(0.5)^{2}}{4\times10}=\frac{0.25}{40}=000625$ After removal of mass, length of spring decrease is equal to extension produced in spring. By using equilibrium condition, $F=mg$ $\Rightarrow kx=mg$ $x=\frac{m}{k}g$ Substituting the values, we get $x=0.00625\times10$ $=0.0625\ \mathrm{m}$ $=6.25\ \mathrm{cm}$ Hence, the spring is shortened by $6.25\ \mathrm{cm}$ after removal of mass. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$ rd part of body is above the water surface. ∴ Volume of body outside the water $=\frac{1}{3}$ (volume of body) $V_{0}=\frac{1}{3} V$ ∴ Volume of body inside, $V_{i}=V-V_{0}=V-\frac{V}{3}=\frac{2V}{3}$ Let mass of body $=M$ Density of bod $y=\sigma$ Density of water, $\rho=10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ According to the law of floatation, body will float into the liquid (water) when weight of body is balanced by Buoyant force. $\therefore W=F_{0}$ $\Rightarrow Mg=V_{i} \rho g$ $V \sigma g=V_{i} \rho g$ $V \sigma=V_{i} \rho$ $\sigma = \frac{V \rho}{V}$ Subscituting the values, we get $\sigma = \frac{2V}{3V} \rho$ $=\frac{2}{3} \times 10^{3} = \frac{2000}{3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ Hence, density of liquid, $\sigma = \frac{2000}{3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We know that, at constant volume, Heat supplicd, $\Delta Q_{1}=\Delta U=C_{y} \Delta T$ At constant pressure, heat supplied, $\Delta Q=C \cdot \Delta T=\Delta U+\Delta W$ Ratio of heat capacity at constant pressure to constant volume is $\gamma=\frac{C_{r}}{C_{y}}$ Now, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U}=\frac{C_{p} \Delta T}{C_{V} \Delta T}=\frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}=\gamma$ $\text{Now}, \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta W}=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta Q-\Delta U}$ $=\frac{C_{p} \Delta T}{C_{p} \Delta T-C_{V} \Delta T}$ $=\frac{C_{r}}{C_{p}-C_{v}}=\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}\left(\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}}-1\right)}$ $=\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}$ For refrigerator, coefficient of performance, $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{W}=\frac{\text{Heat absorbed from food stuff}}{\text{Electrical work done}}$ ∴ $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ Coefficient of heat pump $=\frac{\text{Heat released}}{\text{Electrical work}}$ i.e. $\alpha=\frac{Q_{1}}{W}=\frac{Q_{4}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ We know that, $\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ So, we get, $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}=\frac{\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{4}}}{1-\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}}}$ $=\frac{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}{1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ and $\alpha=\frac{Q}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ $=\frac{\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}}{\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}-1}=\frac{\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}}{\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}-1}$ $=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ Hence, we get the best match as given by $A \rightarrow 4, B \rightarrow 3, C \rightarrow 2$ and $D \rightarrow 1$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given that, number of turns, $N=25$ Radius of coil, $r=1.8\,\mathrm{cm}=1.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$ Resistance of coil, $R=5\ \Omega$ Magnetic field, $B=(0.2\,t-0.05\,t^{2})\,\mathrm{T}$ Now, area of coil, $A=\pi r^{2}=3.14\times(1.8\times10^{-2})^{2}$ $=1.02\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$ Induced emf, $\varepsilon = \frac{-Nd}{d t}(BA) = -NA \frac{dB}{d t}$ $= -NA \frac{d}{d t}(0.2t-0.05t^{2})$ $\varepsilon = -NA(0.2-0.1t)$ Substituting the values, we get $\varepsilon = -25 \times 1.02 \times 10^{-3} (0.2-0.1t)$ $= -2.55 \times 10^{-2} (0.2-0.1t)$ Now, instantaneous power, $P = \frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{R} = \frac{[-2.55 \times 10^{-2} (0.2-0.1t)]^{2}}{5}$ At, $t=35$ , power dissipated is $P = \frac{(2.55 \times 10^{-2})^{2}(0.2-0.1 \times 3)^{2}}{5}$ $= 1.30 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{W} = 1.30 \mu \mathrm{W}$ It is close to option $(d)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $f(x)=\frac{\log (1+x)^{1+x}}{x^{2}}-\frac{1}{x}$ ⇒ $f(x)=\frac{(1+x) \log (1+x)}{x^{2}}-\frac{1}{x}$ $=\frac{(1+x) \log (1+x)-x}{x^{2}}$ $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$ ∴ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)=f(0)$ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{(1+x) \log (1+x)-x}{x^{2}}$ Apply L-Hospital's rule $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{(1+x)\left(\frac{1}{1+x}\right)+\log (1+x)-1}{2 x}$ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\log (1+x)}{2 x}=\frac{1}{2}$ ∴ $f(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ $6 f(0)=6 \times \frac{1}{2}=3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $x=y^{2}$ and $xy=a^{3}$ Solving, we get $x=a^{2}$ and $y=a$ $\text{Now}, y^{2}=x$ ⇒ $2y\frac{dy}{dx}=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2y}$ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(a^{2}, a)}=\frac{1}{2a}$ and $xy=a^{3}$ $x\frac{dy}{dx}+y=0$ ⇒ $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{y}{x}$ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(a^{2}, a)}=\frac{-a}{a^{2}}=\frac{-1}{a}$ Curves intersect orthogonally. ∴ $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{1}\times\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{2}=-1$ ⇒ $\left(\frac{1}{2a}\right)\left(\frac{-1}{a}\right)=-1$ ⇒ $a^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $\int \frac{5 \tan x}{\tan x-2} \, dx = x + a \log \left| \sin x - 2 \cos x \right| + K$ On differentiating, we get $\frac{5 \tan x}{\tan x-2} = 1 + \frac{a(\cos x + 2 \sin x)}{\sin x - 2 \cos x}$ ⇒ $\frac{5 \tan x}{\tan x-2} = 1 + \frac{a(l + 2 \tan x)}{\tan x-2}$ ⇒ $\frac{5 \tan x}{\tan x-2} = \frac{\tan x - 2 + a + 2a \tan x}{\tan x-2}$ ⇒ $5 \tan x = (2a+1) \tan x + a - 2$ Equating the coefficient of $\tan x$ and constant terms, we get $2a+1=5$ $a-2=0$ $\therefore a = 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $\int \frac{2x+3}{x(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)+1} \, dx = -\frac{1}{a x^{2}+b x+c} + \alpha$ LHS $= \int \frac{2x+3}{x(x+3)(x+1)(x+2)+1} \, dx$ $= \int \frac{(2x+3) \, dx}{(x^{2}+3x)(x^{2}+3x+2)+1}$ Put $x^{2}+3x = t$ $\Rightarrow (2x+3) \, dx = dt$ ∴ $\text{LHS} = \int \frac{dt}{t^{2}+2t+1}$ $= \int \frac{dt}{(t+1)^{2}} = -\frac{1}{t+1} + \alpha$ $= -\frac{1}{x^{2}+3x+1} + \alpha$ $a=1, b=3, c=1$ ∴ $a+b+c=1+3+1=5$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $\int \frac{2 \cos x+3 \sin x}{4 \cos x+5 \sin x} = \frac{23}{41} x + K \log \left|4 \cos x+5 \sin x\right| + C$ On differentiating, we get $\frac{2 \cos x+3 \sin x}{4 \cos x+5 \sin x} = \frac{23}{41} + \frac{K(-4 \sin x+5 \cos x)}{4 \cos x+5 \sin x}$ $2 \cos x+3 \sin x$ $= \frac{92 \cos x+115 \sin x-164 K \sin x+205 K \cos x}{41}$ $\Rightarrow 2 \cos x+3 \sin x = \left(\frac{92+205 K}{41}\right) \cos x + \left(\frac{115-164 K}{41}\right) \sin x$ Equating the coefficient of $\cos x$ and $\sin x$ , we get $\frac{92+205 K}{41}=2$ and $\frac{115-164 K}{41}=3$ ⇒ $92+205 K=82$ $K=\frac{-10}{205}=\frac{-2}{41}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Area of region enclosed by the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ and line $x=2$ and $x=3$ is $A=\int\limits_{2}^{3}\sqrt{16-x^{2}}\,dx$ $A=\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{16-x^{2}}+8\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{4}\right]_{2}^{3}$ $\Rightarrow 3\sqrt{7}-4\sqrt{3}-\frac{8\pi}{3}+k$ $=\left(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{7}+8\sin^{-1}\frac{3}{4}\right)-\left(2\sqrt{3}+8\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{4}\right)$ $\Rightarrow 3\sqrt{7}-4\sqrt{3}-\frac{8\pi}{3}+k$ $=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{7}+8\sin^{-1}\frac{3}{4}-2\sqrt{3}-\frac{8\pi}{6}$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left(3\sqrt{7}+16\sin^{-1}\frac{3}{4}-4\sqrt{3}-\frac{8\pi}{3}\right)$ ∴ $k=16\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, the coefficient of friction between A and $B, \mu_{1}=0.35$ The coefficient of friction between B and surface, $\mu_{2}=0.5$ Mass of block $A, m_{a}=100 \text{ kg}$ Mass of block $B, m_{b}=300 \text{ kg}$ Frictional force between blocks A and B, $f_{1}=\mu_{1} m_{2} g$ $=0.35 \times 100 \times 9.8$ $=0.35 \times 980$ = 343 N Frictional force between block B and surface, $f_{2}=\mu_{2}(m_{\alpha}+m_{b}) g$ $=0.5(100+300) 9.8$ $=0.5 \times 4 \times 980 = 1960 \text{ N}$ Minimum force required to move block B, $F=f_{1}+f_{2}=343+1960$ ⇒ = 2303 N Which is nearest to $2350 \text{ N}$ . Hence, option (c) is correct. © examsnet.com

Solution: The velocity acquired by a mass $m$ falling freely under the influence of gravity from the heigh $h$ is $v=\sqrt{2 g h}$ Momentum of first body, $p_{1}=m_{1} v_{1}$ ⇒ $=m_{1} \sqrt{2 g h_{1}}$ Momentum of second body $p_{2}=m_{2} v_{2}$ $\Rightarrow = m_{2} \sqrt{2 g h_{2}}$ The ratio of their linear momenta on touching the ground is $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}} = \frac{m_{1} \sqrt{2 g h_{1}}}{m_{2} \sqrt{2 g h_{2}}}$ $= \frac{2}{3} \times \sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$ or $1:2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of the body, $m=0.15\ \mathrm{kg}$ Velocity of the body, $v=15\ \mathrm{m}\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Spring constant, $k=1500\ \mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{m}^{-1}$ According to law of conservation of energy, the change in kinetic energy is equal to the change in potential energy, i.e. $\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} - 0 = 0 + \frac{1}{2} k x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2} = \frac{m}{k} v^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x = v \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 15 \times \sqrt{\frac{0.15}{1500}}$ = 0.15 m © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the mass of the body be $m$ and velocity of the body be $v$ , such that it has momentum $p$ and kinetic energy E. Momentum, $p=m v$ $\Rightarrow p^{2}=m^{2} v^{2}$ Kinetic energy, $E=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ $\Rightarrow E=\frac{p^{2}}{2 m}$ Hence, the nature of the graph between momentum of a body and its kinetic energy is parabola. i,e., $E \propto p^{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the mass of the particle be $m$ . If the particle slides from height $y$ under the action of gravity, the velocity acquired by the particle is given by, $v=\sqrt{2 g y}$ Hence, kinetic energy, $KE=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ $\Rightarrow KE=\frac{1}{2} m(\sqrt{2 g y})^{2}$ $= mgy$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of disc $=m$ Radius of disc $=a$ Angular speed $=\omega$ Moment of inertia of the disc, $I=\frac{1}{2} m a^{2}$ Initial angular momentum, $L_{i}=I \times \omega = \frac{1}{2} m a^{2} \omega$ Let $\omega'$ be the angular momentum of the disc when the particle of mass $m$ is attached at the rim. Final angular momentum, $L_{f}=I \omega' + m a v'$ $=\frac{1}{2} m a^{2} \omega' + m a^{2} \omega'$ $[\therefore v' = \omega' a]$ Applying conservation of angular momentum, $L_{i}=L_{f}$ $\frac{1}{2} m a^{2} \omega = \frac{1}{2} m a^{2} \omega' + m a^{2} \omega'$ $\Rightarrow \omega' = \frac{\omega}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let, M be the mass of the thin rod and L be the length of thin rod. Moment of inertia of thin rod about its centre of mass, $I_{\text{сom}}=\frac{1}{12} ML^{2}$ By parallel axis theorem, Moment of inertia about an axis = Moment of inertia about centre of mass $+$ Mass $\times 1$ distance from axis $)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow I=I_{com}+M(d)^{2}$ $=\frac{1}{12} ML^{2}+M\left(\frac{L}{4}\right)^{2}$ (Given, $d=\frac{L}{4})$ $=\left(\frac{4+3}{48}\right) ML^{2}=\frac{7}{48} ML^{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $F=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-\hat{k}, r=8\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\tau = v \times F = (8\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \times (3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-\hat{k})$ $\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 8 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}$ $=\hat{i}(-2+6)-\hat{j}(-8-9)+\hat{k}(-16-6)$ $=4\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-22\hat{k}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: (A) Time-period in spring-block system is given by, $T=2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ If mass is doubled, $T'=2\pi \sqrt{\frac{2m}{k}}$ ⇒ $T'=\sqrt{2} T$ Hence, time period becomes $\sqrt{2}$ times, if the mass of the block is doubled. $(A \rightarrow 4)$ (B) For spring, $PE=\frac{1}{2} k x^{2}$ If spring constant is increased 4 times, PE becomes 4 times. $(B \rightarrow 3)$ (C) Speed of the block, $v=\omega A$ Hence, velocity of the block becomes twice when amplitude of the oscillation is doubled. $(C \rightarrow 2)$ (D) Energy of the oscillation, $E=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} a^{2}$ $E'=\frac{1}{2} m \omega'^{2} a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow E'=\frac{1}{2} m (2\omega)^{2} a^{2}=\frac{4}{2} m \omega^{2} a^{2}$ $(\because)'=2\omega)$ ⇒ E' = 4E Energy of the oscillation becomes 4 times when angular frequency is doubled. $(D \rightarrow 1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of the particle, $m = 0.4\ \text{kg}$ Amplitude, $A = 0.4\ \text{m}$ Initial phase, $\phi = \frac{\pi}{4}$ Kinetic energy at mean position KE $= 256 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}$ As, $KE = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} A^{2}$ where, $\omega$ is angular frequency. $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} A^{2} = 256 \times 10^{-3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times \omega^{2} \times (0.4)^{2} = 256 \times 10^{-3}$ $\Rightarrow \omega^{2} = 8$ $\Rightarrow \omega = 2\sqrt{2}\ \text{rad}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ Equation of simple harmonic motion is given by $x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$ $= 0.4 \sin \left[ (2\sqrt{2}) t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: At surface, gravitational potential energy, $U_{1} = \frac{-GMm}{R}$ At height $nR, U_{2} = \frac{-G Mm}{R+nR}$ $\left|U_{2}-U_{1}\right|=\left|\left(\frac{-G Mm}{R+n R}\right)-\left(\frac{-G Mm}{R}\right)\right|$ $= \frac{GMm}{R} - \frac{GMm}{R+nR}$ $= \frac{GMm}{R} \left( i - \frac{1}{n+1} \right) = \left( \frac{n}{n+1} \right) \frac{GMm}{R}$ For height $x = \frac{R}{3}, n = \frac{1}{3}$ Work done $= \left|U_{2}-U_{1}\right| = \left( \frac{ \frac{1}{3} }{ \frac{1}{3} + 1 } \right) \frac{GMm}{R} = \frac{GMm}{4R}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, diameter of tap, $D=1.25 \text{cm}$ $=1.25 \times 10^{-2} \text{m}$ Density of water, $\rho = 10^{3} \text{kgm}^{-3}$ Coefficient of viscosity, $\eta = 10^{-3} \text{Pa-s}$ Volume of water flowing out per second $Q=3 \text{L/min}$ $=\frac{3 \times 10^{-3}}{60}=5 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$ As, $Q=vA=v \times \frac{\pi D^{2}}{4}$ ⇒ $v=\frac{4Q}{D^{2} \pi}$ Reynold's number is given by $R_{r}=\frac{\rho v D}{n}=\frac{4 \rho Q}{\pi D \eta}=\frac{4 \times 10^{3} \times 5 \times 10^{-5}}{314 \times 1.25 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{-3}}$ = 5095 For Reynold's number, the flow of liquid is turbulent if $R_{c}>3000$ . Hence, the nature of flow of water is turbulent. © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $a$ be area of hole, $v_{c}$ be the velocity of efflux, $h$ be the height of liquid above the hole. Let $v$ be the speed with which level decreases in the container. From equation of continuity, $a v_{e}=Av \Rightarrow v=\frac{a v_{e}}{A}$ Using Bernoulli's theorem, $p_{0}+h\rho g+\frac{1}{2}\rho v^{2}=p_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{e'}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow h\rho g+\frac{1}{2}\rho\left(\frac{a v_{c}}{A}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{e}^{2}$ or $v_{e}^{2}=\frac{2 g h}{1-\frac{a^{2}}{A^{2}}}=\frac{2 \times (3-0.525) \times 10}{1-(01)^{2}}$ ⇒ $v_{e}^{2}=50\ \text{m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The density of water is maximum at $4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . As the temperature increases or decreases, the density of water decreases, which increases its volume. Hence, water overflows either when heated about $4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or cooled below $4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $K_{A}$ and $K_{B}$ be the thermal conductivity of material A and B, respectively. Let $T_{1}$ be the temperature of A and $T_{2}$ be the temperature of B. At steady state, rate of flow of heat is given by, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta Q_{A}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta Q_{B}}{\Delta t}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{K' A(T_{2}-T_{1})}{l_{A}+l_{B}} = \frac{K_{A} A(T-T_{1})}{l_{A}}$ $= \frac{K_{B} A(T_{2}-T)}{l_{B}}$ ...(i) where K is thermal conductivity of both material and A and l are area and length of the material respectively. Using Eq. (i), we get $\frac{K_{A} A}{l_{A}} (T-T_{1}) = \frac{K_{B} A(T_{2}-T)}{l_{B}}$ ⇒ $2 K_{B} (T-T_{1}) = K_{B} (T_{2}-T)$ $(\because l_{A}=l_{B}$ and $K_{A}=2 K_{B})$ ⇒ $2 T - 2 T_{1} = T_{2} - T$ ⇒ $3 T = T_{2} + 2 T_{1}$ $\Rightarrow T = \frac{2T_{1}+T_{2}}{3}$ Again using Eq. (i). we get $\frac{K' A(T_{2}-T_{1})}{l_{A}+l_{A}} = \frac{K_{A} A(T-T_{1})}{l_{A}}$ ⇒ $\frac{K' (T_{2}-T_{1})}{2 J_{A}} = \frac{K_{A} \left( \frac{2 T_{1}+T_{2}}{3} - T_{1} \right)}{I_{A}}$ ⇒ $\frac{K' (T_{2}-T_{1})}{2} = \frac{K_{A} (T_{2}-T_{1})}{3}$ ⇒ $K' = \frac{2}{3} K_{A} = \frac{2}{3} \times 2 K_{2}$ ⇒ $K' = \frac{4}{3} K_{a}$ Using Eq. (i) to evaluate $(T_{2} - T)$ , $\frac{K' A(T_{2}-T_{1})}{l_{A}+l_{B}} = \frac{K_{B} A(T_{2}-T)}{l_{B}}$ ⇒ $\frac{K' A(T_{2}-T_{1})}{2 l_{A}} = \frac{K_{B} A(T_{2}-T)}{l_{A}}$ ⇒ $\left( \frac{4}{3} K_{B} \right) \frac{A(T_{2}-T_{1})}{2} = K_{B} A(T_{2}-T)$ ⇒ $\frac{2}{3} (T_{2}-T_{1}) = T_{2} - T$ ⇒ $T_{2} - T = \frac{2}{3} (T_{2} - T_{1}) = \frac{2}{3} \times 24^{\circ} = 16^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

(ii) by Eq. (i), we get $\frac{P'}{P} = \frac{\left(\frac{\mu_t}{\mu_m}-1\right)}{\left(\frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s}-1\right)} = \frac{\frac{1.5}{1.6}-1}{\frac{1.5}{1}-1}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{P'}{P} = \frac{-1}{16} \times \frac{2}{1}$ $\Rightarrow P' = \frac{-1}{8} \times (-5)$ ⇒ $P'=0.625\,\text{D}$ This is close to oprion (a)., © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, length of wire, $l=3\ \mathrm{m}$ Cross-sectional area, $A=6.14 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}^2$ Current in the wire, $I=6\ \mathrm{A}$ Atomic weight of silver $=108\ \mathrm{amu}$ Density of silver, $\rho=10500\ \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$ Number of electrons per $\mathrm{kg}$ of silver $=\frac{N_A}{108}$ $=\frac{6.023 \times 10^{23}}{108}$ Number of electrons per unit volume of silver. $n=\frac{6.023 \times 10^{23}}{108} \times 10500$ Drift current, $I=Anev_{d}$ where $v_{d}$ is drift velocity and $n$ is number of electrons per unit volume. ⇒ $v_{d}=\frac{I}{neA}$ $=\frac{6 \times 108}{6.023 \times 10^{23} \times 10500 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.14 \times 10^{-6}}$ $=0.1\ \mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, inner radius, $r_{1}=20\ \mathrm{cm}=0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ Outer radius, $r_{2}=25\ \mathrm{cm}=0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ Number of turns, $N=800$ Current in the toroid, $I=12\ \mathrm{A}$ Magnetic field due to N circular rings ( coroid), $B=\frac{\mu_{0} N I}{2 \pi r}$ Magnetic field is maximum at $r_{\min}=0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ $B_{\max}=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 800 \times 12}{2 \pi (0.2)}=9.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T}$ $=9.6\ \mathrm{mT}$ Magnetic field is minimum at $r_{\max}=0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ $B_{\min}=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-1} \times 800 \times 12}{2 \pi \times (0.25)}=7.68 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T}$ $=7.68\ \mathrm{mT}$ So, the maximum value of magnetic field within the toroid is $9.6\ \mathrm{mT}$ and minimum value of magnetic field within the toroid is $7.68\ \mathrm{mT}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Magnetic field due to first coil and second coil is same at centre. Then, magnetic field al centre is $B=\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2(2 r)}=\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2(r)}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{I_1}{I_2}=2$ ...(i) As we know that, resistance of the coil is related as $R=\frac{\rho l}{A}$ where, $\rho=$ resistivity $l=$ length $A=$ area of cross-section $\rho$ and A are same for both coils but $l_1=2 \pi(2 r)$ and $l_2=2 \pi(r)$ ⇒ $\frac{l_2}{l_1}=\frac{1}{2}$ ...(ii) If $V_1$ and $V_2$ are potential difference applied across first and second coil, then $I_1=\frac{V_1}{R_1}$ and $I_2=\frac{V_2}{R_2}$ $I_1=\frac{V_1}{\rho \frac{1}{A}}$ ...(iii) and $l_2=\frac{V_2}{\frac{\rho l_2}{A}}$ ...(iv) From Eqs. (i), (iii) and (iv), we get $\frac{V_1}{I_1}\times\frac{I_2}{V_2}=2$ ⇒ $\frac{V_1}{V_2}\times\frac{l_2}{l_1}=2$ ⇒ $\frac{V_1}{V_2}\times\frac{1}{2}=2$ [Form Eq. (ii)] ⇒ $\frac{V_1}{V_2}=4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: When a copper rod is moved in magnetic field, an emf is induced in such a way that current induced will try to oppose the motion of the rod. As we know, $e \propto \frac{d\phi}{dt}$ $\Rightarrow iR \propto \frac{d\phi}{dt}$ $(\because e=iR)$ ⇒ $\frac{dQ}{dt} \times R \propto \frac{d\phi}{dt}$ $\left(\because i = \frac{dQ}{dt}\right)$ ⇒ $\frac{dQ}{dt} \propto \frac{d\phi}{dt}$ Hence, charge developed across the ends of the rod will be proportional to rate of change of magnetic flux. © examsnet.com

(i), (ii) and (iii), we get $u_{E}=u_{B}$ Hence, energy contributions of both electric and magnetic fields are equal. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, wavelength of light, $\lambda = 4900\,\text{\AA}$ Stopping potential, $V = 2\ \mathrm{V}$ Energy of the incident light, $E=\frac{12400\ \mathrm{eV}}{\lambda\ \text{\AA}}$ ∴ $E=\frac{12400}{4900}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.53\ \mathrm{eV}$ Kinetic energy, KE $=$ Stopping potential $\times$ Charge of electron $=2 \times e = 2\ \mathrm{eV}$ Using Einstein's photoelectric equation, Kinetic energy = Energy of incident light $-$ Work function $2 = 2.53 - \phi$ ⇒ $\phi = 2.53 - 2 = 0.53\ \mathrm{eV}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, current gain, $\alpha=0.96$ Emitter current, $I_{E}=7.2\,\mathrm{mA}=7.2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$ We know that, $\alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E}$ ⇒ $I_{C}=\alpha\times I_{E}=0.96\times7.2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$ $=6.91\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$ $\text{Also},\ I_{E}=I_{C}+I_{B}$ ⇒ $I_{B}=I_{E}-I_{C}=(7.2-6.91)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$ $=0.29\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}=0.29\,\mathrm{mA}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Sequence of series in hydrogen spectrum are Lyman series $(n=1)$ , Balmer series $(n=2)$ , Paschen series $(n=3)$ , Bracket series $(n=4)$ and Pfund series $(n=5)$ . For Lyman series, $n_{1}=1$ For shortest wavelength in Lyman series i.e., the energy difference in two states showing transition should be maximum i.e., $n_{2}=\infty$ Using formula, $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R_{H}\left[\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right]$ here $R_{H}=\text{Rydberg constant}$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R_{H}\left[\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}}\right]$ ⇒ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R_{H}$ $\lambda=\frac{1}{R_{H}}=\frac{1}{109678}$ $=9.117 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{cm}=91.2\,\text{nm}$ Hence, Lyman series is a spectral series of transitions and resulting ultraviolet emission lines of $\mathrm{H}$ -atom. © examsnet.com

Solution: According to de-Broglie's wavelength, $\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$ Now, de-Broglic's wavelength of particle A is $\lambda_{A} = \frac{h}{m_{A} v_{A}}$ Similarly, de-Broglie's wavelength of particle B is $\lambda_{A} = \frac{h}{m_{B} v_{B}}$ ∴ Ratio of de-Broglic wavelength of A and B is $2: 1$ i.e., $\frac{\lambda_{A}}{\lambda_{B}} = \frac{h}{m_{A} V_{A}} \times \frac{m_{B} v_{B}}{h}$ $\frac{2}{1} = \frac{h}{m_{A} \times 0.05} \times \frac{m_{B} \times 0.02}{h}$ $\frac{2}{1} = \frac{m_{B} \times 0.02}{m_{A} \times 0.05}$ $\frac{2}{0.02} = \frac{m_{B}}{m_{A} \times 0.05}$ $\frac{1}{0.01} = \frac{m_{A}}{m_{B} \times 0.05}$ ⇒ $\frac{m_{A}}{m_{B}} = \frac{1}{5}$ Hence, the ratio of their masses $m_{A}: m_{B}$ is $1: 5$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The threshold energy for production of a particle is the minimum K.E., a pair of travelling particles must have when they collide. Absorbed energy $= KE +$ threshold energy $h v' = KE + h v_0'$ $h v_0' = h v' - KE$ $6.26 \times 10^{-34} \times v_0$ $= 6.26 \times 10^{-34} \times 4 \times 10^{14} - 6.63 \times 10^{-20} \, \mathrm{J}$ ∴ $v_0 = 2.999 \times 10^{13} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1} = 3 \times 10^{14} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Hence, threshold frequency $(v_0')$ of metal is $3 \times 10^{14} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $f(x)=\sqrt{\;\frac{x^2+2 x+8}{x^2+2 x+4}}$ Let $y=\;\frac{x^2+2 x+8}{x^2+2 x+4}$ $[ \because f(x)=\sqrt{y}]$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; y x^2+2 x y+4 y=x^2+2 x+8$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; (y-1) x^2+2 x(y-1)+4 y-8=0$ For $x$ to be real, discriminant of equation must be greater than equals to zero. $\;\{ [2(y-1)]^2-4(y-1)(4 y-8) \} \ge 0$ $\Rightarrow 4(y-1)^2-4(y-1) 4(y-2) \ge 0$ $\Rightarrow\;(y-1)^2-(y-1) 4(y-2) \ge 0$ $\Rightarrow\;(y-1)[y-1-4 y+8] \ge 0$ $\Rightarrow\;(y-1)(-3 y+7) \ge 0$ $\Rightarrow\;y\;=1,\;\frac{7}{3}$ $\therefore \;\; (y-1)(-3 y+7) \ge 0 \Rightarrow y \in (1,\;\frac{7}{3}]$ $[ \because .$ At $y=1, x^2+2 x+4 \neq x^2+2 x+8]$ $\; \because \;\; y \in (1,\;\frac{7}{3}]$ $\therefore\; f(x) \in (1, \sqrt{\;\frac{7}{3}}] .$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\cos^{4} \theta = a \cdot \cos 4\theta + b \cos 2\theta + c$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \cos^{4} \theta = a [2 \cos^{2} 2\theta - 1] + b [2 \cos^{2} \theta - 1] + c$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \cos^{4} \theta = a \cdot 2 \cos^{2} 2\theta - a + 2 b \cos^{2} \theta - b + c$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \cos^{4} \theta = 2 a (\cos 2\theta)^2 + 2 b \cos^{2} \theta - a - b + c$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \cos^{4} \theta = 2 a (2 \cos^{2} \theta - 1)^2 + 2 b \cos^{2} \theta - a - b + c$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \cos^{4} \theta = 2 a (4 \cos^{4} \theta + 1 - 4 \cos^{2} \theta) + 2 b \cos^{2} \theta - a - b + c$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{4} \theta = 8 a \cos^{4} \theta \; + 2 a - 8 a \cos^{2} \theta \; + 2 b \cos^{2} \theta - a - b + c$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{4} \theta = 8 a \cos^{4} \theta + \cos^{2} \theta (-8 a + 2 b) + a - b + c$ On comparing the corresponding coefficients, we get $8 a = 1, -8 a + 2 b = 0$ and $a - b + c = 0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; a = \frac{1}{8}$ $\therefore \; -8 \left(\frac{1}{8}\right) + 2 b = 0$ gives $b = \frac{1}{2}$ $\; \text{ and } \;\; \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{2} + c = 0$ gives $c = \frac{3}{8}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\frac{x^4+24 x^2+28}{(x^2+1)^3} = \frac{A x+B}{x^2+1} + \frac{C x+D}{(x^2+1)^2} + \frac{E x+F}{(x^2+1)^3}$ Let $x^2+1=k$ Substituting $x^2=k-1$ in LHS, we get $\frac{(k-1)^2+24(k-1)+28}{k^3} = \frac{k^2+22k+5}{k^3}$ $= \frac{1}{k} + \frac{22}{k^2} + \frac{5}{k^3}$ $= \frac{1}{x^2+1} + \frac{22}{(x^2+1)^2} + \frac{5}{(x^2+1)^3}$ On comparing with RHS, we get $A x+B=1, C x+D=22$ and $E x+F=5$ At $x=1,$ $A+B=1, C+D=22$ and $E+F=5$ $herefore A+B+C+D+E+F=1+22+5=28$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, height, $h = 1 \text{ m}$ mass, $m = 1 \text{ kg}$ spring constant, $k = 15 \text{ Nm}^{-1}$ The kinetic energy of mass after falling on the platform will be converted into potential energy of the spring. Thus, $m g (h+x) = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$ $1 \times 10(1+x) = \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times x^2$ $\Rightarrow 10 \times \frac{2}{15} (1+x) = x^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} (1+x) = x^2$ $\Rightarrow 4+4x = 3x^2$ $\Rightarrow 3x^2 - 4x - 4 = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3x^2 - 6x + 2x - 4 = 0$ $\Rightarrow 3x(x-2) + 2(x-2) = 0$ $\Rightarrow (x-2) = 0$ or $\; \;(3x+2) = 0$ $\; x = 2 \text{ m}$ or $x = \frac{-2}{3} \text{ m}$ Since, $x$ is the compression, which cannot be negative, thus $x = 2 \text{ m}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: According to question, a disc of $r = \;\frac{R}{3}$ is removed from the bigger disc of radius $R$ . The mass of reduced disc is $\;\frac{M}{9}$ because mass is directly proportional to the area for uniform disc. Moment of inertia of total disc, $I_{\;\text{total }\;} = \;\frac{M R^2}{2}$ Moment of inertia of removed disc $I_{\;\text{removed }\;} = I_{CM} + \;\frac{M}{9} \times \left(\;\frac{R}{3}\right)^2$ $I_{\;\text{removed}\;} = \;\frac{M}{9} \cdot \frac{\left(\frac{R}{3}\right)^2}{2} + \;\frac{M R^2}{81}$ $= \;\frac{M R^2}{81} \left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) = \;\frac{M R^2}{81} \times \frac{3}{2} = \;\frac{M R^2}{54}$ The moment of inertia of remaining disc $=$ $\;I_{\;\text{total}\;} - I_{\;\text{removed}\;}$ $\;=\;\frac{M R^2}{2} - \;\frac{M R^2}{54} = \;\frac{M R^2(27-1)}{54}$ $\;=\;\frac{26}{54} M R^2 = \;\frac{13}{27} M R^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let initially the cone be in equilibrium i.e. floating From the diagram, it is clear that Buoyant force $(F_b) =$ weight of the cone. $(F_w)$ $\rho_w \times \left(\frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 x\right) \times g = \rho_c \times \left(\frac{1}{3} \pi R^2 H\right) \times g$ $\Rightarrow 2 r^2 x = R^2 H$ $\left(\because \rho_c = \frac{\rho_w}{2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow x = \frac{R^2 H}{2 r^2}$ ........(i) From the diagram, $\tan \theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{R}{H}$ $\Rightarrow x = \frac{r H}{R}$ .....(ii) From Eqs. In simple harmonic motion, the buoyancy force acts as restoring force which is given as $F_b = \text{density} \times \text{volume} \times \text{gravity}$ Since, the displacement is very small, the excess submerged shape of cone. can be considered as a cylinder whose volume is given by $\pi r^2 \delta$ . $\therefore F_b = \rho_w \pi r^2 \delta g = \rho_w \pi \left[ \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1/3} R \right]^2 \delta g$ Thus, force is equal to restoring force, hence $F_b = k \delta = m \omega^2 \delta$ $\rho_w \pi \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3} R^2 \delta g = \rho_c \frac{1}{3} \pi R^2 H \delta \omega^2$ $2 \times 3 \times \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3} \delta g = H \delta \omega^2 \quad \left(\because \rho_c = \frac{\rho_w}{2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{6 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3} g}{H} = \omega^2$ or $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{6 g}{H} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3}} \Rightarrow 2 \pi f = \sqrt{\frac{6 g}{H} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3}}$ $\Rightarrow f = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{6 g}{H} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/3}} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{6 g}{H} \cdot \frac{1}{4^{1/3}}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, current density, $J=\beta (r+r_0)^2=\beta (r^2+2 r r_0+r_0^2)$ We know that, current density, $J=\frac{\text{Current }(I)}{\text{Area}(A)}$ $\Rightarrow$ Current, $I=J \cdot A$ or $dI=J \cdot dA$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\int dI=\int J \cdot dA$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;I=\int \beta (r^2+2 \pi r_0+r_0^2) \cdot dA$ Where, $dA$ is area element in cartesian coordinate. In polar coordinates $dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$ $\therefore\;\;I=2\beta \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/6} d\theta \int\limits_{0}^{R} (r^2+2 r_0+r_0^2) r dr$ ( $\because$ for $\theta, 0$ to $\pi/6$ and $5\pi/6$ to $\pi$ is symmetric) $\;=2\beta[\theta]_0^{\pi/6}\left[\int\limits_{0}^{R} r^3 dr+2 r_0 \int\limits_{0}^{R} r^2 dr+r_0^2 \int\limits_{0}^{R} r dr\right]$ $\;2\beta\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\left[\left(\frac{r^4}{4}\right)_0^R+2 r_0\left(\frac{r^3}{3}\right)_0^R+r_0^2\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\right)_0^R\right]$ $\;=\beta\frac{\pi}{3}\left[\frac{R^4}{4}+2 r_0\frac{R^3}{3}+\frac{r_0^2 R^2}{2}\right]$ $\;=\pi\beta\left[\frac{R^4}{12}+\frac{2 r_0 R^3}{9}+\frac{r_0^2 R^2}{6}\right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: When compass needle oscillates 20 times per minute, then its time period, $T_1 = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{\frac{20}{60}} = 3\ \text{s}$ Angle of dip, $\delta_1 = 45^{\circ}$ When the same oscillates 30 times per min then, its time period. $T_2 = \frac{1}{f_2} = \frac{1}{\frac{30}{60}} = 2\ \text{s}$ and angle of dip, $\delta_2 = 30^{\circ}$ we know that, time period of compass needle $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{I}{M B_H}}$ where, $I=$ moment of inertia $B_H=$ horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field. $\Rightarrow T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{B_H}}$ $\Rightarrow T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{B \cos \delta}} \Rightarrow \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\frac{B_1 \cos \delta_1}{B_2 \cos \delta_2}}$ $= \sqrt{\frac{B_1 \cos 45^{\circ}}{B_2 \cos 30^{\circ}}} = \sqrt{\frac{B_1}{B_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{B_1}{B_2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{T_2^2}{T_1^2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \cdot \frac{B_1}{B_2} \Rightarrow \frac{2^2}{3^2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \frac{B_1}{B_2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{9} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \frac{B_1}{B_2} \Rightarrow \frac{B_1}{B_2} = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{9}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{B_1}{B_2} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow B_1 : B_2 = 2\sqrt{2} : 3\sqrt{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $\Delta x=$ uncertainty in position $\Delta v=$ uncertainty in velocity we know, $\Delta p=m \Delta v$ , where $\Delta p$ is the uncertainty in momentum and $m$ is the mass of particle. Using Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, $\Delta x \cdot m \Delta v = \frac{h}{4 \pi}$ As $\Delta x = \Delta v,$ So, $\Delta v \cdot m \Delta v = \frac{h}{4 \pi}$ On multiplying both sides with $m$ , we get $m \Delta v \cdot m \Delta v = \frac{m h}{4 \pi}$ Thus, $\;\;  \Delta p^2 = \frac{m h}{4 \pi} \Rightarrow \Delta p = \sqrt{\frac{m h}{4 \pi}}$ . Solution: 👈: Video Solution Bond length $\propto \; \frac{1}{\;\text{ Bond order }\;(BO)}$ Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{C}_2$ i.e. $X_1$ is $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma l s^{*2} \sigma 2s^2 \sigma 2s^{*2} \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2$ So, bond order Number of bonding orbital electrons - $= \frac{\text{ Number of antibonding orbital electrons }}{2}$ $= \frac{8-4}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = 2$ Electronic configuration of i.e. $\mathrm{N}_2$ i.c. $X_2$ is $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma 1s^{*2} \sigma 2s^2 \sigma 2s^{+2} \;\; \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2$ Bond order $= \frac{10-4}{2} = \frac{6}{2} = 3$ Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{B}_2$ i.e. $X_3$ is $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma l s^{*2} \sigma 2s^2 \sigma 2s^{*2} \pi 2p_x^1 .2 \pi 2p_y^1$ Bond order $= \frac{6-4}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1$ So, order of bond order $(BO)$ is $BO_2 > BO_1 > BO_3$ Now, since bond order and bond lengths are inversely proportional. Hence, order of bond length is $X_3 > X_1 > X_2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Multiplicative inverse of complex number $\;(\sin \theta, \cos \theta)\; \text{ is }\;$ $z\;= \sin \theta + i \cos \theta$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{z} \; = \; \frac{\sin \theta - i \cos \theta}{(\sin \theta + i \cos \theta)(\sin \theta - i \cos \theta)}$ $\; = \frac{\sin \theta - i \cos \theta}{\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta} = (\sin \theta - i \cos \theta)$ Thus, multiplicative inverse of $(\sin \theta, \cos \theta)$ is $(\sin \theta, -\cos \theta)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\;\text{(a)}\;\sin 5\theta=\;\sin (3\theta+2\theta)$ $=\;\sin 3\theta \cos 2\theta+\cos 3\theta \cdot \sin 2\theta$ $=\;(3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta)\cdot(1-2\sin^2\theta)+(4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta)\cdot(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)$ $=\;3\sin\theta-6\sin^3\theta-4\sin^3\theta+8\sin^5\theta+8\sin\theta\cos^4\theta-6\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$ $=3\sin\theta-10\sin^3\theta+8\sin^5\theta+8\sin\theta\cos^4\theta-6\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$ $=3\sin\theta-10\sin^3\theta+8\sin^5\theta+8\sin\theta(1-\sin^2\theta)^2-6\sin\theta(1-\sin^2\theta)$ $=3\sin\theta-10\sin^3\theta+8\sin^5\theta+8\sin\theta(1+\sin^4\theta-2\sin^2\theta)-6\sin\theta+6\sin^3\theta$ $=-3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta+8\sin^5\theta+8\sin\theta+8\sin^5\theta-16\sin^3\theta$ $\;=5\sin\theta-20\sin^3\theta+16\sin^5\theta$ $\;=5\sin\theta-20\sin\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)+16(1-\cos^2\theta)^2\sin\theta$ $\;=5\sin\theta-20\sin\theta+20\sin\theta\cos^2\theta+16\sin\theta\;(1+\cos^4\theta-2\cos^2\theta)$ $\;=-15\sin\theta+20\sin\theta\cos^2\theta+16\sin\theta+16\cos^4\theta\sin\theta-32\cos^2\theta\sin\theta$ $\;=16\cos^4\theta\sin\theta-12\cos^2\theta\sin\theta+\sin\theta$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $e^{i \theta} = \operatorname{cis} \theta = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta$ $\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos(n\theta)}{2^{n}}$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos n\theta}{2^{n}} \right]$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \left( \frac{\cos \theta}{2} \right)^n \right] \text{ [Using De-moivre theorem] }$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \left( \frac{e^{i \theta}}{2} \right)^n \right]$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ 1 + \frac{e^{i \theta}}{2} + \left( \frac{e^{i \theta}}{2} \right)^2 + \dots \infty \right]$ $1 + \frac{e^{i \theta}}{2} + \left( \frac{e^{i \theta}}{2} \right)^2 + \dots$ is an GP $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \frac{1}{1 - \frac{e^{i0}}{2}} \right] = \operatorname{Re} \left[ \frac{2}{2 - e^{i \theta}} \right]$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \frac{2}{2 - \cos \theta - i \sin \theta} \right]$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \frac{2(2 - \cos \theta - i \sin \theta)}{(2 - \cos \theta)^2 - i^2 \sin^2 \theta} \right]$ $= \operatorname{Re} \left[ \frac{4 - 2 \cos \theta}{4 + \cos^2 \theta - 4 \cos \theta + \sin^2 \theta} \right.$ $= \frac{i \sin \theta}{4 + \cos^2 \theta - 4 \cos \theta + \sin^2 \theta}$ $= \frac{4 - 2 \cos \theta}{5 - 4 \cos \theta}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ be roots of the equation $x^{2}+a x+b=0$ Therefore, $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=-a$ and $\alpha_1 \alpha_2 = b$ and $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ be the roots of the equation $x^{2}+b x+a=0$ Therefore, $\beta_1+\beta_2=-b$ and $\beta_1, \beta_2 = a$ Given that $\alpha_1-\alpha_2=\beta_1-\beta_2$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha_1+\alpha_2)^2-4\alpha_1\alpha_2 = (\beta_1+\beta_2)^2-4\beta_1\beta_2$ $\Rightarrow (-a)^2-4b = b^2-4a$ $\Rightarrow a^2-b^2+4a-4b=0$ $\Rightarrow (a-b)(a+b)+4(a-b)=0$ $\Rightarrow (a-b)(a+b+4)=0$ Therefore, $a-b=0$ and $a+b+4=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $(x+a)(x+1991)+1$ $\; \therefore (x+a)(x+1991)-1=0$ $\; \Rightarrow (x+a)(x+1991)=-1$ Multiplication of two integers is $-1$ , this implies that either $(x+a)$ is $+1$ and $(x+1991)$ is $-1$ or $(x+a)$ is $-1$ and $(x+1991)$ is $+1$ . Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\;\;\text{(b)}\; \int\; \frac{e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}} (\dot{x}+\sqrt{x}) \, dx$ $\;=\int (\sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} + e^{\sqrt{x}}) \, dx = \int \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} \, dx + \int e^{\sqrt{x}} \, dx$ Now, $\int \sqrt{x} \cdot e^{\sqrt{x}} \, dx$ Let $x=p^2$ $\Rightarrow dx = 2 p \, dp$ $\;= \int \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} \, dx = \int p e^p (2 p \, dp) = 2 \int p^2 e^p \cdot dp$ $\;=2 \left[ p^2 e^p - 2 \int p e^p \, dp \right]$ $\;=2 \left[ p^2 e^p - 2 \{ p e^p - e^p \} \right] + K$ $\;=2 \left[ p^2 p^p - 2 p e^p + 2 e^p \right] + K$ $\;=2 \left[ x e^{\sqrt{x}} - 2 \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} + 2 e^{\sqrt{x}} \right] + K$ $\; \int e^{\sqrt{x}} \, dx = 2 \int p e^p \, dp = 2 \left[ p e^p - e^p \right] = 2 \left[ \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} - e^{\sqrt{x}} \right]$ $\; \therefore \int\; \frac{e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}} (x+\sqrt{x}) \, dx$ $\;=2 x e^{\sqrt{x}} - 4 \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} + 4 e^{\sqrt{x}} + 2 \sqrt{x} e^{\sqrt{x}} - 2 e^{\sqrt{x}} + K$ $\;=e^{\sqrt{x}} (2 x - 2 \sqrt{x} + 2) + K$ $\; \therefore A=2, B=-2, C=2$ $\; \therefore A+B+C=2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $I_n=\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^n x dx$ $I_{n+2}=\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^{n+2} x dx$ $\;\; \text{ Now, } \; I_n+I_{n+2}=\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^n x dx+\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^n x \tan^2 x dx$ $\;\; \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^n x (1+\tan^2 x) dx=\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan^n x \sec^2 x dx$ Put $\tan x = t \Rightarrow \sec^2 x dx = dt$ $\therefore I_n+I_{n+2}=\int\limits_{0}^{1} t^n dt=\frac{1}{n+1}$ $\;\; \text{ Now, } \;\; \frac{1}{I_2+I_4}+\frac{1}{I_3+I_5}+\frac{1}{I_4+I_6}$ $\;=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{3}}+\frac{1}{\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{1}{\frac{1}{5}}$ $\;=3+4+5=12=\frac{1}{I_{11}+I_{13}}$ $\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Initial temperature of the sink, $T_2=250 \text{ K}$ Initial efficiency of carnot engine, $\eta_1=25\%=0.25$ If $T_1$ be the temperature of the sink, then $\; \eta_1 = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ $\;0.25 = 1 - \frac{250}{T_1} \Rightarrow \frac{250}{T_1} = 0.75$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; T_1 = \frac{1000}{3} \text{ K}$ When efficiency is increased by $50\%$ i.e $\; \; \eta_2 = 50\% = 0.5$ Then if $T_2'$ be temperature of sink, then $\eta_2 = 1 - \frac{T_2'}{T_1}$ $\Rightarrow 0.5 = 1 - \frac{T_2'}{\frac{1000}{3}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{T_2'}{\frac{1000}{3}} = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5 = \frac{1}{2} .$ $\Rightarrow T_2' = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1000}{3} = \frac{500}{3} \text{ K}$ Here we see that to increase the efficiency of carnot engine temperature of the sink should be decreased, but in question, asked about increasing temperature of sink to increase efficiency, which is not possible. Solution: We know that, Modulation index, $\mu = \; \frac{A_m}{\dot{A}_c} \dots (i)$ Where, $A_m=$ amplitude of message signal $A_c=$ amplitude of carrier signal When $A_m$ is increased by $1\%$ then, new, $A_m' = A_m + \frac{A_m}{100} = \frac{101 A_m}{100}$ Similarly, $A_c$ is increased by $3\%$ . $\because$ New value of amplitude of carrier wave, $A_c' = A_c + 3\% \; \text{ of }\; A_c$ $= A_c + \frac{3 A_c}{100}$ $= \frac{103 A_c}{100}$ New modulation index; $\mu' = \frac{A_m'}{A_c'} = \frac{ \frac{101 A_m}{100} }{ \frac{103 A_c}{100} }$ $= \frac{101}{103} \cdot \frac{A_m}{A_c}$ $= \frac{101}{103} \mu$ [From Eq. (i)] $\%$ change in modulation index $= \frac{\mu' - \mu}{\mu} \times 100$ $= \frac{ \frac{101}{103} \mu - \mu }{ \mu } \times 100$ $= -2\%$ © examsnet.com

Solution: (b) Formal charge ( $\text{FC})$ can be calculated by using formula : $\text{FC} =$ (number of electrons in neutral atom) $-\frac{1}{2}$ (number of electrons in covalent bonds) - (number of electrons in lone pairs) Formal charge on lst atom i.e., oxygen is $\text{FC} = 6 - \frac{1}{2} \times 4 - 4 = 6 - 2 - 4 = 0$ Formal charge on 2nd atom i.e., nitrogen is $\text{FC} = 5 - \frac{1}{2} \times 8 - 0 = 5 - 4 = +1$ Formal charge on 3rd atom i.e., oxygen is $\text{FC} = 6 - \frac{1}{2} \times 4 - 4 = 6 - 2 - 4 = 0$ Hence, formal charge of atoms 1,2 and 3 in the ion $\left[ \mathrm{O}_1 = \mathrm{N}_2 = \mathrm{O}_3^{+} \right].$ is $0,+1$ and 0 respectively. © examsnet.com

Solution: (a) $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{NO}_3^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+} + \mathrm{NH}_3$ The complete balanced equation of the given . reaction is $4\,\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{NO}_3^{-} + 9\,\mathrm{H}^{\oplus} \rightarrow 4\,\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} + \mathrm{NH}_3 + 3\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ Given, conc. of $\mathrm{NO}_3^{-} = 0.1\,\text{M}$ Volume of $\mathrm{NO}_3^{-} = 100\,\text{mL}$ We know that, Molarity $= \frac{\text{Number of moles}}{\text{Volume of solution (in L)}}$ $\text{Hence, number of moles} = \text{molarity} \times \text{volume of solution (in L)}$ $\text{So, number of moles} = 0.1 \times 100 \times 10^{-3} = 10\,\text{mmol} = 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}$ From above Eq., 1 mole $\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}$ reacts with 4 moles $\mathrm{Mg}$ . So, $\mathrm{IO}^{-2}$ mole $\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}$ reacts with $4 \times 10^{-2}$ moles $\mathrm{Mg}$ . Now, to calculate the mass of $\mathrm{Mg}$ required, use the formula, Number of moles $= \frac{\text{Given mass}}{\text{Molar mass}}$ Molar mass of $\mathrm{Mg} = 24\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}$ On substituting the value, $4 \times 10^{-2} = \frac{\text{Mass of } \mathrm{Mg}}{24}$ We will get, $\text{Mass of } \mathrm{Mg} = 24 \times 4 \times 10^{-2}$ $\text{Mass of } \mathrm{Mg} = 0.96\,\text{g}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: A. Frenkel defects is a defect in which an atom/ion occupies a normally vacant site other. than its own. Size of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ is equal to size of $\mathrm{Cl}^{\ominus}$ so, it shows Schottky defect. C. Vacancy defects is a defect in which crystals have vacant sites. D. Metal deficiency defects, in this solids have less number of metals, FeO shows metal deficiency defect due to variable oxidation state of $\mathrm{Fe}$ . Hence, the correct match is List I (Defects) List II (Examples) A. Frenkel defects (III) $\mathrm{AgCl}$ B. Solution: (c) Given, current, $I=38.6\,\mathrm{A}$ , Time, $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ Cathode $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+2e^{\ominus}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cu}(s)$ Anode $2\overline{O}H(aq)\rightarrow\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(l)+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2(g)+2e^{\ominus}$ Using Faraday's Ist law, $W\;=Z I t,\;\; (Z \rightarrow\; \text{ electrochemical equival\'{e}nt }\;)$ $\;=\;\frac{E I t}{96500}=\;\frac{M I t}{2 \times 96500}$ $\;=\;\frac{63.5 \times 38.6 \times 100}{2 \times 96500}=1.27\,\mathrm{g}$ $1.27\,\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{Cu}$ is deposited. Then, $x_1+\dot{x}_2+x_3+x_4$ $=3n(0\leq x_1, x_2, x_3, \leq n \; \text{ and } \; 0\leq x_4\leq 2n)$ Using multinomial theorem, Number of ways $=$ Coefficient of $x^{3n}$ in $\; \underbrace{(1+x+...+x^n)^3}_{\text{GP series}} (1+x+...+x^{2n}) \swarrow \underbrace{}_{\text{GP series}}$ $\Rightarrow \left(\frac{1-x^{n+1}}{1-x}\right)^3 \left(\frac{1-x^{2n+1}}{1-x}\right)$ $\Rightarrow (1-x^{3(n+1)}-3x^{n+1}(1-x^{n+1})(1-x^{2n+1})(1-x)^{-4}.$ $\Rightarrow (1-x^{3(n+1)}-3x^{n+1}+3x^{2n+2})(1-x^{2n+1})(1-x)^{-4}$ $\Rightarrow (1-x^{3(n+1)}-3x^{n+1}+3x^{2n+2}-x^{2n+1}+x^{5n+4}+3x^{3n+2}-3x^{4n+3}(1-x)^{-4})$ Finding the coefficient of $x^{3n}$ using binomial expansion, we get ${}^{3n+3}C_3 - 3^{2n+2}C_3 + 3^{n+2}C_3 - {}^{n+3}C_3$ $=\frac{1}{6}(n+1)(5n^2+10n+6)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $(x, y)$ be on the parabola $y=x^2+4x+3$ which is closet to the line $y=3x+2$ Perpendicular distance between a point $(x_1, y_1)$ and a line $(a x+b y+c=0)$ $D = \left| \frac{a x_1+b y_1+c}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} \right|$ $[ \therefore .$ line $3x-y+2=0$ at point $(x_1, y_1) ]$ $D = \left| \frac{3x-y+2}{\sqrt{(3)^2+(-1)^2}} \right| = \frac{\left| 3x - (x^2+4x+3) +2 \right|}{\sqrt{9+1}}$ $\Rightarrow D = \frac{\left| -x^2 - x -1 \right|}{\sqrt{10}}$ $\Rightarrow D = \frac{x^2+x+1}{\sqrt{10}} = \frac{\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{4}}{\sqrt{10}}$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , $\frac{dD}{dx} = \frac{\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}{\sqrt{10}} + \frac{\frac{3}{4}}{\sqrt{10}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dD}{dx}=0, x=\frac{-1}{2} \Rightarrow y=x^2+4x+3$ $\Rightarrow y = \left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)^2 + (4)\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right) + 3 \Rightarrow y = \frac{1}{4} + 3 - 2 = 0$ $\Rightarrow y = \frac{1+12-8}{4} \Rightarrow y = \frac{5}{4}$ $\frac{dD}{dx} = \frac{2\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{10}} \Rightarrow \frac{d^2D}{dx^2}>0$ Hence, minimum at $\left(\frac{-1}{2}, \frac{5}{4}\right)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\int\;\frac{3x+4}{x^3-2x+4}\,dx=\log f(x)+C$ $I=\int\;\frac{3x+4}{x^3-2x+4}$ Since, $x^3-2x-4=(x-2)(x^2+2x+2)$ $\;\frac{3x+4}{x^3-2x+4}=\;\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+2x+2}$ $\Rightarrow 3x+4=A(x^2+2x+2)+(Bx+C)(x-2)$ On putting $x=2,\;A=1$ and comparing coefficients of $x^2$ , we get $0=A+B \Rightarrow B=-1$ On putting $x=0$ , we have $2A-2C$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;C=-1$ $\;\int\;\frac{3x+4}{x^3-2x+4}\,dx=\int\;\frac{dx}{x-2}-\int\;\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+2}\,dx$ $\;=\log|x-2|-\;\frac{1}{2}\log|x^2+2x+2|+C$ $\;=\log f(x)+C=\log\;\frac{|x-2|}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}+C$ So, $f(x)\;=\;\frac{|x-2|}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}$ $f(3)\;=\;\frac{|3-2|}{\sqrt{(3)^2+2(3)+2}}$ $f(3)\;=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{9+6+2}}=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Here, $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left[\begin{array}{l l}\frac{n}{(n+1)\sqrt{2n+1}}+ & \frac{n}{(n+2)\sqrt{2(n+2)}} \\ +\cdots \text{ upto } n \text{ terms} & \end{array}\right]$ $=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\frac{n^{2}}{(n+k)\sqrt{k(2n+k)}}$ $=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\frac{n^{2}}{(n+k)\sqrt{k(2n+k)}}\times\frac{n^{2}}{n^{2}}$ $=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left(\frac{n+k}{n}\right)\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}\left(\frac{2n+k}{n}\right)}}$ $=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{k}{n}\right)\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}\left(2+\frac{k}{n}\right)}}$ $=\int\limits_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+x)\sqrt{x(2-x)}}\,dx=\int\limits_{0}^{1}f(x)\,dx$ $f(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x)\sqrt{2x+x^{2}}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Here, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos^2(3x+y)$ On putting $3x+y=t$ $3+\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}-3 \Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dx}-3=\cos^2 t$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dx}=\cos^2 t+3 \Rightarrow \frac{dt}{\cos^2 t+3}=dx$ Integrate both side, $\int\limits \frac{dt}{\cos^2 t+3}=\int dx$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{\sec^2 t \, dt}{1+3\sec^2 t}=\int dx \Rightarrow \int \frac{\sec^2 t}{4+3\tan^2 t}=\int dx$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{\sec^2 t \, dt}{4+3\tan^2 t}=\int dx$ On putting $\tan t=m$ , $\sec^2 t \, dx = dm = \frac{1}{4} \int \frac{dm}{1+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}m\right)^2} x+C$ $= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}m\right)=x+C$ $= \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\tan t\right]=x+C \quad [\because m=\tan t]$ $= \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\tan(3x+y)\right]=2\sqrt{3}(x+C) \quad [\therefore t=3x+y]$ So, $f(x)=2\sqrt{3}(x+C)$ © examsnet.com
