Solution: Let $v$ be the minimum velocity of student so, that he could catch the bus If student catch the bus in time $t$ , then distance travelled by student in time $t$ $=16+$ distance travelled by bus in time $t$ . $\; \Rightarrow v t = 16 + \left(u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2\right)$ $\; \Rightarrow v t = 16 + 0 \times t + \frac{1}{2} \times 9 \times t^2$ $\; \Rightarrow v t = 16 + \frac{9}{2} t^2 \Rightarrow 9 t^2 - 2 v t + 32 = 0$ The above equation must have real roots. i.e its discriminant $\geq 0$ i.e $(2v)^2 - 4 \times 9 \times 32 \geq 0$ $\Rightarrow 4 v^2 - 4 \times 288 \geq 0 \Rightarrow v^2 - 288 \geq 0$ $\Rightarrow v^2 \geq 288$ . $v \geq 12\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ Minimum velocity of student to catch the bus $\; = 12\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m/s} = \alpha\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m/s}\; \text{ (given) }\;$ $\; \therefore \alpha = 12$ $\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to law of conservation of energy at point $B$ shown in the figure given in question part, Loss in $\text{PE}=$ Gain in $\text{KE}$ $\;\Rightarrow m g(H-h)=\;\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; v=\sqrt{2 g(H-h)}$ Now, $h=\frac{1}{2} g t^2 \Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\frac{\dot{2h}}{g}}$ $\therefore$ Distance covered in horizontal portion, $s\;=v \times t$ $\;=\sqrt{2 g(H-h)} \times \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ $\Rightarrow\;\; s\;=\sqrt{4 h(H-h)}$ ......(i) For maximum value of $s$ $\;\frac{ds}{dh}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2\sqrt{4 h(H-h)}} \times 4[(H-h)\cdot 1+h(-1)]=0$ $\Rightarrow 2(H-2h)=0 \Rightarrow H=2h$ $\Rightarrow h=\frac{H}{2}$ Substituting the value of $h$ in Eq. Solution: For ball $A$ , $m_A=1\ \mathrm{kg},\ v_A=4\ \mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ for ball $B,\ m_B=3\ \mathrm{kg},\ v_B=0$ $\therefore$ Total momentum before collision, $p_i\;=m_A v_A+m_B v_B$ $\;=1 \times 4+3 \times 0=4\ \mathrm{kg}-\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ Since, after collision, both body stick together, therefore, it is the case of perfectly enelastic collision. Let $v$ be the common velocity, then total momentum after collision, $p_f\;= (m_A+m_B) v$ $\;=(l+3) v=4 v$ According to law of conservation of linear momentum, $\;\;\;   \;\;  p_i=p_f$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;  4=4 v \Rightarrow v=1\ \mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ $\;\;\text{ Time of impact, }\; \Delta t=0.1\ \mathrm{s}$ $\;\;\text{ Force exerted on the body B, }\;$ $\; \;\;\;\;  F_B=\;\frac{\Delta p_B}{\Delta t}=\;\frac{m_B (v_B-u_B)}{\Delta t}=\;\frac{3(v-0)}{0.1}$ $\;\Rightarrow \cdot F_B=\;\frac{3(1-0)}{0.1}=\;\frac{3}{0.1}=30\ \mathrm{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown below Let $v$ be the velocity of solid cylinder on reaching the ground. According to conservation of energy, Total energy at point $A=$ Total energy at point $B$ $\;\; \text{ i. e } \; m g h + 0 = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + 0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; m g h = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} M R^2 \right) \left( \frac{v}{R} \right)^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $\Rightarrow \left( \text{ Where, } I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 \text{ and } \omega = \frac{v}{R} \right)$ $\Rightarrow \;\; g h = \frac{v^2}{4} + \frac{v^2}{2} \Rightarrow g h = \frac{3 v^2}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; v^2 = \frac{4 g h}{3} \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{4 g h}{3}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, instantaneous displacement of particle executing SHM. $x\; = A \sin^{2}(\omega t - 4)$ $\Rightarrow x\; = A \left[ \frac{1 - \cos(2(\omega t - 4))}{2} \right]$ $\; \left( \; \text{ Since, } \; \sin^{2} \theta = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2} \right)$ $\Rightarrow x = \; \frac{A}{2} [1 - \cos(2\omega t - 8)]$ Here, angular velocity of particle $\omega' \; = 2 \omega$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \; \frac{2\pi}{T'} \; = 2 \times \; \frac{2\pi}{T} \Rightarrow T' = \frac{T}{2}$ $= \; \frac{ \frac{2\pi}{\omega} }{2} = \; \frac{\pi}{\omega}$ $\left( \therefore T = \; \frac{2\pi}{\omega} \right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We know that, the radius $(R)$ of nucleus is given as $R=R_0 A^{1/3}$ or $R \propto A^{1/3}$ Where, $R_0=\text{constant}$ $A=\text{mass number}$ $\therefore$ Nuclear density, $\rho=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}=\frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$ (here, $m$ is mass of each nucleon) $\Rightarrow \;\; \rho=\frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (R_0 A^{1/3})^3}=\frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A}$ $\rho=\frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$ Hence, it is clear from above formula, nuclear density is independent of mass number $A$ . Equating the bottom-left entries gives $x^2+x+1=7$ , i.e. $x^2+x-6=0$ . Thus $(x+3)(x-2)=0$ , so $x=-3$ or $x=2$ . The value $x=-3$ fails $x^3=8$ , so it is rejected. Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ Let $A \; = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 \end{bmatrix}, X = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix}.$ $B \; = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ $|A| \; = 1(24-18) - 2(-12-9) - 3(12+12)$ $\; = 6 + 42 - 72$ $\; = -24$ $\text{Adj} A \; = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 21 & 24 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & -9 & -8 \end{bmatrix}^{T}$ $\; = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 & -6 \\ 21 & 3 & -9 \\ 24 & 0 & -8 \end{bmatrix}$ $A^{-1} \; = \; \frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj} A$ $\; = \; \frac{-1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 & -6 \\ 21 & 3 & -9 \\ 24 & 0 & -8 \end{bmatrix}$ $X = \; A^{-1} B$ $\; = \; \frac{-1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 & -6 \\ 21 & 3 & -9 \\ 24 & 0 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ $\; = \; \frac{-1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} 6-6-24 \\ 21+3-36 \\ 24-32 \end{bmatrix}$ $\; = \; \frac{-1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} 6-6-24 \\ 21+3-36 \\ 24-32 \end{bmatrix}$ $\; = \; \frac{-1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} -24 \\ -12 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}$ $\therefore \alpha = 1, \beta = 2, \gamma = 3$ $\; \text{Now,} \; \alpha^2 + \gamma^2 = 1 + 9$ $= 10 = 5 \beta$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution We have, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^{6} \sin \left(\frac{2\pi k}{7}\right) - i \cos \left(\frac{2\pi k}{7}\right)$ $= -i \left[ \sum\limits_{k=1}^{6} \cos \left(\frac{2\pi k}{7}\right) + i \sin \left(\frac{2\pi k}{7}\right) \right] = -i \sum\limits_{k=1}^{6} c^{\frac{i2\pi k}{7}}$ $= -i \left[ e^{i2\pi/7} + e^{i4\pi/7} + \dots + e^{i12\pi/7} \right]$ This forms a GP $= -i \left[ e^{i2\pi/7} \cdot \frac{1-(e^{i2\pi/7})^6}{1-e^{i2\pi/7}} \right]$ $= -i \left[ \frac{e^{i2\pi/7} - e^{i14\pi/7}}{1-e^{i2\pi/7}} \right]$ $= -i \left[ \frac{e^{i2\pi/7} - 1}{1-e^{i2\pi/7}} \right]$ $\left[ \because e^{i14\pi/7}=1 \right]$ $=i$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution We have, $(x-iy)^{\frac{1}{3}}=a-ib$ $\Rightarrow x-iy=(a-ib)^{3}$ $\Rightarrow x-iy=a^{3}-i^{3}b^{3}-3a^{2}ib+3i^{2}b$ $\Rightarrow x-iy=a^{3}+ib^{3}-3a^{2}bi-3ab^{2}$ Comparing real part and imaginary part on both sides, we get $x=a^{3}-3ab^{2}, y=3a^{2}b-b^{3}$ Now, $\frac{x}{2a}+\frac{y}{2b}=\frac{a(a^{2}-3b^{2})}{2a}+\frac{b(3a^{2}-b^{2})}{2b}$ $=\frac{a^{2}-3b^{2}+3a^{2}-b^{2}}{2}=2(a^{2}-b^{2})$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of $x^2 - 10x - 8 = 0$ $\alpha + \beta = 10,\ \alpha \beta = -8$ Also, $\alpha^2 - 10\alpha - 8 = 0$ or $\alpha^2 - 8 = 10 \alpha$ and $\beta^2 - 10\beta - 8 = 0$ or $\beta^2 - 8 = 10 \beta$ Now, $\; \frac{a_{10} - 8 a_8}{5 a_4}$ $= \; \frac{ (\alpha^{10} - \beta^{10}) - 8 (\alpha^8 - \beta^8) }{5 (\alpha^9 - \beta^9) }$ $\; = \; \frac{ (\alpha^{10} - 8\alpha^8) - (\beta^{10} - 8\beta^8) }{5 (\alpha^9 - \beta^9) }$ $\; = \; \frac{ \alpha^8 (\alpha^2 - 8) - \beta^8 (\beta^2 - 8) }{5 (\alpha^9 - \beta^9) }$ $\; = \; \frac{ \alpha^8 \times 10 \alpha - \beta^8 \times 10 \beta }{5 (\alpha^9 - \beta^9) }$ $\; = \; \frac{ 10 [\alpha^9 - \beta^9] }{5 (\alpha^9 - \beta^9) }$ $\; = 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $f(x)$ is continuous at $\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} f(x) = f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ $= \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} \left(\frac{1-\sin^3 x}{3\cos^2 x}\right)$ $= \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} \left(\frac{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin^2 x+\sin x)}{3(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}\right)$ $= \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} \left[\frac{1+\sin^2 x+\sin x}{3(1+\sin x)}\right] = \frac{3}{3(2)}$ $= \frac{1}{2}$ and $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{+}}{2}} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{+}}{2}} \frac{\beta(1-\sin x)}{(\pi-2x)^2}$ $= \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}} \frac{\beta\left(1-\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)\right)}{\left(\pi-2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)\right)^2}, \quad h = x-\frac{\pi}{2}$ $= \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}} \beta\left(\frac{1-\cos h}{4h^2}\right)$ $= \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}} \frac{\beta\left(2\sin^2\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)\right)}{4\times 4\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^2} = \frac{\beta}{8}$ $\therefore \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\beta}{8} = \alpha$ $\Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \beta = 4$ $\therefore \alpha\beta = 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int\; \frac{dx}{1 + a \cos x}$ $= \int\; \frac{1}{1 + a \left( \frac{1 - \tan^2 \frac{x}{2}}{1 + \tan^2 \frac{x}{2}} \right)} \; dx$ $\; = \int\; \frac{\sec^2 \frac{x}{2} \, dx}{1 + \tan^2 \frac{x}{2} + a \left(1 - \tan^2 \frac{x}{2}\right)}$ $\; = \int\; \frac{\sec^2 \frac{x}{2} \, dx}{(1 + a) - \tan^2 \frac{x}{2} (a - 1)}$ $\; = \frac{1}{a + 1} \int\; \frac{\sec^2 \frac{x}{2}}{1 - \left( \frac{a - 1}{a + 1} \right) \tan^2 \frac{x}{2}} \, dx$ $\; \text{ Let } \sqrt{\frac{a - 1}{a + 1}} \tan \frac{x}{2} = t$ $\; \Rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{a - 1}{a + 1}} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \sec^2 \frac{x}{2} \, dx = dt$ $\; \Rightarrow \sec^2 \frac{x}{2} \, dx = 2 \sqrt{\frac{a + 1}{a - 1}} \, dt$ $\; I = \frac{2}{a + 1} \sqrt{\frac{a + 1}{a - 1}} \int\; \frac{1}{1 - t^2} \, dt$ $\; I = \frac{2}{\sqrt{a^2 - 1}} \times \frac{1}{2} \log \left| \frac{1 + t}{1 - t} \right| + C$ $\; = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - 1}} \log \left| \frac{1 + \sqrt{\frac{a - 1}{a + 1}} \tan \frac{x}{2}}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{a - 1}{a + 1}} \tan \frac{x}{2}} \right|$ $\; = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - 1}}$ $\; \log \left| \frac{\sqrt{a + 1} \cos \frac{x}{2} + \sqrt{a - 1} \sin \frac{x}{2}}{\sqrt{a + 1} \cos \frac{x}{2} - \sqrt{a - 1} \sin \frac{x}{2}} \right| + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\;\frac{x^2-2}{x^3\sqrt{x^2-1}} dx=\int\;\frac{(x^2-2) x dx}{x^4\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ Let $x^2-1=t^2$ $\Rightarrow \; \; x dx=t dt$ $I=\int\;\frac{(t^2-1) t dt}{(t^2+1)^2 t}=\int\;\frac{t^2-1}{(t^2+1)^2} dt=\int\;\frac{1-\frac{1}{t^2}}{\left(t+\;\frac{1}{t}\right)^2} dt$ Let $t+\;\frac{1}{t}=u$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; \left(1-\;\frac{1}{t^2}\right) dt = d u$ $\; \therefore \; \; I=\int\;\frac{1}{u^2} d u = -\;\frac{1}{u}+C$ $\; = - \left(\;\frac{t}{t^2+1}\right) + C = - \;\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x^2} + C$ $\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=f(x)-g(x)$ $=\int\;\frac{e^{3x}dx}{4+8e^{2x}+e^{4x}}-\int\;\frac{2}{e^{3x}+8e^{x}+4e^{-x}}dx$ $=\int\;\frac{e^{3x}dx}{4+8e^{2x}+e^{4x}}-\int\;\frac{2e^{x}}{e^{4x}+8e^{2x}+4}dx$ $=\int\left(\frac{e^{3x}-2e^{x}}{e^{4x}+8e^{2x}+4}\right)dx=\int\;\frac{e^{x}(e^{2x}-2)}{e^{4x}+8e^{2x}+4}dx$ Let $e^{x}=t$ , then $e^{x}dx=dt$ $=\int\;\frac{t^{2}-2}{t^{4}+8t^{2}+4}dt=\int\left(\frac{1-\frac{2}{t^{2}}}{t^{2}+8+\frac{4}{t^{2}}}\right)\cdot dt$ $=\int\;\frac{1-\frac{2}{t^{2}}}{t^{2}+\frac{4}{t^{2}}+4}dt=\int\;\frac{\left(1-\frac{2}{t^{2}}\right)dt}{\left(t+\frac{2}{t}\right)^{2}+\left(2^{2}\right)}$ Let $t+\frac{2}{t}=u$ $\Rightarrow\;\;\left(1-\frac{2}{t^{2}}\right)dt=du$ $I=\int\;\frac{1}{u^{2}+2^{2}}du=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{t^{2}+2}{2t}\right)$ $=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left[\frac{e^{2x}+2}{2e^{x}}\right)$ $=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{e^{x}+2e^{-x}}{2}\right)+C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $\;\frac{a t+b}{c t+d}=x$ in the function $f\left(\;\frac{a t+b}{c t+d}\right)=t$ $a t+b=c t x+d x$ $\Rightarrow \;\; t(a-c x)=d x-b$ $\Rightarrow \;\; t\;=\;\frac{d x-b}{a-c x}$ $\; \int f(x) dx = \int \; \frac{d x-b}{a-c x} dx = \int \; \frac{b-d x}{c x-a} dx$ $\; = b \int \; \frac{1}{c x-a} dx - \; \frac{d}{c} \int \; \frac{c x-a+a}{c x-a} dx$ $\; = \; \frac{b}{c} \log (c x-a) - \; \frac{d}{c} \int 1 \, dx - \; \frac{a d}{c} \int \; \frac{1 dx}{c x-a}$ $\; = \; \frac{b}{c} \log \left| (c x-a) - \frac{d x}{c} - \frac{a d}{c^2} \log \left| c x-a \right| \right|$ $\; = \; \frac{-d x}{c} + \left(\frac{b c - a d}{c^2}\right) \log (c x-a) + K$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\int\limits_{\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{18}}[x] dx=a+b\sqrt{2}+c\sqrt{3}$ $\;\;\text{ As }\;\sqrt{3}=1.732$ and $\sqrt{18}=4 \cdot 24$ $\therefore \int\limits_{\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{4}} 1 dx+\int\limits_{\sqrt{4}}^{\sqrt{9}} 2 dx+\int\limits_{\sqrt{9}}^{\sqrt{16}} 3 dx+\int\limits_{\sqrt{16}}^{\sqrt{18}} 4 dx$ $\;\; =2-\sqrt{3}+2(3-2)+3(4-3)+4(\sqrt{18}-4)$ $\;\; =2-\sqrt{3}+2+3+4\sqrt{18}-16$ $\;\; =-9+12\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3}$ $\therefore   \;\; a=-9, b=12, c=-1$ $\;\; a+b+c=-9+12-1=2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\limits_{0}^{4} \frac{x+2}{\sqrt{4x-x^{2}}} \, dx$ $=\int\limits_{0}^{4} \frac{x+2}{\sqrt{4-(x-2)^{2}}} \, dx$ Let $x-2=t$ $\Rightarrow \; dx = dt$ When $x \rightarrow 0,\; t \rightarrow -2$ and $x \rightarrow 4,\; t \rightarrow 2$ $I = \int\limits_{-2}^{2} \frac{t+4}{\sqrt{4-t^{2}}} \, dt$ $= -\frac{1}{2} \int\limits_{-2}^{2} \frac{-2t}{\sqrt{4-t^{2}}} \, dt + 4 \int\limits_{-2}^{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-t^{2}}} \, dt$ $= -\left[ \sqrt{4-t^{2}} \right]_{-2}^{2} + 4 \left[ \sin^{-1} \frac{t}{2} \right]_{-2}^{2}$ $= 0 + 4 \left[ \sin^{-1} 1 - \sin^{-1}(-1) \right]$ $= 0 + 4 \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} \right] = 4\pi$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x(1+\sin x)}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx$ . $\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x\,dx}{\cos^{2} x}+\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x \sin x\,dx}{1+\cos^{2} x}$ As $\frac{2x}{1+\cos^{2} x}$ is an odd function. So, $\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx=0$ As $\frac{2x \sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}$ is an even function. So, $\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \frac{2x \sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx=2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{2x \sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx$ $I=4 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx$ ......(i) $=4 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \sin(\pi-x)}{1+\cos^{2}(\pi-x)}$ $\Rightarrow I=4 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x) \sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}$ .....(ii) On adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), $2I=4\pi \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^{2} x}\,dx$ Let $\cos x=t$ $\Rightarrow -\sin x\,dx=dt$ When $x \rightarrow 0, t \rightarrow 1$ and $x \rightarrow \pi, t \rightarrow -1$ $I=-2\pi \int\limits_{1}^{-1} \frac{1}{1+t^{2}}\,dt$ $I=2\pi \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{1+t^{2}}\,dt=2\pi \left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_{-1}^{1}$ $=2\pi \left[\tan^{-1}(1)-\tan^{-1}(-1)\right]=2\pi \left[\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right]$ $=\pi^{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{\sin \; x - x^{2}}{3-|x|} dx$ $= \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{\sin \; x}{3-|x|} dx - \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{x^{2}}{3-|x|} dx$ As $\; \frac{\sin \; x}{3-|x|}$ is an odd function. $\therefore \; \; \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{\sin \; x}{3-|x|} dx = 0$ As $\; \frac{x^{2}}{3-|x|}$ is an even function, $\therefore \; \; \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{\sin \; x}{3-|x|} dx = 0$ As $\; \frac{x^{2}}{3-|x|}$ is an even function, $\; \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \; \frac{x^{2}}{3-|x|} dx = 2 \int\limits_{0}^{1} \; \frac{x^{2}}{3-|x|} dx$ $\; I = -2 \int\limits_{0}^{1} \; \frac{x^{2}}{3-x}$ $\; \; = 2 \int\limits_{0}^{1} \; \frac{x^{2} - 3x + 3x - 9 + 9}{x-3} dx$ $\; \; \; = 2 \int\limits_{0}^{1} \left( x + 3 + \; \frac{9}{x-3} \right) dx$ $\; = 2 \left[ \; \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 3x + 9 \log(x-3) \right]_{0}^{1}$ $\; = 2 \left[ \frac{1}{2} + 3 + 9 \log(-2) - 9 \log(-3) \right]$ $\; = 2 \left[ \frac{7}{2} - 9 \log\left( \frac{3}{2} \right) \right] = 7 - 18 \log \frac{3}{2} + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $y=\text{IF}$ $\Rightarrow y=e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \Rightarrow \log y=\log e^{\int P(x)\,dx}$ $\Rightarrow \log y=\int P(x)\,dx$ On differentiating both sides, $\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=P(x)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=P(x)y \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}-P(x)y=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution We have, $\;\frac{dy}{dx} = \;\frac{y-4}{x-3}$ $\; \Rightarrow \int\; \frac{1}{y-4} dy = \int\; \frac{1}{x-3} dx$ $\; \Rightarrow \log(y-4) = \log(x-3) + \log C$ $\; \Rightarrow y-4 = C(x-3) \Rightarrow y = C(x-3) + 4$ The curve passes through $(4,3)$ $\; 3 = C(4-3) + 4$ $\Rightarrow \;\; C\; = -1$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y\; = 3 - x + 4$ $\Rightarrow \;\; = 7 - x$ Substitute $y = x$ inequation $y = 7 - x$ $\; x = 7 - x$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 2x = 7$ $\Rightarrow \;\; x\; = \frac{7}{2}$ The intersecting point of curve and line is $\left(\;\frac{7}{2}, \;\frac{7}{2}\right)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, mass of object, $m=10 \text{kg}$ distance travelled by object, $s=2 \text{m}$ Time, $t=1 \text{s}$ According to given situation, $s\;=u t+\;\frac{1}{2} a t^2$ $\Rightarrow \;\; s\;=0+\;\frac{1}{2} a t^2$ $[ \therefore u=0]$ $s\;=\;\frac{1}{2} a t^2$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 2\;=\;\frac{1}{2} \times a \times 1^2$ $a\;=4 \text{m s}^{-2}$ Net force on the object in liquid, $F_{\;\text{net }\;}=m a=10 \times 4=40 \text{N}$ Weight of the object, $w\;=m g$ $\;=10 \times 10=100 \text{N}$ Upthrust force on the object, $F'=w-F_{\;\text{net }\;}=100-40=60 \text{N}$ According to Archimedes' principle, Weight liquid displaced = Upthrust force $\Rightarrow \;\; m'=\;\frac{F'}{g}=\;\frac{60}{10}=6 \text{kg}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $s_{\text{ice}}=2100\,\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ $s_{\text{water}}=4186\,\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ Latent heat of fusion of ice, $L_{\text{kee}}=3.35\times10^5\,\mathrm{Jkg}^{-1}$ Mass of ice, $m=200\,\mathrm{g}=0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ Temperature of ice, $T_1=-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Final temperature of water, $T_2=30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Total required heat, $Q=m\,s_{\text{lie}}(0-T_1)+m\,L_{\text{lce}}+m\,s_{\text{water}}(T_2-0)$ $=0.2\times2100[0-(-10)]+0.2\times3.35\times10^5+0.2\times4186(30-0)$ $=0.2\times2100\times10+0.2\times3.35\times10^5+0.2\times4186\times30$ $=9.6316\times10^4\,\mathrm{J}$ $=96316\,\mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For Carnot engine, $T_1=600\text{ K},\ T_2=300\text{ K}$ Heat absorbed, $Q=800\text{ J}$ If $W$ be the mechanical work done by Carnot engine, then using the formula, $\eta\;=\;\frac{W}{Q}=1-\;\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ $\Rightarrow\;\; \;\frac{W}{Q}\;=1-\;\frac{T_2}{T_1} \Rightarrow \;\frac{W}{800}=1-\;\frac{300}{600}$ $\Rightarrow\;\; \;\frac{W}{800}\;= \left(1-\;\frac{1}{2}\right) \Rightarrow \;\frac{W}{800}=\;\frac{1}{2}$ $W\;=\;\frac{800}{2}=400\text{ J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to Newton's law of cooling, $m c \left( \frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} \right) = K \left( \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0 \right)$ For the first condition, $m c \left( \frac{75-65}{10} \right) \; = K \left( \frac{75+65}{2} - T_0 \right)$ $\Rightarrow \; m c \left( \frac{10}{10} \right) \; = K (70 - T_0)$ $\Rightarrow \; m c \; = K (70 - T_0)$ ......(i) According to second condition, $m c \left( \frac{65-55}{t'} \right) \; = K \left( \frac{65+55}{2} - T_0 \right)$ $\Rightarrow \; m c \left( \frac{10}{t'} \right) \; = K (60 - T_0)$ .....(ii) Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\; \frac{\; \frac{1}{10}}{t'} = \frac{70-T_0}{60-T_0}$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \frac{t'}{10} = \frac{70-T_0}{60-T_0} \Rightarrow t' = 10 \left( \frac{70-T_0}{60-T_0} \right)$ $\text{ clearly, } \; \Rightarrow \; \frac{70-T_0}{60-T_0} > 1$ $\therefore t' > 10 \text{ minutes.}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given $(v_{\text{rms}})_{\text{O}_2} = 500 \text{m/s}$ $(v_{\text{rms}})_{\text{H}_2} = ?$ We know that, $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$ $\Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(v_{\text{ms}})_{\text{H}_2}}{(v_{\text{rms}})_{\text{O}_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{M_{\text{O}_2}}{M_{\text{H}_2}}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(v_{\text{ms}})_{\text{H}_2}}{500} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{2}}$ $= \sqrt{16} = 4$ $\Rightarrow (v_{\text{ms}})_{\text{H}_2} = 4 \times 500 = 2000 \text{ms}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: A wave which travels continuously in a medium in the same direction without the change in its amplitude is called a progressive wave. Equation of progressive wave is given as $y(x,t)=A \sin (\omega t - k x + \varphi)$ We can write the above equation as a linear combination of sine and cosine function as, $y(x,t)=A \sin (k x - \omega t)+B \cos (k x - \omega t)$ Hence, among the given options $y=3 \sin (5x-0.5t)+4 \cos (5x-0.5t)$ represents the equation of progressive wave. © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown below According to Snell's law, $\;2\mu_1\;=\;\frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin r}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}\;=\;\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\sin r}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{1}{2}\;=\;\frac{1}{2\sin r}$ $\Rightarrow\sin r\;=1=\sin 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow r\;=90^{\circ}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $Q$ be divided into two charges $q$ and $Q-q$ i.e $q_1=q$ and $q_2=Q-q$ $\therefore$ Electrostatic force between $q$ and $Q-q$ is given as $F = \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q(Q-q)}{r^2}$ $F$ will be maximum if $\\;\\;\frac{dF}{dq}=0$ $\Rightarrow \\;\frac{d}{dq} \cdot \left[ \frac{q(Q-q)}{r^2} \right] =0$ $\Rightarrow q(0-1)+(Q-q) \cdot 1=0$ $\Rightarrow Q-2q=0$ $\Rightarrow q=\frac{Q}{2}$ $\\;\text{Hence,}\\; q_1=q=\frac{Q}{2}$ $\\;q_2=Q-q=Q-\frac{Q}{2}=\frac{Q}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: From the given situation, $V_A - V_0 = -\int\int E \, dx\,dy$ $0 - V_0 = -\int\limits_{0}^{10} \int\limits_{0}^{20} (A x \hat{i} + A y \hat{j}) \,dx\,dy$ $\Rightarrow \; -V_0 = -\int\limits_{0}^{10} \int\limits_{0}^{20} A x \hat{i} \,dx \hat{i} + A \hat{j} \,dy \hat{j}$ $V_0 = -\int\limits_{0}^{10} \int\limits_{0}^{20} A x \,dx + A y \,dy$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{10} A x \,dx + \int\limits_{0}^{20} A y \,dy$ $= \left[ A \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{10} + \left[ \frac{A y^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{20}$ $= A \frac{10^2}{2} + A \frac{20^2}{2} = 50 A + 200 A$ $= 250 A = 250 \times 10 \; [ \because A = 10 \, \text{Vm}^{-2} ]$ $= 2500 \, \text{V}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Electric potential, $\phi(x, y, z)=\phi_1\;\frac{x_0}{x}$ where, $x_0=5\,\text{m},\;\phi_1=8\,\text{V}$ Electric field is given as $\text{bo}\,E\;=\;-\frac{dV}{dx}\hat{i}-\frac{dV}{dx}\hat{j}-\frac{dV}{dx}\hat{k}$ $\;=\;-\frac{dV}{dx}\hat{i}$ $\;=\;-\frac{d}{dx}\phi\hat{i}$ $(\because V=\phi)$ $=\frac{-d}{dx}\phi_0\;\frac{x_0}{x}\hat{i}=\frac{\phi_0 x_0}{x^2}\hat{i}$ At point ( $10\,\text{m},\;5\,\text{m},\;5\,\text{m}$ ) $\text{bo}\,E = \frac{\phi_0 x_0}{10^2}\hat{i} = \frac{8 \times 5}{100}\hat{i} = 0.4\hat{i}\,\text{Vm}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $V=12\,\text{V}$ $\;q=80\ \text{Ah}=80 \times 60 \times 60\ \text{As}$ $\;P=120\ \text{W}$ We know delivered energy, $\;E=W=V q$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; E=12 \times 80 \times 60 \times 60\ \text{J}$ We know that, $P\;=\;\frac{W}{t}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; t\;=\;\frac{W}{P}=\;\frac{E}{P} \;\; (\because W=E)$ $\;=\;\frac{12 \times 80 \times 60 \times 60}{120}$ $\;=8 \times 60 \times 60\ \text{s}=8\ \text{h}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, magnetic field, $B = 28.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{T}$ Torque, $\tau = 3.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{J}$ Magnet moment, $M =$ ? $\theta = 45^{\circ}$ We know that, torque on bar magnet in magnetic field, $\tau\; = M B \sin\;\theta$ $\Rightarrow \;\; M\;=\;\frac{\tau}{B \sin\;\theta} = \;\frac{3.6 \times 10^{-5}}{28.3 \times 10^{-3} \sin\;45^{\circ}}$ $\;=\;\frac{\sqrt{2} \times 3.6}{28.3} \times 10^{-2} = 1.79 \times 10^{-3} \text{J T}^{-1}$ $\;\; \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{J T}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Area of metal loop, $A=10\ \text{cm}^{2}=10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{2},\ \vec{A}=10^{-3}\ \hat{k}$ Magnitude of magnetic field; $B=1.73\ \text{T}$ Magnetic field is directed along, $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ Unit vector along the direction of magnetic field, $\;\ \hat{\vec{n}} = \frac{\hat{i+\hat{j}+\hat{k}}}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}}} = \frac{\hat{i+\hat{j}+\hat{k}}}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\therefore\ \vec{B}=B\ \hat{\vec{n}}$ $= 1.73\ \frac{\hat{(i+\hat{j}+\hat{k})}}{\sqrt{3}} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ Magnetic flux linked with coil, $\begin{aligned} \phi = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A} \end{aligned}$ $(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot (10^{-3} \hat{k}) = 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ $\text{ Induced emf, } |e| = \frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{\phi - \phi_{2}}{10}$ $= \frac{10^{-3}-0}{10} = \frac{10^{-3}-0}{10} = 10^{-4}\ \text{V}$ $= 0.1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V}$ $= 0.1\ \text{mV}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Frequency of EM wave, $f=50\ \mathrm{MHz}$ $=5 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$ In free space, the energy density of a static electric field, $K_E=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ ........(i) Again, in free space, the energy density of a static magnetic field, $K_B=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=\frac{\left(\frac{E}{c}\right)^2}{2\mu_0}$ $\left(\therefore B=\frac{E}{c}\right)$ $=\frac{E^2}{2 c^2 \mu_0}=\frac{E^2}{2 \frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} \mu_0}\qquad \left(\because c^2=\frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\right)$ $=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ [From Eq. (i)] $\;=K_E$ $\therefore \;\; K_E\;=K_B$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Mass of particle, $m = 2 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{kg}$ de-Broglie wavelength, $\lambda = 3.3 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{m}$ Planck's constant $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{J}\cdot\mathrm{s}$ we know that, de-Broglie wavelength $\; \lambda = \frac{h}{p}$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m K}}$ $( \because p = \sqrt{2 m K})$ Where, $K$ is kinetic energy of particle $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda^2 = \frac{h^2}{2 m K}$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; K = \frac{h^2}{2 m \lambda^2} = \frac{(6.6 \times 10^{-34})^2}{2 \times 2 \times 10^{-27} \times (3.3 \times 10^{-10})^2}$ $\; = 1 \times 10^{-21} \mathrm{J}$ $\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Disproportionation reactions are the reactions in which a compound undergoes oxidation as well as reduction. $\mathrm{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_2$ is an example of decomposition reaction. Hence, are examples of disproportionation reactions. © examsnet.com

Solution: $2\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O},(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})$ Given, $\Delta_r G = -128\,\mathrm{kJ}$ $\Delta_r S^{\circ}\; = -40\,\mathrm{K} \Rightarrow \Delta_r U = ?$ $\Delta G\; = \Delta H - T \Delta S$ ....(i) $\Delta H\; = \Delta U + \Delta n R T$ .......(ii) From (i) and (ii), $\Delta G\; = \Delta U + \Delta n R T - T \Delta S$ $-128000\; = \Delta U + (-1) \times 8.314 \times 300 - 300 \times (-40)$ $-128000\; = \Delta U - 2494.2 + 12000$ $-128000\; = \Delta U - 9505.8$ $\Delta U\; = -128000 - 9505.8$ $\; = -137505.8\,\mathrm{J} \cong -137.50\,\mathrm{kJ}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For the given reaction, $A(g)+\;\frac{1}{2} B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)+\;\text{ Heat }\;$ Low temperature will favour the forward reaction as it is an exothermic reaction. According to Le-Chatelier's principle, if there is any change in the conditions of equilibrium, then the equilibrium shifts in the direction that can reduce the effect of the change. As given reaction is. exothermic, increase temperature will favour backward/reverse reaction and decrease temperature will favour forward reaction. Number of moles of reactant $=1+0.5=1.5$ Number of moles of product $=1$ $\therefore$ High pressure will favour forward reaction as the effect of increased pressure can be minimised, if it goes in forward reaction. © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution We have, $\;\;\frac{y}{x} \cos^{4}\alpha + \frac{x}{y} \sin^{4}\alpha = 2 \sin^{2}\alpha \cdot \cos^{2}\alpha$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\frac{y}{x} \cot^{2}\alpha + \frac{x}{y} \tan^{2}\alpha = 2$ $\;\Rightarrow y^{2} \cot^{2}\cdot\alpha + x^{2} \tan^{2}\alpha = 2xy$ $\;\Rightarrow y^{2} \cot^{2}\alpha - 2xy + x^{2} \tan^{2}\alpha = 0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; (y \cot\alpha - x \tan\alpha)^{2} = 0$ $\;\Rightarrow y \cot\alpha = x \tan\alpha$ $\;\Rightarrow y = x \tan^{2}\alpha$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\;\frac{d y}{d x}\; = \tan^{2}\alpha$ $\;=\;\frac{\sin^{2}\alpha}{\cos^{2}\alpha}$ © examsnet.com

eq 0$ So, $x^2 = \frac{h^2}{2}$ or $x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d^2 A'}{d x^2} = \frac{1}{4} [2 h^2 - 12 x^2]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d^2 A'}{d x^2} \big|_{x=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}} = \frac{1}{4} \left[ 2 h^2 - 12 \times \frac{h^2}{2} \right] < 0$ A is maximum at $x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}$ $y^2 = h^2 - x^2$ $= h^2 - \frac{h^2}{2} = \frac{h^2}{2}$ $\Rightarrow y = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}$ Area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \times x \times y$ $= \\frac{1}{2} \\times \\frac{h}{\\sqrt{2}} \\times \\frac{h}{\\sqrt{2}} = \\frac{h^2}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $\int \frac{\sin^{3} x (\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x))^{-1}}{\cos^{4} x + 3 \cos^{2} x + 1} \, dx = f(x) + C$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{\sin^{3} x (\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x))^{-1}}{\cos^{2} x \left(\cos^{2} x + \frac{1}{\cos^{2} x} + 2 + 1\right)}$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{\sin^{3} x (\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x))^{-1}}{\cos^{2} x \left[(\sec x + \cos x)^2 + 1\right]}$ Let $\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x) = t$ $\left[ \frac{1}{(\sec x + \cos x)^2 + 1} \right] [\sec x \tan x - \sin x] \, dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \left[ \frac{1}{(\sec x + \cos x)^2 + 1} \right] \left[ \frac{\sin^{3} x}{\cos^{2} x} \right] \cdot dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \int t^{-1} \, dt = f(x) + C$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{1}{t} \, dt = f(x) + C$ $\Rightarrow \log |t| + C = f(x) + C$ $\Rightarrow f(x) = \log | \tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x) |$ $e^{f(x)} = \tan^{-1}(\sec x + \cos x)$ $\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\;\frac{1}{(\sin\;x+\cos x+\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\sin\;2x})^{2}} dx$ $\;=\int\;\frac{1}{((\sqrt{\sin\;x})^{2}+(\sqrt{\cos x})^{2}+2\sqrt{\sin\;x}\sqrt{\cos x})^{2}} dx$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{(\sqrt{\sin\;x}+\sqrt{\cos x})^{4}} dx$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{\cos^{2}x(\sqrt{\tan x}+1)^{4}}=\int\;\frac{\sec^{2}x}{(1+\sqrt{\tan x})^{4}} dx$ Let $\tan x=t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \sec^{2}x dx=2t dt$ $I\;=\int\;\frac{2t dt}{(1+t)^{4}}$ $\;=2\int\;\frac{t+1}{(1+t)^{4}} dt-2\int\;\frac{1}{(1+t)^{4}} dt$ $\;=2\int\;\frac{1}{(1+t)^{3}} dt-2\int\;\frac{1}{(1+t)^{4}} dt$ $\;=-\;\frac{1}{(1+t)^{2}}+\;\frac{2}{3}\times\;\frac{1}{(1+t)^{3}}+C$ $\;=\;\frac{2-3(1+t)}{3(1+t)^{3}}+C$ $\;=\;\frac{2-3(1+\sqrt{\tan x})}{3(1+\sqrt{\tan x})^{3}}+C$ $\;=\;\frac{-(1+3\sqrt{\tan x})}{3(1+\sqrt{\tan x})^{3}}+C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x}{\sin x} (3\cos^2 x+2\sin x+\sin^3 x-3) dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x}{\sin x} (3-3\sin^2 x+2\sin x+\sin^3 x-3) dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} x (\sin^2 x-3\sin x+2) dx$ .......(i) $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x) (\sin^2(\pi-x)-3\sin(\pi-x)+2) dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x) (\sin^2 x-3\sin x+2) dx$ .....(ii) On adding both equations $2 I = \pi \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} (\sin^2 x-3\sin x+2) dx$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \int \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2} dx + [3\cos x+2x]_0^\pi \right]$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} \right]_0^\pi + (-3-3) + (2\pi)$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} - 6 + 2\pi \right]$ $= \frac{\pi}{4} \left[ \pi - 12 + 4\pi \right]$ $= \frac{\pi}{4}(5\pi-12)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $p^{\circ}=25$ torr, mass of urea $=12\,\text{g}$ Mass of glucose $=36\,\text{g}$ , mass of water $=100\,\text{g}$ Moles of urea $=\;\frac{\text{ Mass }}{\text{ Molecular mass }}\;=\frac{12}{60}=0.2$ Moles of glucose $=\;\frac{\text{ Mass }}{\text{ Molecular mass }}\;=\frac{36}{180}=0.2$ Moles of water $=\;\frac{\text{ Mass }}{\text{ Molecular mass }}\;=\frac{100}{18}=5.55$ Mole fraction of urea $=\;\frac{0.2}{0.2+0.2+5.55}\;=\frac{0.2}{5.95}=0.0336$ Mole fraction of glucose $=\;\frac{0.2}{0.2+0.2+5.55}\;=\frac{0.2}{5.95}=0.0336$ $\;\frac{p^{\circ}-p}{p^{\circ}}=$ mole fraction of solute $\Rightarrow\;\frac{25-p}{25}\;=0.0336+0.0336$ $\Rightarrow\;25-p\;=25 \times 0.0672$ $\Rightarrow\;p\;=25-16.8$ $\;=23.32\;\text{ torr }\;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The solution which produces the least number of ions on the dissociation of solute particles will show lowest depression in the freezing point. Hence, such a solution will have the highest freezing point.' Since, $\mathrm{KCl}$ and $\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$ are ionic compounds, they will dissociate into ions in aqueous solution and will cause larger depression in freezing points as compared to non-electrolytes urea and glucose. Urea and glucose will remain as molecules in solution. Since, concentration of urea is lower than glucose, it will show lowest depression in the freezing point, therefore, highest freezing point. © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown below. According to given situation we have to find electric field at point $P(0,0,1)$ . Distance of point $P$ from each charges is equal to $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt{2}$ $E_{A P}\;=E_{B P}=E_{C P}=E_{D P}=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{(\sqrt{2})^2}$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{2}$ $E_{A P}$ and $E_{B P}$ are perpendicular to each other. Let $E'$ be the resultant electric field of $E_{A P}$ and $E_{B P}$ , then $E'\;=\sqrt{E_{A P}^2+E_{B P}^2}=\sqrt{2 E_{A P}^2} . \; \; [\because E_{A P}=E_{B P}]$ $\;=E_{A P} \sqrt{2}$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q\sqrt{2}}{2}=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ $E'\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ In the similar way, net electric field due to $E_{C P}$ and $E_{p p}$ $E''=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ Again $E'$ and $E''$ are directed in same direction i.e along $+z$ direction, hence net electric field, $E_{\;\text{net }\;}=E'+E''=2 E'$ $[\because E'=E'']$ $=2\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}=\;\frac{q}{2\sqrt{2} \pi \varepsilon_0} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $C_{1}\;=10\;\mu\text{F}$ $\;=10^{-5}\;\text{F}$ $V_{1}\;=9\;\text{V}$ Charge on capacitor $C_{1}$ , $q_{1}\;=C_{1}V_{1}$ $\;=9\times10^{-5}\;\text{C}$ $C_{2}\;=20\;\mu\text{F}=2\times10^{-5}\;\text{F}$ when uncharged capacitor $C_{2}$ is connected with charged capacitor $C_{1}$ , then charges will flow from capacitor $C_{1}$ to $C_{2}$ till both gain the same potential i.e common potential. Common potential, $V=\frac{\;\text{ total charge }\;}{\;\text{ total capacitance }\;}$ $\;=\frac{q_{1}}{C_{1}+C_{2}}=\frac{9\times10^{-5}}{10^{-5}+2\times10^{-5}}$ $\;=\frac{9\times10^{-5}}{3\times10^{-5}}=3\;\text{V}$ Charge on capacitor $C_{2},\;q_{2}=C_{2}V$ $=2\times10^{-5}\times3=6\times10^{-5}\;\text{C}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $C_1\;=C_2=8\,\mu\mathrm{F}=8\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$ $V\;=10\,\mathrm{V}$ Since, $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in parallel. Equivalent capacitance, $C_{ev}=C_1+C_2=8\times 10^{-6}+8\times 10^{-6}=1.6\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{F}$ Total charge, $q_i=C_{eq}\cdot V$ $\;=1.6\times 10^{-5}\times 10$ $\;=1.6\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{C}$ We know that, capacitance $C=\;\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ $\Rightarrow C\propto\frac{1}{d}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{C'}{C''}=\;\frac{d''}{d'}=\;\frac{d'-40\%\ \text{of}\ d}{d'}=\;\frac{\frac{3}{5}d'}{d'}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{C^r}{C''}=\;\frac{3}{5}$ $\Rightarrow C''=\;\frac{5}{3}C'$ $\;=\;\frac{5}{3}\times 8\times 10^{-6}=\;\frac{40}{3}\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$ New capacitance, $C'''=C''+C_2$ $\;=\;\frac{40}{3}\times 10^{-6}+8\times 10^{-6}$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$ Now value of total charge, $q_f=C'''\times V$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-6}\times 10$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$ Increased value of charge, $\Delta q\;=q_f-q_1$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-5}-1.6\times 10^{-4}$ $\;=\;\frac{160}{3}\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: length of metal wire, $l_1=1\ \mathrm{cm}=10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$ $r_1\;=1\ \mathrm{mm}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$ $R_1\;=3 \times 10^{-3}\ \Omega$ Resistivity of wire is given as $\rho=R\;\frac{A}{l}$ $\;=3 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{\pi r_1^2}{l_1}=3 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{314 \times (10^{-3})^2}{10^{-2}}$ $\;=9.42 \times 10^{-7}\ \Omega-\mathrm{m}$ Again for second case, $l_2\;=3\ \mathrm{cm}=3 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m},\ r_2=0.5\ \mathrm{mm}=5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}$ $\therefore R_2\;=\rho\;\frac{l_2}{A_2}=\rho\;\frac{l_2}{\pi r_2^2}$ $\;=9.42 \times 10^{-7} \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-2}}{314 \times (5 \times 10^{-4})^2}$ $\;=0.36 \times 10^{-1}\ \Omega$ $\;=0.036\ \Omega$ © examsnet.com

Given, $v=1000 \text{ m/s}$ $\;q=10^{-16} \text{ C}$ $\;m=1 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ $N=$ Number of turns $=5000$ $I=5 \text{ A}$ $R=$ Radius of circular path of charge Magnetic field, $B=\mu_0 n I$ (where, $n=$ number of turns per unit length) $\Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \; \frac{N}{L} I$ (where, $n=\;\frac{N}{L}$ ) $\; \Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \times \; \frac{5000}{L} \times 5$ $\; \Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \times \; \frac{25000}{L}$ ........(i) Also we know that, Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time $L=v_x \times t$ (where, $v_x$ is the component of velocity along the axis of the solenoid) $\Rightarrow \;\; L=500 t$ ......(ii) Also, radius of circular path of a charged particle in uniform magnetic field is given by the formula $R=\; \frac{m v_y}{9 B}$ $(.$ where, $v_y=500 \sqrt{3})$ Putting, $B=\; \frac{\mu_0 \times 25000}{L}$ [from Eq .(i)] $\Rightarrow \;\; R=\; \frac{10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} L}{50 \mu_0}$ ......(ii) Now, time taken by the charged particle to exit the solenoid moving along the circular path making $N^{'}$ number of revolutions. $\;t^{'}=\frac{\; \text{circular distance} \;}{v_y} \Rightarrow t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi R \times \; \text{no. of revolutions} \;}{v_y}$ $\;t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi R \times N^{'}}{v_y}$ $t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi \times 10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} L \times N^{'}}{50 \mu_0 \times 500 \sqrt{3}}$ .....(iii) Now, since time taken to cover linear distance and circular distance before exiting the solenoid are same $t=t^{'}$ So, from Eqs. (i) and (ii) $\;\frac{L}{500}=\frac{2 \pi \times 10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} \times L \times N^{'}}{50 \times 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 500 \sqrt{3}} \;\; (\because \mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7})$ On solving, we get $N^{'} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-7}}{10^{-11}} = \frac{10^{-5}}{10^{-11}} = 10^6$ Hence, total number of revolution along helical path by the time it emerges the solenoid $=1 \times 10^6$ . Solution: Velocity of particle, $v = e^{-\beta x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dt} = e^{-\beta x}$ or $\frac{dx}{e^{-\beta x}} = dt$ or $e^{\beta x} dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow$ Integrating, we get $\int\limits_{0^x e}^{\beta x} dx = \int\limits_{0}^{t} dt$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\beta} \left[ e^{\beta x} \right]_{0}^{x} = \left[ t \right]_{0}^{t}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\beta} (e^{\beta x} - e^{0}) = t - 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\beta} (e^{\beta x} - 1) = t$ $e^{\beta x} = \beta t + 1$ Taking log, we get $\log (e^{\beta x}) = \log (\beta t + 1)$ $\Rightarrow \beta x = \log (\beta t + 1)$ $\Rightarrow x = \frac{1}{\beta} \cdot \log (\beta t + 1)$ So, displacement function for the particle is $x = \frac{1}{\beta} \cdot \log (\beta t + 1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: An object started to slide down an inclined plane when angle of incline (also called angle of repose) is just equals to angle of friction. Let $\theta=$ angle at which a mass started to slide down an incline. Then, force of friction $=$ downward force. $\Rightarrow \mu N = m g \sin \theta$ $\Rightarrow \mu m g \cos \theta = m g \sin \theta$ $\Rightarrow \tan \theta = \mu$ $\Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1} \mu$ Hence, angle does not depend on mass of body. So all three masses slides down at same instant at same inclination angle $(\theta)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Componentof force response for horizontal motion is $F \cos \theta$ So, acceleration of bar, $a = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ As acceleration, $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$ , we have $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ we can also express this as, $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ $\Rightarrow v dv = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m} dx$ Integrating both sides and putting $\theta = kx$ , we get $\int v dv = \int \frac{F \cos kx}{m} dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{F}{m} \int \cos kx \cdot dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{F}{m} \cdot \left(\frac{\sin kx}{k}\right)$ $\Rightarrow v^2 = \frac{2F \sin kx}{m k}$ $\Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2F \sin \theta}{m k}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Block stops on incline plane when its initial K.E is used in doing work against friction and partly it is converted into potential energy. As angle of incline is given $45^{\circ}$ so, distance covered on incline $(s)$ is related to height of block (h) as, $\Rightarrow \sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{h}{s}$ or $s=\sqrt{2} h$ Let block covers a distance $s$ over block and reaches up-to height $h$ . Then, $\text{Initial K.E of block} = \text{Work done against friction} + \text{Potential energy gained by block}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = \mu m g \cos \theta \cdot s + m g h$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = \mu m g \cos \theta \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot h + m g h$ $\Rightarrow h = \frac{\; \frac{1}{2} m u^2}{\sqrt{2} \mu m g \cos \theta + m g}$ Here, initial $\text{K.E} = \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = 100\text{ J}$ $m=5\text{ kg},\ \theta=45^{\circ},\ g=10\text{ m/s}^2$ So, $h = \frac{100}{\sqrt{2} \times 0.5 \times 5 \times 10 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 5 \times 10}$ $= \frac{100}{50 \times 1.5} = \frac{4}{3}$ Hence, distance covered over block, $s=\sqrt{2} h$ $\Rightarrow s = \frac{\sqrt{2} \times 4}{3}\text{ m} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: If earth shrinks to $\frac{1}{64}$ of its original volume; $\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 = \frac{1}{64} \left( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \right)$ Here, $r=$ new radius and $R=$ original radius $\Rightarrow r^3 = \frac{R^3}{64}$ or $r = \frac{R}{4}$ As there is no external torque, angular momentum of earth remains constant i.e., $I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$ $\ldots \left[ \because I_{\text{sphere}} = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 \right]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2}{5} M R^2 \cdot \frac{2 \pi}{T_1} = \frac{2}{5} M r^2 \frac{2 \pi}{T_2}$ $\ldots \left[ \therefore \omega = \frac{2 \pi}{T}, T = \text{time of revolution about axis} \right]$ $\Rightarrow T_2 = \frac{r^2 T_1}{R^2}$ $\Rightarrow T_2 = \frac{ \frac{R^2}{16} \times T_1 }{R^2}$ $\ldots \left[ \therefore r = \frac{R}{4} \right]$ $\Rightarrow T_2 = \frac{T_1}{16} = \frac{24}{16} \text{h}$ or $T_2 = 1.5 \text{h}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let, $I_1=$ Inertia of first (rotating)  wheel $\omega_1=$ Angular speed of first wheel $I_2=3 I_1=$ Inertia of second wheel $\omega_2=0=$ Angular speed of second wheel let $\omega=$ Angular speed of coupled wheels. According to conservation of angular momentum, total initial angular momentum $=$ total final angular momentum $\Rightarrow I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \times 0 = (I_1+I_2) \omega$ $\Rightarrow \omega = \frac{I_1 \omega_1}{I_1+I_2} = \frac{I_1 \omega_1}{I_1+3 I_1} \Rightarrow \omega = \frac{\omega_1}{4}$ Now, initial rotational energy of system is $K_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} I_2 (0)^2$ $\Rightarrow K_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2$ Final rotational kinetic energy of system is $K_2 = \frac{1}{2} (I_1+I_2) \omega^2$ $= \frac{1}{2} (I_1+3 I_1) \cdot \frac{\omega_1^2}{16}$ or $K_2 = \frac{1}{4} K_1$ $= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 I_1 \times \frac{\omega_1^2}{16}$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 \right)$ Hence, fraction of lost energy $= \frac{\Delta K}{K_1} = \frac{K_1 - K_2}{K_1} = \frac{\frac{3}{4} K_1}{K_1}$ $= \frac{3}{4} = 0.75$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let, $d=$ Density of planet, $M=$ Mass of planet $R=$ Radius of planet then density, $d=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}$ $\Rightarrow d=\frac{M}{\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right)}$ $\Rightarrow R^3=\frac{3M}{4\pi d}$ $\Rightarrow R=\left(\frac{3M}{4\pi d}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ $\ldots(i)$ Now, acceleration due to gravity $g$ is given by $g=\frac{GM}{R^2}$ Substituting $R$ from $\text{Eq. (i)}$ we gẹt, $\Rightarrow g=\frac{GM}{R^2}=\frac{GM}{\left(\frac{3}{4\pi}\cdot\frac{M}{d}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}$ $\Rightarrow g \propto M^{\frac{1}{3}} d^{\frac{2}{3}}$ Hence, ratio of acceleration due to gravity on surface of planet and that on surface of earth will be $\frac{g'}{g}=\frac{M^{\frac{1}{3}}}{M^{\frac{1}{3}}}\frac{d^{\frac{2}{3}}}{d^{\frac{2}{3}}}=\left(\frac{M'}{M}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot\left(\frac{d'}{d}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}$ Given, $\frac{M'}{M}=8$ and $\frac{d'}{d}=27$ So $\frac{g'}{g}=8^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot27^{\frac{2}{3}}=2\times9$ or $g'=18 g$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, position of particle of mass $(m = 3\,\text{kg})$ is $x = 0.3 \cos \omega t$ Velocity of particle, $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$ $\Rightarrow v = \frac{d}{dt} 0.3 \cos \omega t$ $= 0.3 \frac{d}{dt} \cos \omega t = 0.3(-\sin \omega t) \times \omega$ $= -0.3 \omega \sin \omega t$ Now, at $t = \frac{\pi}{6\omega}$ , Velocity, $v_1 = -0.3 \omega \sin \left(\omega \times \frac{\pi}{6\omega}\right)$ $\Rightarrow v_1 = -0.3 \omega \cdot \sin \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{-0.3\omega}{2}$ At $t = \frac{\pi}{3\omega}$ , $\text{Velocity, } v_2 = -0.3 \omega \sin \frac{\pi}{3}$ $v_2 = -\frac{-0.3 \sqrt{3} \omega}{3}$ Ratio of kinetic energies, $\frac{K\left(\frac{\pi}{6\omega}\right)}{K\left(\frac{\pi}{3\omega}\right)} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2}{\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2} = \left(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^2$ $\frac{K\left(\frac{\pi}{6\omega}\right)}{K\left(\frac{\pi}{3\omega}\right)} = \frac{\left(-\frac{0.3\omega}{2}\right)^2}{\left(-0.3\omega \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2} = \frac{1}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to work-energy theorem, $K\ E$ of stone $=$ Elastic potential energy of rubber band. Now, for rubber band; Young's modulus $=5 \times 10^{8} \, \text{N} / \text{m}^{2}$ Length, $L=2 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{m}$ Change of length, $\Delta L=2 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{m}$ Area of cross-section, $A=5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}^{2}$ Elastic potential energy of rubber band $=\frac{1}{2} \times Y \times (\text{strain})^{2} \times \text{volume}$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times Y \times \left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right)^{2} \times A \times L$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{8} \times \left(\frac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-2}}\right)^{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-2}$ $=25 \, \text{J}$ This energy is given to stone ( mass $=20 \, \text{g}$ ); $\Rightarrow \text{KE}\,(\text{stone}) = \text{E. P. E}\,(\text{Rubber band})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times m v^{2} = 25$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \times v^{2} = 25$ $\Rightarrow v^{2} = \frac{25 \times 2}{20 \times 10^{-3}} \Rightarrow v^{2} = 25 \times 10^{2}$ $\Rightarrow v = 5 \times 10 = 50 \, \text{m/s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As density, $\rho \propto \frac{1}{V}$ Where, $V=$ volume We have, $\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{V_1}{V_1(1 + r \Delta \theta)}$ $r=$ coefficient of cubical expansion $\Delta \theta =$ rise of temperature Since, $\rho_2 = \rho_1 (1 - r \Delta \theta)$ Here, $r = 5 \times 10^{-4} {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$ $\Delta \theta = 40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ So, in given case $\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = 1 - 5 \times 10^{-4} \times 40$ $= 1 - 2 \times 10^{-2} = 0.08$ Hence, fractional change in density $= \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_1}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_1} = \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_1} = \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} - 1$ $\Rightarrow$ Fractional change is $\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_1} = 0.08 - 1 = -0.02$ Hence, negative sign shows decrease in density. © examsnet.com

Solution: For a gas mixture, $r_{mixture}=\frac{C_{p_{(mix)}}}{C_{V_{(mix)}}}$ $=\frac{\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1+n_2}}{\frac{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}}{n_1+n_2}}$ $\Rightarrow r_{mix} =\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}}$ $...(i)$ Now, in given mixture we have $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of oxygen $(\mathrm{O}_2)$ and $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of helium $(\mathrm{He})$ Now, number of moles of oxygen, $n_1=\frac{m}{M}$ $=\frac{\text{Sample mass}}{\text{Molar mass}}$ $\Rightarrow n_1= \frac{4}{32}= \frac{1}{8}$ Similarly number of moles of helium, $n_2= \frac{4}{4}=1$ Also oxygen is a diatomic gas so, $C_{p_1}=\frac{7}{2} R$ and $C_{V_1}= \frac{5}{2} R$ Helium is monoatomic, hence $C_{p_2}=\frac{5}{2} R, C_{V_2}=\frac{3}{2} R$ Substituting these values in eq. (i) we get, $r_{mix} =\frac{\frac{1}{8} \times \frac{7}{2} R+1 \times \frac{5}{2} R}{\frac{1}{8} \times \frac{5}{2} R+1 \times \frac{3}{2} R}$ $= \frac{\frac{7}{16}+\frac{5}{2}}{\frac{5}{16}+ \frac{3}{2}}$ or $r_{mix} =\frac{7+40}{5+24}=\frac{47}{29}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Process undergone by $1$ mole gas is as shown : For an ideal monoatomic gas, ratio of specific heat $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$ For adiabatic process $A \rightarrow B$ $p_A V_A^\gamma = p_B V_B^\gamma$ Substituting values of $p_A, p_B$ and $V_B$ from graph, $\Rightarrow 32 \times 10^5 \times V_A^\gamma = 1 \times 10^5 \times (1)^\gamma$ $\Rightarrow V_A^\gamma = \left(\frac{1}{32}\right)^\gamma$ Here, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$ $\Rightarrow (V_A)^{\frac{5}{3}} = \frac{1}{32}$ or $V_A = \left(\frac{1}{32}\right)^{\frac{3}{5}} = \frac{1}{(2^5)^{\frac{3}{5}}} = \frac{1}{8} \, \text{m}^3$ Similarly for adiabatic compression $C \rightarrow D$ , $p_C V_C^\gamma = p_D V_D^\gamma$ We substitute values from graph, $\Rightarrow (1 \times 10^5) \times (8)^{\frac{5}{3}} = (32 \times 10^5) (V_D)^{\frac{5}{3}}$ $\Rightarrow V_D^{\frac{5}{3}} = 1$ $\Rightarrow V_D = 1^{\frac{3}{5}} = 1 \, \text{m}^3$ Now, Work done in process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A$ $= W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W_{DA}$ Here we substitute work done for adiabatic process, $W_{\text{adiabatic}} = \frac{p_i V_i - p_f V_f}{\gamma - 1}$ and work done of isobaric process, $W_{\text{isobaric}} = p (V_f - V_i)$ so, work done in given cycle $A B C D A$ $= W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W_{DA}$ $= \frac{p_A V_A - p_B V_B}{\gamma - 1} + p_B (V_C - V_B)$ $+ \frac{p_C V_C - p_D V_D}{\gamma - 1} + p_D (V_A - V_D)$ Substituting values of pressures and volumes, we get $W_{ABCDA} = \frac{32 \times 10^5 \times \frac{1}{8} - 1 \times 10^5 \times 1}{\frac{5}{3} - 1}$ $+ 1 \times 10^5 (8-1) + \frac{1 \times 10^5 \times 8 - 32 \times 10^5 \times 1}{\frac{5}{3} - 1}$ $+ 32 \times 10^{5} \left(\frac{1}{8} - 1\right)$ $= \frac{3 \times 10^{5} \times 3}{2} + 7 \times 10^{5} + \frac{-24 \times 10^{5} \times 3}{2} + 4 \times 10^{5} \times x - 7 = -52.5 \times 10^{5} \, \text{J}$ © examsnet.com

Also final pressure $=400\,\mathrm{mm}$ of $\mathrm{Hg}$ Now, for an isothermal change $p_i V_i = p_f V_f$ $\Rightarrow 760 \times 100 = 400 \times V_f$ $\Rightarrow V_f = \frac{760 \times 100}{400}$ $=190\,\mathrm{cm}^3 = 190\,\mathrm{cc}$ $\ldots [\because 1\,\mathrm{cm}^3 = 1\,\mathrm{cc}]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Current through a wire is given by $I=n e v_d A=n e v_d \pi R^{2}$ Here, $n=$ number density of free charge carriers $v_d=$ drift speed of electrons $R=$ radius of wire $e=$ charge on an electron Here, for two wires $A$ and $B$ $I_A=I_B$ (given) $n_A=n_B$ (wires have same material) $R_A=2 R_B$ (given) so we have, $I_A=I_B$ $\Rightarrow n e v_A \pi R_A^{2}=n e v_B \pi R_B^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v_A}{v_B}= \left(\frac{R_B}{R_A}\right)^2= \left(\frac{R_B}{2 R_B}\right)^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v_A}{v_B}= \frac{1}{4}=0.25$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Due to solenoid a magnetic filled exists around coil placed at Centre Magnetic field intensity produced by solenoid, $B = \mu_0 n I$ Flux linked with coil is $\phi_B = N \cdot B \cdot A,$ Where, $N =$ Number of turns in coil $A = \text{Area of coil}$ As current in solenoid is reversed, change in flux is $\Delta \phi_B = 2 N \cdot B \cdot A$ This change in flux produces an emf in coil given by Induced emf $e =$ Rate of change of flux $\Rightarrow e = \frac{2 N B A}{\Delta t} = \frac{2 N (\mu_0 n I) A}{\Delta t}$ Here $N = 200, A = 25 \mathrm{cm}^{2} = 25 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{m}^{2}$ $I = \frac{4}{\pi} \mathrm{A}, n = 100 \text{ tuns/cm} = 100 \times 100 \text{ turns/m}$ $\mu_0 = 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{T} \cdot \mathrm{mA}^{-1}$ and $\Delta t = 0.04 \mathrm{s}$ So induced $\text{emf}$ : $e = \frac{2 \times 200 \times 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{4} \times \frac{4}{\pi} \times 25 \times 10^{-4}}{0.04} = 0.4 \mathrm{V}$ Induced $\text{emf}$ in coil is $0.4 \mathrm{V}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The ionic radii of electronic species increases with decrease in magnitude of nuclear charge. Also, the magnitude of nuclear charge decreases with decrease in number of electrons. Therefore, more the negative charge on atom, higher will be the radii. Similarly, more the positive charge on atom, lesser will be the radii. Solution: Depression in freezing point is given as $\Delta T = i K_f \times m$ where, $i=$ van't Hoff factor $K_f=$ molal freezing point depression constant $m = \text{molality}$ Molar mass of glucose $(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_6)$ $=12 \times 6+12 \times 1+6 \times 16=180\ \text{g/mol}$ Molality of glucose $= \frac{\;\text{ Mass of solute }\;}{\;\text{ Molar mass of solute }\;} \times \frac{1}{\;\text{ Mass of solvent (kg) }\;}$ $= \frac{1.8}{180} \times \frac{1}{0.1} = 0.1\ \text{m}$ $\therefore \Delta T = 1 \times 1.86\ \text{K kg / mol} \times 0.1\ \text{m}$ $=0.186^{\circ}\ \text{C}$ $\therefore$ $\text{Freezing point of solution = Freezing point of water - Depression in freezing point}$ $=0^{\circ}\ \text{C} - 0.186^{\circ}\ \text{C} = \therefore 186^{\circ}\ \text{C}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\int \frac{x^8+4}{x^4-2 x^2+2} dx = \int \frac{x^8+4 x^4+4-4 x^4}{x^4-2 x^2+2} dx$ $= \int \frac{ (x^4+2)^2 - (2 x^2)^2 }{x^4-2 x^2+2} dx = \int x^4+2+2 x^2 dx$ $= \frac{x^5}{5} + \frac{2 x^3}{3} + 2 x + k$ $\Rightarrow A=\frac{1}{5}, B=\frac{2}{3}, C=2$ $\therefore 5A+3B+C=5$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $(\sqrt{x^2+2}+x)(\sqrt{x^2+2}-x)=2$ $I=\int \sqrt{x+\sqrt{x^2+2}} \, dx$ On putting $\sqrt{x^2+2}+x=t$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{x^2+2}-x=\frac{2}{t}$ $\therefore \sqrt{x^2+2}=\frac{t+\frac{2}{t}}{2}$ $\text{Also } \left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+2}}+1\right) dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow dx = \frac{t+\frac{2}{t}}{2t} \, dt$ $\therefore I=\int \sqrt{t} \cdot \left(\frac{t+\frac{2}{t}}{2t}\right) \, dt = \int \left(\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2}+t^{-3/2}\right) \, dt$ $\therefore = \frac{t^{3/2}}{3} - \frac{t^{1/2}}{\frac{1}{2}} + C$ $= \frac{t^2-6}{3 t^{1/2}} + C$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(\sqrt{x^2+2}+x)^2-6}{3 \sqrt{\sqrt{x^2+2}+x}} + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $I=\int \frac{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{2+\sin 2x} \, dx = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}(f(x))+C$ $I=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \int \frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+(\sin x+\cos x)^2} \, dx$ On putting $\sin x+\cos x=t$ $(\cos x-\sin x) \, dx=dt$ $\Rightarrow I=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \int \frac{dt}{1+t^2}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1} t+C$ $=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \tan^{-1}(\sin x+\cos x)+C$ $\therefore f(x)=\sin x+\cos x=\sqrt{2} \cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $I = \int\limits_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \frac{1}{\cos^8 x} \, dx = \int\limits_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} (\sec^6 x)(\sec^2 x) \, dx$ On putting $\tan x = t \Rightarrow \sec^2 x \, dx = dt$ $\therefore I = \int\limits_{-1}^{1} (t^2+1)^3 \, dt = \int\limits_{-1}^{1} (t^6 + 3t^4 + 3t^2 + 1) \, dt$ $= 2 \int\limits_{0}^{1} (t^6 + 3t^4 + 3t^2 + 1) \, dt$ $= 2 \left[ \frac{t^7}{7} + \frac{3t^5}{5} + t^3 + t \right]_{0}^{1} = 2 \left[ \;\frac{1}{7} + \frac{3}{5} + 2 \right]$ $= \frac{192}{35}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $I=\int\limits_{\alpha+1}^{\alpha} \frac{e^{x}(\alpha-x)}{(x-\alpha+1)^{2}}\,dx=\int\limits_{\alpha+1}^{\alpha} \frac{e^{x}(\alpha-x-1+1)}{(x-\alpha+1)^{2}}\,dx$ $=\int\limits_{\alpha+1}^{\alpha} e^{x} \left[\frac{1}{(x-\alpha+1)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x-\alpha+1)}\right]\,dx$ $= \left[-\frac{e^{x}}{(x-\alpha+1)}\right]_{\alpha+1}^{\alpha}$ $=-e^{\alpha}+\frac{e^{\alpha+1}}{2}=e^{\alpha} \left[\frac{e-2}{2}\right]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Consider $I_n = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin n x}{\sin x} dx, n \in N$ $I_n = \left[ \frac{2}{n-1} \sin (n-1) x \right]_{0}^{n} + I_{n-2} = I_{n-2}$ $\Rightarrow I_1 = I_3 = I_5 = I_7 \ldots$ and $I_2 + I_4 = I_6 = I_8$ Now, $I_1 = \int^{\pi}_{0} \sin x \frac{\sin x}{\sin} dx = \pi$ and $I_2 = \int_{0}^{\pi} 2 \cos x dx = 0$ $\therefore I_1 = I_3 = I_5 \ldots$ $= \pi = 2 \cdot \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = (1-(-1)^n) \frac{\pi}{2}, n \in$ odd and $I_2 = I_4 = I_6 \ldots = 0$ $= (1-(-1)^n) \frac{\pi}{2}, n$ is even. © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution On putting $y = m x$ $\Rightarrow m + x \cdot \frac{dm}{dx} = \frac{m^2}{m - m^2 - 1}$ $\Rightarrow x \frac{dm}{dx} = \frac{m^3 + m}{m - m^2 - 1}$ $\therefore \int \frac{m - m^2 - 1}{m^3 + m} \, dm = \int \frac{dx}{x}$ $\Rightarrow \int \left( \frac{1}{m^2+1} - \frac{1}{m} \right) \, dm = \ln|x| + C$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) - \ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right| = \ln|x| + C$ $\Rightarrow \tan^{-}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \ln|y| + C$ $\therefore f(y) = \ln|y|$ $\therefore f(e^3) = \ln|e^3| = 3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As, $P = \frac{a^{1/2} \cdot b^{1/2} \cdot d^{\alpha}}{c^{1/2}}$ So $\%$ error in $P = \frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\Delta a}{a}\right) \times 100 + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\Delta b}{b} \times 100\right)$ $+ \alpha \left(\frac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\Delta c}{c} \times 100\right)$ $\Rightarrow \%$ error in $P = \frac{1}{2} \times \%$ error in $a + \frac{1}{2} \times \%$ error in $b + \frac{1}{2} \times \%$ error in $c + \alpha \times \%$ error in $d$ $...(i)$ Now given, $\%$ Error in $P = 2 \%$ % Error in $a = \%$ error in $b$ $= \%$ Error in $c = \%$ error in $d = 0.5 \%$ Substituting these values in $\text{Eq. (i)}$ , we get $2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 + \alpha \times 0.5$ $\Rightarrow 2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} + \alpha\right) \Rightarrow 4 = \frac{3}{2} + \alpha$ or $\alpha = 4 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$ $\therefore \alpha$ is $\frac{5}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The gievn situation is shown below From above figure we can observe that velocity vector (tangential to circle) can be resolved into horizontal $\left(\frac{v \cos \theta}{2}\right)$ and vertical $\left(\frac{v \sin \theta}{2}\right)$ components. As, particle is executing uniform circular motion, magnitudes of components remains same but direction of vertical component is reversed. So, Initial velocity $v_1 = \frac{v \cos \theta}{2} \hat{i} + \frac{v \sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}$ and final velocity, $v_2 = \frac{v \cos \theta}{2} \hat{i} - \frac{v \sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}$ $\text{Change in velocity} = \text{final velocity} - \text{Initial velocity}$ $= v_2 - v_1$ $= \left(\frac{v \cos \theta}{2} \hat{i} - \frac{v \sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}\right) - \left(\frac{v \cos \theta}{2} \hat{i} + \frac{v \sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}\right)$ $= -2v \frac{\sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}$ Magnitude of change of velocity will be $|\Delta v| = |v_2 - v_1|$ $= 2v \frac{\sin \theta}{2} \hat{j}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As, block has a tendency to slide downwards, friction acts in upward direction. Box will not slide if friction balances component of weight acting in downward direction. $\Rightarrow f \ge m g \sin \theta$ $\text{...(i)}$ Here, $f=$ friction $=\mu N$ or $f=\mu[(m g \cos \theta)+F]$ $\text{...(ii)}$ As, applied force is perpendicular to surface of incline. Normal reaction, $N=$ net perpendicular to surface force $=m g \cos \theta+F$ Hence, by $\text{Eqs. (i)}$ and $(ii)$ we have $\mu(m g \cos \theta)+\mu F \ge m g \sin \theta$ or $F \ge \frac{m g \sin \theta - \mu m g \cos \theta}{\mu}$ $\text{...(iii)}$ here, $m=2\,\text{kg}$ $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$ $\sin \theta = \sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$ $\mu = 0.2$ So, $F \ge \left( \frac{2 \times 10 \times \frac{1}{2} - 0.2 \times 2 \times 10 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{0.2} \right)$ $\Rightarrow F \ge 50-17.32$ $\Rightarrow F \ge 3267$ or $F \ge 327$ Hence, minimum value of $F$ is $32.7\,\text{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For an elastic collision of 2 masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ with initial velocities $u_1$ and $u_2$ , final velocities of masses after collision are $v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \frac{2 m_2 u_2}{(m_1+m_2)}$ and $v_2 = \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2 + \frac{2 m_1 u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ These are obtained as standard results by applying conservation of energy and momentum equations. Now, in given case at first bullet is embedded in mass $M_1$ . Let speed of bullet + Block system be $v_1$ after collision. Then by conservation of momentum we have. $m v = (m + M_1) v_1$ or $v_1 = \frac{m v}{m + M_1}$ Note Here we are not using standard result as first collision is perfectly inelastic. Now, bullet $+M_1$ strikes $M_2$ and it is given in problem that this collision is elastic. Now, by formula we have, $v_2 = \left(\frac{(m + M_1) - M_2}{m + M_1 + M_2}\right) v_1 + 0$ and $v_3 = \left(\frac{M_2 - (m + M_1)}{M_2 + m + M_1} \times 0\right) + \left(\frac{2 (m + M_1) v_1}{m + M_1 + M_2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow v_3 = \frac{2 (m + M_1)}{m + M_1 + M_2} \cdot \frac{m v}{(m + M_1)}$ $= \frac{2 m v}{m + M_1 + M_2}$ Note You can remember these standard and useful results for finding final velocities in case of elastic collisions. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, displacement of block, $x=5 t^{2}$ As, velocity $v=\frac{d x}{d t}$ Velocity of block, $v=\frac{d}{dt}(5 t^{2})$ $=5 \times 2 t=10 t\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Now, velocity of block at $t=5\,\text{s}$ , $v_{2}=10 \times 5=50\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ and velocity of block at $t=3\,\text{s}$ is $v_{1}=10 \times 3=30\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Also, velocity of block at $t=0\,\text{s}$ , $v_{0}=10 \times 0=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Now, by work- K.E theorem, work done by a force = Change in kinetic energy So work done by force in first $3\,\text{sec}$ , $W_{1}=\frac{1}{2}m v_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m v_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m(v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})$ And work done by force in first $5\,\text{sec}$ , $W_{2}=\frac{1}{2}m v_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m v_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m(v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})$ Hence, ratio $\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}m(v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})}{\frac{1}{2}m(v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})}$ $=\frac{v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2}}{v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2}}$ or $\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\frac{v_{1}^{2}}{v_{2}^{2}}$ $...[\text{As}, v_{0}=0]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\left(\frac{30}{50}\right)^{2}=\frac{9}{25}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As rod falls, its loss of gravitational potential energy appears as gain of angular rotational energy. If rod is rotating at angular speed $\omega$ when it is horizontal then, Rotational $K E = \text{Loss of gravitational PE}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = m g h$ $\ldots(i)$ Now for rod, Moment of inertia of a solid rod about its one end, $I = \frac{M L^2}{3}$ and $h = \frac{l}{2} \sin \theta$ $\ldots[\text{see fig } \theta = 30^{\circ}]$ $= \frac{l}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{l}{4}$ So from $\text{Eq. (i)}$ , we have $\frac{1}{2} M \frac{l^2}{3} \times \omega^2 = M g \frac{l}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \omega^2 = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{g}{l}$ Here, $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $l = 0.6\,\text{m}$ So, $\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{10}{0.6} = 25$ or $\omega = 5\,\text{rad/s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\omega=314\;\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$ Let $\alpha=$ constant angular acceleration Then using $\omega_1=\omega_0+\alpha t$ We have, $\omega_1=\alpha t$ $\cdots [\because \omega_0=0]$ $\therefore 314=\alpha(2)$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{314}{2}\;\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}^2}$ Now, angle covered in 20 seconds is given by, $\theta_1=\omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ $\Rightarrow\theta_1=\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ So, $\theta_1=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{314}{2}\times(20)^2=3.14\text{ rad}$ At $t=20\text{ s},\text{ angular speed of wheel,}$ $\Rightarrow\omega_2=\omega_0+\alpha t$ $\Rightarrow\omega_2=0+\frac{314}{2}\times 20$ As, acceleration does not operates after $t=20\text{ s}$ . So, wheel now rotates freely (with constant angular speed) upto $40\text{ s}$ . Angular displacement in radians covered in another 20s of freewheeling is $\theta_2\;=\omega_1\times t$ $=314\times 20=628\text{ rad}$ Total angle covered by wheel, $\theta=(314+628)\text{ rad}$ $=942\text{ rad}$ $\therefore$ Number of revolutions of wheel $n=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}=\frac{942}{2\pi}$ $=\frac{314\times 3}{2\times 314}=150$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Amplitude of a damped oscillator varies with time as $A = A_0 \cdot e^{-\alpha t}$ $\dots(i)$ Here, $\alpha = \frac{b}{2m}, b=$ damping constant and $m=$ mass of oscillator. Solution: Radius of sphere given $=R$ Mass of sphere $=M$ Density of sphere, $d=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$ Radius of each of cavity $=\frac{R}{2}$ Mass of each of portion removed to create a cavity $=$ density $\times$ volume $=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} \times \frac{4}{3}\pi \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{M}{8}$ Now, force of gravity on $m$ , $F=$ force due to complete sphere of mass $M$ -force of mass of cavity of sphere Centre at $A$ - force of mass of cavity of sphere Centre at $B$ . $=\frac{G M m}{d^2}=\frac{G M' m}{\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{G M' m}{\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}$ $\Rightarrow F=\frac{G M m}{d^2}-\frac{GM m}{8\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{G M m}{8\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}$ $=G M m \left(\frac{1}{d^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}\right)$ $=\frac{G M m}{d^2}\left(1-\frac{1}{8\left(1+\frac{R}{2d}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(1-\frac{R}{2d}\right)^2}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: If radius $(r)$ of a circle made two times $(2 r)$ then change in area $=\pi(2 r)^2-\pi r^2$ $=3\pi r^2=3\times\;\text{ initial area }\;$ Here, initial area of soap film, $A_1=10\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ Final area has a radius twice that of initial radius. Solution: For an adiabatic change, $p V^\gamma =\;\text{ constant }\;$ $\Rightarrow T^\gamma p^{1-\gamma} =\;\text{ constant or }\; T_1^\gamma, p_1^{1-\gamma}=T_2^\gamma \cdot p_2^{1-\gamma}$ $\Rightarrow p_2^{1-\gamma}= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^\gamma \cdot p_1^{1-\gamma}$ $\Rightarrow p_2= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}} \cdot p_1$ $\;\text{ Here, }\; p_1=4\,\text{atm} ; \gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ $T_1=27^{\circ}\,\text{C}=300\,\text{K}$ $T_2=327^{\circ}\,\text{C}=600\,\text{K}$ Now, substituting values in Eq. (i), we get $p_2= \left(\frac{300}{600}\right)^{\frac{\frac{5}{3}}{1-\frac{5}{3}}} \times 4 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{-5}{2}} \times 2^2$ $=2^{2+\frac{5}{2}} =2^{\frac{9}{2}}$ Hence, the pressure of the gas in its final state is $2^{\frac{9}{2}}$ atm. © examsnet.com

Solution: Translational kinetic energy of a gas volume is $U = \frac{f}{2} R T$ Where, $f =$ degrees of freedom of gas molecules. - Now, $f = 3$ for He or Ar monoatomic and $f = 5$ for $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ or $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ Diatomic. Hence, for 3 moles of He, 1 mole Ar, 5 moles of $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ and 3 moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ . $U = 3 \times \frac{3}{2} R T + 1 \times \frac{3}{2} R T + 5 \times \frac{5}{2} R T + 3 \times \frac{5}{2} R T$ $= \left( \frac{9}{2} + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{25}{2} + \frac{15}{2} \right) R T$ $= \frac{52}{2} R T = 26 R T$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given arrangement is shown below : Distance of conductor I from origin, is $d=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{1+1}$ $\Rightarrow d=\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}=\sqrt{2}\times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}$ Magnetic field due to wire Iat origin is $B_1=\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$ or $B_1=B_0=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}$ $\ldots [\therefore I_1=I_2=1\,\text{A}]$ Now, in vector form, $bo B_1=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}\right)$ $=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi \times \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-2}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}\right)$ And field of conductor II is $bo B_2=\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi y}(-\hat{k})$ $=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi \times 10^{-2}}(-\hat{k})$ $\ldots[\therefore y=1\,\text{cm}=1\times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}]$ Hence, magnetic field due to both conductors, $bo B=bo B_1+bo B_2$ $=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}\right) \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\times 10^{-2}}+\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}(-\hat{k})\times \frac{1}{10^{-2}}$ $\Rightarrow bo B=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi \times 10^{-2}} \hat{\frac{i}{2}-\frac{j}{2}-k}$ Hence, ratio $\frac{bo B}{B_0}$ is $\frac{bo B}{B_0}= \frac{ \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi \times 10^{-2}} \left(\frac{\hat{i}}{2}-\frac{\hat{j}}{2}-\hat{k}\right) }{ \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi \times \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-2}} } = \left(\frac{\hat{i}}{2}-\frac{\hat{j}}{2}-\hat{k}\right) \sqrt{2}$ $\frac{\hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}\hat{k}$ $\frac{bo B}{B_0}= \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\sqrt{2}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Torque on a magnet (dipole moment $\text{bo} m$ ) when it is placed in region of magnetic field (Intensity B) is $\tau = \text{bo} M \times \text{bo} B$ Where, $\text{bo} M = M \cdot \hat{\text{bo} u}$ $M =$ magnitude of dipole moment and $\hat{\text{bo} u} =$ unit vector in direction of $\text{bo} M$ Now in case I given, $\text{bo} B = \dot{B} \hat{i} \; \text{ and } \; \text{bo} M = \frac{M}{2} (\sqrt{3} \hat{i} + \hat{j})$ Hence, torque is $\tau_1 = \frac{M}{2} (\sqrt{3} \hat{i} + \hat{j}) \times B \hat{i}$ $= \frac{MB}{2} (\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) = \frac{MB}{2} (-\hat{k})$ Now, given, $\left| \tau_1 \right| = 0.06\ \mathrm{N} - \mathrm{m}$ So, $0.06 = \frac{M B}{2}$ or $M B = 0.12$ units Now, when $\text{bo} M = M \left( \frac{\hat{i} + \sqrt{3} \hat{j}}{2} \right)$ and $\text{bo} B = 2 B \hat{j}$ then, torque will be $\tau_2 = \text{bo} M \times \text{bo} B$ $= \frac{M}{2} (\hat{i} + \sqrt{3} \hat{j}) \times 2 B \hat{j} = M B (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) = M B (\hat{k})$ $\therefore$ Magnitude of torque is $\left| \tau_2 \right| = M B = 0.12\ \mathrm{N} - \mathrm{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: de-Broglie wavelength is given by $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$ $\Rightarrow \text{Momentum of particle,}$ $p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6.60 \times 10^{-9}} = 1 \times 10^{-27} \, \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ $\Rightarrow m v = 1 \times 10^{-27}$ or $v = \frac{1 \times 10^{-27}}{1 \times 10^{-30}} \Rightarrow v = 10^{3} \, \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ $\therefore$ Kinetic energy of particle is $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 10^{-30} \times (10^{3})^{2}$ $= 0.5 \times 10^{-24} \, \mathrm{J}$ As, $1 \, \mathrm{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \mathrm{J}$ Kinetic energy of particle, $K = \frac{0.5 \times 10^{-24}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \, \mathrm{eV} = 0.3125 \times 10^{-5}$ $= 3.25 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{eV} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{eV}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Alkali metals are strong reducing agents because after the removal of the only valence electron $(n s^{1})$ they can gain the electronic configuration of noble gases $(n-1) p^{6}$ , that is more stable electronic configuration. $\mathrm{KO}_{2}$ is paramagnetic oxide due to the presence of 1 unpaired electrons. Solution: Ag crystallises in an fcc lattice, so each unit cell contains 4 Ag atoms and 8 tetrahedral voids. Solution: For the zero order reaction, $A \rightarrow 3B$ the half-life is given by the formula $t_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{A_0}{2k}$ where, $A_0$ is the initial concentration and $k$ is the rate constant. After $15\ \text{s}$ the concentration of $A\ (0.1\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})$ is reduced to its half value $(0.05\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})$ , So, $t_{\frac{1}{2}} = 15\ \text{s}$ $k = \frac{01}{2\times 15} = 0.0033\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ For zero order reaction after time ' $t$ ' the concentration of reactant $A$ is given by formula $[A] = [A_0] - kt$ After $t = 20\ \text{s}$ $[A] = 0.1\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1} - 0.0033\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1} \times 20\ \text{s}$ $= 0.033\ \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}$ This implies that $(0.1 - 0.033) = 0.067$ moles of reactant $A$ are converted to product $B$ . Since, 1 mole of $A$ gives 3 moles of $B$ , so $0.067$ moles of reactant $A$ will give $(0.066 \times 3) = 0.198$ moles of $B$ , i.e. $1.98 \times 10^{-1}$ moles. © examsnet.com

Solution: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is the mathematical representation for the variation of the extent of adsorption $\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)$ with pressure $(p)$ at a given temperature. $\frac{x}{m}=k \cdot p^{1/n}(n>l)$ where ' $x$ ' is the mass of the gas adsorbed on mass ' $m$ ' of the adsorbent at pressure ' $p$ '. ' $k$ ' and ' $n$ ' are constants that depend on the nature of the adsorbent and the gas at a particular temperature. Experimentally, it was determined that the extent of gas adsorption varies with pressure raised to the power $\frac{1}{n}$ until saturation pressure $p_s$ is reached. At high pressure, $\frac{x}{m}$ becomes independent of pressure. Hence, Freundlich equation becomes $\frac{x}{m}=k \cdot p^0 \Rightarrow \frac{x}{m}=k$ Thus, the Freundlich adsorption isotherm fails at higher pressure. © examsnet.com

Solution: One of the most important properties of colloidal solutions is that colloidal particles possess a definite type of electrical charge. Solution: Acidic character of oxides in group 15 to 18 . elements decreases down the group. As we move down the group, the atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases. In $\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}(I), \mathrm{P}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$ (II) and $\mathrm{As}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$ (IV), N, $\mathrm{P}$ and As are in $+3$ oxidation state respectively whereas in $\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ (III) the $\mathrm{N}$ is in $+5$ oxidation state. So, the acidity order is $\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5} > \mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} > \mathrm{P}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} > \mathrm{As}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} \; \text{, i.e. III } \; > \; \text{ I } \; > \; \text{ II } \; > \; \text{ IV } \;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Whenever one of the halogens is involved in oxidising a species in solution, the halogen is reduced to a halide ion associated with water molecules. The following reactions illustrate this process $\mathrm{F}_2(g) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{F}^{-}(aq)$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}_2(g) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}(aq)$ $\mathrm{Br}_2(l) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Br}^{-}(aq)$ $\mathrm{I}_2(g) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{I}^{-}(aq)$ Smaller the size of ion, higher is the energy released when the ion is hydrated. Since, the size of ions increases in the order $\mathrm{F}^{-} < \mathrm{Cl}^{-} < \mathrm{Br}^{-} < \mathrm{I}^{-}$ . The order of hydration energy is $\mathrm{F}^{-}(aq) > \mathrm{Cl}^{-}(aq) > \mathrm{Br}^{-}(aq) > \mathrm{I}^{-}(aq)$ Because of very high hydration enthalpy of the fluoride ion, $\mathrm{F}_2$ gets very easily reduced followed by $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ , then $\mathrm{Br}_2$ and $\mathrm{I}_2$ . Therefore, the correct order of oxidising power of halogens is $\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $\cos A = \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$ $2bc \cos A = b^2+c^2-a^2$ Let $bc = k^2$ ⇒ $c = \frac{k^2}{b}$ ⇒ $2k^2 \cos A = b^2 + \frac{k^4}{b^2} - a^2$ ⇒ $b^4 - a^2b^2 - 2k^2 b^2 \cos A + k^4 = 0$ If triangle exists, then $(a^2+2k^2 \cos A)^2 - 4 \times 1 \times k^4 \geq 0$ ⇒ $(a^2+2k^2 \cos A - 2k^2)(a^2+2k^2 \cos A + 2k^2) \geq 0$ ⇒ $[a^2+2k^2(\cos A-1)][a^2+2k^2(\cos A+1)] \geq 0$ ⇒ $\left(a^2-4k^2 \sin^2 \frac{A}{2}\right)\left(a^2+4k^2 \cos \frac{A}{2}\right) \geq 0$ Since, $a^2+4k^2 \cos^2 \frac{A}{2} \geq 0$ or $a^2-4k^2 \sin \frac{A}{2} \geq 0$ ⇒ $a^2 \geq 4k^2 \sin^2 \frac{A}{2}$ ⇒ $\sin^2 \frac{A}{2} \leq \frac{a^2}{4k^2}$ ⇒ $\sin \frac{A}{2} \leq \frac{a}{2k}$ ⇒ $\sin \frac{A}{2} \leq \frac{a}{2\sqrt{bc}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, equation is $x^2-5x-14=0$ ⇒ $x^2-7x+2x-14=0$ ⇒ $(x-7)(x+2)=0$ $c=7, -2$ Length of semi - conjugate $= 7$ Length of semi - tranverse axis $= (-2)^2=4$ ∴ $a=4, b=7$ Equation of hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{16} - \frac{y^2}{49} = 1$ $e=\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^2} = \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^2}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{16+49}{16}} = \frac{\sqrt{65}}{4}$ Coordinate of focus on positive X - axis $=(ae, 0)$ $=\left(4 \times \frac{\sqrt{65}}{4}, 0\right)=(\sqrt{65}, 0)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Equation of chord of contact drawn a point p is $\frac{\alpha x}{a^{2}} - \frac{\beta y}{b^{2}} = 1$ ⇒ $\frac{x}{\frac{a^{2}}{\alpha}} + \frac{y}{\frac{b^{2}}{\beta}} = 1$ ∴ x - intercept is $\frac{a^{2}}{\alpha}$ and y - intercept is $-\frac{b}{\beta}$ . ∴ The sum of square of intercept $= \frac{a^{4}}{\alpha^{2}} + \frac{b^{4}}{\beta^{2}}$ © examsnet.com
