Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let the coordinate of $Q$ be $(x, y, z)$ . $OP = \sqrt{3^2+(12)^2+4^2} = 13$ $QP=13-3=10$ $Q$ divides $OP$ in the ratio $3:10$ or $3:13$ $Q\left(\pm \frac{3\times 3}{13}, \pm \frac{3\times 12}{13}, \pm \frac{3\times 4}{13}\right)$ $Q\left(\pm \frac{9}{13}, \pm \frac{36}{13}, \pm \frac{12}{13}\right)$ Sum of all coordinates of $Q=\pm \left(\frac{9}{13}+\frac{36}{13}+\frac{12}{13}\right)=\pm \frac{57}{13}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let the intersection point of a plane and a line be $p(x,y,z)$ . Coordinate of $P=\left(\frac{2\times 3+1\times(-3)}{2+1}, \frac{2\times 1+1\times(-2)}{2+1}, \frac{2\times(-2)+1\times 7}{2+1}\right)$ $=(1,0,1)$ $\text{DE's}$ of line $AB$ is $3-(-3),1-(-2),-2-7$ $=\langle 6,3,-9\rangle$ Equation of plane is $6(x-1)+3(y-0)-9(z-1)=0$ ⇒ $6x-6+3y-9z+9=0$ ⇒ $6x+3y-9z=-3$ ⇒ $\frac{x}{\frac{-1}{2}} + \frac{y}{-1} + \frac{z}{\frac{1}{3}} =0$ ∴ y - intercept is $-1$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $x_{n+1} = \frac{a+bx_n}{b+cx_n}$ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_{n+1}= \frac{a+b\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_n}{b+c\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_n}$ ∴ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_{n+1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_n = y$ (let) $y=\frac{a+by}{b+cy}$ ⇒ $by+cy^2=a+by\Rightarrow cy^2=a$ ⇒ $y^2=\frac{a}{c}\Rightarrow y=\sqrt{\frac{a}{c}}$ ∴ $\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}x_n = \sqrt{\frac{a}{c}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{(\cos x-1)(\cos x-e^{x})}{x^{n}}$ $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0}\left(\frac{\cos x-1}{x^2}\right) \times \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0}\frac{\cos x-e^{x}}{n^{n-2}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{-2 \sin^2 \frac{x}{2}}{4 \times \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2} \times \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{\cos x - e^{x}}{x^{n-2}}$ $= -\frac{1}{2} \times \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{\cos x - e^{x}}{x^{n-2}} [\text{0/0 form}]$ Apply L'hospital rule $-\frac{1}{2} \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{-\sin x - e^{x}}{(n-2) x^{n-3}}$ $= -\frac{1}{2} \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{-\sin x - e^{x}}{(n-2)} \times \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{1}{x^{n-3}}$ $= \frac{1}{2}(n-2) \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0} \frac{1}{x^{n-3}}$ The above limit is finite if $n-3=0$ . ∴ $n=3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0}\frac{x^2 \log(\cos x)}{\log (1+x^2)}$ Apply L'hospital rule $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0}\frac{x^2 \times \frac{1}{\cos x} (-\sin x)+\log(\cos x) \times 2x}{\frac{1}{1+x^2}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow0}(1+x^2)[-x^2 \tan x+2x \log \cos x]$ Substitute $0$ for $x$ $(1+0)[0+0]=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $y=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ ⇒ $cxy+yd=ax+b\Rightarrow x(cy-a)=b-yd$ ⇒ $x=\frac{b-yd}{cy-a}$ ⇒ $\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{(cy-a)(-d)-(b-yd)c}{(cy-a)^2}$ $=\frac{-cdy+ad-bc+cdy}{c^2y^2+a^2-2acy} = \frac{ad-bc}{c^2y^2+a^2-2acy}$ Here, $P=c^2, R=a^2, Q=-2ac$ $P+Q+R= c^2-2ac+a^2$ $=(c-a)^2 \text{ or } (a-c)^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $f(x) = \begin{cases} \tan^{-1}x, & \text{ when }|x|<1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(|x|-1), & \text{ when }|x|>1 \end{cases}$ $= \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(x-1), & \text{ when } x>1 \\ \tan^{-1}, & \text{ when } -1 < x<1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(-x-1), & \text{ when } x<-1 \end{cases}$ $f'(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}, & \text{ when } x>1 \\ \frac{1}{1+x^2}, & \text{ when } -1 < x<1 \\ \frac{-1}{2}, & \text{ when } x<-1 \end{cases}$ $\lim\limits_{x\to -1^{-}} f'(x) = \frac{-1}{2}$ $\lim\limits_{x\to -1^{+}} f'(x) = \lim\limits_{x\to -1^{+}} \frac{1}{1+x^2} = \frac{1}{2}$ ∴ $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $-1$ $\lim\limits_{x\to -1^{+}} f'(x) = \frac{1}{2}$ $\lim\limits_{x\to -1^{-}} f'(x) = \lim\limits_{x\to -1^{-}} \frac{1}{1+x^2} = \frac{1}{2}$ $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=1$ ∴ $f'(-1)$ does not exist. ∴ The domain of the function is $R-(-1)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $x=a\cos^{3}\theta$ $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=3a\cos^{2}\theta(-\sin\theta)$ and $y=a\sin^{3}\theta$ Similarly, $\frac{dy}{d\theta}=3a\sin^{2}\theta\cos\theta$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}}=\frac{3a\sin^{2}\theta\cos\theta}{-3a\cos^{2}\theta\sin\theta}=-\tan\theta$ Again differenciating w.rt.x, $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\sec^{2}\theta\times\frac{d\theta}{dx}$ $=-\sec^{2}\theta\times\frac{1}{-3a\cos^{2}\theta\sin\theta}$ $=\frac{\csc\theta\sec^{4}\theta}{3a}$ $\left.\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right|_{\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\times4}{3a}=\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3a}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, equation of curve $\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^x +\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^x=2$ On differentiating w.r.t. x to determine the slope $n\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^{n-1} \times \frac{1}{a}+n\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^{n-1} \times \frac{1}{b} \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ ⇒ $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{b}{a} \left(\frac{xb}{ya}\right)^{n-1}=-\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{n-1} \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^n$ $\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(a,b)} = -\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{n-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^n=-\frac{b}{a}$ Equation of tangent is $y-b=\left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)(x-a)$ ⇒ $ay-ab=-bx+ab \Rightarrow bx+ay=2ab$ ⇒ $\frac{b}{2a} + \frac{y}{2b} =1$ ∴ $x$ -intercept is $2a$ and $y$ - intercept is $2b$ . ∴ Sum of intercept $= 2(a+b)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution The curve $2y = e^{-x/2}$ can be determined by differentiate w.r.t. x $2 \frac{dy}{dx} = e^{-x/2} \left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)$ ⇒ $m = \left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{(0,1/2)} = \frac{-1}{4}$ Angle made with Y - axis $= \frac{\pi}{2} + \tan^{-1} |m|$ ⇒ $\tan^{-1}(k) = \frac{\pi}{2} + \tan^{-1} \frac{1}{4}$ $k = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \tan^{-1} \frac{1}{4}\right) = \cot\left(\tan^{-1} \frac{1}{4}\right)$ $= \cot(\cot^{-1}4) = 4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, radius of circle $=10\,\text{cm}\,(OB=OD)$ Diagonal of rectangle $=$ Diameter of circle $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}=20$ ⇒ $l^2+b^2 = 400$ ⇒ $l^2 =400-b^2$ Area of rectangle $(A) = l \times b$ Let $A'=A^2=l^2b^2$ ⇒ $A' = (400-b^2)b^2=400b^2-b^4$ ⇒ $\frac{dA'}{db} = 800b-4b^3 \Rightarrow \frac{dA'}{db}=0$ ⇒ $b^2=200\ [\because b\neq 0]$ $b=10\sqrt{2}$ $\frac{dA'}{db^2} = 800 - 12b^2$ $\left.\frac{dA'}{db^2}\right|_{b=10\sqrt{2}} = 800-12\times(10\sqrt{2})^2$ $=800-12\times200<0$ Area is maximum when $b=10\sqrt{2}$ $l^2=400-b^2=400-200=20$ $l=10\sqrt{2}$ Area $=l \times b$ $= 10\sqrt{2} \times 10\sqrt{2} = 200\text{ cm}^3$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution $f(x) = \cos x - 1 + \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}$ $f'(x) = -\sin x + \frac{2x}{2} - \frac{3x^2}{3} = -\sin x + x - x^2$ $f'(x) = 0, \text{ when } x = 0$ $f''(x) = -\cos x + 1 - 2x$ $f''(0) = -\cos 0 + 1 - 2 \times 0$ $= -1 + 1 - 0 = 0$ ∵ $0$ has no extremum value. © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $y = \left(1+\frac{1}{\sin^{n}\alpha}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{\cos^{n}\alpha}\right)$ $y = 1 + \frac{1}{\sin^{n}\alpha} + \frac{1}{\cos^{n}\alpha} + \frac{1}{\sin^{n}\alpha \cos^{n}\alpha}$ $y = 1 + \sin^{-n}\alpha + \cos^{-n}\alpha + \sin^{-n}\alpha \cos^{-n}\alpha$ $\frac{dy}{d\alpha} = \frac{-n}{\sin^{n+1}\alpha} \cos \alpha + \frac{n}{\cos^{n+1}\alpha} \sin \alpha + \frac{1}{\sin^{n}\alpha} \left[ \frac{n}{\sin^{n+1}\alpha} \sin \alpha \right]$ $+ \frac{1}{\cos^{n}\alpha} \left[ \frac{-n}{\sin^{n+1}\alpha} \cos \alpha \right]$ $= \frac{-n \cos \alpha}{\sin^{n+1}\alpha} \left(1+\frac{1}{\cos^{n}\alpha}\right) + \frac{n \sin \alpha}{\cos^{n+1}\alpha} \left(1+\frac{1}{\sin^{n}\alpha}\right)$ $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0, \text{ where } \alpha = \frac{\pi}{4}$ $y$ at $\alpha = \frac{\pi}{4} = (1+\sqrt{2^n})^2 (1+\sqrt{2})^2$ $= (1+\sqrt{2^n})^2 = (1+2^{n/2})^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Given, $\int 	an^{-1}(1-x+x^2) \, dx + \int 	an^{-1} x \, dx + \int 	an^{-1}(1-x) \, dx$ $= \int \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} - \cot^{-1}(1-x+x^2) \right] dx + \int \tan^{-1} x \, dx + \int \tan^{-1}(1-x) \, dx$ $= \frac{\pi x}{2} - \int \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1-x+x^2} \right) dx + \int \tan^{-1} x \, dx + \int \tan^{-1}(1-x) \, dx$ $= \frac{\pi x}{2} - \int \tan^{-1} \left[ \frac{x+(1-x)}{1-x(1-x)} \right] dx + \int \tan^{-1} x \, dx + \int \tan^{-1}(1-x) \, dx$ $\frac{\pi x}{2} - \int \left[ \tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1}(1-x) - \tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1}(1-x) \right] dx$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} x + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} - x^{5}}}$ $I = \int \frac{1}{x \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}} dx$ Let $x^{3} = \sin^{2} t$ $3 x^{2} dx = 2 \sin t \cos t dt$ $\Rightarrow I = \frac{1}{3} \int \frac{3 x^{2} dx}{x^{3} \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}$ $= \frac{2}{3} \int \frac{1}{\sin^{2} t \cos t} \sin t \cos t dt$ $= \frac{2}{3} \int \csc t dt$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log |\csc t - \cot t| + C$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log \left| \frac{1 - \cos t}{\sin t} \right| + C$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2} t}}{\sqrt{\sin^{2} t}} \right| + C$ $= \frac{1}{3} \log \left( \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}{\sqrt{x^{3}}} \right|^{2} \right) + C$ Here, $f(x) = \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}{\sqrt{x^{3}}} \right|^{2}$ $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}}}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3/2}} \right|^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{1 - \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8}}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}} \right)^{2} = (\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7})^{2}$ From option (a) $\colon \left( \frac{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{7}} \right) \times \left( \frac{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}} \right)$ $= (\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7})^{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I=\int\frac{1}{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}\,dx$ $I=2\int\frac{\cos\frac{\pi}{3}}{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}\,dx=2\int\frac{\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}-x\right)}{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}\,dx$ $=2\int\left[\frac{\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}+\frac{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\sin x}{\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos x}\right]\,dx$ $=2\int\left[\cot\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+\tan x\right]\,dx$ $=2\left[\log\left|\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right|-\log\left|\cos x\right|\right]+C$ $=2\left[\log\left|\frac{\sin x\cos\frac{\pi}{3}}{\cos x}-\frac{\cos x\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{\cos x}\right|\right]+C$ $=2\left[\log\left|\frac{\tan x-\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|\right]+C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int (1+x) \log (1+x^{2}) \, dx$ Using by parts $\log (1+x^{2}) \left[ \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right] - \int \frac{2x}{1+x^{2}} \times \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int \frac{x^{2} (x+2)}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int \frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2}}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int (x+2) - \frac{x+2}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 2x \right) + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{2x}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $+ 2 \int \frac{1}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x +$ $\frac{1}{2} \log (1+x^{2})$ $+ 2 \tan^{-1} x$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x + \frac{1}{2} \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x + 2 \tan^{-1} x + C$ $\text{Compare I with } \left( x + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \right)$ $\log (1+x^{2}) + g(x) + C, \text{ we get }$ $g(x) = -2x - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 2 \tan^{-1} x$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}} \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}\,dx$ $= \int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}} \frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sqrt{\sin x} + \sqrt{\cos x}}\,dx$ $\dots(i)$ $= \int_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}} \frac{\sqrt{\cos x\left(\frac{9\pi}{22}+\frac{\pi}{11}-x\right)}}{\sqrt{\sin\left(\frac{9\pi}{22}+\frac{\pi}{11}-x\right) + \sqrt{\cos\left(\frac{9\pi}{22}+\frac{\pi}{11}-x\right)}}}\,dx$ $= \int_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}} \frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\cos x} + \sqrt{\sin x}}\,dx$ $\dots(ii)$ On adding both Eqs. (i) and (ii), $2I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}} dx = \left[ x \right]_{\frac{\pi}{11}}^{\frac{9\pi}{22}}$ $= \frac{9\pi}{22} - \frac{\pi}{11}$ $I = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{7\pi}{22} \right] = \frac{7\pi}{44}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution When, $m=n, m \in Z$ Let $I = \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \cos^{2}(m x) \, dx + \frac{1}{2} \int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} 2 \sin(m x) \cos(m x) \, dx$ $\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \cos^2 m x dx + \frac{1}{2} \int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin 2 m x dx$ Using the formula. $\int\limits_{0}^{2a} f(x) = \begin{cases} 2\int\limits_{0}^{a} f(x) dx & \text{if } f(2a-x)=f(x) \\ 0 & \text{if } f(2a-x)=-f(x) \end{cases}$ and $\int\limits_{-a}^{a} f(x) = \begin{cases} 2\int\limits_{0}^{a} f(x) dx & \text{if } f(-x)=f(x) \\ 0 & \text{if } f(-x)=-f(x) \end{cases}$ $I = 2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \cos^2 m x dx + 0$ $= \int_{0}^{\pi} (1 + \cos 2 m x) \, dx$ $= \left[ x + \frac{\sin 2 m x}{2 m} \right]_0^{\pi} = \pi$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int\limits_{2}^{5} \left[ \sqrt{x+2\sqrt{x-1}} + \sqrt{x-2\sqrt{x-1}} \right] \, dx$ $= \int\limits_{2}^{5} \left[ \sqrt{x-1+1+2\sqrt{x-1}} + \sqrt{x-1+1-2\sqrt{x-1}} \right] \, dx$ $= \int\limits_{2}^{5} \left[ \sqrt{(\sqrt{x-1}+1)^2} + \sqrt{(\sqrt{x-1}-1)^2} \right] \, dx$ $= \int\limits_{2}^{5} \left[ \sqrt{x-1}+1+\sqrt{x-1}-1 \right] \, dx$ $= 2 \int\limits_{2}^{5} \sqrt{x-1} \, dx$ $= 2 \int\limits_{2}^{5} (x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}} \, dx$ $= 2 \times \frac{2}{3} \left[ (x-1)^{3/2} \right]_{2}^{5}$ $= \frac{4}{3} \left[ 4^{3/2} - 1^{3/2} \right]$ $= \frac{4}{3} \left[ 8-1 \right]$ $= \frac{28}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: To find height of building we have to analyze vertical motion of ball. Now in given case, Initial velocity, $u_y = u \sin \theta$ $\Rightarrow u_y = 15 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 15 \times \frac{1}{2} = 7.5\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ Acceleration, $a_y = -g = -10\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$ Time to reach the ground $=3\ \mathrm{s}$ . Now using $h = u_y t + \frac{1}{2} a_y t^2$ , we get $h = 7.5 \times 3 - \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 3^2$ $= 225 - 45 = -22.5\ \mathrm{m}$ So, height of building $=22.5\ \mathrm{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\text{bo } u = (-\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \, \text{m}/\text{s}$ $a = (6\hat{i}+4\hat{j}) \, \text{ms}^{-2}, t=2 \, \text{s}$ using $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$ , we get Displacement, $s = (-\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times 2 + \frac{1}{2}(6\hat{i}+4\hat{j}) \times 2^2$ $= -2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+12\hat{i}+8\hat{j}$ $\text{s} = (10\hat{i}+10\hat{j}) \, \text{m}$ or magnitude of displacement vector $|s| = \sqrt{10^2+10^2} = 10\sqrt{2}$ $= 14.14 \, \text{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As speed is constant, net force on block is zero. Downward force $=$ upward pull $\Rightarrow m g \sin\theta = F$ Here, $\theta=30^{\circ}$ and $F=500\ \mathrm{N}$ $\text{ so, } m g \sin 30^{\circ} = 500$ $\Rightarrow m g \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 500$ $\Rightarrow m g = 1000\ \mathrm{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given arrangement of block and rope is as shown Free body diagram of block is shown. Tension can be resolved into components (shown in FBD). for equilibrium, $T \cos \theta = m g$ and $T \sin \theta = F$ $\Rightarrow$ Dividing these, we get $\frac{T \sin \theta}{T \cos \theta} = \frac{F}{m g}$ or $\tan \theta = \frac{F}{m g}$ Here, $F = 40\,\text{N}$ and $m g = 80\,\text{N}$ Hence, $\tan \theta = \frac{40}{80}$ or $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown  below: As block is pulled at a constant speed, the net force on block is zero. $\Rightarrow F=m g \sin \theta$ Now work done by this force $(F=$ tension $)$ in displacing block by a distance $d$ along the incline, Work done $=$ Force $\times$ Displacement $\Rightarrow W=m g \sin \theta \times d$ Here, $m=2\ \text{kg}, \theta=30^{\circ}, d=4\ \text{m}$ $W=2 \times 10 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 4=40\ \text{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, Force on block, $\text{bo} F = F \hat{i}$ Acceleration of block, $a = \beta \cdot x = 5 x$ Now, let instantaneous velocity of block is $v$ , then $\frac{d v}{d t} = a$ $\Rightarrow \Rightarrow \frac{d v}{d x} \frac{d x}{d t} = a$ $\Rightarrow v \frac{d v}{d x} = a$ $\text{ or } v d v = a d x$ Now, integrating between limits $x_1 = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ to $x_2 = 5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ $\Rightarrow \int_{v_1}^{v_2} v \cdot d v = \int\limits_{x_1}^{x_2} 5 x \cdot d x$ $\Rightarrow \left[ \frac{v^2}{2} \right]_{v_1}^{v_2} = \frac{5}{2} \left[ x^2 \right]_{x_1}^{x_2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} (v_2^2 - v_1^2) = \frac{5}{2} (x_2^2 - x_1^2)$ Here, $x_1 = 2 \text{ cm}$ and $x_2 = 5 \text{ cm}$ so $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} (v_2^2 - v_1^2) = \frac{5}{2} (5^2 - 2^2) \times (10^{-2})^2$ Multiplying with mass of body $m = 1 \text{ kg}$ , we get $\frac{1}{2} m (v_2^2 - v_1^2) = \frac{5}{2} \times m \times 21 \times 10^{-2}$ $\Rightarrow$ Change in kinetic energy $= \frac{5}{2} \times 1 \times 21 \times (10^{-2})^2 = 525 \times 10^{-4}$ As change in $KE = \text{Work done}$ $\therefore \text{Work done} = 52.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Torque on a particle, $\tau = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ $\vec{r} =$ position vector of particle $\vec{F} =$ Force vector As particle is located at $(1,1,1)$ m; position vector of particle, $\vec{r} = x \hat{i} + y \hat{j} + z \hat{k} = (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\,\text{m}$ And direction of force is along vector $(\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ Hence, unit vector in direction of force, $\hat{n} = \frac{\hat{i} + \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$ force in vector form, $\vec{F} = \text{magnitude} \times \text{direction}$ $= 2 \hat{n}$ $= 2 \frac{\hat{i} + \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} (\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \,\text{N}$ So torque, $\tau = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ $= \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{vmatrix}$ $= \hat{i}(1 \times 0 - \sqrt{2} \times 1) - \hat{j}(1 \times 0 - \sqrt{2} \times 1)$ $+ \hat{k}(1 \times \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} \times 1)$ $= -\sqrt{2} \hat{i} + \sqrt{2} \hat{j} + 0 \hat{k}$ $\text{Torque} = (-\sqrt{2} \hat{i} + \sqrt{2} \hat{j})\,\text{N-m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For a rectangular lamina moment of inertia about its centroidal axis given by $I_{CM}=\frac{V_c}{12}(a^2+b^2)$ Now, moment of inertia of lamina about an axis passing through one of vertices is obtained by using parallel axis theorem. Now, moment of Inertia about any vertex, $I_{\text{corner}}=I_{CM}+m \cdot d^2$ $d=$ distance between axes $I_{\text{corner}}=\frac{m}{12}(a^2+b^2)+m d^2$ Now from diagram, $d^2=\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$ $I_{\text{corner}}=\frac{m}{12}(a^2+b^2)+m \left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{4}\right)$ $=m \left(\frac{a^2+a l^2+b^2+3b^2}{12}\right)$ $=m \left(\frac{4(a^2+b^2)}{12}\right)$ $=m \left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{3}m(a^2+b^2)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is given below : Block stops when net force on block is zero. $\Rightarrow$ Component of weight along incline $=$ Spring force $\Rightarrow m g \sin\theta=k x$ Substituting $m=10\text{ kg},\theta=45^{\circ}$ $k=100\sqrt{2}\text{ Nm}^{-1}$ , we get $10\times10\times\sin45^{\circ}=100\sqrt{2}\times x$ $\Rightarrow x=0.5\text{ m}$ As, unstretched length of spring is $0.8\text{ m}$ , total length of spring (or distance of block from top) in equilibrium, $l=0.5+0.8=1.3\text{ m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let at some extension $x$ centre of sphere has a speed $v$ and angular speed of rotation of sphere be $\omega$ . Then Total energy of system, $E=$ Rotational Energy + Translational energy + Spring energy $\Rightarrow E=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2+\frac{1}{2}Mv^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ $\text{ for sphere, } I=\frac{2}{5}MR^2$ Also no ship condition is, $v=R\omega$ So, total energy, $E=\frac{1}{2}Mv^2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{5}MR^2\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ As total energy remains constant, $\frac{dE}{dt}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx} \left\{ \frac{1}{2}Mv^2+\frac{1}{5}Mv^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \right\} =0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{7}{10}Mv^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \right) =0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{7}{10}M \cdot 2v \frac{dv}{dt} + \frac{1}{2}k \cdot 2x \frac{dx}{dt} =0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{7}{5}M v a + \frac{kx}{2} v =0 \Rightarrow a = -\frac{5}{7} \frac{k}{M} \cdot x$ As, acceleration $\propto$ - displacement so, motion is $\text{SHM}$ . Hence, $\omega^2 = \frac{5}{7} \frac{k}{M}$ Time period of oscillation, $\Rightarrow T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{ \frac{7}{5} \frac{M}{k} }$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $v=$ escape speed So, $v_{\text{escape}}=v=\sqrt{\frac{G M}{R} \times 2}$ $...(i)$ $M=$ mass of earth, $R=$ Radius of earth Now, when an object is projected with speed $4 v$ from surface of earth, let its speed at infinity is $v^{'}$ Then by energy conservation, $\text{Initial energy}=\text{final energy}$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{G M m}{R}+\frac{1}{2}m(4v)^2=0+\frac{1}{2}m(v^{'})^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{-G M m}{R}+16\left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2\right)=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $...(ii)$ Substituting value of $v$ from Eq. (i) in Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{-G M m}{R}+16\left(\frac{1}{2} m \frac{G M \times 2}{R}\right)=\frac{1}{2} m (v^{'})^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{15 G M m}{R}=\frac{1}{2} m (v^{'})^2$ $\Rightarrow v'^{2}=15 \times \frac{2 G M}{R}$ $\Rightarrow v'^{2}=15 \times v^2$ $\ldots \left[\therefore v^2=\frac{2 G M}{R}\right]$ $\Rightarrow v'=\sqrt{15} \cdot v$ © examsnet.com

Solution: When a spring is stretched from some initial extension $x_i$ to some final extension $x_f$ , then work done in stretching $=$ change in potential energy of spring. Work done, $W=\Delta U$ $=\;\frac{1}{2} k (x_f^2-x_i^2)$ Here, $k=50\ \text{N}/\text{m},\ x_f=60\ \text{cm}=60\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ $x_i=50\ \text{cm}=50\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ So, work done $W=\frac{1}{2}\times 50\left[(60\times 10^{-2})^2-(50\times 10^{-2})^2\right]$ $\Rightarrow W=\frac{1}{2}\times 50\times 10^{-4}(3600-2500)$ $=1.5\ \text{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For evaporation water pressure (excess pressure due to surface tension) is greater than vapor pressure. $\Rightarrow$ Excess pressure in drop $\geq$ vapor pressure $\Rightarrow \frac{2 T}{R} \geq p$ where, $T=$ surface tension $p=$ vapor pressure $R=$ Radius of drop $\Rightarrow R=\frac{2 T}{p}$ Here, surface tension, $T=8 \times 10^{-2} \ \text{N/m}$ vapor pressure, $p=25 \times 10^{3} \ \mathrm{Pa}$ Hence, radius of drop $R=\frac{2 \times 8 \times 10^{-2}}{25 \times 10^{3}}$ $\Rightarrow R=\frac{16}{25} \times 10^{-4} \ \mathrm{m}$ $\Rightarrow R=64 \times 10^{-6} \ \mathrm{m}=64 \mu\mathrm{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In water, by Archimedes principle, Weight $=$ Upthrust Weight of fluid displaced $=$ Volume inside water $\Rightarrow m g = \frac{2}{3} V \cdot \rho_w \cdot g \times p_w \times g$ $\dots(i)$ let $x$ part of volume be above surface in liquid of density $\rho$ then, $m g = (1-x) V \cdot \rho \cdot g$ $\dots(ii)$ $\Rightarrow (1-x) V \rho g = \frac{2}{3} V \rho_w g$ $\Rightarrow 1-x = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\rho_w}{\rho} = \frac{2}{3} \times \left( \frac{1}{\text{ specific gravity }} \right)$ As, specific gravity $= \frac{\rho_{\text{fluid }}}{\rho_{\text{water }}}$ Here, specific gravity $=1.5$ Hence, $x = \frac{2}{3 \times 1.5} = \frac{4}{9}$ $V - \frac{4}{9} V = \frac{5}{9} V$ part of volume of object lies above the surface of liquid. © examsnet.com

Solution: As density $\propto \frac{1}{\text{volume}}$ or $\rho \propto \frac{1}{V}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\rho'}{\rho} = \frac{V'}{V'} = \frac{V}{V + r V \Delta \theta} \Rightarrow \rho' = \rho \left( \frac{1}{1 + r \Delta \theta} \right)$ $\Rightarrow \rho' \approx \rho (1 + r \Delta \theta)^{-1} \Rightarrow \rho' = \rho (1 - r \Delta \theta)$ $\text{Here, } r = 18.2 \times 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{K}^{-1} \text{.}$ $\text{and } \Delta \theta = 60 - 10 = 50 \, \mathrm{K}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\rho'}{\rho} = 1 - (18.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 50)$ $= 0.9909$ so, percentage change in density, $\Rightarrow \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho} - 1 \right) \times 100 = \frac{\rho' - \rho}{\rho} \times 100$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100$ $= (0.9909 - 1) \times 100$ $= 0.0091 \times 100 = 0.91\%$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Efficiency of a carnot engine is given by, $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ $T_2=\text{ Temperature of sink }$ $T_1=\text{ temperature of source }$ Here, $T_2=127^{\circ}  \mathrm{C}=127+273=400  \mathrm{K}$ and So $\frac{20}{100}=1-\frac{400}{T_1}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{400}{T_1}=\frac{80}{100}$ $\Rightarrow T_1=\frac{400 \times 100}{80}=500  \mathrm{K}$ or $\text{''}T_1=500-273=227^{\circ}  \mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In a cyclic process, change in internal energy is zero. $\Rightarrow \Delta U=0$ Hence, by first law of thermodynamics $ $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ \text{ < br>} $\Delta Q = \Delta W$ (\because \Delta U=0) $< br>Now, work done by a gas$ = $area under$ p V $graph.    < br> Also work done is negative if cycle is anticlockwise. < br>$ \text{In given cycle, area } = \frac{1}{2} \times BC \times AC $< br>$ = \frac{1}{2}(20-5) \times (30-10) $< br>$ = \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 20 = 150 \text{N} - \text{m} $< br>So, work done in 10 such complete cycles < br>$ = -10 \times 150 $< br>$ = -1500 \text{J} = -1.5 \text{kJ} $< br>Heat absorbed$ = $Work done < br>$ = -1.5 \text{kJ}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{R . m. s}$ speed is given by $v_{\text{rms}}=v_1=\sqrt{\;\frac{3RT}{M}}$ Average speed is given by, $v_{\text{avg}}=v_2=\sqrt{\;\frac{8}{\pi}\cdot\frac{RT}{M}}$ $\;\text{Given,}\;\;v_1=1.5 v_2$ $\Rightarrow (v_1)^2=(1.5)^2\cdot v_2^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3RT}{M_1}=\frac{9}{4}\cdot\frac{8}{\pi}\cdot\frac{RT}{M_2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{M_1}{M_2}=\frac{3\times4\times\pi}{9\times8}=\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{M_1}{M_2}=0.52$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In a closed organ pipe, only odd  harmonics are present. ⇒ $f_1:f_2:f_3 \dots = 1:3:5$ Where, $f_1 = \frac{v}{4l'} v =$ speed of sound and $l =$ length of pipe. In an open organ pipe, both odd and even harmonics are present. ⇒ $f_1:f_2:f_3 \dots = 1:2:3$ ....... Also $f_1 = \frac{v}{2l}$ In given question length of open pipe, $l_1 = 80\text{ cm}$ and $(f_2)_{\text{open pipe}} = (f_1)_{\text{closed pipe}}$ $(2 \times f_1)_{\text{open pipe}} = (f_1)_{\text{closed pipe}}$ ⇒ $2 \times \frac{v}{2l_1} = \frac{v}{4l_2}$ So, length of closed pipe, ⇒ $l_2 = \frac{l_1}{4} = \frac{80}{4} = 20\text{ cm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Power of a combination of lenses, $P=P_1+P_2$ Here, $P_1=-1.75 D$ and $P_2 = 2.25D$ So, power of combination, $P=(-1.75+2.25)D=0.5D$ Also, focal length of lens in cm is given by $f=\frac{100}{P}=\frac{100}{0.5}$ ⇒ $f=200\text{ cm}$ Focal length of combination is 200 cm. © examsnet.com

Solution: Intensity is energy per unit area per unit time. So, intensity ∝ $\frac{1}{\text{Area of wavefront}}$ So, Intensity $I \propto \frac{1}{4\pi r^{2}}$ or $I \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}$ Where, $r=$ radius of wavefront Therefore, assertion A is incorrect. Reason $R$ is correct as a point source emits an spherical wavefront. © examsnet.com

Solution: Electric field of plate is uniform and is in . $+ z$ direction $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} \hat{k}$ where, $\sigma =$ charge density Flux through area of area vactor A is given by, Electric flux $\phi_E = EA$ ⇒ $\phi_E = EA \cos \theta$ $= \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} \pi r^2 \cos \theta = 2 \frac{\sigma}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \pi^2 r^2 \cos \theta$ Here, $\sigma = 4.9 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{C}/\mathrm{m}^2$ $r = 1 \, \mathrm{cm} = 1 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{m}$ ⇒ $\cos \theta = \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$ Also $\pi^2 \approx 10$ So, Flux linked with area given is $\phi_E = 2 \times 4.9 \times 10^{-6} \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times 10 \times (1 \times 10^{-2})^{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$ $= 4.9 \times 9 \times 10^{-10+10} = 44.1 \, \mathrm{N-m}^2 / \mathrm{C}$ Nearest option is (a) © examsnet.com

Solution: Capacity of an air capacitor is given by, $C=\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ Given, $C=12\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ If distance between plates is doubled and a dielectric of dielectric constant $K$ is filled between Given, $K=4$ So, $C'=\frac{4\varepsilon_0 A}{2d} = 2 \times \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ ∴ $C'=2C$ or $C'=2\times 12=24\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown as; For a system of charges potential energy is given by $U=\sum\limits_{i=j} \frac{K q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$ ⇒ Hence for given system potential energy, $U=\frac{K q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{K q_2 q_2}{r_{13}}$ $=\frac{K(-q)(q)}{x} + \frac{K(q)(Q)}{x} + \frac{K(-q)(Q)}{\sqrt{2}x}$ $=\frac{Kq}{x} \left(-q+Q-\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ So, potential energy will be zero if $-q+Q-\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}=0$ or $Q\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=q$ ⇒ $Q=(\sqrt{2}-1)=\sqrt{2}q$ ⇒ $Q=\frac{\sqrt{2}q}{\sqrt{2}-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given situation is shown below. Note Earth's field goes from South to North: At neutral point horizontal component of earth, is opposed by field of magnet so, at neutral point, $B_H=B_{\text{magnet}}$ ⇒ $B_H = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \cdot \frac{M}{r^3}$ Where, $M=$ magnetic dipole moment of magnet and $r=$ distance of neutral point from centre of magnet Here, $B_H = 3.2\times 10^{-5}\text{T}$ $r-6\ \text{cm}=6\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ Hence, $3.2 \times 10^{-5} = 10^{-7} \times \frac{M}{(6 \times 10^{-2})^3}$ ⇒ $M=\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 216 \times 10^{-6}}{10^{-7}}$ $=6. \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A-m}^2$ If length of magnet is taken $2l$ , then $M=m \cdot 2l$ , (∵ m= pole strength) Here, $2l=16\ \text{cm}=16\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ ⇒ $6.9 \times 10^{-2} = m \times 16 \times 10^{-2}$ ⇒ $m = \frac{6.9}{16} = 0.43\ \text{A-m} \simeq 0.5\ \text{A-m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given circuit can be shown as. Total resistance in above case, $R_S=R_1+R_2+.......+R_{10}$ ⇒ $R_s = 10\Omega$ Current in circuit , $I=\frac{V}{R_s}$ ⇒ $I=\frac{10}{10} = 1\ \mathrm{A}$ Power consumption of circuit, $P_s=I^2\times 10\times 10\Omega$ In second case, $\frac{1}{R_P} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + .....$ ⇒ $\frac{1}{R_P} = \frac{10}{1}$ ⇒ $R_P - \frac{1}{10}\Omega$ Power consumption, $P_P = \frac{V^2}{R_P} = \frac{100}{\frac{1}{10}} = 10^3\ \mathrm{W}$ ⇒ $\frac{P_S}{P_P} = \frac{10}{1000} = 0.01$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Magnetic field near centre of a solenoid is given by $B=\mu_0 n I$ Here, $n =$ Number of turn per unit length $\frac{N}{L} = \frac{5 \times 500}{I} = 2500$ $B=4.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{T}$ $\mu_0=4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T-m/A}$ So, substituting the values , we get $4.4 \times 10^{-3} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2500 \times I$ ⇒ Current in solenoid, $I=\frac{4.4 \times 10^{-3}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2500}$ $= \frac{4.4}{\pi} \approx 1.4\ \text{A}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The situation given can be shown as Magnetic field at some point $P$ with position vector $r$ due to a straight long current carrying wire is given by $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$ Where, $d=$ Perpendicular distance of point from wire. Here, $r=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}\,\text{m}$ ⇒ for wire on X - axis, $d=d_x=4\,\text{m}$ and for wire on Y-axis $d=d_y=2\,\text{m}$ As magnetic fields due to wires along $X$ and along $Y$ -axis are in opposite direction ( $RH$ rule) so, $B_{\text{net}} = B+B_x$ $=\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi d_y}(\hat{k}) + \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d_x}(-\hat{k})$ $= \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} \left(\frac{I_2}{d_y} - \frac{I_1}{d_x}\right) \hat{k}$ $= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi} \left(\frac{6}{2} - \frac{8}{4}\right) \hat{k}$ $= 2 \times 10^{-7} \hat{k} \,\text{T}$ ∴ $\left|B_{\text{net}}\right| = 2 \times 10^{-7} \,\text{T}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Intensity at a point is equals to the average value of magnitude of poynting vector, $I = S_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} C \varepsilon_0 E^2_0$ Here, $E_0 = 4.4 \ \text{V/m}$ So, Intensirty $I = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 10^8 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times (4.4)^2$ ⇒ $I = 25.7 \times 10^{-3} \ \text{W/m}^2$ or $I = 25.7 \ \text{mW/m}^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Average power loss in a rotating coil in 1 rotation is $P_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{max}} I_{\mathrm{max}}}{2} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{max}}^2}{2R}$ $= \frac{(NBA\omega)^2}{2R}$ ......(i) Here, number of turns, $N=40$ Intensity of magnetic field, $B=0.05\ \mathrm{T}$ Area of coil, $A=0.01\ \mathrm{m}^2$ Angular speed, $\omega = 50\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ Resistance of closed loop of coil, Average power loss, $P_{\mathrm{avg}} = 25\ \mathrm{mW}$ $=25\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W}$ So, fromeq. (i) we have $25\times 10^{-3} = \frac{(40\times 0.05\times 0.01\times 50)^2}{2R}$ ⇒ Resistance of coil, $R=\frac{(40\times 0.0\times 0.01\times 50)^2}{2\times 25\times 10^{-3}}$ $=20\ \Omega$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Capacitive reactance of a capacitor, $X_C=\frac{1}{C\omega}$ Where, $\omega=$ frequency $C=$ Capacity of capacitor $X_C \propto \frac{1}{\omega},\ \text{if } C =$ constant Hence, in given case when frequency is doubled, reactance becomes half. ∴ Now capacitive reactance, $X'_C=\frac{6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{2}=3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Intensity of an electromagnetic wave in terms of amplitude of magnetic field, $I = \frac{1}{2} c \varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = \frac{c B_0^2}{2 \mu_0}$ Here, $B_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-4} \ \text{T}$ $c = 3 \times 10^8 \ \text{m/s}$ $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \ \text{T -m/A}$ So intensity of wave, $I = \frac{3 \times 10^8 \times (2.2 \times 10^{-4})^2}{2 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7}}$ $= 5.8 \times 10^6 \ \text{W/m}^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: By parallelogram law of vector addition, angle made by resultant with $P$ is given by; $\tan\alpha = \frac{Q \sin\theta}{P+Q \cos\theta}$ Here $\alpha=90^{\circ}$ . So ; $\tan 90^{\circ} = \infty = \frac{Q \sin\theta}{P+Q \cos\theta}$ $\Rightarrow P+Q \cos\theta = 0$ or $Q \cos\theta = -P$ Now, magnitude of resultant, $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q \cos\theta}$ Here, we have $R = 2P$ and $Q \cos\theta = -P$ and $Q = 10\ \text{m}$ So, $2P = \sqrt{P^2 + 100 - 2P^2}$ $\Rightarrow 4P^2 = 100 - P^2 \Rightarrow 5P^2 = 100$ or $P = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\ \text{m}$ Magnitude of $P$ is $2\sqrt{5}\ \text{m}$ . © examsnet.com

First, we need to find the value of $g\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)$ : $g\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \sin\left(2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ We know that $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$ , so: $g\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$ Next, we need to find the value of $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ : $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8} - \frac{4}{8} = -\frac{3}{8}$ Therefore, the value of $f\left(g\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\right)$ is: $f\left(g\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\right) = -\frac{3}{8}$ The correct answer is: $-\frac{3}{8}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution To determine the domain of the function $f(x) = \sqrt{\log_{10}\left(\frac{3-x}{x}\right)}$ , we need to ensure that the expression inside the square root is non-negative and that the argument of the logarithm is positive. Let's break this down step by step. 1. Argument of the Logarithm Must Be Positive: The argument of the logarithm, $\frac{3-x}{x}$ , must be positive. This gives us the inequality: $\frac{3-x}{x} > 0$ To solve this inequality, we need to determine where the expression $\frac{3-x}{x}$ is positive. The critical points are $x = 0$ and $x = 3$ . We can test the intervals determined by these points: $(-\infty, 0)$ , $(0, 3)$ , and $(3, \infty)$ . For $x \in (0, 3)$ , both $3-x$ and $x$ are positive, so $\frac{3-x}{x} > 0$ . For $x \in (-\infty, 0)$ or $x \in (3, \infty)$ , the expression $\frac{3-x}{x}$ is not positive. Therefore, the inequality $\frac{3-x}{x} > 0$ is satisfied for $0 < x < 3$ . 2. Expression Inside the Square Root Must Be Non-Negative: The expression inside the square root, $\log_{10}\left(\frac{3-x}{x}\right)$ , must be non-negative. This means: $\log_{10}\left(\frac{3-x}{x}\right) \ge 0$ Since the logarithm base 10 of a number is non-negative if and only if the number is at least 1, we have: $\frac{3-x}{x} \ge 1$ Simplifying this inequality: $\frac{3-x}{x} - 1 \ge 0 \Rightarrow \frac{3-x-x}{x} \ge 0 \Rightarrow \frac{3-2x}{x} \ge 0$ The critical points are $x = 0$ and $x = \frac{3}{2}$ . We test the intervals determined by these points: $(-\infty, 0)$ , $\left(0, \frac{3}{2}\right)$ , and $\left(\frac{3}{2}, \infty\right)$ . For $x \in \left(0, \frac{3}{2}\right)$ , both $3-2x$ and $x$ are positive, so $\frac{3-2x}{x} > 0$ . For $x \in \left(\frac{3}{2}, \infty\right)$ , $3-2x$ is negative, so $\frac{3-2x}{x} < 0$ . Therefore, the inequality $\frac{3-2x}{x} \ge 0$ is satisfied for $0 < x \le \frac{3}{2}$ . Combining the two conditions, we get that the domain of $f(x)$ is: $0 < x \le \frac{3}{2}$ Thus, the domain of $f$ is $(0, \frac{3}{2}]$ . The correct option is $B$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Since $X^{\mathrm{T}}B^{\mathrm{T}}=(BX)^{\mathrm{T}}$ , the equation $X^{\mathrm{T}}B^{\mathrm{T}}=A^{\mathrm{T}}$ is equivalent to $BX=A$ . Thus $D$ satisfies $BD=A$ . Write $D=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$ . The system is: $3x+5y-7z=0$ $-y+8z=-6$ $6x-y=8$ From $-y+8z=-6$ , we get $y=8z+6$ . Then $y=8(-1)+6=-2$ and $x=-11(-1)-10=1$ . Thus $D=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ . For $f$ to be one-to-one, $A$ must be restricted to one side of the vertex, so either $A=\left(-\infty,\frac{3}{2}\right]$ or $A=\left[\frac{3}{2},\infty\right)$ . If $A=\left(-\infty,\frac{3}{2}\right]$ , then $f$ is decreasing on $A$ and its range is $\left[-\frac{1}{4},\infty\right)$ . Thus for $f:A\to B$ to be onto, we need $B=\left[-\frac{1}{4},\infty\right)$ . This matches option B. Option D is not injective because the unrestricted quadratic is not one-to-one. Solution: Let $t=\tan A$ , so $\cot A=\frac{1}{t}$ . Then the expression becomes $\frac{1/t}{1-t}+\frac{t}{1-1/t}$ . Simplify each fraction: $\frac{1/t}{1-t}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}$ and $\frac{t}{1-1/t}=\frac{t^2}{t-1}=-\frac{t^2}{1-t}$ . So the sum is $\frac{1}{t(1-t)}-\frac{t^2}{1-t}=\frac{1-t^3}{t(1-t)}$ . Factor: $1-t^3=(1-t)(1+t+t^2)$ . Thus the sum is $\frac{(1-t)(1+t+t^2)}{t(1-t)}=\frac{1+t+t^2}{t}=t+1+\frac{1}{t}$ . Therefore it equals $\tan A+1+\cot A$ . Now $\tan A+\cot A=\frac{\sin A}{\cos A}+\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\frac{\sin^2 A+\cos^2 A}{\sin A\cos A}=\frac{1}{\sin A\cos A}=\sec A\csc A$ . Hence the expression simplifies to $\sec A\csc A+1$ , which is option option D. © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Use $\sqrt{1-\sin^2 x}=\sqrt{\cos^2 x}=|\cos x|$ . So the integrand becomes $\frac{\cos x}{|\cos x|}$ wherever $\cos x\ne 0$ . Step 2: Split the integral at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ , where the original integrand is undefined. For $0\le x < \frac{\pi}{2}$ , $\cos x>0$ , so $\frac{\cos x}{|\cos x|}=1$ . For $\frac{\pi}{2} < x\le \pi$ , $\cos x<0$ , so $\frac{\cos x}{|\cos x|}=-1$ . Step 3: $\int_0^{\pi} \frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2 x}}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx+\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(-1)\,dx$ $=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2}=0$ Therefore the correct option is $0$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Count the bond pairs first. In $\mathrm{XeOF}_4$ , the central $\mathrm{Xe}$ atom forms four single bonds to $\mathrm{F}$ atoms and one double bond to $\mathrm{O}$ . The four single bonds contribute $4$ bond pairs, and the double bond contributes $2$ bond pairs. So the number of bond pairs is $4+2=6$ . Now count lone pairs. $\mathrm{Xe}$ has $1$ lone pair. $\mathrm{O}$ has $2$ lone pairs. Each $\mathrm{F}$ atom has $3$ lone pairs, so the four $\mathrm{F}$ atoms contribute $4\times3=12$ lone pairs. Total lone pairs $=1+2+12=15$ . Therefore, the required numbers are $(6,15)$ , which matches option D. © examsnet.com

Solution: Since $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, $A \cap B = \varnothing$ . Thus $A \cap B^c = A$ . By the conditional probability formula, $P(A \mid B^c)=\frac{P(A\cap B^c)}{P(B^c)}$ . So $P(A \mid B^c)=\frac{P(A)}{1-P(B)}$ . Therefore, the correct option is $\frac{P(A)}{1-P(B)}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The square-root function is defined only for non-negative inputs, so $9-x^2 \ge 0$ . This gives $x^2 \le 9$ , i.e. $x \in [-3,3]$ . For $x \in [-3,3]$ , the expression $9-x^2$ ranges from $0$ at the endpoints to $9$ at $x=0$ . Therefore $\sqrt{9-x^2}$ ranges from $\sqrt{0}=0$ to $\sqrt{9}=3$ . Hence the range is $[0,3]$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Prime factorize: $6300=2^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 7$ . For a divisor to be even, it must contain at least one factor of $2$ , so the exponent of $2$ can be $1$ or $2$ , giving $2$ choices. The exponents of $3$ , $5$ , and $7$ can be chosen from $0$ up to their maximum exponents, giving $3$ , $3$ , and $2$ choices respectively. Thus the number of positive even divisors is $2\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 2=36$ . Therefore, the correct option is $36$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Take the basis $\{\overline{a},\overline{b},\overline{c}\}$ and write each point as an ordered triple of its coefficients. Let $L_1$ join $P_1=\overline{a}+\overline{b}+\overline{c}=(1,1,1)$ and $Q_1=\overline{a}-\overline{b}+3\overline{c}=(1,-1,3)$ . Then $L_1: (1,1,1)+t(0,-2,2)=(1,1-2t,1+2t)$ . Let $L_2$ join $P_2=2\overline{a}-\overline{b}+\overline{c}=(2,-1,1)$ and $Q_2=\overline{a}-2\overline{b}+4\overline{c}=(1,-2,4)$ . Then $L_2: (2,-1,1)+s(-1,-1,3)=(2-s,-1-s,1+3s)$ . At the intersection, equate coordinates: $1=2-s$ , $1-2t=-1-s$ , and $1+2t=1+3s$ . From the first equation, $s=1$ . Substitute in the second: $1-2t=-2$ , so $t=\frac{3}{2}$ . Check in the third: $1+2\cdot\frac{3}{2}=4$ and $1+3\cdot1=4$ , so the lines do intersect. The intersection is $(1,1-2t,1+2t)$ with $t=\frac{3}{2}$ , that is $(1,-2,4)$ . Converting back to vector form gives $\overline{a}-2\overline{b}+4\overline{c}$ . Hence the correct option is the one with option C. © examsnet.com

Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $l,m,n$ be the direction cosines of the line. Since the line makes the same angle $\theta$ with all three coordinate axes, we have $|l|=|m|=|n|=\cos\theta$ . Using the direction cosine identity $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$ , we get $3\cos^{2}\theta=1$ . Thus $\cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{3}$ . Then $\tan^{2}\theta=\sec^{2}\theta-1=\frac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}-1=3-1=2$ . Since $\theta$ is the acute angle between the line and an axis, $\tan\theta=\sqrt{2}$ . Therefore the correct option is $\sqrt{2}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The alkaline earth metals are $\mathrm{Be}$ , $\mathrm{Mg}$ , $\mathrm{Ca}$ , $\mathrm{Sr}$ , $\mathrm{Ba}$ and $\mathrm{Ra}$ . Densities of the first four members are: $\mathrm{Be} = 1.85\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ , $\mathrm{Mg} = 1.74\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ , $\mathrm{Ca} = 1.55\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ , $\mathrm{Sr} = 2.64\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ . Comparing these values, $\mathrm{Ca}$ has the smallest density, which is lower than even that of $\mathrm{Be}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}$ . This is due to the comparatively large atomic size and relatively weak metallic bonding of $\mathrm{Ca}$ in its crystal lattice, which gives it an unusually open structure. Hence the alkaline earth metal with the lowest density is $\mathrm{Ca}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Correct answer: Phenylamine (option C) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis prepares only primary amines that can be formed through an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction on an alkyl/benzylic halide. Step 1: Phthalimide is treated with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ to form potassium phthalimide: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{CO})_2\text{NH} + \text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{CO})_2\text{N}^-\text{K}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ Step 2: The phthalimide anion attacks an alkyl halide $R-X$ by an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ pathway to give $N$ -alkylphthalimide. Step 3: Alkaline hydrolysis (or hydrazinolysis) of the $N$ -alkylphthalimide liberates the primary amine $R\text{NH}_2$ . Ethylamine ( $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ ) comes from ethyl halide, propylamine ( $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{NH}_2$ ) from propyl halide, and benzylamine ( $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ ) from benzyl halide. All three of these halides are $\text{sp}^3$ (or benzylic) halides that readily undergo $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution, so their amines can be prepared this way. Phenylamine (aniline) would require chlorobenzene to react with the phthalimide anion. In chlorobenzene the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, and the planar aryl carbon is shielded from backside attack, so nucleophilic substitution by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ does not occur. Therefore the phthalimide anion cannot be attached to a benzene ring, and phenylamine cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis. Phenylamine is instead prepared by reduction of nitrobenzene, e.g. $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Sn/HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ . Hence the amine that cannot be prepared by the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is phenylamine, option C. © examsnet.com

Solution: For one-one: $f(-1)=(-1)^3-(-1)=0$ , $f(0)=0$ , and $f(1)=0$ . Since $f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)$ , different inputs give the same output, so $f$ is not one-one. For onto: $f(x)=x^3-x$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ . As $x\to \infty$ , $f(x)=x^3-x\to \infty$ . As $x\to -\infty$ , $f(x)=x^3-x\to -\infty$ . Since $f$ is continuous and takes arbitrarily large positive and negative values, its range is all of $\mathbb{R}$ . Therefore, $f$ is onto. Hence $f$ is onto but not one-one, so the correct option is onto but not one - one . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given $f(x)=\sqrt{x}-1$ and $g(f(x))=x+2\sqrt{x}+1$ . We must express $g(f(x))$ entirely in terms of $f(x)$ . First, simplify the given expression using the perfect square identity: $x+2\sqrt{x}+1=(\sqrt{x}+1)^2$ Now relate $\sqrt{x}$ to $f(x)$ : since $f(x)=\sqrt{x}-1$ , we have $\sqrt{x}=f(x)+1$ . Substituting this into the expression gives: $g(f(x))=((f(x)+1)+1)^2=(f(x)+2)^2$ Since this holds for every $x$ in the domain, replacing $f(x)$ by a general variable $x$ yields: $g(x)=(x+2)^2$ Check: $g(f(x))=(\sqrt{x}-1+2)^2=(\sqrt{x}+1)^2=x+2\sqrt{x}+1$ , which matches the given condition. Therefore, the correct answer is $(x+2)^2$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The given expression is $f(n) = 3 \cdot 5^{2n+1} + 2^{3n+1}$ . Since $f(n)$ is divisible by $k$ for every positive integer $n$ , $k$ must divide both $f(1)$ and $f(2)$ . Compute $f(1) = 3 \cdot 5^{3} + 2^{4} = 375 + 16 = 391$ . Compute $f(2) = 3 \cdot 5^{5} + 2^{7} = 9375 + 128 = 9503$ . So $k = \text{HCF}(391, 9503)$ . Applying the Euclidean algorithm: $9503 = 24 \times 391 + 119$ , $391 = 3 \times 119 + 34$ , $119 = 3 \times 34 + 17$ , $34 = 2 \times 17 + 0$ . Hence $\text{HCF}(391, 9503) = 17$ , so $k = 17$ . Verification: working modulo $17$ , we have $5^{2} = 25 \equiv 8$ and $2^{3} = 8$ . Therefore $f(n) = 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 25^{n} + 2 \cdot 8^{n} \equiv 15 \cdot 8^{n} + 2 \cdot 8^{n} = 17 \cdot 8^{n} \equiv 0 \pmod{17}$ . So $17$ divides $f(n)$ for all positive integers $n$ , confirming $k = 17$ . The prime numbers less than or equal to $17$ are $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17$ . Counting them gives $7$ primes. Therefore, the number of prime numbers less than or equal to $k$ is $7$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $D=\begin{vmatrix}1-x&-2&1\\-2&4-x&-2\\1&-2&1-x\end{vmatrix}.$ Apply $R_1\to R_1+R_2+R_3$ : $D=\begin{vmatrix}-x&-x&-x\\-2&4-x&-2\\1&-2&1-x\end{vmatrix}.$ Taking $-x$ common from $R_1$ : $D=-x\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\-2&4-x&-2\\1&-2&1-x\end{vmatrix}.$ Apply $C_2\to C_2-C_1$ and $C_3\to C_3-C_1$ : $D=-x\begin{vmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&6-x&0\\1&-3&-x\end{vmatrix}.$ Expanding along $R_1$ : $D=-x(6-x)(-x)=x^2(6-x).$ Thus, $x^2(6-x)=0$ , so the roots are $\alpha=0$ , $\beta=0$ , and $\gamma=6$ . Therefore, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=0\cdot0+0\cdot6+6\cdot0=0.$ Hence, the correct option is $0$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: To find $a+i b = \frac{\sqrt{-5-12i} + \sqrt{5+12i}}{\sqrt{-8-6i}}$ and calculate $2a+b$ : Calculate $\sqrt{-5-12i}$ and $\sqrt{5+12i}$ : Since the real parts of $\sqrt{-5-12i}$ and $\sqrt{5+12i}$ are positive: $\sqrt{-5-12i} = \sqrt{\frac{13-5}{2}} + i \sqrt{\frac{13+5}{2}} = 2-3i$ $\sqrt{5+12i} = \sqrt{\frac{13+5}{2}} + i \sqrt{\frac{13-5}{2}} = 3+2i$ Calculate $\sqrt{-8-6i}$ : Given that the real part is negative: $\sqrt{-8-6i} = -\sqrt{\frac{10-8}{2}} + i \sqrt{\frac{10+8}{2}} = -1+3i$ Find $a+i b:$ Using the calculations from the previous steps: $a+i b = \frac{(2-3i)+(3+2i)}{-1+3i} = \frac{5-i}{-1+3i}$ Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: $= \frac{(5-i)(-1-3i)}{(-1+3i)(-1-3i)}$ Simplify: $\; = \;\frac{-5+i-15i-3}{1+9} = \frac{-8-14i}{10}$ $\; = -\frac{4}{5} - \frac{7i}{5}$ Thus, $a = -\frac{4}{5}$ and $b = -\frac{7}{5}$ . Calculate $2a+b$ : $2a+b = 2\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) + \left(-\frac{7}{5}\right) = -\frac{8}{5} - \frac{7}{5} = -3$ Hence, the result is -3 . © examsnet.com

Solution: The given equation $z \overline{z}+(4-3i) z+(4+3i) \overline{z}+c=0$ is analyzed to determine the real values of $c$ that form a circle. Key Steps Identifying the Circle's Center: $z \overline{z}$ is the modulus squared of $z$ , and the terms $(4-3i) z$ and $(4+3i) \overline{z}$ suggest the transformation involves the complex number $4-3i$ . Thus, the center of the circle is at $4-3i$ . Finding the Radius: To find the radius, use the formula that incorporates the modulus of the center: $\sqrt{(4)^2+(-3)^2-c}=\sqrt{25-c}$ The radius needs to be non-negative for the equation to represent a circle: $\sqrt{25-c} \geq 0$ which simplifies to: $25-c \geq 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; c \leq 25$ Conclusion The real values of $c$ for which the equation represents a circle are in the interval: $(-\infty, 25]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given the equation $z^3+\overline{z}=0$ , where $z=x+iy$ is a complex number, we can find the distinct solutions as follows: Rewrite the Equation: Start with: $z^3+\overline{z}=0$ This implies: $z^3=-\overline{z}$ Equate Magnitudes: Taking the magnitude of both sides, we have: $|z^3|=|-\overline{z}|$ This simplifies to: $|z|^3=|\overline{z}|$ Since $|\overline{z}|=|z|$ , the equation becomes: $|z|^3=|z|$ Solve for Magnitude: This equation leads to: $|z|(|z|^2-1)=0$ Therefore, either $|z|=0$ or $|z|^2=1$ . Consider Each Case: If $|z|=0$ , then $z=0$ . This gives one distinct solution: $z=0$ . If $|z|^2=1$ , then $|z|=1$ and consequently $z\overline{z}=1$ . This implies: $z=\frac{1}{z}$ Substitute Back: Substituting $\overline{z}=\frac{1}{z}$ into the original equation: $z^3+\frac{1}{z}=0$ Multiply through by $z$ to clear the fraction: $z^4+1=0$ Solve $z^4+1=0$ : This equation has four roots: $z=e^{i(\pi/4)}, e^{i(3\pi/4)}, e^{i(5\pi/4)}, e^{i(7\pi/4)}$ Count Distinct Solutions: Including $z=0$ , we have: One solution for $z=0$ Four solutions from $z^4+1=0$ Therefore, the number of distinct solutions to the equation is 5 . © examsnet.com

Solution: The roots of the quadratic equation $x^2-35 x+c=0$ are given to be in the ratio 2:3. Let's assume the roots are $2 \alpha$ and $3 \alpha$ . The sum of the roots is given by the equation: $2 \alpha+3 \alpha=5 \alpha=35$ Solving for $\alpha$ , we get: $\alpha=7$ The product of the roots can be expressed as: $(2 \alpha)(3 \alpha)=6 \alpha^2=c$ Substituting the value of $\alpha$ , we find: $c=6 \times 7^2=6 \times 49$ Given that $c=6 K$ , we equate to find $K$ : $6 \times 49=6 K$ $K=49$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We are given the polynomial equation $x^4-x^3-8 x^2+2 x+12=0$ with roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ , and $\delta$ . It is known that the sum of two of the roots, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , is zero, i.e., $\alpha+\beta=0$ . From Vieta's formulas, the sum of all roots is: $S_1=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=1$ Given $\alpha+\beta=0$ , we find: $\gamma+\delta=1$ Similarly, from Vieta's formulas, the sum of the products of the roots taken two at a time is: $S_2=\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta=-8$ Using $\alpha+\beta=0$ , simplify to: $\alpha\beta+\gamma\delta=-8$ From the sum of the products of the roots taken three at a time, we have: $S_3=\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta\delta+\alpha\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma\delta=-2$ Substitute $(\alpha+\beta)\gamma\delta+\alpha\beta(\gamma+\delta)=-2$ and rearrange: $\alpha\beta=-2$ From Vieta's formulas, the product of the roots is given by: $S_4=\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=12$ Use $\alpha\beta=-2$ to find: $\gamma\delta=-6 \; \; \ldots (v)$ Next, solve the system of equations obtained from (ii) and (v): $\gamma+\delta=1$ $\gamma\delta=-6$ These are the equations for a quadratic: $t^2-(\gamma+\delta)t+\gamma\delta=0 \Rightarrow t^2-t-6=0$ Solving, we find the roots to be: $t = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+24}}{2} = \frac{1 \pm 5}{2}$ Thus, $t=3$ or $t=-2$ . Since $\gamma > \delta$ , we assign $\gamma = 3$ and $\delta = -2$ . Finally, compute: $3\gamma+2\delta=3 \times 3+2 \times (-2)=9-4=5$ © examsnet.com

Solution: To find the value of $h$ that removes the $x^3$ term from the polynomial $f(x)=x^4+2x^3-19x^2-8x+60=0$ when transformed to $f(x+h)=0$ , follow these steps: Polynomial Transformation: The transformation affects each term in the original polynomial. For the $x^3$ term in the polynomial, apply the transformation: $f(x+h)=(x+h)^4+2(x+h)^3-19(x+h)^2-8(x+h)+60$ Focus on the $x^3$ Terms: When expanding, consider only the terms involving $x^3$ : From $(x+h)^4$ : ${}^{4}C_{1} \cdot x^{3} \cdot h = 4 h x^{3}$ From $2(x+h)^3$ : $2 \times 1 \times x^{3} = 2 x^{3}$ Collect $x^3$ Terms: Adding these terms together gives: $4 h x^{3} + 2 x^{3} = (4 h + 2) x^{3}$ Set the Coefficient to Zero: To eliminate the $x^3$ term from the polynomial, the coefficient must be zero: $4 h + 2 = 0$ Solve for $h$ : $4 h = -2 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad h = \frac{-2}{4} = \frac{-1}{2}$ Thus, the value of $h$ that removes the $x^3$ term is $h = -\frac{1}{2}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: To prepare a garland using 6 distinct white roses and 6 distinct red roses such that no two red roses are adjacent, follow these steps: Arranging White Roses: Since we have 6 distinct white roses, they can be arranged in a garland. The formula to arrange flowers in a garland using circular permutations is $\;\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$ , where $n$ is the number of items. For the white roses, this gives us: $\;\frac{(6-1)!}{2} = \;\frac{5!}{2} = \;\frac{120}{2} = 60$ Arranging Red Roses: Placing Red Roses: The number of ways to arrange these 6 distinct red roses in these 6 positions is given by the permutation of 6 distinct items, which is 6 !. Thus, the calculation is: $6!=720$ Calculating Total Arrangements: Finally, combine the permutations of both sets of roses. The total number of ways to arrange the garland while maintaining the condition is: $60 \times 720=43200$ Thus, there are 43,200 different ways to prepare the garland with the given conditions. © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $(3+x+x^2)^6$ General term of the expansion $=\;\frac{6!}{r!s!t!} \times 3^r \times x^5 \times (x^2)^t$ Where, $\;r+s+t=6$ $\;=\;\frac{6!}{r!s!t!} \times 3^r \times x^{5+2t}$ For the coefficient of $x^5$ , $s+2t=5$ But $r+s+t=6$ $\;r+5-t=6$ $\;r-a=1+t \; \text{ and } \; s=5-2t$ Now, $t=0$ , then $r=1, s=5$ $t=1$ , then $r=2, s=3$ $t=2$ then $r=3, s=1$ $\therefore$ There are only 3 terms that contain $x^5$ $\therefore$ Coefficient of $x^5$ $\;=\;\frac{6!}{0!1!5!} \times 3^1 + \;\frac{6!}{1!2!3!} \times 3^2 + \;\frac{6!}{2!3!!!} \times 3^3$ $\;=18+540+1620=2178$ © examsnet.com

Solution: To determine the absolute value of the difference between the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^6$ in the expansion of the given expression, we start with: $x^{2}-2x^{2}+(x+1)^{4}(x^{2}-1)^{2}$ We simplify the function as follows: $f(x)=\frac{2x^{2}}{(x^{2}+1)(x^{2}+2)}$ Expanding, we have: $f(x)=2x^{2}(x^{2}+1)^{-1}(x^{2}+2)^{-1}$ Simplifying further gives: $f(x)=\frac{2x^{2}}{2}(1+x^{2})^{-1}\left(1+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)^{-1}$ This can be expanded into: $f(x)=x^{2}\left[1-x^{2}+x^{4}-x^{6}+\cdots\right]\cdot\left[1-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{4}}{4}-\frac{x^{4}}{8}+\cdots\right]$ Now, let's find the coefficients. For $x^4$ : Coefficient calculation: $\left[-\frac{1}{2}-1\right]=\frac{-3}{2}$ For $x^6$ : Coefficient calculation: $\left[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}+1\right]-\frac{7}{4}$ Now calculate the absolute difference: $\text{Difference}=\left|\frac{7}{4}-\left(\frac{-3}{2}\right)\right|=\left|\frac{7}{4}+\frac{3}{2}\right|$ $=\left|\frac{7}{4}+\frac{6}{4}\right|=\left|\frac{13}{4}\right|=\frac{13}{4}$ This process allows us to correctly determine the absolute value of the difference between the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^6$ in the expansion. © examsnet.com

Solution: To solve the given expression $\tan 6^{\circ}+\tan 42^{\circ}+\tan 66^{\circ}+\tan 78^{\circ}$ , we can apply some identities and symmetry properties of the tangent function. First, let's use the identity for tangent of a sum and difference of angles: $\tan (A+B) \tan (A-B)= \left( \;\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A \tan B} \right) \left( \;\frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A \tan B} \right)$ This can be simplified to: $\tan (A+B) \tan (A-B)=\;\frac{\tan^2 A-\tan^2 B}{1-\tan^2 A \tan^2 B}$ Now, substitute $A=60^{\circ}$ and $B=18^{\circ}$ into equation (i): $\tan 78^{\circ} \times \tan 42^{\circ}=\;\frac{\tan^2 60^{\circ}-\tan^2 18^{\circ}}{1-\tan^2 60^{\circ} \tan^2 18^{\circ}}=\;\frac{3-\tan^2 18^{\circ}}{1-3 \tan^2 18^{\circ}}$ Simplifying: $=\;\frac{1}{\tan 18^{\circ}} \left[ \;\frac{3 \tan 18^{\circ}-\tan^3 18^{\circ}}{1-3 \tan^2 18^{\circ}} \right]$ So, $\tan 78^{\circ} \tan 42^{\circ}=\;\frac{\tan 54^{\circ}}{\tan 18^{\circ}}$ Next, substitute $A=60^{\circ}$ and $B=54^{\circ}$ in equation (i): $\tan 114^{\circ} \times \tan 6^{\circ}=\;\frac{3-\tan^2 54^{\circ}}{1-3 \tan^2 54^{\circ}}=\;\frac{1}{\tan 54^{\circ}} \left[ \;\frac{3 \tan 54^{\circ}-\tan^3 54^{\circ}}{1-3 \tan^2 54^{\circ}} \right]$ This gives: $=\;\frac{\tan 162^{\circ}}{\tan 54^{\circ}}$ Since $\tan 114^{\circ}=\tan (180^{\circ}-66^{\circ}) =-\tan 66^{\circ}$ and $\tan 162^{\circ}=\tan (180^{\circ}-18^{\circ}) =-\tan 18^{\circ}$ , we have: $\tan 66^{\circ} \times \tan 6^{\circ}=\;\frac{\tan 18^{\circ}}{\tan 54^{\circ}}$ Multiplying equations (ii) and (iii): $\tan 6^{\circ} \tan 42^{\circ} \tan 66^{\circ} \tan 78^{\circ}=\;\frac{\tan 54^{\circ}}{\tan 18^{\circ}} \times \;\frac{\tan 18^{\circ}}{\tan 54^{\circ}}=1$ Therefore, $\tan 6^{\circ}+\tan 42^{\circ}+\tan 66^{\circ}+\tan 78^{\circ}$ sums up to a neat result based on symmetrical properties of angles and tangent function identities. © examsnet.com

Solution: To find the maximum value of the expression $12 \sin\;x-5 \cos x+3$ , we start by considering the form $a \sin\;x+b \cos x$ , which achieves its maximum value at $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ . For our specific expression, we have $a=12$ and $b=-5$ . The calculation for the maximum value of $12 \sin\;x-5 \cos x$ is: $\sqrt{12^2+(-5)^2}=\sqrt{144+25}=\sqrt{169}=13$ Therefore, the maximum value of the entire expression $12 \sin\;x-5 \cos x+3$ is: $13+3=16$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Use $A=76^{\circ}$ and $B=16^{\circ}$ . Then $A+B=92^{\circ}$ and $A-B=60^{\circ}$ . Then $E=1-\frac{c}{2}-\frac{\frac12-c}{2}$ . Simplifying, $E=1-\frac{c}{2}-\frac14+\frac{c}{2}$ . Therefore $E=\frac34$ . Hence the correct option is $\frac{3}{4}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: To solve the given series equation: $1+ \sin x+ \sin^2 x+ \sin^3 x+ \dots = 4+2\sqrt{3}$ we recognize that this is an infinite geometric series with the first term $a=1$ and the common ratio $r= \sin x$ . The sum of an infinite geometric series is given by: $S=\frac{a}{1-r}$ Here, substituting the given values: $\frac{1}{1- \sin x}=4+2\sqrt{3}$ To find $\sin x$ , we solve: $1- \sin x=\frac{1}{4+2\sqrt{3}}$ Rationalizing the denominator gives: $1- \sin x=\frac{4-2\sqrt{3}}{4}=1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ Thus: $\sin x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ Given the constraints $0< x< \pi$ and $x \neq \frac{\pi}{2}$ , we find that $x$ could be $\frac{\pi}{3}$ or $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ . The solutions within this range are: $x=\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{2\pi}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: To solve the expression $\tan^{-1} 2+\tan^{-1} 3$ , we can use the formula for the sum of inverse tangents: $\tan^{-1} a+\tan^{-1} b=\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{a+b}{1-ab} \right)$ Applying this formula to our problem, we have: $\tan^{-1} 2+\tan^{-1} 3=\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2+3}{1-2 \times 3} \right)$ Simplify the fraction: $=\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{5}{1-6} \right) =\tan^{-1}(-1)$ We know that $\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{4}$ . However, we typically express angles in the range 0 to $\pi$ . Thus: $\tan^{-1} 2+\tan^{-1} 3=\frac{3\pi}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We have, $A B C$ is a triangle $\;\cos A+\cos B+\cos C$ $\;=2\cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)+1-2\sin^2 \frac{C}{2}$ $\;=1+2\sin\frac{C}{2}\cos\left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)-2\sin^2\frac{C}{2}$ $\;=1+2\sin\frac{C}{2}\left[\cos\left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)-\sin\frac{C}{2}\right]$ $\;=1+2\sin\frac{C}{2}\left[\cos\left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)-\cos\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)\right]$ $\;=1+2\sin\frac{C}{2}\left[2\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\right]$ $\;=1+4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}$ $\;=1+4\left[\sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}} \sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{ac}}\right]$ $\;=\frac{1+4(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{abc}$ $\;=\frac{1+4 s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{sabc}\left[\therefore \text{ multiply and divide by } s\right]$ $\;=1+4\frac{\Delta^2}{sabc},\;\text{ where } \Delta \text{ is area of triangle }$ $\;=1+\left(\frac{\Delta}{s}\right)\left(\frac{4\Delta}{abc}\right)\;\;\left[\because r=\frac{\Delta}{s}\text{ and }R=\frac{abc}{4\Delta}\right]$ $\;=1+\frac{r}{R}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In triangle $\triangle ABC$ , given $a=26, b=30$ , and $\cos C=\;\frac{63}{65}$ , we need to find the length of side $c$ . We know the cosine rule for any triangle is given by: $\cos C=\;\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$ Substituting the known values: $\;\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2 \times a \times b}=\;\frac{63}{65}$ This implied expression becomes: $\;\frac{26^2+30^2-c^2}{2 \times 26 \times 30}=\;\frac{63}{65}$ Now, solve this step-by-step: Calculate $26^2$ and $30^2$ : $26^2=676, \;\; 30^2=900$ Substitute these into the equation: $\;\frac{676+900-c^2}{1560}=\;\frac{63}{65}$ Simplify the numerator: $676+900=1576$ Substitute back: $\;\frac{1576-c^2}{1560}=\;\frac{63}{65}$ Cross-multiply to solve for $c^2$ : $65 (1576-c^2) =63 \times 1560$ Compute $63 \times 1560$ : $63 \times 1560=98280$ Now, solve for $c^2$ : $65 \times (1576-c^2)=98280$ Simplify the expressions: $102440-65c^2=98280$ Rearrange to find $c^2$ : $102440-98280=65c^2$ Solve: $4160=65c^2$ Divide by 65 to isolate $c^2$ : $c^2=\;\frac{4160}{65}=64$ Take the square root: $c=\sqrt{64}=8$ Thus, the value of $c$ is 8 . © examsnet.com

Solution: In $\triangle AFC$ $\;\cos A=\;\frac{AF}{AC}=\;\frac{AF}{b}$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; AF=b\cos A$ In $\triangle AFH$ $\;\cos (90^{\circ}-2B)=\;\frac{AF}{AH}\Rightarrow \sin B=\;\frac{b\cos A}{x}.$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; x=\left(\frac{b}{\sin B}\right)\cos A$ Using sine rule, we get $\;x=\left(\frac{a}{\sin A}\right)\cos A$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{a}{x}=\tan A$ Similarly, $\;\frac{b}{y}=\tan B$ and $\;\frac{c}{z}=\tan c$ $\therefore\;\;\;\frac{akc}{xyz}\;=\tan A\tan B\tan C$ $\;=\tan A+\tan B+\tan C\;\; [\because A+B+C=\pi]$ $\;=\;\frac{a}{x}+\;\frac{b}{y}+\;\frac{c}{z}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Concept: Three points are collinear if the vectors joining them are parallel (proportional components). Formula: If $\vec{AB} \parallel \vec{AC}$ , then $\frac{AB_x}{AC_x} = \frac{AB_y}{AC_y} = \frac{AB_z}{AC_z}$ Solution: Let $A = \alpha\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+13\hat{k}$ , $B = 6\hat{i}+11\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$ , $C = \frac{9}{2}\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}-8\hat{k}$ $\vec{AB} = (6-\alpha)\hat{i} + 1\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ $\vec{AC} = \left(\frac{9}{2}-\alpha\right)\hat{i} + (\beta-10)\hat{j} - 21\hat{k}$ For collinearity, set the ratios equal: $\frac{6-\alpha}{\frac{9}{2}-\alpha} = \frac{1}{\beta-10} = \frac{-2}{-21} = \frac{2}{21}$ Finding $\beta$ : $\frac{1}{\beta-10} = \frac{2}{21} ⇒ \beta - 10 = \frac{21}{2} ⇒ \beta = \frac{41}{2}$ Finding $\alpha$ : $\frac{6-\alpha}{\frac{9}{2}-\alpha} = \frac{2}{21}$ $21(6-\alpha) = 2\left(\frac{9}{2}-\alpha\right)$ $126 - 21\alpha = 9 - 2\alpha$ $117 = 19\alpha ⇒ \alpha = \frac{117}{19}$ Computing the expression: $19\alpha = 117, \quad 6\beta = 6 \times \frac{41}{2} = 123$ $(19\alpha - 6\beta)^2 = (117 - 123)^2 = (-6)^2 = 36$ Answer: Option B — $(19\alpha - 6\beta)^2 = 36$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the equal magnitude of the mutually orthogonal vectors be $m$ . Since $\overline{f},\overline{g},\overline{h}$ are mutually orthogonal, $\overline{f}\cdot\overline{g}=\overline{g}\cdot\overline{h}=\overline{h}\cdot\overline{f}=0$ . Let $\overline{a}=\overline{f}+\overline{g}+\overline{h}$ and $\overline{b}=\overline{h}$ . The dot product is $\overline{a}\cdot\overline{b}=(\overline{f}+\overline{g}+\overline{h})\cdot\overline{h}=\overline{h}\cdot\overline{h}=m^2$ . The magnitude of $\overline{a}$ is $|\overline{a}|=\sqrt{m^2+m^2+m^2}=m\sqrt{3}$ . The magnitude of $\overline{b}$ is $|\overline{b}|=m$ . Therefore, if $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors, $\cos\theta=\frac{\overline{a}\cdot\overline{b}}{|\overline{a}||\overline{b}|}=\frac{m^2}{m\sqrt{3}\cdot m}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ . Hence $\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ . Thus the correct option is the one with $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given two unit vectors $a$ and $b$ , we know that: $|a|=|b|=1$ Consider the vectors $c=a+2b$ and $d=5a-4b$ . These vectors are perpendicular, meaning: $c \cdot d=0$ Let's compute the dot product: $(a+2b) \cdot (5a-4b)=a \cdot (5a-4b)+2b \cdot (5a-4b)$ Expanding this, we have: $=a \cdot 5a - a \cdot 4b + 2b \cdot 5a - 2b \cdot 4b$ This simplifies to: $=5|a|^2 - 4 a \cdot b + 10 a \cdot b - 8|b|^2$ Simplifying further by substituting $|a|=1$ and $|b|=1$ : $=5(1)+6 a \cdot b -8(1)=0$ Which simplifies to: $\;5-8+6(a \cdot b)=0$ $\;-3+6(a \cdot b)=0$ Solving for $a \cdot b$ : $\;6(a \cdot b)=3$ $\; a \cdot b = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ The dot product $a \cdot b = |a||b| \cos \theta$ , so: $\cos \theta = \; \frac{1}{2}$ Thus, the angle $\theta$ between $a$ and $b$ is: $\theta = \; \frac{\pi}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & p & 5 \end{vmatrix}=0$ Calculate the determinant: $=2(2 \cdot 5-(-3) \cdot p)-(-1)(1 \cdot 5-(-3) \cdot 3)+1(1 \cdot p-2 \cdot 3)$ Simplify each term: The first term: $2(10+3p)=20+6p$ The second term: $-1(5+9)=-14$ The third term: $1(p-6)=p-6$ Combining these terms gives: $20+6p-14+p-6=0$ Simplifying further: $20+6p-14+p-6=0 \Rightarrow 7p=-28 \Rightarrow p=-4$ Thus, the value of $p$ is -4 . © examsnet.com

Solution: To find the variance given the coefficient of variation (CV) and the mean, we can use the following relationship: The formula for the coefficient of variation (CV) is given by: $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\mu} \times 100$ where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation and $\mu$ is the mean. In this problem, the coefficient of variation is 25 , and the mean $(\mu)$ is 44 . Substituting these values into the equation, we have: $\frac{\sigma}{44} \times 100 = 25$ Solving for $\sigma$ , we get: $\sigma = \frac{25 \times 44}{100} = 11$ The variance $(\sigma^2)$ is the square of the standard deviation: $\sigma^2 = 11^2 = 121$ Therefore, the variance is 121 . © examsnet.com
