Solution: $P = |P| = 25 \text{ units}$ $P_y = 7$ $\text{ Since, } \sqrt{P_x^2 + P_y^2} = P$ $\Rightarrow P_x^2 + P_y^2 = P^2$ $\Rightarrow P_x^2 + 7^2 = 25^2$ $\Rightarrow P_x = \sqrt{25^2 - 7^2}$ $= \sqrt{625 - 49}$ $= \sqrt{576} = 24 \text{ units}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Height of auditorium is 30 m and ball just reaches to this height so this is the maximum height of projectile. Let angle of projection is $\theta$ . $\;\;\text{ So, }\; H_{max}=30=\;\frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$ $\;\;\;\;\;   30\;=\;\frac{(30)^2 \sin^2\theta}{2 \times 10}$ $\sin^2\theta\;=\;\frac{600}{900}=\;\frac{2}{3}$ $\;\Rightarrow  \sin\theta=\sqrt{\;\frac{2}{3}}$ $\;\;\text{ and }\; \cos\theta=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ Now, length of auditorium will be equal to range of projectile. $\;\text{ So, }\;\;R=\frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ $\;=\;\frac{u^2 (2 \sin\theta \cos\theta)}{g}$ $R\;=\;\frac{(30)^2 \times 2 \times \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{0.10}$ $R\;=\;\frac{1800 \sqrt{2}}{30}$ $\;=60 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: When the balloon is descending, the net force acting on it is given by $F_{\text{net}} = mg - B = ma$ , where $B$ is the Buoyant force. Thus, $B = mg - ma$ For the balloon to move upwards with the same acceleration $a$ , a mass $\Delta m$ must be removed. The new net force equation becomes $B - (m-\Delta m)g = (m-\Delta m)a$ $mg - ma - (m-\Delta m)g = (m-\Delta m)a \quad [\text{From Eq. (i)}]$ $\Rightarrow \quad \Delta m = \frac{2ma}{g+a}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Frictional force $f_s\; = \mu m g = 0.2 \times 10 \times 10$ $\Rightarrow \;\; f_s\; = 20 \mathrm{N}$ ∴ deceleration, $a = \frac{f_s}{m}$ $= \frac{20}{10} = 2 \mathrm{m/s^2}$ Using, $v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s$ $\Rightarrow \;\; s = \frac{v^2-u^2}{2a}$ $= \frac{0^2-2^2}{2 \times (-2)} = 1 \mathrm{m}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let's use the work-energy theorem, which says: $K\;=W$ $\Rightarrow \;\; K\;=F \times s \;\; \ldots (i)$ Here, $K$ is kinetic energy, $F$ is force, and $s$ is distance. When a force acts and the body starts from rest, the distance $s$ covered in time $t$ is: $s = \frac{1}{2} a t^2$ Since acceleration $a = \frac{F}{m}$ (where $m$ is mass), we get: $s = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{F}{m} \times t^2$ Now, substitute $s$ from (ii) into our equation (i): $K = F \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{F}{m} \times t^2$ So, $K = \frac{F^2}{2 m} t^2$ We are told both bodies $A$ and $B$ get the same kinetic energy ( $K_A = K_B$ ) using the same force $F = 40\,\mathrm{N}$ , but their masses and times are different. Set up the equation for both bodies and compare: $\frac{F^2}{2 m_A} t_A^2 = \frac{F^2}{2 m_B} t_B^2$ You can cancel out $F^2$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ because they are the same: $\frac{t_A^2}{m_A} = \frac{t_B^2}{m_B}$ Rearrange to solve for time ratio: $\frac{t_A^2}{t_B^2} = \frac{m_A}{m_B}$ Take the square root for the ratio $t_A: t_B$ : $\frac{t_A}{t_B} = \sqrt{\frac{m_A}{m_B}}$ Plug in $m_A = 20\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_B = 5\,\mathrm{kg}$ : $\frac{t_A}{t_B} = \sqrt{\frac{20}{5}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$ So, the ratio $t_A: t_B = 2: 1$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Potential energy gained by crane, $U\;=m g h$ $\;=8000 \times 10 \times 108$ $\;=8.64 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{J}$ ∴ Output power of crane $\;P_0=\;\frac{W}{t}=\;\frac{U}{t}=\;\frac{8.64 \times 10^6}{60 \times 60}$ $\Rightarrow P_0=2.4 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{W}=2.4\,\mathrm{kW}$ Since, efficiency of crane $\eta\;=\;\frac{P_0}{P_i}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 0.8\;=\;\frac{P_0}{P_i}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; P_i\;=\;\frac{P_0}{0.8}$ $\;=\;\frac{2.4}{0.8}\,\mathrm{kW}=3\,\mathrm{kW}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: First we calculate centre of mass of system let block $A$ is at origin ( $x=0$ ) $\;x_{C M}=\;\frac{10(0)+25(10)+15(20)}{10+25+15}$ $\;x_{C M}=\;\frac{550}{50}=11\,\mathrm{m}$ Now, new position of block $A$ with respect to origin is $x=2\,\mathrm{m}$ and new position of block $C, x=20-3=17\,\mathrm{m}$ . Let new position of block $B$ with respect to origin is $Y$ , so that centre of mass remains at same position Then, $x_{CM}\;=11\;\frac{10(2)+25(y)+15(17)}{50}$ $550\;=20+25y+255$ $25y\;=550-275=275$ $y\;=\;\frac{275}{25}=11\,\mathrm{m}$ So, block $B$ should move $11-10=1$ metre towards block $C$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;a_{\;\text{rolling}\;} \;\; =\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\;\frac{I}{M R^2}}=\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\;\frac{\;\frac{2}{5} M R^2}{M R^2}}$ $\;\;\; 3.5 =\frac{5}{7}(g \sin \theta)$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; g \sin \theta=4.9$ Thus, acceleration of the sphere when it slides down without rolling is $g \sin \theta$ $=4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Maximum velocity $v_{\max}=5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ Maximum acceleration $a_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{m/s}^2$ For SHM relationships: $\: v_{\max}= \omega A$ $\: a_{\max}= \omega^2 A$ where $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and $A$ is the amplitude. Step 1: Divide the two equations $\: \: \frac{a_{\max}}{v_{\max}} = \: \frac{\omega^2 A}{\omega A} = \omega$ $\: \Rightarrow \omega = \: \frac{a_{\max}}{v_{\max}} = \: \frac{10}{5} = 2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ Step 2: Find the time period $\: T = \: \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \: \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$ Final Answer: $T = \pi\,\mathrm{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Combined mass, $m=m_1+m_2$ $=1+0.5=1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ Using conservation of momentum, $\;m_1 u_1+m_2 u_2=(m_1+m_2) v$ $\Rightarrow 1 \times 0+0.5 \times 3=1.5 v$ $\Rightarrow v=1\ \mathrm{m/s}$ According to conservation of energy, $\;\;\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\;\frac{1}{2} k A^2$ $\Rightarrow A=\sqrt{\;\frac{m v^2}{k}}$ $\Rightarrow \;\;\sqrt{\;\frac{1.5 \times 1^2}{600}}=\sqrt{\;\frac{1}{400}}=\;\frac{1}{20}\ \mathrm{m}$ $\;=\;\frac{100}{20}\ \mathrm{cm}=5\ \mathrm{cm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Height of satellite $A$ above Earth's surface: $h_A=1.25 R_E$ Height of satellite $B$ above Earth's surface: $h_B=19.25 R_E$ Hence, the orbital radii (distance from Earth's center): $\; r_A=R_E+h_A=R_E+1.25 R_E=2.25 R_E$ $\; r_B=R_E+h_B=R_E+19.25 R_E=20.25 R_E$ Formula for orbital speed For a satellite in a circular orbit around Earth: $v=\sqrt{\frac{G M_E}{r}}$ where $G$ is the gravitational constant and $M_E$ is Earth's mass. Thus, for two satellites $A$ and $B$ : $\frac{v_A}{v_B}=\sqrt{\frac{r_B}{r_A}}$ Substitute $r_A$ and $r_B$ $\frac{v_A}{v_B}=\sqrt{\frac{20.25 R_E}{2.25 R_E}}=\sqrt{\frac{20.25}{2.25}}=\sqrt{9}=3$ Therefore, $v_A : v_B = 3 : 1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Elastic potential energy per unit volume $U \;=\; \frac{W}{V} \;=\; \frac{\frac{1}{2} F \Delta l}{A \cdot l}$ $\;=\; \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{F}{A} \cdot \frac{\Delta l}{l}$ $\;=\; \frac{1}{2} \times \text{ Stress} \times \text{Strain} \;$ $\;=\; \frac{1}{2} \times \text{ Stress } \times \frac{ \text{ Stress } }{Y}$ $\;=\; \frac{1}{2} \times S \times \frac{S}{Y} \;=\; \frac{S^2}{2Y}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Mass of the aeroplane, $m=4.5 \times 10^4 \text{ kg}$ Total wing area, $A=600 \text{ m}^2$ Acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \text{ m/s}^2$ The aeroplane is travelling at a constant height, meaning lift = weight. Step 1. Lift $=$ Pressure difference × Area $L=\Delta P \times A$ Step 2. Lift = Weight $L=m g$ So, $\Delta P \times A=m g$ Step 3. Solve for pressure difference $\Delta P = \frac{m g}{A}$ Substitute the known values: $\Delta P = \frac{4.5 \times 10^4 \times 10}{600}$ $\Delta P = \frac{4.5 \times 10^5}{600}$ $\Delta P = 750 \text{ N/m}^2$ Answer: $750 \text{ N/m}^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to Wien's displacement law. $\; \lambda_m \cdot T = b$ $\Rightarrow \lambda_m \propto \; \frac{1}{T} \Rightarrow \; \frac{ (\lambda_m)_A }{ (\lambda_m)_B } = \; \frac{ T_B }{ T_A }$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{ 0.5 \times 10^{-6} }{ 0.1 \times 10^{-3} } = \; \frac{ T_B }{ T_A }$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{ 5 \times 10^{-3} }{ 1 } = \; \frac{ T_B }{ T_A }$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{ T_A }{ T_B } = \; \frac{ 1 }{ 5 \times 10^{-3} } = \; \frac{ 10^3 }{ 5 } = \; \frac{ 1000 }{ 5 } = 200$ © examsnet.com

Solution: A stretched wire has a fundamental frequency $f$ . When it is divided into $3$ segments, their fundamental frequencies are $f_1, f_2$ , and $f_3$ . Tension $T$ is constant. We need to find the relation among $f, f_1, f_2, f_3$ . Step 1: Formula for fundamental frequency of a stretched string For a string under tension $T$ , length $L$ , and linear density $\mu$ : $f = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Step 2: Frequencies of the three parts Suppose the original length is divided into three parts of lengths $L_1, L_2, L_3$ , so that $L = L_1 + L_2 + L_3$ Then their fundamental frequencies are $f_1 = \frac{1}{2L_1} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}, \quad f_2 = \frac{1}{2L_2} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}, \quad f_3 = \frac{1}{2L_3} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Step 3: Express $L_i$ in terms of $f_i$ From the above, $L_i = \frac{1}{2 f_i} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ and $L = \frac{1}{2 f} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Step 4: Use $L = L_1 + L_2 + L_3$ $\frac{1}{2f} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \left( \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} + \frac{1}{f_3} \right)$ Cancel the common factor $\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ : $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} + \frac{1}{f_3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Magnification of a lens is given as $m=\;\frac{v}{u}$ from lens formula $\;\frac{1}{v}\;-\;\frac{1}{u}=\;\frac{1}{f}$ $\;\frac{1}{v}\;=\;\frac{f+u}{f u}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \;\frac{u}{v}\;=\;\frac{f+u}{f}$ and $m=\;\frac{v}{u}=\;\frac{f}{f+u}$ Now, magnification in both case is equal. So, $m_1=-m_2$ $\;\frac{f}{f-20}\;=\;\frac{-f}{f-10}$ $f-20\;=-f+10$ $2 f\;=30 \Rightarrow f=15\ \text{cm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Fringe width, $\beta=\;\frac{D\lambda}{d}$ $\;\;\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}=\;\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} \cdot \;\frac{d_2}{d_1}$ $\;=\left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+20\%\;\text{ of }\;\lambda_1}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{d_1-25\%\;\text{ of }\;d_1}{d_1}\right)$ $\;=\left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\frac{\lambda_1}{5}}\right) \left(\frac{d_1-\frac{d_1}{4}}{d_1}\right)=\frac{5}{6} \times \frac{3}{4}$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}=\frac{5}{8}$ $\;\Rightarrow \beta_2=\frac{8}{5} \beta_1=\frac{8}{5} \times 0.3=0.48 \text{ mm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Potential at point $C$ , due to charges $+q$ and $-q$ . $V_C=-\frac{k q}{d}+\frac{k q}{d}=0$ and potential of point $D$ $V_0=\frac{-k q}{d}+\frac{k q}{3d}=\frac{-2 k q}{3d}$ So, potential difference between $C$ and $D$ $V_D-V_C=\frac{-2 k q}{3d}$ So, work done in moving charge $Q$ from $C$ to $D$ $W=Q (V_D-V_C)$ $W=\frac{-2 k Q q}{3d}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Length $L=30 \text{m}$ Area of cross-section $A=6 \times 10^{-7} \text{m}^2$ Resistivity $\rho=1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{m}$ Formula: $R=\rho \frac{L}{A}$ Substitution: $R=(1.7 \times 10^{-8}) \times \frac{30}{6 \times 10^{-7}}$ Simplify: $\frac{30}{6 \times 10^{-7}}=5 \times 10^7$ So, $R=1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 5 \times 10^7$ $R=(1.7 \times 5) \times 10^{-1}$ $R=8.5 \times 10^{-1}=0.85 \Omega$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The current $I=80 \text{A}$ , and the length of the conductor $L=10 \text{m}$ . Expression for Current: Current can be written as $I=n e A V_d$ , where $n$ is the number of electrons per unit volume, $e$ is the charge of an electron, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $V_d$ is the drift velocity of electrons. Total Number of Electrons: Let $N$ be the total number of free electrons in the length $L$ of the conductor. $N=n A L$ . Total Momentum: The total momentum of all free electrons is $P_{\text{total}} = N (m_e V_d)$ , where $m_e$ is the mass of an electron. Substitute $N$ : So, $P_{\text{total}} = (n A L) (m_e V_d)$ . Rewrite with Current Expression: Since $I=n e A V_d$ , we can replace $n A V_d$ with $\frac{I}{e}$ . Therefore, $P_{\text{total}} = \frac{I}{e} L m_e$ . Solution: The formula for wavelength is: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$ First Line of Lyman Series: For Lyman series, $n_1 = 1$ . The first line means $n_2 = 2$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2} \right) = R \left( 1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) = R \left( \frac{3}{4} \right) = \frac{3R}{4}$ So, $\lambda_L = \frac{4}{3R}$ Second Line of Balmer Series: For Balmer series, $n_1 = 2$ . The second line means $n_2 = 4$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = R \left( \frac{3}{16} \right) = \frac{3R}{16}$ So, $\lambda_B = \frac{16}{3R}$ Find the Ratio: Now, find $\frac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B}$ : $\frac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B} = \frac{\frac{4}{3R}}{\frac{16}{3R}} = \frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$ This means $\lambda_L : \lambda_B = 1 : 4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We want to find the temperature where the rms (root mean square) speed of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ molecules is equal to the rms speed of $\mathrm{O}_2$ molecules at $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The formula for rms velocity is: $V_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 R T}{M}}$ where $R$ is the gas constant, $T$ is temperature in Kelvin, and $M$ is molar mass. We set the rms speeds equal: $V_{\text{rms}(\mathrm{SO}_2)} = V_{\text{rms}(\mathrm{O}_2)} \text{ So }, \sqrt{\frac{3 R T_{\mathrm{SO}_2}}{M_{\mathrm{SO}_2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 R T_{\mathrm{O}_2}}{M_{\mathrm{O}_2}}}$ Squaring both sides removes the square root: $\frac{T_{\mathrm{SO}_2}}{M_{\mathrm{SO}_2}}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{O}_2}}{M_{\mathrm{O}_2}}$ Rearrange for $T_{\mathrm{SO}_2}: T_{\mathrm{SO}_2}=T_{\mathrm{O}_2} \times \frac{M_{\mathrm{SO}_2}}{M_{\mathrm{O}_2}}$ The temperature given for $\mathrm{O}_2$ is $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Convert this to Kelvin: $27+273=300\,	ext{K}$ The molar mass of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ is 64 , and of $\mathrm{O}_2$ is 32 . Plug in the values: $T_{\mathrm{SO}_2}=300 \times \frac{64}{32}=300 \times 2=600\,\text{K}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The slope of an isochore (a line where volume does not change) for an ideal gas is given by $\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{nR}{V}$ , where: $n =$ number of moles, $R =$ gas constant, $V =$ volume. Here, the slope is $0.082 \text{atm} \text{K}^{-1}, n=1$ , and $R=0.082 \text{L} \text{atm} \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}$ . Substitute the known values into the formula: $0.082 = \;\frac{1 \times 0.082}{V}$ Solve for $V$ : $V = 1 \text{L}$ Now, use the ideal gas equation: $p V = n R T$ . Solution: $W+X\rightleftharpoons Y+Z$ Initial concentrations: W starts at $2 x, X$ starts at $x$ , and both Y and Z start at 0 . At equilibrium: Let the amount of Y and Z formed be $y$ . So, at equilibrium: $\;W=2 x-y$ $\;X=x-y$ $\;Y=y$ $\;Z=y$ Relationship between Y and X at equilibrium: At equilibrium, the amount of Y is four times the amount of X . This gives us: $[Y]_{e q}=4[X]_{e q}$ So, $y=4(x-y)$ Solve for $y$ : $y=4 x-4 y$ $y+4 y=4 x$ $5 y=4 x$ $y=\;\frac{4}{5}x$ Write $K_c$ expression and substitute values: The equilibrium constant is: $K_c=\;\frac{[Y][Z]}{[W][X]}$ Plug in the equilibrium values: $K_c=\;\frac{\left(\frac{4}{5}x\right)\left(\frac{4}{5}x\right)}{\left(2x-\;\frac{4}{5}x\right)\left(x-\;\frac{4}{5}x\right)}$ Simplify: Numerator: $\left(\;\frac{4}{5}x\right)^2=\;\frac{16}{25}x^2$ Denominator: $\;2 x-\;\frac{4}{5}x=\;\frac{10 x-4 x}{5}=\;\frac{6 x}{5}$ $\;x-\;\frac{4}{5}x=\;\frac{5 x-4 x}{5}=\;\frac{x}{5}$ So denominator: $\;\frac{6 x}{5} \cdot \;\frac{x}{5}=\;\frac{6 x^2}{25}$ Therefore, $K_c=\;\frac{\frac{16x^2}{25}}{\frac{6x^2}{25}}=\;\frac{16}{6}=2.666$ © examsnet.com

Water needs to be separated from the alkyl chloride, which can be challenging, especially for lower molecular weight alkyl chlorides that may be soluble in water or form azeotropes. This makes obtaining pure alkyl chloride directly difficult. Option B: $\mathrm{PCl}_5$ (Phosphorus Pentachloride) Reaction: $\mathrm{ROH} + \mathrm{PCl}_5 \longrightarrow \mathrm{RCl} + \mathrm{POCl}_3 + \mathrm{HCl}$ Byproducts: Phosphorus oxychloride $(\mathrm{POCl}_3)$ and hydrogen chloride $(\mathrm{HCl}) . \mathrm{POCl}_3$ is a liquid, and HCl is a gas. The separation of these byproducts from the desired alkyl chloride may require careful distillation or other purification steps, affecting the direct purity. Option C: SOCl ${}_2$ (Thionyl Chloride) Reaction: $\mathrm{ROH} + \mathrm{SOCl}_2 \xrightarrow[]{ \;\text{Pyridine}\;} \mathrm{RCl} + \mathrm{SO}_2 \uparrow + \mathrm{HCl} \uparrow$ Byproducts: Sulfur dioxide $(\mathrm{SO}_2)$ and hydrogen chloride $(\mathrm{HCl})$ . Both of these are gases. They readily escape from the reaction mixture as they are formed. This leaves behind a relatively pure alkyl chloride, making the purification process very simple and efficient. This is often considered the best method for preparing pure alkyl halides because the gaseous byproducts automatically separate from the desired product. This is a non-volatile solid or viscous liquid. It needs to be separated from the alkyl chloride, typically by distillation or extraction, which adds purification steps. Solution: Given, $a: b: c=4: 5: 6$ We can express the sides as $a=4x, b=5x$ and $c=6x$ for some positive constant $x$ . $\;\because \cos A=\;\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}(\;\text{ By Cosine rule }\;)$ $\;=\;\frac{(5x)^2+(6x)^2-(4x)^2}{2 \times 5x \times 6x}=\;\frac{45x^2}{60x^2}=\;\frac{3}{4}$ Similarly, $\cos B=\;\frac{(4x)^2+(6x)^2-(5x)^2}{2(4x)(6x)}$ $=\;\frac{27x^2}{48x^2}=\;\frac{9}{16}$ and $\cos C=\;\frac{(4x)^2+(5x)^2-(6x)^2}{2(4x)(5x)}$ $=\;\frac{5x^2}{40x^2}=\;\frac{1}{8}$ So, $\;\frac{\cos A+3\cos C}{\cos B}=\;\frac{\;\frac{3}{4}+3\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\frac{9}{16}}=\;\frac{\;\frac{6+3}{8}}{\frac{9}{16}}$ $=\;\frac{9}{8} \times \;\frac{16}{9}=2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Use formula for combined variance Let $n_1=15, \mu_1=2, \sigma_1^2=4$ $n_2=10, \mu_2=2, \sigma_2^2=5$ $\; \;\text{ Combined mean }\; \; = \mu = \; \frac{n_1 \mu_1 + n_2 \mu_2}{n_1+n_2}$ $\; = \frac{15 \times 2 + 10 \times 2}{25} = 2$ Combined variance $= \sigma^2$ $= \; \frac{n_1 \sigma_1^2 + n_2 \sigma_2^2 + n_1 (\mu_1-\mu)^2 + n_2 (\mu_2-\mu)^2}{n_1+n_2}$ Since, $\mu_1 = \mu_2 =$ the last two terms becomes zero. Solution: Distinct rational numbers of the form $\frac{p}{q}$ are counted by reducing each fraction, so each distinct value corresponds to a coprime pair $(p,q)$ with $p,q\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ . The provided table is: $q$ Valid $p$ (C.G.D. $(p,q)=1$ Count 1 $2,3,4,5,6$ 5 2 $1,3,5$ 3 3 $1,2,4,5$ 4 4 $1,3,5$ 3 5 $1,2,3,4,6$ 5 6 1,5 2 Total $2\;2$ The table omits $p=1$ when $q=1$ , but $\gcd(1,1)=1$ , so the correct total number of distinct reduced fractions is $6+3+4+3+5+2=23$ . Now count proper fractions, i.e. reduced fractions with $p < q$ . For $q=1$ , there is no proper fraction. For $q=2$ , the valid numerators are $1,3,5$ ; only $p=1$ satisfies $p < q$ , giving $1$ . For $q=3$ , the valid numerators are $1,2,4,5$ ; $p=1,2$ satisfy $p < q$ , giving $2$ . For $q=4$ , the valid numerators are $1,3,5$ ; $p=1,3$ satisfy $p < q$ , giving $2$ . For $q=5$ , the valid numerators are $1,2,3,4,6$ ; $p=1,2,3,4$ satisfy $p < q$ , giving $4$ . For $q=6$ , the valid numerators are $1,5$ ; both satisfy $p < q$ , giving $2$ . Total proper fractions $=1+2+2+4+2=11$ . Therefore the required probability is $\frac{11}{23}$ . Hence the correct option is $\frac{11}{23}$ (option option C). © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\sum x^2 \cdot P(X=x) = (-1)^2 \cdot \;\frac{1}{3} + 0^2 \cdot \;\frac{1}{6} + 1^2 \cdot \;\frac{1}{6} + 2^2 \cdot \;\frac{1}{3} = 1 \cdot \;\frac{1}{3} + 0 + 1 \times \;\frac{1}{6} + 4 \times \;\frac{1}{3} = \;\frac{11}{6}$ $\;E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(X) = (-1) \cdot \;\frac{1}{3} + 0 \cdot \;\frac{1}{6} + 1 \times \;\frac{1}{6} + 2 \times \;\frac{1}{3} = \;\frac{1}{2}$ $\; \therefore \operatorname{var}(X) = E(X^2) - (E(X))^2$ $\; \;\; = \;\frac{11}{6} - \;\frac{1}{4} = \;\frac{19}{12}$ Hence, $6 \cdot \sum x^2 \cdot P(X=x) - \operatorname{var}(X)$ $= 6 \times \;\frac{11}{6} - \;\frac{19}{12} = \;\frac{132-19}{12} = \;\frac{113}{12}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Average number of accidents per weeks $(\lambda)=5$ We want to find the probability of at most one accident i.e. $P(X \leq 1)=P(0)+P(1) .$ As we know that, poisson probability formula, $P(X=k)=\;\frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k}{k!}$ $\therefore \;\;  P(0)=\;\frac{e^{-5} \cdot 5^0}{0!}=e^{-5}$ $P(1)=\;\frac{e^{-5} \cdot 5^1}{1!}=5 e^{-5}$ $\therefore  P(X \leq 1)=e^{-5}(1+5)=6 e^{-5}=\;\frac{6}{e^5}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\; y = \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{\sqrt{1+\sin x} + \sqrt{1-\sin x}}{\sqrt{1+\sin x} - \sqrt{1-\sin x}} \right)$ $\Rightarrow y = \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{(\sqrt{1+\sin x} + \sqrt{1-\sin x})^2}{(\sqrt{1+\sin x})^2 - (\sqrt{1-\sin x})^2} \right)$ $= \; \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{1+\sin x+1-\sin x+2\sqrt{1-\sin^2 x}}{1+\sin x-1+\sin x} \right)$ $= \; \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{2+2|\cos x|}{2 \sin x} \right) = \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x} \right) \binom{ \because \; \frac{-3\pi}{2} < x < \frac{-\pi}{2} }{ \therefore |\cos x| = -\cos x }$ $= \; \sin^{-1} \left( \; \frac{2 \sin^2 \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)}{2 \sin \left( \frac{x}{2} \right) \cos \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)} \right) = \sin^{-1} \left( \tan \left( \frac{x}{2} \right) \right)$ $\therefore \;\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \tan^2 \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)}} \times \sec^2 \left( \frac{x}{2} \right) \times \frac{1}{2}$ $= \;\; \frac{\left|\cos^{\frac{x}{2}}\right|}{\sqrt{\cos^2 \frac{x}{2} - \sin^2 \frac{x}{2}}} \times \frac{1}{\left|\cos \frac{x}{2}\right|^2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \; \frac{\left|\sec \frac{x}{2}\right|}{2 \sqrt{\cos x}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $x=\sqrt{2} e^t(\sin t-\cos t)$ and $y=\sqrt{2} e^t(\sin t+\cos t)$ On differentiating both side, we get $\therefore \;\; \frac{dx}{dt}=\sqrt{2} e^t[2\sin t] \;\text{ and }\; \frac{dy}{dt}=\sqrt{2} e^t(2\cos t)$ $\therefore \;\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}} = \cot t$ Again, differentiating both side, $\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} = \frac{d \cot t}{d x} = \frac{d \cot t}{d t} \times \frac{dt}{dx}$ $= -\csc^2 t \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} e^t (2\sin t)} = \frac{-1}{2 \sqrt{2} e^t \cdot \sin^3 t}$ $\therefore \left. \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \right|_{t=\frac{\pi}{4}} = \frac{-1}{2 \sqrt{2} \times e^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^3} = -e^{\frac{-\pi}{4}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, equation of circle is $x^2+y^2=a^2 \;\; \;\; \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot (i)$ Also $P$ and $Q$ are end points of diameter. Let $P \equiv (a \cos \theta, a \sin \; \theta)$ $Q \equiv (-a \cos \theta, -a \sin \; \theta)$ According to the question, $s \;=\; \frac{|a \cos \theta + a \sin \; \theta - 1|}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\;=\; \frac{|a(\cos \theta + \sin \; \theta) - 1|}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\; \text{ and } \; t \;=\; \frac{|-a(\cos \theta + \sin \; \theta) - 1|}{\sqrt{2}} = 1$ $\; \text{ Now, st } \;\; = \; \frac{| 1 - a^2 (\cos \theta + \sin \; \theta)^2 |}{2}$ $\; = \; \frac{| 1 - a^2 (1 + \sin \; 2\theta) |}{2}$ So, ( $s t$ ) will be maximum, if ( $1 + \sin \; 2\theta$ ) minimum, $\; \because (\sin \; 2\theta)_{\min} = -1 (\; \text{ i.e. } \; \sin \; 2\theta \ge -1)$ $\; \Rightarrow 1 + \sin \; 2\theta \ge 0 \; \therefore (1 + \sin \; 2\theta)_{\min} = 0$ $\; \therefore (a^2 (1 + \sin \; 2\theta))_{\min} = 0 \; \text{ and hence, } \; s t = \frac{1}{2}$ $\;\; \text{ Also, } \; (a^2 (1 + \sin \; 2\theta))_{\max} = 2 a^2$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; s t = \frac{| 1 - 2 a^2 |}{2} > \frac{1}{2} \; \text{ for } \; a > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ So, $(s t)_{\text{max}}$ occurs when $a^2 \; (1 + \sin \; 2\theta) = 2 a^2$ $\Rightarrow 1 + \sin \; 2\theta = 2 \left( \because a > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \; \therefore |a| = a\right)$ $\Rightarrow \cos \theta + \sin \; \theta = \sqrt{2}$ $\Rightarrow \theta = 45^{\circ}$ $\therefore \;\;\; s = \frac{|\sqrt{2} a - 1|}{\sqrt{2}}, \; \text{ and } \; t = \frac{|\sqrt{2} a + 1|}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore \;\;\; a > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{2} a > 1$ $\therefore \;\;\; s = \frac{\sqrt{2} a - 1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $t = \frac{\sqrt{2} a + 1}{\sqrt{2}} = a + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ Clearly, $t > s$ $\therefore \;\; \left(a + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ is the final answer. © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{(\sec x + \tan x)^{\frac{5}{2}}} dx$ Put $\sec x + \tan x = t$ $\therefore \sec x - \tan x = \frac{1}{t}$ $\therefore \sec x = \frac{1}{2} \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right)$ and $\tan x = \frac{1}{2} \left( t - \frac{1}{t} \right)$ Differentiate w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\Rightarrow \left( \sec x \tan x + \sec^2 x \right) dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow dx = \frac{dt}{\sec x \tan x + \sec^2 x}$ $I = \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\frac{5}{t^2}} \times \frac{dt}{\sec x \tan x + \sec^2 x}$ $= \int \frac{\sec x}{t^{\frac{5}{2}}} \times \frac{dt}{(\sec x + \tan x)}$ $= \int \left( \frac{1}{2} \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right) \right) \cdot \frac{1}{t^{\frac{5}{2}}} \times \frac{1}{t} dt$ $= \frac{1}{2} \int \left( t + \frac{1}{t} \right) t^{-\frac{7}{2}} dt$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \int t^{-\frac{5}{2}} dt + \int t^{-\frac{9}{2}} dt \right]$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{t^{-\frac{3}{2}}}{-\frac{3}{2}} + \frac{t^{-\frac{7}{2}}}{-\frac{7}{2}} \right] + C$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ -\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}} - \frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{\frac{7}{2}} \right] + C$ $= -\frac{1}{3} (\sec x - \tan x)^{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{1}{7} (\sec x - \tan x)^{\frac{7}{2}} + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int \frac{1}{\cos x} \left[ \frac{1}{\sin x} - \frac{1}{\sin x+3\cos x} \right] dx$ $= \int \frac{2}{\sin 2x} dx - \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x+3} dx$ $= 2 \int \csc 2x \, dx - \int \frac{dz}{z+3}, \quad \text{ where }$ $z = \tan x$ $= \frac{2 \log_e |\csc 2x - \cot 2x|}{2} - \ln |z+3| + C$ $= \ln |\csc 2x - \cot 2x| - \ln |\tan x+3| + C$ $= \ln \left| \frac{ \frac{1}{\sin 2x} - \frac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} }{ \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} + 3 } \right| + C$ $= \ln \left| \frac{ \frac{1-\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} }{ \frac{\sin x+3\cos x}{\cos x} } \right| + C$ $= \ln \left| \frac{2 \sin 2}{2 \sin x \cdot \cos x} \times \frac{\cos x}{\sin x+3\cos x} \right| + C$ $= \ln \left| \frac{\sin x}{\sin x+3\cos x} \right| + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I=\int\limits_{0}^{x} \frac{t^{2}}{\sqrt{a^{2}+t^{2}}} \, dt$ Put $t = a \sinh \theta \Rightarrow dt = a \cosh \theta \, d\theta$ Now, $\sqrt{a^{2}+t^{2}} = \sqrt{a^{2}+a^{2} \sinh^{2} \theta}$ $= a \sqrt{1+\sinh^{2}\theta} = a \cosh \theta$ and $t^{2} = a^{2} \sinh^{2} \theta$ $t$ 0 $x$ $\theta$ 0 $\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)$ $\therefore I = \int\limits_{0}^{\sinh^{-1}(x/a)} \frac{a^{2} \sinh^{2} \theta}{a \cosh \theta} \cdot a \cosh \theta \, d\theta$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{\sinh^{-1}(x/a)} a^{2} \sinh^{2} \theta \, d\theta$ $\because \sinh^{2} \theta = \frac{\cosh(2\theta) - 1}{2}$ So, $I = a^{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\sinh^{-1}(x/a)} \frac{\cosh(2\theta)-1}{2} \, d\theta = \frac{a^{2}}{2}$ $\left[ \begin{array}{l} \sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) \\ \int\limits_{0}^{\cosh(2\theta) d\theta - \int\limits_{0}^{\sinh^{-1}(x/a)}} \int\limits_{1} 1 \cdot d\theta \end{array} \right]$ $= \frac{a^{2}}{2} \left[ \frac{1}{2} \sinh(2\theta) - \theta \right] = \frac{a^{2}}{2}$ $= \frac{a^{2}}{2} \left[ \frac{x}{a} \times \frac{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}{a} - \sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) \right]$ $= \frac{x}{2} \sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}} - \frac{a^{2}}{2} \sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Required area (A) $= \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (\cos x - \sin x) dx + \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} (\sin x - \cos x) dx$ $= (\sin x + \cos x)_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} + (-\cos x - \sin x)_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ $= \left[ \left( \sin \frac{\pi}{4} + \cos \frac{\pi}{4} \right) - \left( \sin 0 + \cos 0 \right) \right] - \left[ \left( \cos \frac{\pi}{2} + \sin \frac{\pi}{2} \right) - \left( \cos \frac{\pi}{4} + \sin \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \right]$ $= (\sqrt{2} - 1) - (1 - \sqrt{2})$ $= \sqrt{2} - 1 - 1 + \sqrt{2}$ $= 2 \sqrt{2} - 2 = 2(\sqrt{2} - 1) \; \text{ sq. unit } \;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{ Let } I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \cos^4 x dx$ $= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \frac{1}{\cos^4 x} dx = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \sec^4 x dx$ $= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \sec^2 x (1+\tan^2 x) dx = \int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} (1+u^2) du$ $x$ $\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\frac{\pi}{3}$ $u$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sqrt{3}$ where $u = \tan x$ $= \left( u + \frac{u^3}{3} \right)_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}$ $= \left( \sqrt{3} + \frac{(\sqrt{3})^3}{3} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)^3}{3} \right)$ $= \frac{3\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{3}}{3} - \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{1}{9\sqrt{3}} \right)$ $= \frac{6\sqrt{3}}{3} - \left( \frac{9+1}{9\sqrt{3}} \right) = 2\sqrt{3} - \frac{10\sqrt{3}}{27}$ $= \frac{54\sqrt{3}-10\sqrt{3}}{27} = \frac{44\sqrt{3}}{27} = \frac{44}{9\sqrt{3}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $I = \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} \; \frac{\cos^3 x}{\cos^3 x + \sin^3 x} \, dx \; \cdots (i)$ $\; I = \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} \; \frac{ \left( \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) \right)^3 }{ \left( \cos\left(\; \frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) \right)^3 + \left( \sin\; \left( \; \frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) \right)^3 } \, dx$ $= \; \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} \; \frac{-\sin^3 x}{-\sin^3 x - \cos^3 x} \, dx$ $= \; \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} \; \frac{\sin^3 x}{\sin^3 x + \cos^3 x} \, dx \; \cdots (ii)$ On adding in Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\Rightarrow 2I = \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} dx = \; \frac{3\pi}{2}$ $\therefore \; I = \; \frac{3\pi}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, differential equation is $\sec(x-y+1) dy = dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \cos(x-y+1) \cdots (i)$ Put $x-y=z$ $\Rightarrow 1 - \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dz}{dx} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 - \frac{dz}{dx}$ So, Eq. (i), $\Rightarrow 1 - \frac{dz}{dx} = \cos(z+1)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dz}{dx} = 1 - \cos(z+1) = 2 \sin^2\left( \frac{z+1}{2} \right)$ $\Rightarrow dx = \frac{1}{2} \csc^2\left( \frac{z+1}{2} \right) dz$ On integrating, $x = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \left( -\cot\left( \frac{z+1}{2} \right) \right) + C$ $\Rightarrow x + \cot\left( \frac{x-y+1}{2} \right) = C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $y^2=4 a(x+a)\;\;\; \cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (i)$ Differentiate w.r.t $x$ , we get $\;2 y \;\frac{dy}{dx}=4 a(1+0)=4 a$ $\Rightarrow  \;\;  y \;\frac{dy}{dx}=2 a \Rightarrow a=\frac{y}{2} \;\frac{dy}{dx}$ From Eq. (1) $\;y^2=4 \times \;\frac{y}{2} \cdot \;\frac{dy}{dx} \left(x+\;\frac{y}{2} \;\frac{dy}{dx}\right)$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  y^2=2 y \;\frac{dy}{dx} \times x + y^2 \left(\;\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  y=2 x \;\frac{dy}{dx}+y \left(\;\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, differential equation is $\; \frac{d y}{d x} \; = \; \frac{2 x y-4 x+y-2}{2 x y+x-4 y-2}$ $\; = \; \frac{2 x(y-2)+1(y-2)}{2 y(x-2)+1(x-2)}$ $\; = \; \frac{(2 x+1)(y-2)}{(2 y+1)(x-2)}$ $\; \Rightarrow \int\; \frac{2 y+1}{y-2} d y = \int\; \frac{2 x+1}{x-2} dx$ $\; \Rightarrow \int\; \frac{2(y-2)+5}{y-2} d y = \int\; \frac{2(x-2)+5}{x-2} dx$ $\; \Rightarrow \int 2 d y + \int\; \frac{5}{y-2} d y = \int 2 dx + \int\; \frac{5}{x-2} dx$ $\; \Rightarrow 2 y + 5 \log (y-2) = 2 x + 5 \log (x-2) + c$ $\; \Rightarrow 2(y-x) + 5 \log \left| \frac{y-2}{x-2} \right| = C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\text{ Stress }\;=\;\frac{F}{A}$ $\;\Rightarrow[\;\text{ Stress }\;]=\;\frac{[F]}{[A]}=\;\frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L^2]}=[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ Linear momentum, $p=mv$ $[p]=[m][v]$ $=[M][LT^{-1}]=[MLT^{-1}]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: For a freely falling body starting from rest, the distance covered in the $n$ -th second is given by $S_n=u+\frac{1}{2}g(2n-1)$ . Here $u=0$ and $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ , so $S_n=\frac{1}{2}\times10(2n-1)=5(2n-1)$ . Step 2: Let the last but one second be the $n$ -th second of the motion. The distance travelled in this second is given as $5\ \mathrm{m}$ . Therefore, $5=5(2n-1)$ . Step 3: Solving this equation gives $2n-1=1\Rightarrow2n=2\Rightarrow n=1$ . Thus, the last but one second is the 1st second of the fall. Hence, the last second is the 2nd second. So the correct option is the $2^{\text{nd}}$ second. © examsnet.com

Solution: Range of projectile $R=40\,\text{m}$ $R\;=40=\;\frac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$ $\Rightarrow u^{2}\;=\;\frac{40g}{\sin 2\theta}$ and from equation of trajectory $\;Y=x \tan\theta-\;\frac{1}{2} g \;\frac{x^{2}}{u^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}$ $\;Y=x \tan\theta-\;\frac{1}{2} \;\frac{g x^{2}\sin 2\theta}{40g\times\cos^{2}\theta}$ $\;20=30 \tan\theta-\;\frac{1}{80} \times \;\frac{900 \times 2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}$ $\;20=30 \tan\theta-\;\frac{1800}{80} \tan\theta$ $\;20=30 \tan\theta-\;\frac{45}{2} \tan\theta$ $\;20=\;\frac{15 \tan\theta}{2}$ $\;\Rightarrow 15 \tan\theta=40$ $\;\;\;  \tan\theta=\;\frac{40}{15}=\;\frac{8}{3}$ $\;\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y = A x - B x^2$ Comparing with equation of trajectory, $y = x \tan \theta - \; \frac{g x^2}{2 u^2 \cos^2 \theta}$ we get, $\; A = \tan \theta \; \text{ and } \; B = \; \frac{g}{2 u^2 \cos^2 \theta}$ $\; \therefore \;\;\; \frac{H}{R} = \frac{ \frac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g} }{ \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} } = \frac{ \sin^2 \theta}{2 \sin 2\theta}$ $\; \;\; = \frac{ \sin^2 \theta}{4 \sin \theta \cos \theta} = \frac{1}{4} \tan \theta = \frac{A}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Tension in the wire $= \text{centripetal force} = m r \omega^2$ $= 4 \times 2.5 \times (2 \pi f)^2 = 10 \times 4 \pi^2 f^2$ $= 10 \times 4 \pi^2 \times \left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)^2 = 160 \text{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Using Lami's theorem $\frac{T}{\sin 90^{\circ}} = \frac{30}{\sin (180^{\circ}-30^{\circ})} = \frac{W}{\sin (90^{\circ}+30^{\circ})}$ $\Rightarrow T = \frac{30}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \frac{W}{\cos 30^{\circ}}$ $\Rightarrow T = 60 = \frac{2W}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\therefore T = 60\,\text{N}$ $\frac{2W}{\sqrt{3}} = 60 \Rightarrow W = 30\sqrt{3}\,\text{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to work energy theorem $W\;=\;\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $\therefore \;\; P\;=\;\frac{W}{t}$ $P\;=\;\frac{1}{2} m \frac{v^2}{t} \Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\;\frac{2 P t}{m}}$ $\;=\sqrt{\;\frac{2 \times 10 \times 10^3 \times 10}{2000}}=10 \text{ m/s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The body moves at a steady speed, which means its speed does not change. This only happens if the total (net) force on the body is zero. So, $F_1 - F_2 = 0$ which means $F_1 = F_2$ Work and Energy: Because the body's speed is not changing, its kinetic energy also stays the same. The workenergy theorem tells us that the total work done on the body is equal to the change in its kinetic energy. $W\; = \Delta E_k$ $W\; = 0$ Net Power: Power is the work done divided by time. Since the total work ( $W$ ) is zero, the net power is also zero: $P = \; \frac{W}{t} = 0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: A thin uniform rod of length $L$ , and we need the radius of gyration $k$ about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. Formulae: Moment of inertia (M.I.) about the given axis for a uniform rod is: $I=\; \frac{1}{12} M L^2$ The radius of gyration $k$ is related to the moment of inertia by $I=M k^2$ Substituting: $\;M k^2=\; \frac{1}{12} M L^2$ $\;k^2=\; \frac{L^2}{12}$ $\;k=\; \frac{L}{\sqrt{12}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $K_{\text{disc}}=6\,\text{J}$ $\therefore \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2+\frac{1}{2}mv^2=6$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \cdot \left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 6$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{4} m v^2 = 6 \Rightarrow m v^2 = 8\,\text{J} \cdots (i)$ $\text{ Thus, } K_{\text{Ring}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $= \frac{1}{2} \times (mR)^2 \left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $= \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ $= m v^2 = 8\,\text{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Mass $m=4\ \mathrm{kg}$ Force constant (spring constant) $k=64\ \mathrm{N/m}$ Formula for time period of a mass-spring system: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ Substitute the values: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{4}{64}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}}=2\pi\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let angular frequency of SHM is $\omega$ and when is at distance $x$ from mean position, its velocity will be given as $v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} \;\;\; \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot (i)$ When its velocity becomes double, let new amplitude is $A'$ . So, $2 v=\omega \sqrt{A'^2 - x^2}$ Putting the value of $v$ from equation (i) $\; 2\omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \omega \sqrt{A'^2 - x^2}$ $\; 2 \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \sqrt{A'^2 - x^2}$ $\Rightarrow 4 (A^2 - x^2) = A'^2 - x^2$ $\Rightarrow A'^2 = 4A^2 - 3x^2 \Rightarrow A' = \sqrt{4A^2 - 3x^2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Escape velocity is given as $v=\sqrt{2 g R}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}}$ $M \rightarrow$ Mass of sphere, $R \rightarrow$ Radius of sphere $\;3 \times 10^4 = \sqrt{\;\frac{2 \times 6.66 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}{R}}$ $\; \;\; R = \frac{2 \times 6.66 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}{9 \times 10^8}$ $\; R = 8.88 \times 10^5 \text{ metre }$ $\; R = 888 \times 10^3 \text{ metre } = 888 \text{ km}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = 10^6 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$ $R = 100 r$ $\Rightarrow \quad r = \frac{R}{100}$ ∴ Change in surface energy $\Delta E = T \times \Delta A$ $= 35 \times 10^{-3} \left[ 10^6 \times 4 \pi r^2 - 4 \pi R^2 \right]$ $= 35 \times 10^{-3} \left[ 10^6 \times 4 \pi \times \left( \frac{R}{100} \right)^2 - 4 \pi R^2 \right]$ $= 35 \times 10^{-3} \left[ 400 \pi R^2 - 4 \pi R^2 \right]$ $= 35 \times 10^{-3} \times 396 \pi R^2$ $= 35 \times 10^{-3} \times 396 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 1 \times 10^{-4}$ $= 4356 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{J} = 4356 \, \mu \mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: According to the principle of calorimetry, $\;Q_{\;\text{gained }\;}=Q_{\;\text{lost }\;}$ $\Rightarrow m_{\;\text{water }\;}\times C_{\;\text{water }\;}\times\Delta T=m_{\;\text{steam }\;}\times L_{\;\text{steam }\;}+m_{\;\text{steam }\;}\times C_{\;\text{water }\;}\times\Delta T$ $\Rightarrow 114\times1\times(70-30)=m_{\;\text{steam }\;}\times540+m_{\;\text{steam }\;}\times1\times30$ $\Rightarrow m_{\;\text{steam }\;}=8\,\mathrm{g}$ $\therefore\;\;\text{ Total mass of water }\;=m_{\;\text{water }\;}+m_{\;\text{steam }\;}$ $=\;114+8=122\,\mathrm{g}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: If $W_1$ and $W_2$ represents work done during isothermal compression and isothermal expansion. Then, $\;\; W_2 = W_1 + 25\%$ of $W_1$ $\; = W_1 + \frac{25}{100} W_1 = \; \frac{5 W_1}{4}$ $\therefore \;\; Q_2 \; = \; \frac{5 Q_1}{4}$ $\; \text{Thus,}\; \eta \; = 1 - \; \frac{W_1}{W_2} = 1 - \; \frac{Q_1}{Q_2} = 1 - \; \frac{Q_1}{\frac{5 Q_1}{4}}$ $\; = 1 - \frac{4}{5} = \frac{1}{5} = 0.20 \; \text{or}\; 20\%$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The work done when a gas changes its volume at constant temperature (isothermal process) is given by: $W = n R T \ln \left( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right)$ First Case: From $V$ to $2 V$ We have $n=2, V_1=V$ , and $V_2=2 V$ . So, the work done is: $W = 2 R T \ln \left( \frac{2V}{V} \right) = 2 R T \ln(2)$ Second Case: From $2 V$ to $4 V$ Now, $n=2, V_1=2 V$ , and $V_2=4 V$ . So, the work done here is: $W' = 2 R T \ln \left( \frac{4V}{2V} \right)$ $= 2 R T \ln(2) = W$ The work done in increasing the volume from $2 V$ to $4 V$ is the same as the work done from $V$ to $2 V$ , both are $W$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Write the adiabatic equation An adiabatic process for an ideal gas can be written as: $p V^\gamma = \text{constant}$ Step 2: Take logarithms on both sides If we take the logarithm of both sides, we get: $\log(p) + \gamma \log(V) = \;\text{constant}\;$ This can be rearranged as: $\log(p) = -\gamma \log(V) + \;\text{constant}\;$ Step 3: Compare to the standard line equation This equation looks like the equation of a straight line: $y = m x + c$ Here, $y = \log(p), x = \log(V)$ , and the slope $m = -\gamma$ . Step 4: Find the slope from the graph The slope of the line is: $m = \;\frac{\Delta \log p}{\Delta \log V}\;$ From the graph, pick two points and subtract their values: $= \;\frac{2.20-2.48}{1.4-1.2} = \;\frac{-0.28}{0.2} = -1.4$ Step 5: Interpret the value of $\gamma$ The slope $m = -\gamma = -1.4$ , so: $\gamma = 1.4$ Step 6: Final answer The ratio of the specific heat capacities of the gas is 1.4 . © examsnet.com

Solution: For surface $X Y$ , $\;\mu_a \sin 45^{\circ} = \mu g \sin \; r_1$ $\;\mu_g \sin \;r_1 = \;\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; \sin \;r_1 = \;\frac{1}{\mu_g \sqrt{2}} \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (i)$ ∴ From figure, $i_2 = 90 - r_1$ For total internal reflection $\;\sin \;i_2 = \;\frac{1}{\mu_g}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \; (90-r_1) = \;\frac{1}{\mu_g} \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (ii)$ $\Rightarrow \cos r_1 = \;\frac{1}{\mu_g}$ From eqn. (i) and (ii), $\sin^2 r_1 + \cos^2 r_1 = 1$ $\Rightarrow \;\frac{1}{2 \mu_g^2} + \;\frac{1}{\mu_g^2} = 1 \Rightarrow \;\frac{3}{2 \mu_g^2} = 1$ $\Rightarrow \mu_g^2 = \;\frac{3}{2} ; \therefore \mu_g = \sqrt{\;\frac{3}{2}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Capacitance of small conducting sphere $C=4\pi \varepsilon_0 r=10 \mu\mathrm{F}$ Since, $27 \times \; \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 = \; \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \Rightarrow R=3 r$ ∴ Capacitance of big sphere $C' \; = 4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R = 4 \pi \varepsilon_0 (3 r)$ $\; = 3 (4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r) = 3 \times 10 = 30 \mu\mathrm{F}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $b-a=1\,\text{cm}=1 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m},$ $b = (a+1 \times 10^{-2})\, \text{m}$ $C = 4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \left(\frac{ab}{b-a}\right)$ $\Rightarrow 100 \times 10^{-12} = \frac{1}{9 \times 10^9} \times \frac{a(a+1 \times 10^{-2})}{1 \times 10^{-2}}$ $9 \times 10^{-3}=a^2+10^{-2} a$ $\Rightarrow 0.9=100 a^2+a$ $\Rightarrow 100 a^2+a-0.9=0$ $\Rightarrow a = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2-4 \times 100(-0.9)}}{2 \times 100}$ $= \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{361}}{200} = \frac{-1 \pm 19}{200}$ $= \frac{-1+19}{200} = \frac{18}{200}\,\text{m}$ $= 0.09\,\text{m}=9\,\text{cm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $R_1 \;=\; \frac{3R}{4} \; \text{ and } \; R_2=\; \frac{R}{4}$ $\therefore \;\; \frac{1}{R_{eq}} \;=\; \frac{1}{R_1}+\; \frac{1}{R_2}=\; \frac{1}{\frac{3R}{4}}+\; \frac{1}{\frac{R}{4}}$ $\frac{1}{R_{eq}} \;=\; \frac{4}{3R}+\; \frac{4}{R}=\; \frac{16}{3R} \Rightarrow R_{eq}=\; \frac{3R}{16}$ Heat generated in the wire per second $P \;=\; \frac{H}{t}=\; \frac{E^2}{R_{eq} \cdot t}=\; \frac{E^2}{ \left( \frac{3R}{16} \right) \times 1} \;\; [t=1\,\text{s}]$ $\;=\; \frac{16E^2}{3R}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $R_1$ be the initial resistance of the wire in the left gap. $R_2$ be the resistance in the right gap $l_1$ be the initial balancing length ( 40 cm ) Let $l_2$ be the remaining length ( $100-40=60 \text{ cm}$ ) The initial ratio is $\; \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \; \frac{40}{60} = \; \frac{2}{3}$ When the wire is stretched to double its length, its resistance becomes $4 R_1$ Let $l_1$ " be the new balancing length $l_2$ 'be the new remaining length (100- $l_1$ ) The new ratio is $\; \frac{4 R_1}{R_2} = \; \frac{l_1'}{100 - l_1'}$ $\; 4 \cdot \left( \; \frac{2}{3} \right) = \; \frac{l_1'}{100 - l_1'}$ $\; 8 (100 - l_1') = 3 l_1'$ $\; 800 - 8 l_1' = 3 l_1'$ $\; 11 l_1' = 800$ $\; l_1' = \; \frac{800}{11}$ The new balancing point is approximately $\left( \; \frac{800}{11} \right) \text{ cm}$ from the left end. © examsnet.com

Solution: When a charged particle moves into a magnetic field at a right angle (normally), it starts moving in a circle because the magnetic force keeps turning it. The time it takes to complete one full circle (the time period $T$ ) is given by: $T = \; \frac{2\pi m}{B q}$ Here, $m$ is the mass of the particle, $q$ is its charge, and $B$ is the magnetic field strength. You can also write it as: $T = \; \frac{2\pi}{B \cdot \left( \; \frac{q}{m} \right)}$ This means the time period $T$ is inversely related to the specific charge $\left( \; \frac{q}{m} \right)$ (charge divided by mass). So, if the specific charge increases, the time period decreases, and if the specific charge decreases, the time period increases. © examsnet.com

Solution: Magnetic field at a point inside the wire $B_{in}=\;\frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}$ Here, $a \rightarrow$ radius of wire $r \rightarrow$ distance from centre of wire Here, $r=0.5 a$ $\therefore \;\; B_{in}=\;\frac{\mu_0 I \cdot (0.5 a)}{2\pi a^2}=\;\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}$ Magnetic field at a point outside the wire, $B_{\;\text{out}\;} = \;\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ Here, $\;\; r=1.5 a$ $\therefore \; B_{\;\text{out}\;} = \;\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(1.5 a)} = \;\frac{\mu_0 I}{3\pi a}$ $\therefore \;\; \frac{B_{\;\text{in}\;}}{B_{\;\text{out}\;}} = \;\frac{\;\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}}{\frac{\mu_0 I}{3\pi a}} = \;\frac{3}{4} \;\text{ or }\; 3:4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The induced emf in a rotating spoke $e\;=\;\frac{1}{2} B \omega r^2$ $\therefore   \;\; e_1\;=\;\frac{1}{2} B \left(2 \pi \times \frac{180}{60}\right) (0.4)^2=0.48 \pi B$ $\; \text{ and } \; e_2\;=\;\frac{1}{2} B \left(2 \pi \times \frac{90}{60}\right) \times (0.4)^2$ $\;=0.24 \pi B$ $\;=2 \times 0.24 \pi \times \frac{B}{2}=\;\frac{e_1}{2}=\;\frac{E}{2}=0.5 B$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric field $E$ and the magnetic field $B$ are related by $\;\frac{E}{B}=c$ , where $c$ is the speed of light. Here $c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ . The required ratio is that of $E$ to $10^8 B$ , i.e. $\;\frac{E}{10^8 B}$ . $\;\frac{E}{10^8 B} = \frac{1}{10^8} \times \frac{E}{B} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{10^8} = 3$ So the ratio is $E : (10^8 B) = 3 : 1$ . Solution: We want to find the average velocity (rate) for the reaction as $A$ goes to $B$ when the amount of $A$ drops from $x$ to $y\, \mathrm{mol/L}$ in 100 minutes. The change in the concentration of $A$ is: $\Delta[A]=y-x\, \mathrm{mol/L}$ This tells us how much $A$ has changed in value. The average velocity means how much $A$ changes per minute. We can find it by dividing the total change in $A$ by the time taken: Average velocity $=\; \frac{\Delta[A]}{\Delta t}$ where $\Delta t = 100$ minutes. So, Average velocity $=\; \frac{y-x}{100}\, \mathrm{mol}\, \mathrm{L}^{-1}\, \mathrm{min}^{-1}$ If you need the answer as a positive value (since rates are usually positive), write it as $\; \frac{\left|x-y\right|}{100}\, \mathrm{mol}\, \mathrm{L}^{-1}\, \mathrm{min}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

It is dissolved in molten cryolite ( $\mathrm{Na}_3\mathrm{AlF}_6$ ) and sometimes small quantities of $\mathrm{CaF}_2$ are also added. The zone refining method is used for metals that need to be extremely pure and are less reactive, such as silicon, germanium, gallium, indium, etc. Zirconium (and hafnium) are purified by the van Arkel (iodide) process, not by zone refining. Solution: $\because \lfloor 2x - 2 \rfloor = \lfloor (2x - 1) - 1 \rfloor$ $= \lfloor 2x - 1 \rfloor - 1$ $\text{ let, } \lfloor 2x - 1 \rfloor = a$ $\Rightarrow \lfloor 2x - 2 \rfloor = a - 1$ $\text{ so, } 3(a-1) + 1 = 2a - 1$ $\Rightarrow 3a - 3 + 1 = 2a - 1 \Rightarrow a = 1$ thus $\lfloor 2x - 1 \rfloor = 1$ $\Rightarrow 1 \leq (2x - 1) < 2 \Rightarrow 2 \leq 2x < 3$ $\Rightarrow 1 \leq x < 1.5$ so, $x \in [1, 1.5)$ Now, $k = 2\lfloor 2x - 1 \rfloor - 1 = 2(1) - 1 = 1$ for $x \in [1, 1.5)$ $f(x) = \lfloor k + 5x \rfloor = \lfloor 1 + 5x \rfloor$ $\text{ at } x=1, f(x) = \lfloor 6 \rfloor = 6 \quad (\text{ minimum })$ $\text{ at } x=1.5, f(x) = \lfloor 1 + 5 \times 1.5 \rfloor$ $= \lfloor 8.5 \rfloor = 8 \quad \text{ (maximum) }$ so, $f(x)$ can be $6, 7, 8$ Hence, the range of $f(x)=\{6,7,8\}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\frac{z-1}{z-i}\;=\;\frac{(x+iy)-1}{(x+iy)-i}$ $\;=\;\frac{(x-1)+iy}{x+i(y-1)}$ $\;=\;\frac{(x-1)+iy}{x+i(y-1)} \times \;\frac{(x-i(y-1))}{(x-i(y-1))}$ $=\;\frac{\left[x(x-1)+y(y-1)\right]+i\left[xy-(x-1)(y-1)\right]}{x^2+(y-1)^2}$ ∵ The fraction is purely imaginary. Solution: $\; \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}+i}{\sqrt{3}-i}\right)^{n}=-1$ $\; \because\; \text{ Modulus of numerator }\;=\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+1^{2}}$ $\;=2\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6}$ and modulus of denominator $=2$ $\;\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\; \therefore \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}+i}{\sqrt{3}-i}\right)^{n} = \left(\frac{2\text{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{2\text{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}\right)^{n}$ $\;= \left[\text{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\right]^{n}$ $\;= \left[\text{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right]^{n}=\text{cis}\left(\frac{n\pi}{3}\right)$ and $\text{cis}\left(\frac{n\pi}{3}\right) =-1$ $\;=\text{cis}(\pi)$ $\; \therefore \;\; \frac{n\pi}{3}=\pi$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; n=3$ thus, $p=3$ Similarly, second expression $\; \left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{1+\sqrt{3}i}\right)^{m}=\text{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \left[\frac{2\left(\text{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)}{2\left(\text{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)}\right]^{m}=\text{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \left[\text{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right]^{m}=\text{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \text{cis}\left(-\frac{2\pi}{3}\cdot m\right)=\text{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ Therefore, $-\frac{2\pi}{3}\cdot m=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ $\Rightarrow -2\pi m \equiv 2\pi \cdot \bmod(6\pi)$ $\Rightarrow -2m \equiv 2 \bmod(6)$ $\Rightarrow 2m \equiv -2 \equiv 4 \bmod 6$ $\Rightarrow m=2 \bmod 3$ ∴ Least positive integer $=m=2$ thus, $q=2$ Hence, $\sqrt{q^{2}+p^{2}}=\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{13}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let, $a = x \hat{i} + y \hat{j} + z \hat{k}$ then, $a \times i = \widehat{\begin{vmatrix} i & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ x & y & z \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix}}$ $= \hat{i}(0-0) - \hat{j}(0-z) + \hat{k}(0-y)$ $= z \hat{j} - y \hat{k}$ So, $\left| a \times i \right|^2 = z^2 + y^2$ Similarly, $\left| a \times \hat{j} \right|^2 = x^2 + z^2$ and $\left| a \times \hat{k} \right|^2 = x^2 + y^2$ thus, $\left| a \times \hat{i} \right|^2+\left| a \times \hat{j} \right|^2+\left| a \times \hat{k} \right|^2$ $= 2 (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)$ $\because a$ is unit vector So, $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ Hence, $\left| a \times \hat{i} \right|^2+\left| a \times \hat{j} \right|^2+\left| a \times \hat{k} \right|^2$ $= 2 \times 1 = 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $AB = OB - OA = (2-3)\hat{i}+(0-1)\hat{j}+(1-1)\hat{k} = -\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ So, the direction vector of $\text{lin} E A B$ is $d = -\hat{i} - \hat{j}$ $\text{let} P = A + \lambda d$ $= (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) + \lambda(-\hat{i}-\hat{j})$ $= (3-\lambda)\hat{i} + (1-\lambda)\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $PC = C - P = (\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})$ $-[(3-\lambda)\hat{i} + (1-\lambda)\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ $= (\lambda-2)\hat{i} + (4+\lambda)\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ As, given in the question $\because PC \perp AB$ $\Rightarrow PC \cdot AB = 0$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda-2)(-1) + (4+\lambda)(-1) + (-1)(0) = 0$ $\Rightarrow -\lambda+2-4-\lambda = 0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda = -1$ $\therefore P = (3-\lambda)\hat{i} + (1-\lambda)\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ $= (3+1)\hat{i} + (1+1)\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ $= 4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ therefore, $a=4, b=2$ and $c=1$ Hence, $a+b+c=4+2+1=7$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} (x_i-4)=22$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; \sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} x_i - 4 \times 11 = 22$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; \sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} x_i = 66$ So, mean $(\overline{x}) = \frac{66}{11} = 6$ and $\sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} (x_i-4)^2 = 154$ $\because \;\; x_i - \overline{x} = x_i - 6$ $= (x_i-4) - 2$ $\therefore \;\; [x_i - \overline{x}]^2 = [ (x_i-4) - 2 ]^2$ $= (x_i-4)^2 - 4(x_i-4) + 4$ So, $\sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} (x_i-\overline{x})^2 = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} (x-4)^2$ $-4 \sum\limits_{i=1}^{11} (x_i-4) + 11 \times 4$ $= 154 - 4 \times 22 + 44 = 110$ $\;\text{Variance}\; (\sigma) = \frac{1}{n} \sum (x_i-\overline{x})^2 \\ = \frac{1}{11} \times 110 = 10$ Thus, $\alpha = 6, \beta = 10$ Therefore, $\;\frac{\alpha}{\beta} + \;\frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \;\frac{6}{10} + \;\frac{10}{6} = \;\frac{3}{5} + \;\frac{5}{3}$ $= \frac{9+25}{15} = \frac{34}{15} = \;\text{Sum of roots}\;$ and $\;\frac{\alpha}{\beta} \cdot \;\frac{\beta}{\alpha} = 1 =$ product of roots Hence, the quadratic is $\;x^2 - \left(\;\frac{34}{15}\right) x + 1 = 0$ $\Rightarrow 15x^2 - 34x + 15 = 0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Total outcomes $=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}=6$ Prime number $=\{2,3,5\}=3$ So, $P(A)=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ and even numbers $=\{2,4,6\}=3$ $\therefore P(B)=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ Thus, $P(\overline{B})=1-P(B)=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ Total sample for 2 throws $=6 \times 6=36$ Then, $P(A / \overline{B})=\frac{P(A \cap \overline{B})}{P(\overline{B})}$ First throw is prime $=\{2,3,5\}$ Second throw is not even $=\{1,3,5\}$ Pairs where first is in $\{2,3,5\}$ and second is in $\{1,3,5\}=3 \times 3=9$ outcomes So, $P(A \cap \overline{B})=\frac{9}{36}=\frac{1}{4}$ Therefore, $P(A / \overline{B})=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $R_k$ be the event that are exactly $k$ red balls is in bag, where $k=1,2,3,4,5$ So, $P(R_k) = \frac{1}{5}$ for $k=1,2,3,4,5$ Let $A$ be the event that a red ball is drawn. $P(R_1 / A) = \frac{P(R_1 \cap A)}{P(A)}$ $\because\ P(A / R_1) = \frac{1}{5}$ $\text{ and }\ P(R_1 \cap A) = P(R_1) \cdot P(A / R_1)$ $= \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{25}$ $\text{ and }\ P(A) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{5} P(R_k) \cdot P(A / R_k)$ $= \frac{1}{5} \sum\limits_{k=0}^{5} \frac{k}{5} = \frac{1}{25}(1+2+3+4+5)$ $= \frac{1}{25} \times 15 = \frac{15}{25}$ Hence, $P(R_1 / A) = \frac{P(R_1 \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{\frac{1}{25}}{\frac{15}{25}} = \frac{1}{15}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The mean of a binomial distribution is $x$ , and the variance is 5 . We know that the mean, $\mu = n p = x$ . This means $n$ times $p$ is $x$ . The formula for variance is $\sigma^2 = n p (1-p) = 5$ . This means $n$ times $p$ times $(1-p)$ is 5 . From the mean formula, $p = \frac{x}{n}$ . Substitute $p = \frac{x}{n}$ into the variance formula: $x \left(1 - \frac{x}{n}\right) = 5$ If we open the bracket, we get: $x - \frac{x^2}{n} = 5$ Take $\frac{x^2}{n}$ to the other side: $\frac{x^2}{n} = x - 5$ Now, solve for $n$ : $n = \frac{x^2}{x-5}$ To get a whole number for $n, x-5$ must divide $x^2$ exactly. Let's check different $x$ values: If $x=6: n = \frac{36}{1} = 3636$ is an integer. If $x=10: n = \frac{100}{5} = 2020$ is an integer. If $x=30: n = \frac{900}{25} = 3636$ is an integer. So, the possible values for $x$ are: $6,10,30$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $\because x^2+y^2-2x-4y-20=0$ After rotation of axes through $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , it transforms to $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ in the given equation $a=1, h=0, b=1, g=-1, f=-2, c=-20$ After rotation of $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $a' = a\cos^2\theta + b\sin^2\theta + 2h\cos\theta\sin\theta$ $\;\;\; = 1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + 1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + 0 = 1$ $b' = a\sin^2\theta + b\cos^2\theta - 2h\sin\theta\cos\theta$ $\; = 1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + 1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 - 0 = 1$ also, $h' = (b-a)\sin\theta\cos\theta + h(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta)$ $\; = 0+0 = 0$ Similarly, $x' = x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x-y)$ and $y' = x\sin\theta + y\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x+y)$ then ${-2x'-4y'} = \frac{-2x+2y-4x-4y}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\; = \frac{-6x-2y}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\; = -3\sqrt{2}x - \sqrt{2}y = 2gx + 2fy$ then $g = -\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}, f = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, c = -20$ So, $\;\begin{vmatrix} a & h & g \\ h & b & f \\ g & f & c \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -20 \end{vmatrix}$ $\;\;\; = 1\left(-20-\frac{1}{2}\right) - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\left(+\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $\;\;\; = -\frac{41}{2} - \frac{9}{2} = -25$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;4x+3y-1=0$ $\;\;\text{Normal vector}\;=\langle 4,3\rangle$ Direction vectors are perpendicular to the normal vector $d=\langle 3,-4\rangle\;\text{or}\;\langle-3,4\rangle$ Unit vector in direction vector $\;=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}}\langle 3,-4\rangle$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{5}\langle 3,-4\rangle$ So, two points 10 units away from $A=(-2,3)$ along the line are $\; (x_1, y_1)=(-2,3)+10\cdot\frac{1}{5}\langle 3,-4\rangle$ $\;=(-2+6,3-8)=(4,-5)$ $\;\;\text{and}\; (x_2, y_2)=(-2,3)-10\cdot\frac{1}{5}\langle 3,-4)$ $\;=(-2-6,3+8)$ $\;=(-8,11)$ Therefore, $(x_1+y_1)^2+(x_2+y_2)^2$ $=(4-5)^2+(-8+11)^2$ $=1+9=10$ © examsnet.com

(i) $2 x^2+x y-y^2=0$ assume $y=m x$ , and substitute $2 x^2+x(m x)-(m x)^2=0$ Coefficient of $x^2$ should be zero $\Rightarrow \;\; 2+m-m^2=0 \Rightarrow m=2,-1$ $m_1=2 \;\text{ and }\; m_2=-1$ ∵ Both lines are perpendicular their slopes must be $-\;\frac{1}{m_1}=-\;\frac{1}{2} \;\text{ and }\; \frac{-1}{m_2}=1$ So, the perpendicular lines has their slopes $-\frac{1}{2}$ and 1 and passing through $(1,1)$ ∴ Pair of lines are $\; (y-y_1-m_1 (x-x_1) )$ $\; (y-y_1-m_2 (x-x_2) )=0$ $\Rightarrow \left(y-1+\frac{1}{9}(x-1)\right) (y-1-(x-1))=0$ $\Rightarrow \left(\frac{x}{2}+y-\frac{3}{2}\right) (y-x)=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} x y-\frac{1}{2} x^2+y^2-x y-\frac{3}{2} y+\frac{3}{2} x=0$ $\Rightarrow -x^2-x y+2 y^2-3 y+3 x=0$ Compare with $\;\;\; a x^2+2 h x y+b y^2+2 g x+3 y=0$ $\; \therefore \;\; a=-1, h=+\frac{1}{2}, b=2 g=-\frac{3}{2}$ $\;\;\text{ so, }\; \frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2$ $\;\;\text{ and }\; 2(g+h)=2 \left(-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right) =-2$ Hence, $\frac{b}{a}=2(g+h)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Put $x=2-y$ in the given conic $\Rightarrow (2-y)^2+y^2-2(2-y)-4y+2=0$ $\Rightarrow y^2-4y+4+y^2-4+2y-4y+2=0$ $\Rightarrow 2y^2-6y+2=0 \Rightarrow y^2-3y+1$ $\therefore y=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow y_1=\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}, y_2=\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}$ Thus, $x_1=2-\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)=\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $x_2=2-\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ then, $p_1 \equiv \left(\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$ and $p_2 \equiv \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$ The lines $OP_1$ and $OP_2$ will have equation of the form $y=mx$ $\Rightarrow lx+my=0$ $\because m_1=\frac{y_1}{x_1}=\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{1-\sqrt{5}}$ $=\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{1-\sqrt{5}} \times \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{1+\sqrt{5}} = -2-\sqrt{5}$ $\text{ and } m_2=\frac{y_2}{x_2}=\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{1+\sqrt{5}}$ $=\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{1+\sqrt{5}} \times \frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{1-\sqrt{5}} = -2+\sqrt{5}$ ∴ Combined equation of lines are $(m_1x-y_1)(m_2x-y)=0$ will form $\Rightarrow (l_1x+m_1y)(l_2x+m_2y)=0$ Lets expands and compare $m_1m_2x^2-(m_1+m_2)xy+y^2=l_1l_2x^2$ $+(l_1m_2+l_2m_1)xy+m_1m_2y^2$ $\therefore l_1l_2=m_1m_2, \quad l_1m_2+l_2m_1=-(m_1+m_2),$ $m_1m_2=1$ $m_1=-2-\sqrt{5}, \quad m_2=-2+\sqrt{5}$ $\text{ and } m_1+m_2=-4$ $\because l_1l_2=m_1m_2=1$ $\Rightarrow l_1=\frac{1}{l_2}$ $\therefore l_1m_2+\frac{m_1}{l_1}=4$ $\Rightarrow (\sqrt{5}-2)l_1^2+(-\sqrt{5}-2)=4l_1.$ $\Rightarrow l_1=1 \text{ and } l_2=1$ Hence, $l_1+l_2+m_1+m_2=1+1-4=-2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The given equations are $s: x^2 + y^2 + 4x + 7 = 0$ $s': 2x^2 + 2y^2 + 3x + 5y + 9 = 0$ $\Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 + \frac{3}{2}x + \frac{5}{2}y + \frac{9}{2} = 0$ $s'': x^2 + y^2 + y = 0$ Radical axis of $s$ and $s': s - s' = 0$ $\Rightarrow 4x - \frac{3}{2}x - \frac{5}{2}y + 7 - \frac{9}{2} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{5}{2}x - \frac{5}{2}y + \frac{5}{2} = 0$ $\Rightarrow x - y + 1 = 0 \cdots (i)$ Radical axis of $s$ and $s'': s - s'' = 0$ $\Rightarrow 4x - y + 7 = 0 \cdots (ii)$ From Eqs. Solution: $y^2=8 x, a=2$ Equation of tangent $y=mx+\frac{2}{m}$ $\text{ at }(1,3)$ $3=m+\frac{2}{m} \Rightarrow m^2-3m+2=0$ $\Rightarrow m=1,2$ So, equation of tangent (put point $(1,3)$ on $y=mc+c$ ) $y=x+c, y=2x+c$ $\Rightarrow y=x+2 y=2x+1$ to find coordinates of $A$ and $B$ , put the line on parabola. $(x+2)^2=8x \Rightarrow x^2-4x+4=0$ $\Rightarrow x=2,-2$ $\text{ at } x=2, y=\sqrt{8\times2}=4$ So, $A=(2,4)$ and $(2x+1)^2=8x$ $\Rightarrow 4x^2-4x+1=0$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}$ $\text{ at } x=\frac{1}{2}, y=2$ So, $B=\left(\frac{1}{2},2\right)$ Now, area of $\triangle PAB$ $A=\frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$ $=\left| \frac{1}{2} \left(1(4-2)-3\left(2-\frac{1}{2}\right)+1(4-2)\right) \right|..$ $=\left| \frac{1}{2} \left(2-\frac{9}{2}+2\right) \right|=\left| \frac{1}{2} \left(4-\frac{9}{2}\right) \right|$ $=\left| \frac{1}{2} \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \right|=\frac{1}{4}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $4x^2-9y^2=36 \Rightarrow \frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=0$ So, $a^2=9, b^2=4$ Thus, equation of normal $\frac{9x}{x_1}+\frac{4y}{y_1}=(9+4)=13 \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(i)$ and the given equation is $3x+2\sqrt{2}y+k=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 3x+2\sqrt{2}y=-k \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(ii)$ ∵ Both equation are proportional Thus, $\frac{\frac{9}{x_1}}{3}=\frac{\frac{4}{y_1}}{2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{13}{-k}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \frac{3}{x_1}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{y_1} \Rightarrow x_1=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} y_1$ Put in equation of hyperbola $\frac{\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} y_1\right)^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=1 \Rightarrow y_1^2=4 \Rightarrow y_1= \pm 2$ at $y_1=2 \Rightarrow x_1=3\sqrt{2}$ and at $y_1=-2$ $\Rightarrow x_1=-3\sqrt{2}$ Also, $\frac{3}{x_1}=-\frac{13}{k} \Rightarrow -k=\frac{13}{3} \times 3\sqrt{2}=13\sqrt{2}$ Hence, $k=-13\sqrt{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $f(x)=\begin{cases} (1+\sin x)^{\cos x} & -\frac{\pi}{2} < x < 0 \\ a & x=0 \\ \frac{e^{\frac{2}{x}}+e^{\frac{3}{x}}}{a e^{\frac{2}{x}}+b e^{\frac{3}{2}}} & 0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2} \end{cases}$ So, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^{-}} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{-}} (1+\sin x)^{\cos x}$ Let $y = (1+\sin x)^{\cos x}$ $\Rightarrow \ln y = \cos x \ln (1+\sin x)$ $= \frac{\ln (1+\sin x)}{\sin x} = 1$ $\Rightarrow y = e$ $\therefore \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{-}} (1+\sin x)^{\cos x} = e = a = f(0)$ $\text{ and } \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{e^{\frac{2}{x}}+e^{\frac{3}{x}}}{a e^{\frac{2}{x}}+b e^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{e^{\frac{3}{x}} \left(e^{-\frac{1}{x}}+1\right)}{e^{\frac{3}{x}} \left(e \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{x}}+b\right)} = \frac{1}{b}$ So, $e = \frac{1}{b} \Rightarrow b = \frac{1}{e}$ Hence, $a b = e \cdot \frac{1}{e} = 1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{(\csc x-\cot x)(e^{x}-e^{-x})}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2+\cos x}}$ Convert, $\csc x$ and $\cot x$ into $\sin x$ and $e^{x}-e^{-x}=2\sinh x$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{ \left( \frac{2\sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}} \cdot 2\sinh x \right) }{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2+\cos x}}$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{2\tan\frac{x}{2}\cdot\sinh x}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2+\cos x}} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x}}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x}}$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{2\tan\frac{x}{2}\cdot\sinh x(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x})}{1-\cos x}$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{2\tan\frac{x}{2}\cdot\sinh x(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x})}{1-\cos x}$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{ \frac{2\sin\frac{x}{2}}{\cos\frac{x}{2}} \cdot \sinh x(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x}) }{2\sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}}$ $\;=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{ \sinh x(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+\cos x}) }{\cos\frac{x}{2} \cdot \sin\frac{x}{2}}$ $\; \because x \to 0 \Rightarrow \cos\frac{x}{2} \to 1 \;\text{ and }\; \sin\frac{x}{2} \to \frac{x}{2}$ $\; \sinh x \to x$ $\;=\;\frac{x(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2+1})}{\frac{x}{2}} = 2(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3})$ $=2(2\sqrt{3}) = 4\sqrt{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y = \sqrt{\cosh x + \sqrt{\cosh x}}$ Let $\sqrt{\cosh x} = u \Rightarrow y = \sqrt{u^2 + u}$ Now, $\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{u^2+u}} \cdot (2u+1) = \; \frac{2u+1}{2 \sqrt{u^2+u}}$ $\; \frac{dy}{du} = \; \frac{2u+1}{2y}$ Now, $\; \frac{du}{dx} = \; \frac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{\cosh x}) = \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\cosh x}} (\sinh x)$ $= \; \frac{\sinh x}{2u}$ Thus, $\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \; \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \; \frac{du}{dx} = \; \frac{2u+1}{2y} \cdot \; \frac{\sinh x}{2u}$ $= \; \frac{(2u+1) \sinh x}{4 y u}$ put $u = \sqrt{\cosh x}$ Therefore, $\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \; \frac{\sinh x (1+2 \sqrt{\cosh x})}{4 y \sqrt{\cosh x}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y = (\log x)^{\frac{1}{x}} + \underset{v}{\;x}_{v}^{\log x}$ $\;\; \text{ So, } \; \ln(u) = \frac{1}{x} \log(\log x)$ $\frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x \log x} + \log(\log x) \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{x^2}\right)$ $\frac{1}{x^2 \log x} - \frac{\log(\log x)}{x^2}$ $\Rightarrow \left. \frac{du}{dx} \right|_{x=e} = (\log e)^{\frac{1}{e}} \left[ \frac{1}{e^2 \log e} - \frac{\log(\log e)}{e^2} \right]$ $= 1 \left[ \frac{1}{e^2} - 0 \right] = \frac{1}{e^2}$ and $\ln(y) = \log x \cdot \log(x) = (\log x)^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} \frac{dv}{dx} = 2 \log(x) \cdot \frac{1}{x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dx} = \eta \left[ \frac{2 \log x}{x} \right]$ at $x=e$ $= e^{\log x} \left[ \frac{2 \log x}{e} \right]$ $= e \cdot \frac{2}{e} = 2$ Hence, $\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{x=e} = \frac{1}{e^2} + 2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{ Let } I = \int \frac{\sec^2 x - 7}{\sin^7 x} \, dx$ $\Rightarrow I = \int \frac{1 - 7 \cos^2 x}{\sin^7 x \cos^2 x} \, dx$ $\Rightarrow I = \int \frac{\sin^5 x (1 - 7 \cos^2 x) \, dx}{\sin^{12} x \cos^2 x}$ Put $\sin^6 x \cos x = t$ $(6 \sin^5 x \cos^2 x - \sin^7 x) \, dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \sin^5 x (6 \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x) \, dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \sin^5 x (6 \cos^2 x - 1 + \cos^2 x) \, dx = dt$ $\Rightarrow \sin^5 x (1 - 7 \cos^2 x) \, dx = -dt$ $\therefore I = \int \frac{-dt}{t^2}$ $\Rightarrow I = \frac{1}{t} + C$ $\Rightarrow I = \frac{1}{\sin^6 x \cos x} + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int\frac{dx}{2\cos x+3\sin x+4}$ $\text{ Let } t=\tan\frac{x}{2} \Rightarrow \sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$ $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ $\text{ and } dx=\frac{2dt}{1+t^2}$ $=\int\frac{2dt}{(1+t^2)\left[\frac{2(1-t^2)}{1+t^2}+\frac{6t}{1+t^2}+4\right]}$ $=\int\frac{2dt}{2-2t^2+6t+4+4t^2} dt$ $=\int\frac{dt}{t^2+3t+3}=\int\frac{dt}{\left(t+\frac{3}{2}\right)^2+\frac{3}{4}}$ $\text{ put } u=t+\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow du=dt$ $=\int\frac{1}{u^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2} du$ $=\frac{1}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\right)+C$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2u}{\sqrt{3}}\right)+C$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2t+3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)+C$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\tan\frac{x}{2}+3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)+C$ $\text{ Thus, } f(x)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ $\therefore f\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ $=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{3}+3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ $=\tan^{-1}(2+\sqrt{3})=\frac{5\pi}{12}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\int\limits_{1/5}^{1/2} \frac{\sqrt{x-x^2}}{x^3} dx$ $= \int\limits_{1/5}^{1/2} \frac{x \sqrt{\frac{1}{x}-1}}{x^3} dx \int\limits_{1/5}^{1/2} \frac{1}{x^2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{x} - 1 . dx}$ $\text{Put} \frac{1}{x}-1 = t \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x^2} dx = -dt$ $\text{at} x=\frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow t=4 \text{ and at } x=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow t=1$ $= -\int\limits_{4}^{1} t^{1/2} \cdot dt = \int\limits_{1}^{4} \sqrt{t} \cdot dt$ $= \left[ \frac{t^{3/2}}{3/2} \right]_1^4 = \frac{2}{3} \left[ t^{3/2} \right]_1^4$ $= \frac{2}{3} \left[ 4^{3/2} - 1^{3/2} \right] = \frac{2}{3} (8-1)$ $= \frac{14}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $I\;=\int\limits_{0}^{400\pi} \sqrt{1-\cos 2x}\,dx$ $\;=\int\limits_{0}^{400\pi} \sqrt{2\sin^2 x}\,dx$ $\;=\sqrt{2}\int\limits_{0}^{400\pi} \sin x\,dx$ $\;=400\sqrt{2}\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx$ $\;=2\times 400\sqrt{2}\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin x\,dx$ $\;=800\sqrt{2}[-\cos x]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ $\;=800\sqrt{2}\left[-\cos\frac{\pi}{2}+\cos 0\right]$ $\;=800\sqrt{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;x \;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}= \left(1+ \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; \left[x \;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right]^2 = \left[ \left(1+ \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}} \right]^{-2}$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1}{x^2 \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2}=1+ \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; 1=x^2 \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2+x^2 \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^4$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; x^2 \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^4+x^2 \left(\;\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^2-1=0$ $\;\;\text{ so, order }\;=k=2$ $\;\;\text{ and degree }\;=l=4$ Thus, quadratic equation, $\;(x-2)(x-4)=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; x^2-6x+8=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y dx = (x + y^3 \cos y) dy$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} - \frac{x}{y} = y^2 \cos y$ $\therefore IF = e^{\int -\frac{1}{y} dy}$ $= e^{\ln (y)^{-1}} = -\frac{1}{y}$ $\therefore \frac{1}{y} \left( \frac{dy}{dy} \right) - \frac{x}{y^2} = y \cdot \cos y$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{d}{dy} \left( \frac{x}{y} \right) dy = \int y \cdot \cos y \, dy$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{y} = y \sin y - \int \sin y \, dy$ $x = y \sin y + \cos y + C$ $x = y^2 \sin y + y \cos y + c y$ Put point ( $0, \pi$ ) into it $\Rightarrow 0 = 0 - \pi + c \pi \Rightarrow c = 1$ $\therefore x = y^2 \sin y + y \cos y + y$ $\Rightarrow x = y^2 \sin y + y (1 + \cos y)$ $\Rightarrow x = y^2 \sin y + 2 y \cos^2 \left( \frac{y}{2} \right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;(x-(x+y) \log (x+y)) dx+x d y=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\frac{d y}{d x}=\;\frac{(x+y) \log (x+y)-x}{x}$ $\;=\;\frac{x+y}{x} \log (x+y)-1$ $\;\;\text{put.}\;\;\;\;u=x+y \Rightarrow \;\frac{d u}{d x}=\;\frac{d y}{d x}+1$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\frac{d y}{d x}=\;\frac{d u}{d x}-1$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\frac{d u}{d x}-1=\;\frac{u}{x} \log (u)-1$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\int\;\frac{d u}{u \log u}=\int\;\frac{1}{x} dx$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\log (\log u)=\log x+\log (c)$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\log (\log u)=\log (c x)$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\log u=c x$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;\;\log (x+y)=c x \;\; ( \because u=x+y)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let's restate the given problem carefully: The velocity of a particle is given by $v = a t + \frac{b}{t+c}$ We need to find the dimensions of $a, b$ , and $c$ . Step 1. Dimensional formula of velocity $[v] = [L T^{-1}]$ Step 2. Dimensional analysis of first term at In the expression $v = a t + \frac{b}{t+c}$ , both terms on the right-hand side must have the same dimensions as velocity. The first term: $a t$ $[a][t] = [v] = [L T^{-1}]$ $[a] = \frac{[L T^{-1}]}{[T]} = [L T^{-2}]$ So, $[a] = [L T^{-2}]$ Step 3. The second term $\frac{b}{t+c}$ This term must also have the dimensions of velocity: $\left[\frac{b}{t+c}\right] = [L T^{-1}]$ Now, $t+c$ is a sum - you can only add quantities with the same dimensions, so: $[c] = [t] = [T]$ Then, $[b] = [L T^{-1}] \cdot [t+c] = [L T^{-1}] \cdot [T] = [L]$ So, $[b] = [L]$ Final Dimensions: $[a] = [L T^{-2}], \quad [b] = [L], \quad [c] = [T]$ © examsnet.com
