Solution: We know that, $\cos^2 \alpha + \cos^2 \beta + \cos^2 \gamma = 1$ $\Rightarrow 1 - \sin^2 \alpha + 1 - \sin^2 \beta + \cos^2 \gamma = 1$ $\Rightarrow 1 + \cos^2 \gamma - (\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta) = 0$ $\Rightarrow 1 + \cos^2 \gamma = \sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta$ $\Rightarrow \sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta = 1 + \cos^2 \gamma$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{x}{2}=3 t_1$ $\Rightarrow t_1=\frac{x}{6}$ $B C=\frac{x}{2}=B D+D C$ $=4.5 \times \frac{t_2}{2}+7.5 \times \frac{t_2}{2}$ $\frac{x}{2}=6 t_2 \Rightarrow t_2=\frac{x}{12}$ ∴ Average speed $V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\text{ total distance travelled }}{\text{ total time taken }}$ $= \frac{x}{t_1+t_2} = \frac{x}{\frac{x}{6} + \frac{x}{12}}$ $= \frac{x}{\frac{3x}{12}} = 4 \text{ m/s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find the volume of water hitting the wall each second. The formula for flow rate (volume per second) is: Volume per second $=$ Area × Velocity Here, Area $=2 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^2$ and Velocity $=12 \text{ms}^{-1}$ Volume per second $=2 \times 10^{-3} \times 12=24 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^3/\text{s}$ Step 2: Find the mass of water hitting the wall each second. To get the mass per second, multiply the volume flow by the density of water ( $\rho=1000 \text{kg}/\text{m}^3$ ): Mass per second $=$ Density × Volume per second $=1000 \times 24 \times 10^{-3}=24 \text{kg}/\text{s}$ Step 3: Calculate the force on the wall. Force is the change in momentum per second. The water hits the wall at velocity $12 \text{ms}^{-1}$ and stops instantly. Force $=$ Mass per second × Velocity $=24 \times 12=288 \text{N}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find the friction force for each block The friction force is given by: $F_{\;\text{friction}\;}=\mu_k \times m \times g$ For block $A$ (mass $=2\,\text{kg}$ ): $F_{K\,A}=0.3 \times 2 \times 10=6\,\text{N}$ For block $B$ (mass $=4\,\text{kg}$ ): $F_{K\,B}=0.3 \times 4 \times 10=12\,\text{N}$ Step 2: Find the net force on each block The net force is the applied force minus friction: For block $A$ : $F_A=20-6=14\,\text{N}$ For block $B$ : $F_B=20-12=8\,\text{N}$ Step 3: Find the acceleration of each block Use $a=\;\frac{F_{n\,e\,t}}{m}$ for each block. For block $A$ : $a_A=\;\frac{14}{2}=7\,\text{m/s}^2$ For block $B$ : $a_B=\;\frac{8}{4}=2\,\text{m/s}^2$ Step 4: Find the ratio of accelerations $\;\frac{a_A}{a_B}=\;\frac{7}{2}$ So, the ratio is $7: 2$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $W=\int\limits_{x_1}^{x_2} f\,dx$ $=\int\limits_{2}^{4} (6x^2-4x)\,dx$ $=\left[\frac{6x^3}{3}-\frac{4x^2}{2}\right]_{2}^{4}$ $=\left[2x^3-2x^2\right]_{2}^{4}$ $=2 \times 4^3-2 \times 4^2-2 \times 2^3+2 \times 2^2$ $=128-32-16+8$ $=88\,\mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find the volume of water in the well The well is a cylinder. Its diameter is 2 m , so its radius $r=1 \text{m}$ . Its depth (height) $h=14 \text{m}$ . The volume formula for a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2 h$ . So, the volume of water is $V=\pi \times 1^2 \times 14 = 14 \pi$ cubic meters. Step 2: Find the mass of the water The density $(\rho)$ of water is $1000 \text{kg/m}^3$ . So, mass $(m)=$ volume × density $=14 \pi \times 1000 \text{kg}$ . Step 3: Calculate work needed to lift all the water The work to lift water from the bottom to the ground level is $W=m g h$ , where $g=10 \text{m/s}^2$ and $h$ is the height ( 14 m ). So, $W=(1000 \times 14 \pi) \times 10 \times 7$ Step 4: Substitute values and calculate $W=1000 \times \;\frac{22}{7} \times 1^2 \times 14 \times 10 \times 7 = 3.08 \times 10^6 \text{J}$ Step 5: Use the power of the motor to find time Power $(P)$ is 1.4 kW , which is $1.4 \times 10^3 \text{W}$ . Time $(t)=\;\frac{W}{P}=\;\frac{3.08 \times 10^6}{1.4 \times 10^3}$ . $t=22 \times 10^2 \text{s} = 2200 \text{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: If $σ$ be the mass per unit area, Then, $\sigma\;=\;\frac{3}{2\times 1+1\times 1}$ $\;=1 \text{ kg}/\text{m}^2$ ∴ mass of rectangle-1, $m_1=\sigma A_1=1 \times 2 \times 1=2 \text{ kg}$ mass of rectangle-2, $\;m_2=\sigma A_2=1 \times 1 \times 1=1 \text{ kg}$ $\; \therefore  X_{CM}=\;\frac{m_1 x_1+m_2 x_2}{m_1+m_2}$ $\; \;\; =\;\frac{2 \times \frac{1}{2}+1 \times \frac{3}{2}}{2+1}=\;\frac{5}{6} \text{ m}$ and $Y_{ CM }=\;\frac{m_1 y_1+m_2 y_2}{m_1+m_2}$ $=\;\frac{2 \times 1+1 \times \frac{1}{2}}{2+1}=\;\frac{5}{6} \text{ m}$ ∴ Centre of mass $= (X_{CM}, Y_{CM}) = \left(\;\frac{5}{6} \text{ m}, \;\frac{5}{6} \text{ m}\right)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Rotational kinetic energy $K_r\;=\;\frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{2} \times \left(\;\frac{1}{2} M R^2\right)  \omega^2$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{2} \times \;\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 1^2 \times 2^2$ $\;=20\ \mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y_1\;=0.1 \sin \; \left(100 \pi t+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ $\therefore \;\; v_1\;=0.1 \times 100 \pi \cos \left(100 \pi t+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ $\;=10 \pi \times \cos \left(100 \pi t+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ $y_2\;=0.1 \cos \pi t$ $\;=0.1 \sin \; \left(\pi t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ $\therefore \;\; v_2\;=0.1 \times \pi \cos \left(\pi t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ $\;=0.1 \pi \cos \left(\pi t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ $\therefore \;\text{ At }\; t\;=0$ $v_1\;=10 \cos \;\frac{\pi}{3}$ $\;\text{ and }\; v_2\;=0.1 \pi \cos \;\frac{\pi}{2}$ ∴ Phase difference between $v_1$ and $v_2$ at time $t=0$ , is given as, $\phi=\;\frac{\pi}{2}-\;\frac{\pi}{3}=\;\frac{\pi}{6}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find Spring Constant $(k)$ The spring stretches by 0.2 m when a 0.5 kg mass hangs from it. This means the force from the weight $(m_1 g)$ equals the force from the spring $(k x)$ : $k x=m_1 g$ So, $k=\;\frac{m_1 g}{x}=\;\frac{0.5 \times 10}{0.2}=25\ \mathrm{N/m}$ Step 2: Use the New Mass The new hanging mass is $m_2=0.25\ \mathrm{kg}$ . Step 3: Find the New Time Period ( $T$ ) The time period of a mass-spring system is: $T=2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m_2}{k}}$ Substitute the values: $T=2\pi \sqrt{\frac{0.25}{25}}$ $T=2\pi \sqrt{0.01}$ $T=2\pi \times 0.1=0.2\pi\ \mathrm{s}$ Step 4: Calculate the Value Using $\pi \approx 3.14$ : $T=0.2 \times 3.14=0.628\ \mathrm{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;T \propto a^{\frac{3}{2}} g^x R^y \Rightarrow T=k a^{\frac{3}{2}} g^x R^y$ $\; [ M^0 L^0 T^1 ] = [ L^{3/2} ] [ L T^2 ]^x [ L^y ]$ $\; [ M^0 L^0 T^1 ] = \left[ L^{\frac{3}{2}+x+y} T^{-2x} \right]$ $\; \therefore -2x=1$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; x=\frac{-1}{2}$ $\;\;\frac{3}{2}+x+y=0$ $\;\;\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}+y=0$ $\;1+y=0 \Rightarrow y=-1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Longitudinal strain, $ε_L=0.2\%=0.002$ Poisson's ratio, $\mu=0.3$ We are asked to find the volume strain $(ε_V)$ . Step 1: Recall the formula for volume strain For small deformations, Volume strain $= \varepsilon_V = \varepsilon_L (1-2\mu)$ However, to be more precise, the change in volume $\frac{\Delta V}{V}=ε_L+2ε_t$ , where $\varepsilon_t = -\mu \varepsilon_L$ (lateral strain is negative if the material stretches longitudinally). So, $\;\frac{\Delta V}{V}=\varepsilon_L+2(-\mu \varepsilon_L)$ $\;\Rightarrow ε_V=ε_L(1-2\mu)$ Step 2: Substitute the values $\;ε_V=0.002(1-2\times 0.3)$ $\;ε_V=0.002(1-0.6)$ $\;ε_V=0.002\times 0.4=0.0008$ Step 3: Convert to percentage $ε_V=0.0008\times 100=0.08\%$ Final Answer: $0.08\%$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find Extra Pressure Inside a Bubble The extra (excess) pressure inside a soap bubble is $p = \; \frac{4 T}{r}$ , where $T$ is surface tension and $r$ is the radius. So for bubble $A$ : $p_A = \; \frac{4 T}{r_1}$ And for bubble $B$ : $p_B = \; \frac{4 T}{r_2}$ Step 2: Use the Gas Law for Bubbles The usual gas equation is $p V = n R T$ . Here, $p$ is pressure, $V$ is volume, $n$ is the number of moles, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is temperature. Since the temperature is constant, $p V \propto n$ . The number of moles $n$ is related to the mass $m$ of the gas. So, $p V \propto m$ . Step 3: Work Out the Mass for Each Bubble For bubble $A$ : The volume of a sphere is $V_A = \; \frac{4}{3} \pi r_1^3$ . So $p_A V_A \propto m_A$ becomes: $\; \frac{4 T}{r_1} \times \; \frac{4}{3} \pi r_1^3 \propto m_A$ This simplifies to $m_A \propto r_1^2$ . For bubble $B$ : Similarly, $V_B = \; \frac{4}{3} \pi r_2^3$ . So $\; \frac{4 T}{r_2} \times \; \frac{4}{3} \pi r_2^3 \propto m_B$ This gives us $m_B \propto r_2^2$ . Step 4: Find the Ratio of the Masses The ratio is $\; \frac{m_A}{m_B} = \; \frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: When water (at temperature $\theta$ ) is mixed with ice (at $0^{\circ}$ ), heat will flow from the warmer water to the ice. The water cools down from $\theta$ to $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ . The ice melts, using that heat. No heat is lost to surroundings. Step 1: Heat lost by water cooling to $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ $Q_{\;\text{lost }\;}=m s \theta$ Step 2: Heat gained by ice (for melting) If $x$ is the mass of ice melted, then: $Q_{\;\text{gained }\;}=x L$ Step 3: Equating heat lost and gained $m s \theta = x L$ Step 4: Solve for $x$ $x = \;\frac{m s \theta}{L}$ Step 5: Check if $M$ (the large mass of ice) matters Since $M$ is very large, its temperature doesn't rise; it only partly melts. Hence $M$ appears only to indicate that the ice remains at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ . Final Answer: $x = \;\frac{m s \theta}{L}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The efficiency formula for a Carnot engine is: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ Here, $T_1$ is the absolute temperature of the source, and $T_2$ is the absolute temperature of the sink. The problem says the source is $25\%$ hotter than the sink. That means: $T_1 = T_2 + 0.25 \times T_2 = 1.25 T_2$ Now, plug $T_1 = 1.25 T_2$ into the efficiency formula: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{1.25 T_2}$ $\eta = 1 - \frac{1}{1.25}$ $\frac{1}{1.25} = \frac{4}{5}$ So, $\eta = 1 - \frac{4}{5}$ $\eta = \frac{1}{5}$ To change this to a percentage, multiply by $100\%$ : $\eta = \frac{1}{5} \times 100\% = 20\%$ So, the engine's efficiency is $20\%$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Use the ideal gas law We know that $p V = n R T$ describes how pressure, volume, and temperature are related for an ideal gas. Step 2: Set up the formula for work at constant pressure When pressure is constant, the work ( $W$ ) done by the gas is: $W = p \Delta V$ From the ideal gas law, we can find that: $p \Delta V = n R \Delta T$ This means the work done is: $W = n R \Delta T$ Step 3: Insert the given values Number of moles, $n = 6$ Change in temperature, $\Delta T = 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ . (This is the same as 20 K for a temperature difference.) Gas constant, $R = 8.31 \mathrm{J} \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \mathrm{K}^{-1}$ Step 4: Calculate the work $W = 6 \times 8.31 \times 20$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Efficiency of heat engine, $\eta=1-\;\frac{T_2}{T_1} \Rightarrow \eta=\;\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1}$ Coefficient of performance of refrigerator, $\beta\;=\;\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$ $\therefore\;\; \frac{\eta}{\beta}\;=\;\frac{\frac{\;T_1-T_2}{T_1}}{\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}}=\;\frac{(T_1-T_2)^2}{T_1 T_2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For an ideal gas, the internal energy is given by: $U = \frac{f}{2} n R T$ Substitute known values $2250 R = \frac{f}{2} (3) R (300)$ Cancel $R$ from both sides: $2250 = \frac{f}{2} \times 3 \times 300$ Simplify $2250 = \frac{f}{2} \times 900$ $2250 = 450 f$ $f = \frac{2250}{450} = 5$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y_1=3 \sin \;250 \pi t$ $\therefore \;\; \omega_1=250 \pi \text{ rad/s}$ $\; y_2=2 \sin \;260 \pi t$ $\therefore \;\; \omega_2=260 \pi \text{ rad/s}$ $\therefore \;\; f_1=\frac{\omega_1}{2\pi}=\frac{250\pi}{2\pi}=125 \text{ Hz}$ $\; f_2=\frac{\omega_2}{2\pi}=\frac{260\pi}{2\pi}=130 \text{ Hz}$ $\; T=\frac{1}{f_2-f_1}$ $\; =\frac{1}{130-125}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2 \text{ s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Ratio of initial and final fringe widths, i.e. $\frac{\beta_{\;\text{ initial }\;}}{\beta_{\;\text{ final }\;}}$ Calculation: $\;\beta_{\;\text{ initial }\;} = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$ $\;\beta_{\;\text{ final }\;} = \frac{\lambda D}{3d}$ Thus, $\;\frac{\beta_{\;\text{ initial }\;}}{\beta_{\;\text{ final }\;}} = \frac{\frac{\lambda D}{d}}{\frac{\lambda D}{3d}} = 3$ So the ratio of initial : final fringe width is $3 : 1$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Total atoms in the solid $=6 \times 10^{24}$ $0.005 \%$ of atoms lose one electron each. Step 1: Find how many atoms lose an electron Number of affected atoms $=(0.005 \%) \times (6 \times 10^{24})$ $0.005 \% = \; \frac{0.005}{100} = 5 \times 10^{-5}$ ⇒ Number of atoms losing electrons $=6 \times 10^{24} \times 5 \times 10^{-5}=3 \times 10^{20}$ Step 2: Each atom loses one electron Each lost electron corresponds to a positive charge gained by the solid equal to the charge of that electron $(e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C})$ . Step 3: Total charge gained $\;Q= (3 \times 10^{20}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})$ $\;Q=4.8 \times 10^1=48 \mathrm{c}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The energy stored in a capacitor is given by the formula: $U=\frac{q^2}{2C}$ where $U$ is energy, $q$ is charge, and $C$ is capacitance. Step 2: Rearranging to Find Capacitance We can solve for $C$ as follows: $C=\frac{q^2}{2U}$ Here, $q=12 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}$ and $U=6 \mathrm{J}$ . Substitute these values into the formula: $C=\frac{(12 \times 10^{-6})^2}{2 \times 6}$ Step 3: Calculate Capacitance Simplify the above equation: $C=12 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{F}$ Step 4: Capacitance of a Spherical Conductor The capacitance of a spherical conductor is given by: $C=4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r$ Step 5: Find the Radius Rearrange to find the radius $r: r=\frac{C}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}$ We can also use $\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}=9 \times 10^9 \mathrm{N m^2 / C^2}$ so: $r=9 \times 10^9 \times 12 \times 10^{-12}$ Step 6: Solve for the Radius Multiply the values: $r=108 \times 10^{-3}=0.108 \mathrm{m}=10.8 \mathrm{cm}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $V_{A C}\; = I_{A C} \times 20$ $\; = (5-3) \times 20 = 40 \text{ Volt}$ $V_{D E}\; = I_{A D} \times 25 = (5-2) \times 25 = 75 \text{ V}$ $\therefore \; \frac{V_{A C}}{V_{A D}} \; = \; \frac{40}{75} = \; \frac{8}{15}$ $\therefore \; V_{A C}\; : V_{A D} = 8 : 15$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Terminal voltage of the battery during charging, $V=E+I r$ Here, $E=10$ volt Net emf in the circuit $E^{'}\;=V_{\;\text{supply }\;}-E=160-10$ $\;=150\ \mathrm{V}$ $\therefore \;\; I\;=\;\frac{E^{'}}{R+r}\;=\;\frac{150}{24+1}\;=\;\frac{150}{25}=6\ \mathrm{A}$ ∴ From eqn (i) $V\;=E+I r$ $\;=10+6\times 1$ $\;=16\ \mathrm{V}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: An electron moves in a circular orbit of radius $R$ and period $T$ . Step 1: Find the current due to orbital motion The charge of the electron is $e$ (magnitude). In one complete revolution, the charge $e$ passes a given point once in time $T$ . So, current $I=\;\frac{e}{T}$ Step 2: Magnetic moment due to a current loop Magnetic moment of a current loop is given by $\mu=I \times$ area of the loop The area of a circular loop of radius $R$ is $A=\pi R^2$ Thus, $\mu=I \times A=\;\frac{e}{T} \times \pi R^2=\;\frac{\pi e R^2}{T}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The solenoid has 5 closely packed layers and each layer has 700 turns. ∴ Total number of turns, $N\;=700 \times 5=3500$ $\therefore   \;\;  B\;=\mu_0 n I$ $\;=\mu_0 \times \frac{N}{L} \times I$ $\;=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times \frac{3500}{1} \times 5$ $\;=21.9 \times 10^{-3} T$ $\;\simeq 22 \times 10^{-3} T$ $\;\; \approx 22 \mathrm{mT}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $W=M B (\cos \theta_1 - \cos \theta_2)$ Initially, $\theta_1=0^{\circ}, \theta_2=45^{\circ}$ $\therefore W_1\;=M B (\cos 0 - \cos 45^{\circ})$ $\;=M B \left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ $\;= \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) M B$ Again, $\theta_2=45^{\circ}+15^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$ $\therefore W_2\;=M B (\cos 45^{\circ} - \cos 60^{\circ})$ $\;=M B \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\right)$ $\;=M B \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}\right)$ $\therefore \frac{W_2}{W_1}\;=\;\frac{M B \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}\right)}{M B \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow W_2\;=\;\frac{W_1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{W}{\sqrt{2}}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We are given: current $I=4 \mathrm{mA}=4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{A}$ and flux $\phi = 32 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{T} \mathrm{m}^2$ . Step 1: Find the inductance ( $L$ ). The relationship between flux, inductance, and current is $\phi = L I$ . So, $L = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = 8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{H}$ . Step 2: Find the energy stored in the inductor. The formula for energy stored is $E = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$ . Plug in the values: $E = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 10^{-3} \times (4 \times 10^{-3})^2$ . Calculate the value: $E = 64 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{J}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: We need to find: For the power dissipated to become half of its maximum value, what is the current amplitude? Step 1: Relation between Power and Current The average power dissipated in an AC circuit is given by: $P = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R$ At resonance, the impedance is purely resistive ( $Z = R$ ), and the current is maximum ( $I = I_{\text{ max }}$ ). So maximum power is: $P_{\text{max}} = I_{\text{rms, max}}^2 \;\; R = \left( \frac{I_{\text{max}}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^2 R = \frac{I_{\text{max}}^2 \;\; R}{2}$ But we only need relative power, so we can use $P \propto I^2$ . Step 2: Condition for half power We are told $P = \frac{1}{2} P_{\text{ max }}$ So: $I^2 R = \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{max}}^2 R$ Simplify: $I = \frac{I_{\text{max}}}{\sqrt{2}}$ So the current amplitude becomes $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ times its maximum value when the power is half of the maximum. © examsnet.com

Solution: The de-Broglie wavelength is given by: $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m k}}$ Step 2: Rearranging to Find Kinetic Energy We can rearrange the formula to find kinetic energy $k: \lambda^2 = \frac{h^2}{2 m k}$ So, $k = \frac{h^2}{2 m \lambda^2}$ Step 3: Substitute the Values Here, Planck's constant, $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ Js}$ Mass of electron, $m = 9 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ Wavelength, $\lambda = 2 \text{ nm} = 2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ Now substitute these into the formula: $k = \frac{(6.6 \times 10^{-34})^2}{2 \times 9 \times 10^{-31} \times (2 \times 10^{-9})^2}$ Step 4: Calculation Calculate the value: $k = \frac{(6.6 \times 10^{-34})^2}{2 \times 9 \times 10^{-31} \times (2 \times 10^{-9})^2}$ This gives: $k = 0.608 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ Step 5: Convert Joules to Electron Volts 1 electron volt $( \text{eV} ) = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ . So, $k = \frac{0.608 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \text{ eV} = 0.38 \text{ eV}$ The kinetic energy of the electron is about 0.38 eV . © examsnet.com

Solution: $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{3 \rightarrow 2}}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{3^2}\right)$ $\frac{1}{\lambda_{3 \rightarrow 2}}=\frac{5R}{36} \Rightarrow \lambda_{3 \rightarrow 2}=\frac{36}{5R}$ $\text{ and } \frac{1}{\lambda_{2 \rightarrow 1}}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}\right)=\frac{3R}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda_{2 \rightarrow 1}=\frac{4}{3R}$ $\therefore \frac{\lambda_{3 \rightarrow 2}}{\lambda_{2 \rightarrow 1}} = \frac{\frac{36}{5R}}{\frac{4}{3R}}$ $=\frac{36 \times 3R}{5R \times 4}=\frac{27}{5}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: A nucleus has: Radius $R=R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$ , where $R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \,\mathrm{m}$ Each nucleon (proton or neutron) has a mass $m_n \approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \,\mathrm{kg}$ Step 2: Estimate the number of nucleons per unit volume For nuclear matter, the volume per nucleon is roughly the volume of a sphere of radius $R_0$ : $V_{\;\text{per nucleon}\;} \;\; \approx \;\frac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3$ $V_{\;\text{per nucleon}\;} \;\; \approx \;\frac{4}{3} \pi (1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3 \approx 7.2 \times 10^{-45} \,\mathrm{m}^3$ Hence, number density of nucleons: $n=\;\frac{1}{V_{\;\text{per nucleon}\;}} \approx \;\frac{1}{7.2 \times 10^{-45}} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{44} \,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ Step 3: Compute the mass density $\rho = n \times m_n = (1.4 \times 10^{44}) (1.67 \times 10^{-27}) \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17} \,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ Density of nuclear matter $\sim 10^{17} \,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The question tells us that the voltage gain divided by the current amplification factor ( $\beta$ ) equals 4. We know that the formula for voltage gain in a common emitter amplifier is $A_V = \; \frac{\beta \times R_C}{R_B}$ , where $R_C$ is collector resistance and $R_B$ is base resistance. So if we divide $A_V$ by $\beta$ , we get: $\frac{A_V}{\beta} = \frac{ \; \frac{\beta \times R_C}{R_B} }{\beta}$ This simplifies to: $\frac{R_C}{R_B}$ The question gives $\frac{A_V}{\beta}=4$ , so: $\frac{R_C}{R_B}=4$ This means the ratio of collector resistance to base resistance is $4: 1$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The complex ion $[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{Cl})_6]^{3-}$ has a spin-only magnetic moment of 4.90 B.M. Oxidation State and Electron Configuration: For Mn in this ion, the oxidation state is +3 . Finding the Magnetic Moment: The formula for the spin-only magnetic moment is: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \; \text{ В.М. } \;$ Here, $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. For $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}, n=4$ because there are 4 unpaired electrons in the $3d$ orbitals. Plug in the value of $n$ : $\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90 \; \text{ В.М. } \;$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Statement I In the nitration of aniline, more amount of $m$ -nitroaniline is formed than expected. Normally, $-\mathrm{NH}_2$ is an activating, ortho/para-directing group. Hence, we expect mainly $o$ - and $p$ -nitroaniline. However, nitration is carried out in strongly acidic medium ( $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4/\mathrm{HNO}_3$ ), and under these conditions, aniline gets protonated to form the anilinium ion $(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{NH}_3^{+})$ . The $-\mathrm{NH}_3^{+}$ group is an electron-withdrawing, deactivating, meta-directing group. So the nitration mixture now contains protonated aniline, which gives meta nitro product. As a result, the actual nitration product mixture contains a higher proportion of $m$ -nitroaniline than we would expect based on the activating nature of $-\mathrm{NH}_2$ alone. Hence, Statement I is correct. Statement II In the presence of a strongly acidic medium, aniline is protonated to form anilinium ion, which is meta-directing. As discussed above, this is true - in a strongly acidic medium, aniline is converted to the anilinium ion $(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{NH}_3^{+})$ . The anilinium ion is meta-directing because the positively charged nitrogen withdraws electrons from the ring, deactivating it, especially at ortho and para positions. © examsnet.com

Solution: $A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \mid \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{x^2+x+1}) \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \}$ and $B = \{ y \in \mathbb{R} \mid y = \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{x^2+x+1}), x \in A \}$ Since, domain of $\sin^{-1}(x)$ is $[-1,1]$ So, domain of $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}$ is real, so so $\sqrt{x^2+x+1}\;\in[-1,1]$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{x^2+x+1}\;\in[0,1]$ ( ∵ square root is always non-negative) $\Rightarrow x^2+x+1 \le 1$ $\Rightarrow x^2+x \le 0$ $\Rightarrow x(x+1) \le 0$ So, $x \in[-1,0]$ for set $A$ Thus, $A=[-1,0]$ Now, for set $B$ , since $x \in A=[-1,0]$ , the range values for $\sqrt{x^2+x+1}$ for $x \in[-1,0]$ we will find. $\text{At}\; x=-1, \sqrt{(-1)^2-1+1}=\sqrt{1-1+1}=1$ At $x=0, \sqrt{0^2+0+1}=\sqrt{0+1}=1$ At $x=-\frac{1}{2}, \sqrt{\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)^2-\frac{1}{2}+1}$ $= \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}+1} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}$ So, $\sqrt{x^2+x+1} \in \left[\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}, 1\right] = \left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1\right]$ Thus, $y = \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1})$ $\in \left[\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), \sin^{-1}(1)\right]$ $= \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ Hence, $B = \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ $\Rightarrow \text{Now,}\; A \cap B = [-1,0] \cap \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] = \emptyset$ So, $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$ is false. $\Rightarrow A \cap B^C = [-1,0] \cap \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]^C$ and the intersection with any set outside this cannot be $[0,1]$ , So, $A \cap B^C = [0,1]$ is false. $\Rightarrow A^C$ is everything except $[-1,0]$ . Since $B = \left(\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \subset \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1,0)$ $\Rightarrow A^C \cap B$ is true. $\Rightarrow A \cup B = \mathbb{R} \setminus \left\{[-1,0] \cup \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\right\}$ So, union of $A$ and $B$ is the complement of their own union. That's impossible. Thus, $A^C \cap B = \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ , option (c) is correct. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given function, $f(x)=\sqrt{\log_e \left(\frac{1}{x^2-4x+4}\right)} + \sin^{-1}(x^2-2)$ Since, $\log$ is defined for positive values only. So, $\frac{1}{x^2-4x+4}>0$ Also since, $x^2-4x+4=(x-2)^2 \ge 0$ this holds for $x \neq 2$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \ln \left(\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}\right) \ge 0$ Now, we know that $\ln(t)$ is strictly increasing for $t>0$ and $\ln(1)=0$ , the inequality $\ln \frac{1}{(x-2)^2} \ge 0$ is equivalent to $\;\;\frac{1}{(x-2)^2} \ge 1 \Leftrightarrow (x-2)^2 \le 1$ $\Rightarrow \;\; |x-2| \le 1$ i.e., $\;\; 1 \le x \le 3$ But $\log$ is undefined for $x=2$ $\therefore x \in [1,3]-\{2\}$ For $\sin^{-1}(x^2-2)$ to be real, $x^2-2 \in [-1,1]$ $\Rightarrow \;\; -1 \le x^2-2 \le 1$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 1 \le x^2 \le 3 \Rightarrow 1 \le |x| \le \sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; x \in [-\sqrt{3},-1] \cup [1,\sqrt{3}] \Rightarrow x \in [1,\sqrt{3}]$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$ . Given $a = \det(\operatorname{adj}(A))$ and $b = \det(B^{-1})$ . For a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $\det(\operatorname{adj}(A)) = (\det A)^{3-1} = (\det A)^2$ . $\det A = 1\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\3&3\end{vmatrix} - 1\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\2&3\end{vmatrix} + 2\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{vmatrix}$ $= 1(6-9) - 1(3-6) + 2(3-4)$ $= -3 + 3 - 2 = -2$ . So $a = (-2)^2 = 4$ . Now $\det B = \begin{vmatrix}1&2&3\\4&-3&-1\\2&1&-4\end{vmatrix}$ $= 1\begin{vmatrix}-3&-1\\1&-4\end{vmatrix} - 2\begin{vmatrix}4&-1\\2&-4\end{vmatrix} + 3\begin{vmatrix}4&-3\\2&1\end{vmatrix}$ $= 1(12+1) - 2(-16+2) + 3(4+6)$ $= 13 + 28 + 30 = 71$ . Thus $b = \det(B^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det B} = \frac{1}{71}$ . Then $b+1 = \frac{72}{71}$ and $18b = \frac{18}{71}$ . So $\frac{b+1}{18b} = \frac{\frac{72}{71}}{\frac{18}{71}} = \frac{72}{18} = 4$ . Since $a = 4$ , we get $\frac{b+1}{18b} = a$ . Therefore the correct option is $a$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $f(x)=\;\frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}  f(x) & f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) - f(x) \\ 1 & f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right)  \end{vmatrix}$ and $f(2)=33$ Here, $f(x)=\;\frac{1}{2}\left[f(x) \cdot f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) - f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) + f(x)\right]\;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(i)$ Let $f(x)=a_0 x^n+a_1 x^{n-1}+. . .+a_{n-1} x+a_n$ $(a_0 \neq 0)$ Putting this value of $f(x)$ in Eq. (i), $\;f(x)=\;\frac{1}{2}\left[f(x) \cdot f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) - f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) + f(x)\right]$ $\Rightarrow f(x) \cdot f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) = f\left(\;\frac{1}{x}\right) + f(x)$ Hence, $f(x)=x^n+1$ or $-x^n+1$ Now, $f(2)=2^n+1=33$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  2^n=32$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  2^n=2^5$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  n=5$ And $f(2)=-2^n+1=33$ $\Rightarrow  \;\; -2^n=33-1=32=2^5$ which is not possible. $\therefore  f(x)=x^n+1=x^5+1$ So, $f(3)=3^5+1=243+1=244$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $z=x+iy$ . Then $\frac{z-(2-i)}{z+(1+2i)}=\frac{(x-2)+i(y+1)}{(x+1)+i(y+2)}.$ The expression is purely imaginary when its real part is $0$ , with denominator nonzero, so $z\neq -(1+2i)$ , i.e. $(x,y)\neq(-1,-2)$ . Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: $\frac{(x-2)+i(y+1)}{(x+1)+i(y+2)}=\frac{[(x-2)+i(y+1)][(x+1)-i(y+2)]}{(x+1)^2+(y+2)^2}.$ The real part of the numerator is $(x-2)(x+1)+(y+1)(y+2).$ Set it equal to $0$ : $(x-2)(x+1)+(y+1)(y+2)=0.$ Expanding: $x^2-x-2+y^2+3y+2=0.$ So $x^2+y^2-x+3y=0.$ Completing squares: $\left(x-\frac12\right)^2+\left(y+\frac32\right)^2=\frac52.$ This is a circle with centre $\left(\frac12,-\frac32\right)$ and radius $\sqrt{\frac52}$ . The centre lies on $x+y+1=0$ because $\frac12-\frac32+1=0$ . The point $(-1,-2)$ satisfies the circle equation but makes the original denominator zero, so it is deleted from the locus; hence the locus does not contain $(-1,-2)$ . Therefore the correct option is the circle not containing $(-1,-2)$ and having its centre on $x+y+1=0$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $(\sqrt{3}-i)^n=2^n$ , where $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . First find the modulus: $|\sqrt{3}-i|=\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{3+1}=\sqrt{4}=2$ . The argument is: $\arg(\sqrt{3}-i)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$ . So, in polar form: $\sqrt{3}-i=2\left[\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]$ . Using De Moivre's theorem: $(\sqrt{3}-i)^n=2^n\left[\cos\left(-\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)\right]$ . $=2^n\left[\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)-i\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)\right]$ . Given $(\sqrt{3}-i)^n=2^n$ , we get: $2^n\left[\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)-i\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)\right]=2^n$ . Dividing by $2^n\neq0$ : $\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)-i\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)=1$ . Equating real and imaginary parts: $\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)=1$ and $\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{6}\right)=0$ . Both conditions hold when: $\frac{n\pi}{6}=2k\pi$ , $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Thus: $n=12k$ . Since $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the least positive value occurs at $k=1$ : $n=12$ . Therefore, the correct option is $\boxed{12}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $z=1+\sqrt{5}+i\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}$ . $|z|^2=(1+\sqrt{5})^2+(\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}})^2$ $=(1+2\sqrt{5}+5)+(10-2\sqrt{5})=16$ So, $|z|=4$ . Also, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}}{1+\sqrt{5}}$ . Squaring, $\tan^2\theta=\dfrac{10-2\sqrt{5}}{(1+\sqrt{5})^2}=\dfrac{10-2\sqrt{5}}{6+2\sqrt{5}}=5-2\sqrt{5}$ . Since $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)=\sqrt{5-2\sqrt{5}}$ and $z$ lies in the first quadrant, $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ . Thus $z=4\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)$ . By De Moivre's theorem, $z^5=4^5\left(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi\right)$ . $=1024(-1+0)=-1024$ . Therefore, the correct option is $-1024$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, equation is $\sqrt{3 x^2+x+5}=x-3$ Here, $3 x^2+x+5 \geq 0$ (since square root is non-negative) $\Rightarrow x-3 \geq 0$ $\Rightarrow x \geq 3$ Now, squaring to both sides of given equation, we get $\left(\sqrt{3 x^2+x+5}\right)^2=(x-3)^2$ $\Rightarrow 3 x^2+x+5=x^2-6 x+9$ $\Rightarrow 2 x^2+7 x-4=0$ Using quadratic formula, $x=\frac{-7 \pm \sqrt{7^2-4 \cdot 2 \cdot (-4)}}{2 \cdot 2}$ $= \frac{-7 \pm \sqrt{49+32}}{4} = \frac{-7 \pm 9}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{2}{4} \text{ and } x=\frac{-16}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{2} \text{ and } x=-4$ Since domain, $x \geq 3$ , so $x=-4$ And $x=\frac{1}{2}$ are not possible. ∴ There is zero solution. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, the equation is $2x^3+3x^2-5x-7=0$ Since $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are its roots, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{-3}{2}$ $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac{-5}{2}$ $\alpha\beta\gamma=-\frac{-7}{2}=\frac{7}{2}$ Now, $\frac{1}{\alpha^2}+\frac{1}{\beta^2}+\frac{1}{\gamma^2}=\frac{(\beta\gamma)^2+(\gamma\alpha)^2+(\alpha\beta)^2}{(\alpha\beta\gamma)^2}$ $=\frac{(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)^2-2\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)}{(\alpha\beta\gamma)^2}$ $=\frac{\left(\frac{-5}{2}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)\left(\frac{-3}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^2}$ $=\frac{\frac{25}{4}+\frac{21}{2}}{\frac{49}{4}}=\frac{\frac{67}{4}}{\frac{49}{4}}$ $=\frac{67}{49}$ Thus, the correct option is $(3)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the two equal positive roots be $\alpha,\alpha$ and the other two real roots be $\beta,\gamma$ . Given $\beta\gamma=1$ , so $\gamma=\frac{1}{\beta}$ . By Vieta's sum of roots, $2\alpha+\beta+\frac{1}{\beta}=-\frac{b}{a}$ . By Vieta's product of roots, $\alpha^2\beta\gamma=\alpha^2=\frac{e}{a}$ . Since $\alpha>0$ , $\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{e}{a}}$ . By Vieta's sum of pairwise products, $\alpha^2+2\alpha\left(\beta+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)+\beta\gamma=\frac{c}{a}$ . Using $\beta\gamma=1$ , this becomes $\alpha^2+2\alpha\left(\beta+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)+1=\frac{c}{a}$ . From the sum of roots, $\beta+\frac{1}{\beta}=-\frac{b}{a}-2\alpha$ . Substitute this value: $\alpha^2+2\alpha\left(-\frac{b}{a}-2\alpha\right)+1=\frac{c}{a}$ . Simplify: $-3\alpha^2-\frac{2\alpha b}{a}+1=\frac{c}{a}$ . Thus $3\alpha^2+\frac{2\alpha b}{a}+\frac{c}{a}=1$ . Multiplying by $a$ gives $3a\alpha^2+2\alpha b+c=a$ . Using $\alpha^2=\frac{e}{a}$ and $\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{e}{a}}$ , we get $3e+2b\sqrt{\frac{e}{a}}+c=a$ . This is equivalent to $3e+\frac{2b\sqrt{e}}{\sqrt{a}}+c=a$ . Hence option B is the correct relation. © examsnet.com

Solution: The dot in the given terms denotes multiplication, so $y = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 8} + \frac{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7}{4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12} + \cdots$ $= \frac{3}{1!}\cdot\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3\cdot 5}{2!}\cdot\frac{1}{4^2} + \frac{3\cdot 5\cdot 7}{3!}\cdot\frac{1}{4^3} + \cdots$ Compare with the binomial expansion $(1-x)^{-n}=1+nx+\frac{n(n+1)}{2!}x^2+\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3!}x^3+\cdots$ Since the first term in the expansion is $1$ , the given series is $(1-x)^{-n}-1$ . Comparing the first two terms, $nx=\frac{3}{4}$ ... (i) $\frac{n(n+1)}{2!}x^2 = \frac{3\cdot5}{4\cdot8}=\frac{15}{32}$ $\Rightarrow n(n+1)x^2=\frac{15}{16}$ ... (ii) Dividing (ii) by the square of (i), $\frac{n(n+1)x^2}{n^2x^2}=\frac{\frac{15}{16}}{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2}=\frac{15}{16}\cdot\frac{16}{9}=\frac{5}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{n+1}{n}=\frac{5}{3}$ $\Rightarrow 3n+3=5n$ $\Rightarrow n=\frac{3}{2}$ Then $x=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{n}=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$ Thus $y=(1-x)^{-n}-1=\left(1-\frac12\right)^{-3/2}-1=2^{3/2}-1=2\sqrt{2}-1$ $\Rightarrow y+1=2\sqrt{2}$ $\Rightarrow (y+1)^2=8$ $\Rightarrow y^2+2y+1=8$ $\Rightarrow y^2+2y-7=0$ Hence the correct option is $y^2+2y-7=0$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: We will expand $(1+x-x^2)^6$ and find the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^6$ . Multimonial expansion states that $\;(a_1+a_2+a_3)^n=\sum\;\frac{n!}{k_{1}!k_{2}!k_{3}!}$ $\;a_1^k a_2^{k_2} a_3^{k_3}$ where $k_1+k_2+k_3=n$ In our case, $a_1=1, a_2=x, a_3=-x^2$ and $n=6$ From $k_1+k_2+k_3=6$ $\Rightarrow\;\; k_1=6-k_2-k_3$ To get $x^4$ , we can have different combinations of $x$ and $x^2$ $k_1$ : number of times 1 is chosen $k_2$ : number of times $x$ is chosen $k_3$ : number of times $x^2$ is chosen The equation is: $k_2+2k_3=4$ Now, if $k_3=0$ , then $k_2=4$ and $k_1=2$ If $k_3=1$ , then $k_2=2$ and $k_1=3$ If $k_3=2$ , then, $k_2=0, k_1=4$ Now, find the coefficients for each valid combination. Coefficient of $\;x^4=\;\frac{6!}{2!4!0!}-\;\frac{6!}{3!2!1!}+\;\frac{6!}{4!0!2!}$ $\;=15-60+15=-30$ Now, for $x^6, k_2+2k_3=6$ and $k_1+k_2+k_3=6$ If $k_3=0$ , then $k_2=6$ , and $k_1=0$ If $k_3=1$ , then $k_2=4$ , and $k_1=1$ If $k_3=2$ then $k_2=2$ and $k_1=2$ If $k_3=3$ , then $k_2=0$ , and $k_1=3$ So, coefficient of $x^6=\;\frac{6!}{0!6!0!}-\;\frac{6!}{1!4!1!}+\;\frac{6!}{2!2!2!}-\;\frac{6!}{3!0!3!}$ $=1-30+90-20=41$ ∴ Sum of the coefficient of $x^4$ and $x^6=41-30=11$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, expression is $\tan \left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right) \cdot \tan \left(\frac{4\pi}{7}\right)+\tan \left(\frac{4\pi}{7}\right) \cdot \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)+\tan \left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right) \cdot \tan \left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)$ Let $x=\frac{\pi}{7}, y=\frac{2\pi}{7}$ and $z=\frac{4\pi}{7}$ So, the expression becomes $\tan(y) \cdot \tan(z)+\tan(z) \cdot \tan(x)+\tan(x) \cdot \tan(y)$ Now, $x+y+z=\frac{\pi}{7}+\frac{2\pi}{7}+\frac{4\pi}{7}=\frac{7\pi}{7}=\pi$ Since, $x+y+z=\pi$ , we can use the identify $\tan(x) \cdot \tan(y)+\tan(y) \cdot \tan(z)+\tan(z) \cdot \tan(x)=-7$ $\therefore \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right) \tan \left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)+\tan \left(\frac{4\pi}{7}\right) \cdot \tan \left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)+\tan \left(\frac{4\pi}{7}\right) \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)=-7$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\cos 13^{\circ} \cdot \sin 17^{\circ} \cdot \sin 21^{\circ} \cdot \cos 47^{\circ}$ $= (\cos 13^{\circ} \cos 47^{\circ}) \cdot (\sin 17^{\circ} \sin 21^{\circ})$ $= \frac{1}{2} [\cos(34^{\circ}) + \cos(60^{\circ})] \cdot \frac{1}{2} [\cos(4^{\circ}) - \cos(38^{\circ})]$ $\; \left[ \because \sin A \sin B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)] \;\text{ and }\; \cos A \cos B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)].. \right]$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left[\cos 34^{\circ}+\frac{1}{2}\right] [\cos 4^{\circ}-\cos 38^{\circ}]$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left[\cos 34^{\circ} \cos 4^{\circ}-\cos 34^{\circ} \cos 38^{\circ}+\frac{1}{2} \cos 4^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \cos 38^{\circ}\right]$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left[ \frac{1}{2} \{\cos(30^{\circ})+\cos(38^{\circ})\} - \frac{1}{2} \{\cos(4^{\circ})+\cos(72^{\circ})\} + \frac{1}{2} \cos 4^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \cos 38^{\circ} \right]$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left[ \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\cos 38^{\circ}\right) - \frac{1}{2} (\cos 4^{\circ}+\cos 72^{\circ}) + \frac{1}{2} \cos 4^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \cos 38^{\circ} \right]$ $= \frac{1}{8} \left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\cos 72^{\circ}\right] = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}-\frac{\cos 72^{\circ}}{8}$ $= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}-\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4} \times \frac{1}{8} \left( \because \cos 72^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}\right)$ $= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}-\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{32} = \frac{2\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{5} + 1}{32} = \frac{1}{32}(2\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{5} + 1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\; \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{3\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{4\pi}{5}$ $\;= \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \left(\pi- \frac{2\pi}{5}\right) + \sin\; \left(\pi- \frac{\pi}{5}\right)$ $\;= \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}=2 \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}+2 \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5}$ $\;=2 \left[ \sin\; \frac{\pi}{5}+ \sin\; \frac{2\pi}{5} \right] =4 \sin\; \frac{3\pi}{10} \cos\; \frac{\pi}{10}$ $\;=4 \; \frac{(\sqrt{5}+1)}{4} \; \frac{(\sqrt{10+2\sqrt{5}})}{4} = \; \frac{1}{4}(\sqrt{5}+1)(\sqrt{10+2\sqrt{5}})$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\cot(\cos^{-1}x)=\sec\left\{\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}\right)\right\}, b>a$ For the square root to be real, $b^2-a^2>0$ , and with $b>a$ this implies $b>0$ . Let $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}\right)=\theta$ . Then $\tan\theta=\frac{a}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}$ . So $\sec\theta=\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}=\sqrt{1+\frac{a^2}{b^2-a^2}}=\frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}$ . Hence the equation becomes $\cot(\cos^{-1}x)=\frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}$ . Let $\cos^{-1}x=\alpha$ , so $\cot\alpha=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ . Therefore $\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}$ . Since the right side is positive, $\alpha$ is acute and hence $x>0$ . Squaring, $\frac{x^2}{1-x^2}=\frac{b^2}{b^2-a^2}$ . $\Rightarrow x^2(b^2-a^2)=b^2(1-x^2)$ . $\Rightarrow x^2(2b^2-a^2)=b^2$ . $\Rightarrow x=\frac{b}{\sqrt{2b^2-a^2}}$ (positive root). Alternatively, let $\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}\right)=\phi$ . Then $\cot\phi=\frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2-a^2}}$ . From the right triangle, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{b^2+(b^2-a^2)}=\sqrt{2b^2-a^2}$ . Thus $\cos\phi=\frac{b}{\sqrt{2b^2-a^2}}$ . Since $\cos^{-1}x=\phi$ , $x=\cos\phi=\frac{b}{\sqrt{2b^2-a^2}}$ . $\therefore x=\frac{b}{\sqrt{2b^2-a^2}}$ . So the correct option is the first option. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\sinh^{-1} x = \log 3$ $\cosh^{-1} y = \log \frac{3}{2}$ $\sinh^{-1} x = \log(3)$ $\Rightarrow x = \sinh(\log 3)$ $= \frac{e^{\log 3} - e^{-\log 3}}{2}$ $= \frac{3 - \frac{1}{3}}{2} = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3}$ And $\cosh^{-1} y = \log\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow y = \cosh\left(\log \frac{3}{2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{e^{\log\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)} + e^{-\log\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}}{2} = \frac{\frac{3}{2} + \frac{2}{3}}{2} = \frac{13}{12}$ $x - y = \frac{4}{3} - \frac{13}{12}$ $= \frac{16-13}{12} = \frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$ Now, we know that $\tanh^{-1}(z) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right)$ Now, $z = x - y$ So, $\tanh^{-1}(x-y) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1+x-y}{1-(x-y)}\right)$ $= \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1+x-y}{1-x+y}\right)$ $= \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1+\frac{1}{4}}{1-\frac{1}{4}}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{\frac{5}{4}}{\frac{3}{4}}\right)$ $= \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{5}{3}\right) = \ln\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}\right)$ So, $\tanh^{-1}(x-y) = \log\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}\right)$ , which matches option A. © examsnet.com

Solution: Since, $a, b$ and $c$ are in AP So, $2 b=a+c$ Also, $\angle A=2\angle C\;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (i)$ Now, in a $\triangle A B C$ , $a=2 R \sin A, b=2 R \sin B, c=2 R \sin C$ So, $2 b=a+c$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2 \cdot 2 R \sin B=2 R \sin A+2 R \sin C$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2 \sin B= \sin A+ \sin C$ In a $\triangle A B C$ , $\;A+B+C=180^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow 2 C+B+C=180^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow B=180^{\circ}-3 C$ So, $\sin B = \sin (180^{\circ}-3 C)$ $= \sin (3C) \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (ii)$ And $2\sin B = \sin A + \sin C$ $\Rightarrow 2\sin (3C) = \sin (2C) + \sin C$ [using Eq. (i) and (ii)] $=2\sin C \cos C + \sin C$ $\;\;\text{ and }\; \sin (3C)=3\sin C-4\sin^3 C$ $\;\;\text{ So, }\; 2\sin (3C)=2(3-4\sin^2 C)$ $=2\cos C+1$ $=2(4\cos^2 C-1)$ $\Rightarrow 8\cos^2 C-2=2\cos C+1$ $\Rightarrow 8\cos^2 C-2\cos C-3=0$ $\therefore \cos C = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4-4(8)(-3)}}{16}$ $= \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{100}}{16} = \frac{2 \pm 10}{16}$ So, $\cos C = \frac{3}{4}, \cos C = -\frac{1}{2}$ Since, $C$ must be positive, So, $\cos C = \frac{3}{4}$ Now, $\cos A = \cos (2C)$ $= 2\cos^2 C-1 = 2\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2-1 = \frac{1}{8}$ And $B=180^{\circ}-3C$ $\cos B = \cos (180^{\circ}-3C)$ $= -\cos (3C)$ $= -(4\cos^3 C - 3\cos C)$ $= -\left(4\left(\frac{27}{64}\right) - 3\cdot \frac{3}{4}\right)$ $= -\left(\frac{27}{16} - \frac{9}{4}\right)$ $= -\left(\frac{27-36}{16}\right) = \frac{9}{16}$ $\therefore \cos B = \frac{9}{16}$ So, $\cos A : \cos B : \cos C$ $= \frac{1}{8} : \frac{9}{16} : \frac{3}{4}$ $= \frac{2:9:12}{16}$ So, $\cos A : \cos B : \cos C = 2:9:12$ © examsnet.com

Solution: In a triangle $A, B$ and $C$ are in arithmetic progression. So, $B=\frac{\pi}{3}$ Now, $r r_3=r_1 r_2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\Delta}{s} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s-c}=\frac{\Delta}{s-a} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s-b}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{s(s-c)}=\frac{1}{(s-a)(s-b)}$ $\Rightarrow s^2-(a+b)s+ab=s^2-cs$ $\Rightarrow ab=(a+b-c)s$ $\Rightarrow ab=(a+b-c)\frac{a+b+c}{2}$ $\Rightarrow 2ab=(a+b)^2-c^2$ $\Rightarrow 2ab=a^2+b^2+2ab-c^2$ $\Rightarrow a^2+b^2=c^2$ Also, using cosine rule, $b^2=a^2+c^2-2ac\cos B$ $\Rightarrow b^2=a^2+c^2-2ac\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow b^2=a^2+c^2-ac$ $\Rightarrow c^2-a^2=a^2+c^2-ac$ $\Rightarrow 2a^2=ac\Rightarrow 2a=c$ $\Rightarrow a=\frac{c}{2}=\frac{10}{2}=5$ So, $b^2=c^2-a^2=100-25=75$ $\Rightarrow b=5\sqrt{3}$ Now, $a^2+b^2+c^2=25+75+100=200$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\; \text{LHS} \;=\; \frac{2 (r_1+r_3)}{a c (1+\cos B)}$ $\;=\; \frac{2 (r_1+r_3)}{a c \left(1+2 \cos^2 \frac{B}{2} - 1\right)}$ $\;=\; \frac{2 (r_1+r_3)}{a c \left(2 \cos^2 \frac{B}{2}\right)}$ We know that, $r_1 = \frac{\Delta}{s-a}, r_3 = \frac{\Delta}{s-c}$ And $\cos \frac{B}{2} = \sqrt{ \frac{s(s-b)}{a c} }$ Hence, LHS $= \; \frac{2 \left[ \frac{\Delta}{s-a} + \frac{\Delta}{s-c} \right]}{a c \cdot 2 \left( \sqrt{ \frac{s(s-b)}{a c} } \right)^2}$ $\;=\; \frac{2 \Delta \left[ \frac{1}{s-a} + \frac{1}{s-c} \right]}{2 a c \cdot \left( \frac{s(s-b)}{a c} \right)}$ $\;=\; \frac{\Delta \left[ \frac{s-c+s-a}{(s-a)(s-c)} \right]}{s(s-b)}$ $\;=\; \frac{\Delta (2s - a - c)}{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ $\;=\; \frac{\Delta (a+b+c-a-c)}{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ $\;=\; \frac{b \Delta}{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ $\;=\; \frac{b}{\Delta} = \text{RHS}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The position vector of $a$ is $a = -3\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Let, $M$ be the mid-point of the hypotenuse $B C$ . So, the position vector of $M$ is $m = 6\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ Let the centroid be $G$ and its position vector be $g$ . So, $g = \frac{a+b+c}{3}$ Since, the mid-point of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equidistant from all three vertices So, $M$ is the circumcenter of a triangle and $m = \frac{b+c}{2}$ $\Rightarrow b + c = 2m$ Substituting this value in Eq. (i), we get $g = \frac{a + 2m}{3}$ $\Rightarrow g = \frac{\widehat{(-3i+5\hat{j}+2\hat{k})+2(6\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k})}}{3}$ $= \frac{\widehat{-3i+5\hat{j}+2\hat{k}+12\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+10\hat{k}}}{3}$ $= \frac{\widehat{9i+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k}}}{3}$ $= 3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ So, the position vector of centroid is $3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $\;A =3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}-\hat{k}, B =\hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+\hat{k} \;\text{ and }\;$ $\;C =5 \hat{i}+5 \hat{j}+5 \hat{k}$ So, $B C = C - B$ $\;\; =5 \hat{i}+5 \hat{j}+5 \hat{k}-\hat{i}-3 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\;\; =4 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}$ $\;B A = A - B =3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}-\hat{k}-\hat{i}-3 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\;\; = 2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2 \hat{k}$ Now, $B A \times B C =\hat{\begin{vmatrix} i & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix}}$ $\;=(4+4) \hat{i}-(8+8) \hat{j}+(4-4) \hat{k}$ $\;=8 \hat{i}-16 \hat{j}$ And $\left| B A \times B C \right| =\sqrt{8^2+(-16)^2}$ $\;=\sqrt{64+256}$ $\;=\sqrt{320}=8 \sqrt{5}$ So, area of triangle $=\frac{1}{2}\left| B A \times B C \right|$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times 8 \sqrt{5}=4 \sqrt{5}$ Now, $\left| B C \right| =\sqrt{4^2+2^2+4^2}$ $=\sqrt{16+4+16}=\sqrt{36}=6$ Let, the magnitude of the altitude $h$ from $A$ to $B C$ is given by $\;\; \text{Area} \;=\;\frac{1}{2} \times \;\text{base} \times \text{height}\;$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  4 \sqrt{5}=\;\frac{1}{2} \times \left| B C \right| \times h$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  4 \sqrt{5}=\;\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times h$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  h=\;\frac{4 \sqrt{5}}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $a =2 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}-3 \hat{k}$ , $b =-\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k} \;\text{ and }\; c =p \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ Now, $a \cdot (b \times c)=\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ p & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=0$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2(2+6)-4(-1-3p)-3(2-2p)=0$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; 16+4+12p-6+6p=0$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; 18p+14=0$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; p=\frac{-14}{18}=\frac{-7}{9}$ Now, $v =9 p \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}$ $\;=9 \left(\frac{-7}{9}\right) \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}$ $\;=-7 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}$ Now, unit vector $\hat{u}\;=\;\frac{v}{|v|}\;=\;\frac{\widehat{-7 \hat{i} -4 \hat{j} +4 \hat{k}}}{\sqrt{(-7)^2+(-4)^2+4^2}}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \hat{u} = \frac{\widehat{-7 \hat{i} -4 \hat{j} +4 \hat{k}}}{9}$ $\;=\;\frac{-7}{9} \hat{i} -\frac{4}{9} \hat{j} +\frac{4}{9} \hat{k}$ © examsnet.com
