Solution: Let $b = x \hat{i} + y \hat{j}$ and $a$ is perpendicular to $b$ . $\therefore a \cdot b = 0$ $\Rightarrow (4 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) \cdot (x \hat{i}+y \hat{j})=0$ $\Rightarrow 4x+3y=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\lambda$ $\Rightarrow x=3\lambda, y=-4\lambda$ $\therefore b = \lambda(3 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j})$ Let the required vector be $c = c_1 \hat{i}+c_2 \hat{j}$ then the projection of $c$ on $a$ and $b$ are $\frac{c \cdot a}{|a|}$ and $\frac{c \cdot b}{|b|}$ respectively. $\therefore \frac{c \cdot a}{|a|}=1 \;\text{and}\; \frac{c \cdot b}{|b|}=2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\widehat{ (c_1 i + c_2 \hat{j}) \cdot (4 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) }}{\sqrt{4^2+3^2}}=1$ $\Rightarrow 4c_1+3c_2=5 \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(i)$ $\;\text{and}\; \frac{c \cdot b}{|b|}=2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\widehat{ (c_1 i + c_2 \hat{j}) \cdot (3 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}) }}{\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}}=2$ $\Rightarrow 3c_1-4c_2=10 \;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(ii)$ Solving Eq. (i) and (ii), we get $c_1=2, c_2=-1$ So, the required vector $= c_1 \hat{i}+c_2 \hat{j}=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Concept: Mean deviation about the mean is the average of absolute deviations of class marks from the arithmetic mean. Formula: $\overline{x}=\frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i}, \quad MD=\frac{\sum f_i |x_i-\overline{x}|}{\sum f_i}$ Solution: Class marks are $x_i=1,3,5,7,9$ . Frequencies are $f_i=1,3,4,1,2$ . $\sum f_i=11$ . $\sum f_i x_i=1(1)+3(3)+4(5)+1(7)+2(9)=55$ . $\overline{x}=\frac{55}{11}=5$ . Now, $\sum f_i |x_i-\overline{x}|=1|1-5|+3|3-5|+4|5-5|+1|7-5|+2|9-5|$ . $=1(4)+3(2)+4(0)+1(2)+2(4)=4+6+0+2+8=20$ . $MD=\frac{20}{11}$ . Answer: $\frac{20}{11}$ (Option B). © examsnet.com

Solution: Basket I has $5$ apples and $7$ oranges, so it has $5+7=12$ fruits in all. Basket II has $4$ apples and $8$ oranges, so it also has $4+8=12$ fruits in all. Let $A_1$ be the event of picking an apple from basket I and $O_1$ the event of picking an orange from basket I. $P(A_1)=\frac{5}{12}$ and $P(O_1)=\frac{7}{12}$ . Let $A_2$ be the event of picking an apple from basket II and $O_2$ the event of picking an orange from basket II. $P(A_2)=\frac{4}{12}$ and $P(O_2)=\frac{8}{12}$ . The event of getting one apple and one orange occurs in two mutually exclusive ways. Case (i): apple from basket I and orange from basket II. Since the two picks are independent, $P(A_1\cap O_2)=P(A_1)\cdot P(O_2)=\frac{5}{12}\times\frac{8}{12}=\frac{40}{144}$ . Case (ii): orange from basket I and apple from basket II. $P(O_1\cap A_2)=P(O_1)\cdot P(A_2)=\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{4}{12}=\frac{28}{144}$ . Hence the required probability is $\frac{40}{144}+\frac{28}{144}=\frac{68}{144}=\frac{17}{36}$ . Check by the complement method: $1-P(\text{both apples})-P(\text{both oranges})=1-\frac{5}{12}\cdot\frac{4}{12}-\frac{7}{12}\cdot\frac{8}{12}=1-\frac{20}{144}-\frac{56}{144}=\frac{68}{144}=\frac{17}{36}$ . So the probability is $\frac{17}{36}$ , which is the third option. © examsnet.com

Solution: Interpreting the event as the first card being a queen and the second card being a black face card: There are $6$ black face cards in total. If the first card is a black queen, then $2$ choices leave $5$ black face cards among the remaining $51$ cards. This contributes $\frac{2}{52}\cdot\frac{5}{51}$ . If the first card is a red queen, then $2$ choices leave all $6$ black face cards among the remaining $51$ cards. This contributes $\frac{2}{52}\cdot\frac{6}{51}$ . Thus the probability is $\frac{2}{52}\cdot\frac{5}{51}+\frac{2}{52}\cdot\frac{6}{51}=\frac{10}{2652}+\frac{12}{2652}=\frac{22}{2652}=\frac{11}{1326}$ . Hence option B is correct. Note: a strict conditional reading, given that the first card is already a queen, would give $\frac{11}{102}$ , which is not among the options. © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $D$ be the event that the item is defective and $N$ be the event that the item is not defective. Then $P(D) = 0.3$ and $P(N) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$ . Let $R_D$ be the event that the device reports the item as defective and $R_N$ be the event that the device reports the item as not defective. The device gives an accurate result in $8$ out of $10$ tests, i.e. in $\frac{8}{10} = 0.8$ of the tests. So $P\left(\frac{R_D}{D}\right) = P\left(\frac{R_N}{N}\right) = 0.8$ . Hence the inaccurate result probability is $P\left(\frac{R_N}{D}\right) = P\left(\frac{R_D}{N}\right) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2$ . We need $P\left(\frac{D}{R_N}\right)$ . $P(D \cap R_N) = P\left(\frac{R_N}{D}\right) \times P(D) = 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06$ $P(N \cap R_N) = P\left(\frac{R_N}{N}\right) \times P(N) = 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.56$ Now, by the theorem of total probability, $P(R_N) = P(D \cap R_N) + P(N \cap R_N) = 0.06 + 0.56 = 0.62$ By Bayes' theorem, $P\left(\frac{D}{R_N}\right) = \frac{P(D \cap R_N)}{P(R_N)} = \frac{0.06}{0.62} = \frac{6}{62} = \frac{3}{31}$ ∴ The probability that an item is actually defective given that the device reports it as not defective is $\frac{3}{31}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $A, B$ and $C$ be the event that a student is from section $A, B$ and $C$ . So, $P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.3, P(C)=0.5$ Now, section A : 20 girls, 30 boys, total 50 students Section B : 40 girls, 20 boys, total 60 students Section C : 10 girls, 30 boys, total 40 students $P(G / A)\;=\;\frac{20}{50}=0.4, P(G / B)=\;\frac{40}{60}=\;\frac{2}{3}$ $P(G / C)\;=\;\frac{10}{40}=0.25$ $P(G)\;=P(G / A)\cdot P(A)+P(G / B)\cdot P(B)+P(G / C)\cdot P(C)$ $\;=0.4 \times 0.2+\;\frac{2}{3}\times 0.3+0.25 \times 0.5$ $\;=0.08+0.2+0.125$ $\;=0.405$ Now, $P(G\cap A)=P(G / A)\cdot P(A)$ $=0.4 \times 0.2=0.08$ Using Bayes' theorem, $\;P(A / G)=\;\frac{P(A\cap G)}{P(G)}$ $\;=\;\frac{0.08}{0.405}=\;\frac{80}{405}=\;\frac{16}{81}$ So, the probability that a randomly selected girl belongs to section $A$ is $\;\frac{16}{81}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Mean, $\mu=\;\frac{16}{5}$ , variance, $\sigma^2=\;\frac{48}{25}$ We know that, $\mu=n p$ and $\sigma^2=n p(1-p)$ So, $\;\frac{16}{5}=n p$ and $\;\frac{48}{25}=n p(1-p)$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \;\frac{16}{5}(1-p)=\;\frac{48}{25}$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  1-p=\;\frac{48}{25} \times \;\frac{5}{16}=\;\frac{3}{5}$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  p=1-\;\frac{3}{5}=\;\frac{2}{5}, 1-p=\;\frac{3}{5}$ Now, $n p=\;\frac{16}{5}$ $\Rightarrow n \cdot \;\frac{2}{5}=\;\frac{16}{5}$ $\Rightarrow n=8$ Now, $\;P(X \leq 2)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)$ $\;=\binom{8}{0} P^0(1-p)^8+\binom{8}{1} p^1(1-p)^7+\binom{8}{2} p^2(1-p)^6$ $\;=1 \cdot \left(\;\frac{2}{5}\right)^0 \cdot \left(\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^8+8 \cdot \;\frac{2}{5} \cdot \left(\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^7+28 \cdot \left(\;\frac{2}{5}\right)^2 \cdot \left(\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^6$ $\;= \left(\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^8+\;\frac{16 \cdot 3^7}{5^8}+\;\frac{28 \cdot 4 \cdot 3^6}{5^8}$ $\;=\;\frac{3^8+16 \cdot 3^7+28 \cdot 4 \cdot 3^6}{5^8}$ $\;=\;\frac{3^6 (3^2+16 \cdot 3+112)}{5^8}=\;\frac{3^6(169)}{5^8}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the coordinates of the centroid be $G(x, y)$ of the $\triangle APQ$ is $x = \frac{x_A + x_P + x_Q}{3}, y = \frac{y_A + y_P + y_Q}{3}$ Given the points $A(a, 0), P(a \cos \theta, a \sin \theta)$ and $Q(b \sin \theta, -b \cos \theta)$ The coordinates of the centroid are $x = \frac{a + a \cos \theta + b \sin \theta}{3}$ $y = \frac{0 + a \sin \theta - b \cos \theta}{3}$ Let $x = h$ and $y = k$ , then, $h = \frac{a + a \cos \theta + b \sin \theta}{3}, k = \frac{a \sin \theta - b \cos \theta}{3}$ $\Rightarrow 3h - a = a \cos \theta + b \sin \theta$ $3k = a \sin \theta - b \cos \theta$ Squaring and adding these equations $(3h - a)^2 + (3k)^2 = (a \cos \theta + b \sin \theta)^2 + (a \sin \theta - b \cos \theta)^2$ $= a^2 \cos^2 \theta + b^2 \sin^2 \theta + 2ab \cos \theta \sin \theta + a^2 \sin^2 \theta + b^2 \cos^2 \theta - 2ab \cos \theta \sin \theta$ $= a^2 + b^2$ Replacing $h$ with $x$ and $k$ with $y$ , we get the locus of the centroid as $(3x - a)^2 + (3y)^2 = a^2 + b^2$ $\Rightarrow \left(x - \frac{a}{3}\right)^2 + y^2 = \frac{a^2 + b^2}{9}$ $\Rightarrow \left(x - \frac{a}{3}\right)^2 + y^2 = \left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}{3}\right)^2$ So, the locus of the centroid is $\left(x - \frac{a}{3}\right)^2 + y^2 = \left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}{3}\right)^2$ It is a circle with centre at $\left(\frac{a}{3}, 0\right)$ and radius $\frac{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the original coordinates of the point $P$ be $(x_0, y_0) = (4,1)$ . We will apply the transformations in succession and find the coordinates of $P$ after each step. Step (i): Origin is shifted to the point $(1,6)$ by translation of axes. When the origin is shifted to $(h, k)$ , the new coordinates $(x', y')$ of a point $(x, y)$ are given by the formulas: $\; x' = x - h$ $\; y' = y - k$ In this case, $(x, y) = (4,1)$ and $(h, k) = (1,6)$ . So, the coordinates of $P$ after this transformation, let's call them ( $x_1, y_1$ ), are: $\; x_1 = 4 - 1 = 3$ $\; y_1 = 1 - 6 = -5$ The point $P$ is now at $(3,-5)$ with respect to the new coordinate system. Step (ii): Translation through a distance of $2$ units along the positive direction of $X$ -axis. This implies a translation of the point itself within the current coordinate system (established after step (i)). A translation of a point $(x, y)$ by $a$ units along the positive X-axis results in new coordinates ( $x + a, y$ ). Here, the point is $(x_1, y_1) = (3,-5)$ , and the translation distance is $a = 2$ . So, the coordinates of $P$ after this transformation, let's call them $(x_2, y_2)$ , are: $\; x_2 = x_1 + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5$ $\; y_2 = y_1 = -5$ The point $P$ is now at $(5,-5)$ . Step (iii): Rotation of axes through an angle of $90^{\circ}$ in the positive direction. This means the coordinate axes (with respect to which $P$ is currently at $(5,-5)$ ) are rotated by an angle $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ counter-clockwise. If the old coordinates of a point are $(x, y)$ and the axes are rotated by an angle $\theta$ , the new coordinates $(x', y')$ are given by: $\; x' = x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta$ $\; y' = -x \sin \theta + y \cos \theta$ In this case, the point is $(x_2, y_2) = (5,-5)$ and $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ . $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$ $\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$ So, the final coordinates of $P$ , let's call them $(x_3, y_3)$ , are: $\; x_3 = 5 \cos 90^{\circ} + (-5) \sin 90^{\circ} = 5(0) + (-5)(1) = -5$ $\; y_3 = -5 \sin 90^{\circ} + (-5) \cos 90^{\circ} = -5(1) + (-5)(0) = -5$ The final position of the point $P$ is $(-5,-5)$ . Comparing this with the given options, the final coordinates are $(-5,-5)$ , which corresponds to Option C. The final answer is $(-5,-5)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $L_1=a x-3 y+5=0$ , $L_2=4 x-6 y+8=0$ To find $x$ -intercept of line $L_1$ , set $y=0$ , then $\;a x-3(0)+5\;=0$ $\Rightarrow \; x\; =-\; \frac{5}{a}$ So, $x$ -intercept $(p)=-\; \frac{5}{a}$ To find $y$ -intercept $(q)$ , set $x=0$ , then $\;a(0)-3 y+5=0$ $\Rightarrow -3 y=-5$ So, $q=y=\; \frac{5}{3}$ Now, to find $y$ -intercept $(n)$ , set $x=0$ So, $4(0)-6 y+8=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y=\; \frac{-8}{-6}$ So, $n=y=\; \frac{4}{3}$ to find $x$ -intercept $(m)$ , set $y=0$ in equation $L_2$ $\;4(x)-6(0)+8\;=0$ $\Rightarrow \;4 x\; =-8$ $\therefore \; m\; =x=-2$ Also, $L_1: a x-3 y+5=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y=\; \frac{a}{3} x+\; \frac{5}{3}$ ∴ Slope of $L_1=\; \frac{a}{3}$ And $L_2: 4 x-6 y+8=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; y=\; \frac{4}{6} x+\; \frac{8}{6}=\; \frac{2}{3} x+\; \frac{4}{3}$ ∴ Slope of $L_2=\; \frac{2}{3}$ Since, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are parallel, so their slopes are equal. $\therefore \;\; \frac{a}{3}=\; \frac{2}{3}$ $\Rightarrow a=2$ Now, equation of the line passing through $(p, q)= \left(\; \frac{-5}{2}, \; \frac{5}{3}\right)$ And $(m, n)= \left(-2, \; \frac{4}{3}\right)$ is $\;y-\; \frac{4}{3}= \frac{\; \frac{4}{3} - \frac{5}{3}}{-2- \left(\; -\frac{5}{2}\right)} (x-(-2))$ $\Rightarrow y-\; \frac{4}{3}= \frac{ -\frac{1}{3} }{ \frac{1}{2} } (x+2)$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{3 y-4}{3}=\; \frac{-2}{3} (x+2)$ $\Rightarrow 3 y-4=-2 x-4$ $\Rightarrow 3 y+2 x=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given the second pair is $2x^2+xy-6y^2=0$ . Factorizing: $2x^2+xy-6y^2=(2x-3y)(x+2y)$ . So its lines are $2x-3y=0$ and $x+2y=0$ . For exactly one common line, $ax^2-7xy-3y^2=0$ must contain one of these lines but not the other. Substitute $2x-3y=0$ , i.e. $y=\frac{2x}{3}$ , into $ax^2-7xy-3y^2=0$ : $ax^2-7x\left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)-3\left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)^2=0$ $\Rightarrow a-\frac{14}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=0$ $\Rightarrow a-6=0$ $\Rightarrow a=6$ . Substitute $x+2y=0$ , i.e. $y=-\frac{x}{2}$ , gives $a+\frac{11}{4}=0$ , so $a=-\frac{11}{4}$ , not an integer. Hence $a=6$ . Thus the pair is $6x^2-7xy-3y^2=0$ . Factorizing: $6x^2-7xy-3y^2=(2x-3y)(3x+y)$ . So it shares exactly the line $2x-3y=0$ with $2x^2+xy-6y^2=0$ . For $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$ , the angle bisectors are given by $\frac{x^2-y^2}{a-b}=\frac{xy}{h}$ . Here $a=6$ , $2h=-7$ , so $h=-\frac{7}{2}$ , and $b=-3$ . Therefore, $\frac{x^2-y^2}{6-(-3)}=\frac{xy}{-\frac{7}{2}}$ . $\Rightarrow \frac{x^2-y^2}{9}=-\frac{2xy}{7}$ . $\Rightarrow -7x^2+7y^2=18xy$ . $\Rightarrow 7x^2+18xy-7y^2=0$ . Hence the correct option is $7x^2+18xy-7y^2=0$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given equation is $2 x^2+2 h x y+2 y^2-x+y=1$ The angle $\theta$ between the lines is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)=0 \Rightarrow \tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}$ . The angle $\theta$ between the pair of lines $a x^2+2 h x y+b y^2+2 g x+2 f y+c=0$ is $\tan \theta=\left| \frac{2\sqrt{h^2-ab}}{a+b} \right|$ Here $a=2, b=2$ $\tan \theta=\left| \frac{2\sqrt{h^2-4}}{4} \right|$ $=\left| \frac{\sqrt{h^2-4}}{2} \right|$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{h^2-4}}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{h^2-4}{4}=\frac{9}{16}$ $\Rightarrow h^2-4=\frac{9}{16} \times 4=\frac{9}{4}$ $\Rightarrow h^2=\frac{9}{4}+4=\frac{25}{4}$ $\Rightarrow h=\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{4}}=\pm \frac{5}{2}$ Since, $h$ is a positive rational number, $h=\frac{5}{2}$ Thus, the given equation is $2 x^2+2 h x y+2 y^2-x+y-1=0$ $2 x^2+2 \cdot \frac{5}{2} x y+2 y^2-x+y-1=0$ $2 x^2+5 x y+2 y^2-x+y+1=0$ $=F(x, y)$ Now, $\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=4 x+5 y-1=0$ , $\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=4 y+5 x+1=0$ Solving these two equations, we get $x=-1, y=1$ So, the point of intersection is $(-1,1)$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, lines are $x+2y-2=0$ and $2x+3y-1=0$ Solving these two lines, we get $x=-4\;\text{and}\;y=3$ Thus, the center of circle is $(-4,3)$ . Since, the general eq. of circle is $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ , where $(h,k)$ is the center and $r$ is the radius. So, $(x-(-4))^2+(y-3)^2=r^2$ $\Rightarrow\;\;(x+4)^2+(y-3)^2=r^2\;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(i)$ But, the circle passes through the point $(8,8)$ , So, $(8+4)^2+(8-3)^2=r^2$ $12^2+5^2=r^2$ $169=r^2$ $\Rightarrow\;\;r=13$ Now, from Eq. (i), we get $(x+4)^2+(y-3)^2=r^2\;=169$ $\Rightarrow\;\;x^2+8x+16+y^2-6y+9\;=169$ $\Rightarrow\;\;x^2+y^2+8x-6y-144\;=0$ Comparing with the given equation $x^2+y^2+px+qx+r=0$ We get $p=8,\;q=-6,\;r=-144$ $\therefore\;\;p^2+q^2+r\;=8^2+(-6)^2+(-144)$ $\;=64+36-144$ $\;=-44$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The circle is $x^2+y^2-2x+4y+3=0$ . Comparing with $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ , we get $2g=-2$ , $2f=4$ , and $c=3$ . Thus $g=-1$ and $f=2$ . The polar of $P(x_1,y_1)$ with respect to the circle is $xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)+c=0$ . Substituting $g=-1$ , $f=2$ , and $c=3$ : $xx_1+yy_1-(x+x_1)+2(y+y_1)+3=0$ . Simplifying, $(x_1-1)x+(y_1+2)y-x_1+2y_1+3=0$ . This is the same line as $2x-3y+1=0$ . Therefore, for some nonzero constant $\lambda$ , $(x_1-1)x+(y_1+2)y-x_1+2y_1+3=\lambda(2x-3y+1)$ . Comparing coefficients, $x_1-1=2\lambda$ . $y_1+2=-3\lambda$ . $-x_1+2y_1+3=\lambda$ . From $x_1-1=2\lambda$ and $y_1+2=-3\lambda$ , $3x_1+2y_1=-1$ . From $x_1-1=2\lambda=2(-x_1+2y_1+3)$ , $3x_1-4y_1=7$ . Solving $3x_1+2y_1=-1$ and $3x_1-4y_1=7$ , we get $x_1=\frac{5}{9}$ and $y_1=-\frac{4}{3}$ . Hence, $3x_1-y_1=3\left(\frac{5}{9}\right)-\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)$ . $=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{4}{3}=3$ . So the correct option is $3$ , i.e. seq $2$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: The circle $S'$ is $x^2+y^2-6x+6y+2=0$ . Rewriting it gives $(x-3)^2+(y+3)^2=16$ . So, the center of $S'$ is $(3,-3)$ and its radius is $r'=4$ . Since $S$ is a unit circle, its radius is $r=1$ . The point $(-1,-3)$ is the leftmost point of $S'$ because the center $(3,-3)$ is $4$ units to its right. For external tangency, the centers and the point of contact are collinear, with the point of contact between the centers. Hence the center of $S$ is one unit to the left of $(-1,-3)$ : $C=(-2,-3)$ . Thus the equation of $S$ is $(x+2)^2+(y+3)^2=1$ . Expanding: $x^2+y^2+4x+6y+12=0$ . Comparing with $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ : $2g=4 \Rightarrow g=2$ , $2f=6 \Rightarrow f=3$ , and $c=12$ . Therefore, $g+f+c=2+3+12=17$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: $S \equiv x^2+y^2-6 x+8 y+k=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-3)^2+(y+4)^2=25-k$ Thus, the center of the circle $C$ is at $(3,-4)= (x_1, y_1)$ . Let point $P$ as $(x_2, y_2)$ and point $Q$ is the point that divides the line segment $C P$ in the ratio $-1: 2$ Also, $3 x+4 y-43=0$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{-3}{4}x+\frac{43}{3}$ So, slope of tangent line $=\frac{-3}{4}$ And slope of line $C P=-\left(\frac{-4}{3}\right)=\frac{4}{3}$ Thus, equation of line $C P$ is $\Rightarrow y-(-4)=\frac{4}{3}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow y+4=\frac{4}{3}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{4}{3}x-8$ Since, $P$ lies on both the lines $3 x+4 y-43=0$ and the line $C P$ , $\therefore 3x+4\left(\frac{4}{3}x-8\right)-43=0$ $\Rightarrow 3x+\frac{16}{3}x-32-43=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{25}{3}x=75$ $\Rightarrow x=9$ Now, $y=\frac{4}{3}x-8=\frac{4}{3}(9)-8$ $=12-8=4$ So, $P=(9,4)$ Using section formula, we find the coordinates of $Q(x, y)$ . $x=\frac{2x_1-x_2}{2-1}=\frac{2(3)-9}{1}=-3$ $y=\frac{2y_1-y_2}{2-1}=\frac{2(-4)-4}{1}=-12$ So, $Q=(x, y)=(-3,-12)$ The power of point $Q$ w.r.t to circle, $x^2+y^2-6x+8y+k=0$ is $(-3)^2+(-12)^2-6(-3)+8(-12)+k$ $=9+144+18-96+k$ $=75+k \cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot (i)$ Now, the line $3x+4y-43=0$ is tangent to the circle, the radius of the circle is the distance from the center $C(3,-4)$ to the line $3x+4y-43=0$ So, $r=\frac{\left| A x_0+B y_0+C \right|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}$ $=\frac{|3(3)+4(-4)-43|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}$ $=\frac{|9-16-43|}{5}=\frac{50}{5}=10$ Now, $r=\sqrt{25-k}$ $\Rightarrow 10=\sqrt{25-k} \Rightarrow 25-k=100$ $\Rightarrow k=-75$ Put $k=-75$ in Eq. (i), we get The power of $Q$ w.r.t the circle $=75+k=75-75=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $s_1: x^2+y^2+2 g x+2 f y+c=0$ $s_2: 2 x^2+2 y^2+3 x+8 y+2 c=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; x^2+y^2+\frac{3}{2} x+4 y+c=0$ $s_3: x^2+y^2+2 x+2 y+1=0$ Radical axis $s_1-s_2=0$ $\Rightarrow (x^2+y^2+2 g x+2 f y+c)$ $\; - \left(x^2+y^2+\frac{3}{2} x+4 y+c\right)+0$ $\Rightarrow 2 g x+2 f y-\frac{3 x}{2}-4 y=0$ $\Rightarrow \left(2 g-\frac{3}{2}\right) x+(2 f-4) y=0$ $\Rightarrow (4 g-3) x+(4 f-8) y=0$ The radical axis touches the circle $s_3$ , where radius of $s_3$ . $=\sqrt{(-1)^2+(-1)^2-1}=1 \;\text{ and center is }\;(-1,-1)$ The perpendicular distance from the center of $s_3$ to the radical axis $=$ radius of $s_3$ $\;\;\frac{\left|(4 g-3) \cdot(-1)+(4 f-8)(-1)\right|}{\sqrt{(4 g-3)^2+(4 f-8)^2}}=1$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;\frac{\left|-4 g+3-4 f+8\right|}{\sqrt{(4 g-3)^2+(4 f-8)^2}}=1$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;\left|-4 g-4 f+11\right|$ $\;=\sqrt{(4 g-3)^2+(4 f-8)^2}$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;(-4 g-4 f+11)^2$ $\;=(4 g-3)^2+(4 f-8)^2$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;16 g^2+16 f^2+121+32 g f-88 g-88 f$ $\;=16 g^2-24 g+9+16 f^2-64 f+64$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;32 g f-64 g-24 f+48=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;8 g f-16 g-6 f+12=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;8 g(f-2)-6(f-2)=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;(8 g-6)(f-2)=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;4 g-3)(f-2)=0$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\;g=\frac{3}{4} \;\text{ or }\; f=2$ Either $g=\frac{3}{4}$ or $f=2$ is the required condition. © examsnet.com

Solution: Rewrite $y^2=x$ as $y^2=4\cdot \frac14 x$ , so $a=\frac14$ . For the standard parameter $t$ , the tangent is $ty=x+\frac{t^2}{4}$ . Intersection of tangents at $t_i$ and $t_j$ is $\left(\frac{t_i t_j}{4},\frac{t_i+t_j}{4}\right)$ . For $t_1=2,t_2=-4$ : $L=\left(\frac{2(-4)}{4},\frac{2+(-4)}{4}\right)=\left(-2,-\frac12\right)$ . For $t_2=-4,t_3=6$ : $M=\left(\frac{(-4)6}{4},\frac{-4+6}{4}\right)=\left(-6,\frac12\right)$ . For $t_3=6,t_1=2$ : $N=\left(\frac{6\cdot2}{4},\frac{6+2}{4}\right)=\left(3,2\right)$ . Now compute the area: $\text{Area}=\frac12\left|(x_M-x_L)(y_N-y_L)-(y_M-y_L)(x_N-x_L)\right|$ . $\text{Area}=\frac12\left|(-6+2)\left(2+\frac12\right)-\left(\frac12+\frac12\right)(3+2)\right|$ . $\text{Area}=\frac12\left|(-4)\frac52-(1)(5)\right|$ . $\text{Area}=\frac12\left|-10-5\right|=\frac{15}{2}=7.5$ . Therefore, the area of triangle $LMN$ is $7.5$ , so option option C is correct. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, equation: $9x^2+4y^2=72$ Differentiate w.r.t $x$ , we get $18x+8y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-18x}{8y}=\frac{-9x}{4y}$ Slope of tangent at point $(2,3)$ is $m_t=\frac{-9(2)}{4(3)}=\frac{-18}{12}=\frac{-3}{2}$ So, equation of tangent using point-slope form is $(y-3)=-\frac{3}{2}(x-2)$ $\Rightarrow 2y-6=-3x+6$ $\Rightarrow 3x+2y=12$ Now, slope of normal, $m_n=\frac{-1}{m_t}=\frac{2}{3}$ Now, slope of normal, $m_n=\frac{-1}{m_t}=\frac{2}{3}$ So, equation of normal is $(y-3)=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)$ $\Rightarrow 3y-9=2x-4$ $\Rightarrow 2x-3y=-5$ Now, for the $x$ -intercept of the tangent line, put $y=0$ , then $3x+2(0)=12$ $\Rightarrow x=4$ $\text{ so } (4,0)$ For the $x$ -intercept of the normal line, put $y=0$ , then $2x-3(0)=-5$ $\Rightarrow x=-\frac{5}{2}, \text{ so, } \left(-\frac{5}{2},0\right)$ Now, base of triangle $=$ Distance $\text{b / w x}$ -intercepts of the tangent and normal lines $b=4-\left(-\frac{5}{2}\right)=\frac{13}{2}$ And, height of triangles is the $y$ -coordinate of the point $(2,3)$ is $h=3$ So, area $=\frac{1}{2} b h=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{13}{2}\right)\times 3=\frac{39}{4}$ $\therefore \text{ Area }=\frac{39}{4} \text{ sq. units }$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, equation of hyperbola is $\; \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \; \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$ Now, the equation of the tangent to be hyperbola is $\; 3 \sqrt{2} x - 4 y = 12$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; y = \; \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{4} x - 3$ So, slope of the tangent, $m_t = \; \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{4}$ and $y$ -intercept is $c = -3$ Now, the line $y = m x + c$ tangent to the hyperbola is given by $c^{2} \; = a^{2} m^{2} - b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; (-3)^{2} \; = a^{2} \left( \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{4} \right)^{2} - b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; 9 \; = \; \frac{9}{8} a^{2} - b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; 9 a^{2} - 8 b^{2} \; = 72$ Given, eccentricity, $e = \; \frac{5}{4}$ $\; \text{So,} \; b^{2} \; = a^{2} (e^{2} - 1)$ $\; = a^{2} \left( \left( \frac{5}{4} \right)^{2} - 1 \right)$ $\; = a^{2} \left( \frac{25}{16} - 1 \right) = \frac{9}{16} a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; 16 b^{2} \; = 9 a^{2}$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $b^{2} \; = 9 \; \text{and} \; a^{2} = 16$ $\therefore a^{2} - b^{2} \; = 16 - 9 = 7$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given hyperbola equation is $x y=16$ Differentiate it w.r.t $x$ , we get $\;y+x \cdot \;\frac{dy}{dx}\;=0$ $\Rightarrow\;\;\frac{dy}{dx}\;=\;\frac{-y}{x}$ Now, slope of tangent at $(8,2)$ is $m_1=\;\frac{-2}{8}=\;\frac{-1}{4}$ And slope of normal is $m_n=\;\frac{-1}{-\frac{1}{4}}=4$ Now, equation of normal at $(8,2)$ is $\;y-2=4(x-8)$ $\Rightarrow\;\;  y=4x-30$ Normal intersects the hyperbola again at a point $(\alpha, \beta)$ , So, $\alpha \beta=16$ and $\beta=4\alpha-30$ Solving these two equations, we get $\;\alpha(4\alpha-30)=16$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\;  2\alpha^2-15\alpha-8=0$ $\text{So, }\alpha\;=\;\frac{-(-15) \pm \sqrt{(-15)^2-4 \cdot 2 \cdot (-8)}}{2 \cdot 2}$ $\;=\;\frac{15 \pm \sqrt{289}}{4}=\;\frac{15 \pm 17}{4}$ So, $\alpha_1=\;\frac{15+17}{4}=\;\frac{32}{4}=8$ and $\alpha_2=\;\frac{15-17}{4}=\;\frac{-1}{2}$ Since $(8,2)$ is one point, the other point is where $\alpha=\;\frac{-1}{2}$ So, $\beta=4\alpha-30$ $\;=4\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)-30=-32$ $\;\therefore |\beta|+\;\frac{1}{|\alpha|}=|-32|+\;\frac{1}{|-1/2|}$ $\;\; =32+2=34$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let the two fixed points be $A(-3,1,2)$ and $B(1,-2,4)$ . Let $P(x, y, z)$ be the point at which the line segment $A B$ subtends a right angle. Then, $\angle A P B = 90^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; P A \cdot P B = 0$ Now, $P A =(-3-x, 1-y, 2-z)$ $P B =(1-x,-2-y, 4-z)$ So, $P A \cdot P B =(-3-x)(1-x)+(1-y)(-2-y)+(2-z)(4-z)=0$ $\Rightarrow -3+3 x-x+x^2-2-y+2 y+y^2+8-2 z-4 z+z^2=0$ $\Rightarrow x^2+2 x+y^2+y+z^2-6 z+3=0$ $\Rightarrow x^2+y^2+z^2+2 x+y-6 z+3=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, vertices of $\triangle A B C$ are $A(1,2,3), B(2,3,-1)$ and $C(3,-1,-2)$ Now, $A B = B - A = (2,3,-1) - (1,2,3) = (1,1,-4)$ Now, $C B = (3,-1,-2) - (2,3,-1) = (1,-4,-1)$ So, $\left| AB \right|\; = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + (-4)^2}$ $\; = \sqrt{1+1+16} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$ $\left| CB \right|\; = \sqrt{1^2 + (-4)^2 + (-1)^2}$ $\; = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$ So, d.c. of $AB = \frac{AB}{|AB|} = \frac{(1,1,-4)}{3\sqrt{2}}$ $= \left( \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-4}{3\sqrt{2}} \right)$ And d.c. of $CB = \frac{CB}{|CB|} = \frac{(1,-4,-1)}{3\sqrt{2}}$ $= \left( \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-4}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-1}{3\sqrt{2}} \right)$ ∴ d.c.'s of the internal bisector of $\angle A B C$ are $\; \left( \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} - \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-4}{3\sqrt{2}} - \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \right)$ $\; = \left( \frac{2}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-3}{3\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-5}{3\sqrt{2}} \right)$ So, the D.c.'s are $\langle 2, -3, -5 \rangle$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Since, $x \to 0^{+}$ , so, the greatest integer function $\lfloor x \rfloor$ equals 0 as $0 \le x < 1$ . Now, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0+} \frac{\cos \lfloor x \rfloor - \cos(k x - \lfloor x \rfloor)}{x^{2}}=5$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{\cos 0 - \cos(k x)}{x^{2}}=5 \Rightarrow$ $\; \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{1 - \cos(k x)}{x^{2}}=5$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{2 \sin^{2} \left( \frac{k x}{2} \right)}{x^{2}}=5$ $\; \Rightarrow \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}} 2 \; \frac{ \sin^{2} \left( \frac{k x}{2} \right) }{ \left( \frac{k x}{2} \right)^{2} } \cdot \; \frac{k^{2}}{4}=5$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \; \frac{k^{2}}{4}=5 \; \; \left[ \because \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta}=1 \right]$ $\; \Rightarrow \; \; k^{2}= \; \frac{20}{2} \Rightarrow k= \pm \sqrt{10}$ So, $k=\sqrt{10}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x\tan 2x-2x\tan x}{(1-\cos 2x)^2}$ $\;\;\; =\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x \cdot \frac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2 x}-2x\tan x}{(1-(1-2\sin^2 x))^2}$ $\;\;\; =\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{2x\tan x\left(\frac{1}{1-\tan^2 x}-1\right)}{(2\sin^2 x)^2}$ $\;\;\; =\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{\frac{2x\tan x(1-1+\tan^2 x)}{1-\tan^2 x}}{4\sin^4 x}=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{2x\tan x \cdot \tan^2 x}{4\sin^4 x (1-\tan^2 x)}$ $\;\;\; =\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x\tan^3 x}{2\sin^4 x (1-\tan^2 x)}=\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x\sin^3 x}{2(1-\tan^2 x) \cdot \cos^2 x \cdot \sin^2 x}$ $\;\;\; =\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{1}{2\cos^3 x (1-\tan^2 x)} \cdot \lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x}{\sin x}$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{2\cos^3 0 (1-\tan^2 0)} \cdot 1 \;\; \left[\because \lim\limits_{x\to 0}\;\frac{x}{\sin x}=1\right]$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{2(1)(1)}=\;\frac{1}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, function $f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{(e^{a x}-1) \log(1+x)}{\sin^2 x}, & x>0 \\ \frac{\cos 4x - \cos b x}{\tan^2 x}, & x=0 \end{cases}$ is contiuous at $x=0$ Since, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$ So, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = f(0)$ and $f(0)=2$ Now, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^+} \frac{(e^{a x}-1) \log(1+x)}{\sin^2 x}$ Applying L'hospital rule, twice, since it is an indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ . So, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^+} \frac{a e^{a x} \log(1+x) + \frac{E^{a x}-1}{1+x}}{2 \cos x \sin x}$ This limit is again $\frac{0}{0}$ form, so apply L'Hospital rule again. $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^+} \frac{a^2 e^{a x} \log(1+x) + \frac{a e^{a x}(1+x) - (e^{a x}-1)}{(1+x)^2} + \frac{a e^{a x}}{1+x}}{2 \cos^2 x - 2 \sin^2 x}$ $= \frac{0 + \frac{a(1)-(1-1)}{1^2} + \frac{a}{1}}{2(1)-0} = \frac{a+a}{2} = a$ Since, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = f(0) \Rightarrow a=2$ Now, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{\cos 4x - \cos b x}{\tan^2 x}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{-2 \sin\left(\frac{4x+bx}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{4x-bx}{2}\right)}{\tan^2 x}$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{-2 \sin\left(\frac{4x+bx}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{4x-bx}{2}\right) \cdot \cos^2 x}{\frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2} \cdot x^2}$ $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{ \frac{-2 \sin\left(\frac{4x+bx}{2}\right)}{\frac{4x+bx}{2}} \cdot \left(\frac{4x+bx}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{ \sin\left(\frac{4x-bx}{2}\right) }{ \frac{4x-bx}{2} } \cdot \left(\frac{4x-bx}{2}\right) \cdot \cos^2 x }{ \frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2} \cdot x^2 }$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{-2 \cdot 1 \cdot \left(\frac{4x+bx}{2}\right) \cdot 1 \cdot \left(\frac{4x-bx}{2}\right) \cdot \cos^2 x}{1 \cdot x^2} \qquad \left[\because \lim\limits_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1\right]$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{-2 (16 x^2 - b^2 x^2)}{4 x^2} \cdot \cos^2 x$ $= \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \frac{b^2-16}{2} \cdot \cos^2 x = \frac{b^2-16}{2} \cdot 1 \qquad \left[\because \lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} \cos^2 x = 1\right]$ $= \frac{b^2-16}{2}$ Also, $\lim\limits_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = f(0)$ $\Rightarrow \ \frac{b^2-16}{2} = 2 \Rightarrow b^2 = 4+16 = 20$ Now, $\sqrt{b^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{20 - 2^2} = \sqrt{20-4} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $y = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{3x - x^3}{1 - 3x^2} \right) + \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{7x}{1 - 12x^2} \right)$ Let $x = \tan \theta$ $\text{So},\; = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{3\tan\theta - \tan^3\theta}{1 - 3\tan^2\theta} \right) + \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{7\tan\theta}{1 - 12\tan^2\theta} \right)$ $\; = 3 \tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{7x}{1 - 12x^2} \right)$ Now, differentiate $y$ w.r.t $x$ , we get $\; \frac{dy}{dx} \; = 3 \cdot \frac{1}{1+x^2} + \frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{7x}{1-12x^2}\right)^2} \cdot \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{7x}{1-12x^2} \right)$ $\;=\; \frac{3}{1+x^2} + \frac{1}{1 + \frac{49x^2}{(1-12x^2)^2}} \cdot \frac{(1-12x^2) \cdot 7 - 7x(-24x)}{(1-12x^2)^2}$ $\;=\; \frac{3}{1+x^2} + \frac{(1-12x^2)^2}{(1-12x^2)^2 + 49x^2} \cdot \frac{7 - 84x^2 + 168x^2}{(1-12x^2)^2}$ $\;=\; \frac{3}{1+x^2} + \frac{7+84x^2}{(1-12x^2)^2 + 49x^2}$ Now, At $x=0$ $\; \frac{dy}{dx} \Big|_{x=0} = \frac{3}{1+0} + \frac{7+84(0)}{(1-12(0)^2)^2 + 49.0^2} = 3 + \frac{7}{1+0} = 3+7 = 10$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $y=\sqrt{\frac{x^4 \sqrt{3x-5}}{(x^2-3)(2x-3)}}$ Take the natural $\log$ to both sides, we get $\ln(y)=\frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{x^4\sqrt{3x-5}}{(x^2-3)(2x-3)}\right)$ $\ln(y)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\ln(x^4)+\ln(\sqrt{3x-5})-\ln(x^2-3)-\ln(2x-3)\right]$ $=\frac{1}{2}\left[4\ln(x)+\frac{1}{2}\ln(3x-5)-\ln(x^2-3)-\ln(2x-3)\right]$ Now, differentiating w.r.t $x$ , we get $\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{4}{x} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{3x-5} - \frac{2x}{x^2-3} - \frac{2}{2x-3} \right]$ $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{2} \left[ \frac{4}{x} + \frac{3}{2(3x-5)} - \frac{2x}{x^2-3} - \frac{2}{2x-3} \right]$ Now, at $x=2$ $y=\sqrt{\frac{2^4 \sqrt{3\cdot 2-5}}{(2^2-3)(4-3)}}=\sqrt{\frac{16 \cdot 1}{1 \cdot 1}}=4$ So, $\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=\frac{4}{2}\left[ \frac{4}{2}+\frac{3}{2(3\cdot 2-5)}-\frac{2\cdot2}{2^2-3}-\frac{2}{2\cdot 2-3} \right]$ $=2\left[2+\frac{3}{2}-\frac{4}{1}-2\right]=2\left[\frac{3-8}{2}\right]=-5$ $\therefore \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=-5$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $x^2 + y^2 + \sin \; y = 4$ Differentiate both sides w.r.t $x$ , we get $\; 2 x + 2 y \cdot \; \frac{d y}{d x} + \cos y \cdot \; \frac{d y}{d x} = 0 \Rightarrow \; \frac{d y}{d x} (2 y + \cos y) = -2 x$ $\; \; \frac{d y}{d x} = \; \frac{-2 x}{2 y + \cos y}$ Again, differentiate both sides w.r.t $x$ , we get $\; \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \; = \; \frac{d}{d x} \left( \; \frac{-2 x}{2 y + \cos y} \right)$ $\; = \; \frac{(2 y + \cos y) \cdot (-2) - (-2 x) \cdot (2 - \sin \; y) \cdot \frac{d y}{d x}}{(2 y + \cos y)^2}$ $\; = \; \frac{-4 y - 2 \cos y + 2 x \cdot (2 - \sin \; y) \cdot \left( \frac{-2 x}{2 y + \cos y} \right)}{(2 y + \cos y)^2}$ $\; = \; \frac{-4 y - 2 \cos y - \frac{4 x^2 (2 - \sin \; y)}{2 y + \cos y}}{(2 y + \cos y)^2}$ Put $x = -2$ in original equation, we get $\; (-2)^2 + y^2 + \sin \; y = 4$ $\Rightarrow \; \; y^2 + \sin \; y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 0$ Now, from Eq. (i), we get $\; \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \; = \; \frac{-4(0) - 2 \cos(0) - \frac{4(-2)^2 (2 - \sin(0))}{2 \cdot (0) + \cos(0)}}{(2(0) + \cos(0))^2}$ $\; = \; \frac{-2 - \frac{16(2-0)}{1}}{1^2} = \; \frac{-2-32}{1} = -34$ $\therefore \; \; \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} \; \frac{}{} |_{x=-2} \; = -34$ © examsnet.com

Solution: The surface area of sphere is $S=4 \pi r^2, r$ is radius Now, differentiate w.r.t $x$ , we get $\;\frac{ds}{dt}=4 \pi \cdot 2 r \cdot \;\frac{dr}{dt}=8 \pi r \;\frac{dr}{dt}$ Also, given that $\;\frac{ds}{dt}=4 \text{ cm}^2/\text{sec}$ and $r=8 \text{ cm}$ $\; \therefore \;\; \;\frac{ds}{dt}=\pi r \cdot \;\frac{dr}{dt} \Rightarrow 4=8 \pi(8) \cdot \;\frac{dr}{dt}$ $\; \Rightarrow \;\; \;\frac{dr}{dt}=\;\frac{1}{16 \pi} \text{ cm}/\text{sec}$ Volume of Sphere is : $v=\;\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$ Differentiate both sides w.r.t $r$ , we get $\;\frac{dv}{dt}\;=\;\frac{4}{3} \pi \cdot 3 r^2 \cdot \;\frac{dr}{dt}=4 \pi \cdot(8)^2 \cdot \;\frac{1}{16 \pi} \;\text{ [using Eq. }\;$ $\;=16 \text{ cm}^3/\text{sec}$ ∴ Rate of change in the volume of the bubble $=16 \text{ cm}^3/\text{sec}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given curve, $f(x)=2 \cos x - \sin 2x$ $f'(x)=-2 \sin x - 2 \cos 2x$ To find turning points, set $f'(x)=0$ $\Rightarrow -2 \sin x - 2 \cos 2x = 0 \Rightarrow \sin x - \cos 2x = 0$ $\Rightarrow \sin x + 1 - 2 \sin^2 x = 0 \Rightarrow 2 \sin^2 x - \sin x - 1 = 0$ Let $u = \sin x$ , then $\;2u^2 - u - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow (2u+1)(u-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow u = -\frac{1}{2} \text{ or } u = 1$ $\therefore \sin x = \frac{-1}{2} \text{ or } \sin x = 1$ But $x \in [-\pi, \pi]$ So, $\sin x = \frac{-1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow x = -\frac{5\pi}{6}, -\frac{\pi}{6}$ And $\sin x = 1 \Rightarrow x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ Thus, there are three solutions for $x \in [-\pi, \pi]$ ∴ There are 3 turning points. © examsnet.com

Solution: The total surface area of a cone is $A=\pi r^2+\pi r l$ , where $r$ is radius and $l$ is the slant height. $=\pi(7)^2+\pi(7) \cdot \sqrt{7^2+7^2} \quad [ \because l=\sqrt{r^2+h^2} \text{ And } r=7, h=7]$ $=49\pi+49\sqrt{2}\pi=49\pi(1+\sqrt{2})$ But, the error in measuring $r$ and $h$ is $0.002 \times 7=0.014$ feet So, $dr=0.014$ and $dh=0.014$ Now, error in $l$ , denoted by $dl$ and differentiate it w.r.t $r$ and $h$ , we get $dl = \frac{\partial l}{\partial r} dr + \frac{\partial l}{\partial h} \cdot dh$ But $l = \sqrt{r^2+h^2}$ So, $\frac{\partial l}{\partial r} = \frac{1}{2} (r^2+h^2)^{-1/2} \cdot 2r = \frac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+h^2}} = \frac{r}{l}$ And $\frac{\partial l}{\partial h} = \frac{1}{2} (r^2+h^2)^{-1/2} \cdot 2h = \frac{h}{\sqrt{r^2+h^2}} = \frac{h}{l}$ So, $dl = \frac{r}{l} dr + \frac{h}{l} dh = \frac{7}{7\sqrt{2}} \cdot (0.014) + \frac{7}{7\sqrt{2}} (0.014)$ $= \frac{0.014}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{0.014}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} (0.014) = \sqrt{2}(0.014)$ The error in surface area, is $dA$ , i.e., $dA = \frac{\partial A}{\partial r} dr + \frac{\partial A}{\partial l} dl$ Since, $A = \pi r^2 + \pi r l$ $\therefore \frac{\partial A}{\partial r} = 2\pi r + \pi l \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial A}{\partial l} = \pi r$ $dA = (2\pi r + \pi l) \cdot dr + (\pi r) \cdot dl$ $= (2\pi r + \pi l)(0 \cdot 0.14) + (\pi r)(0.014)$ $= (14\pi + 7\sqrt{2}\pi)(0.014) + 7\sqrt{2}\pi(0.014)$ $= 14\pi(0.014) + 7\sqrt{2}\pi(0.014) + 7\sqrt{2}\pi(0.014)$ $= 0.196\pi + 0.098\sqrt{2}\pi + 0.098\sqrt{2}\pi$ $= 0.196\pi + 0.196\sqrt{2}\pi$ $= 0.196\pi(1+\sqrt{2})$ $= (0.616)(\sqrt{2}+1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Since, the slope of tangent to a curve at any point $(x, y)$ is $x+y$ . $\therefore \;\; \;\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y \Rightarrow \;\frac{dy}{dx}-y=x$ This is a linear differentiation equation So, $P=-1$ and $Q=x$ Now, $\text{IF}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\int -d\,x}=e^{-x}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; e^{-x} \cdot \;\frac{dy}{dx}-e^{-x} y=x e^{-x}$ $\Rightarrow \;\; \;\frac{dy}{dx} (y \cdot e^{-x}) =x e^{-x}$ Integrating both sides, we get $y \cdot e^{-x}\;=\int x e^{-x}\,dx$ $\;=-x e^{-x}-\int -e^{-x}\,dx$ $\;=-x e^{-x}+ (-e^{-x}) +c$ where $C=$ constant of integration $\Rightarrow y e^{-x}=-x e^{-x}-e^{-x}+c$ $\Rightarrow y=-x-1+c e^{x}$ , where $c$ is arbitrary constant. © examsnet.com

Solution: $\; ( \sqrt{\tan x} + \sqrt{\cot x} ) dx$ $\; = \int \left( \sqrt{\tan x} + \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tan x}} \right) dx$ $\; = \int \; \frac{\tan x + 1}{\sqrt{\tan x}} dx$ Let $u = \sqrt{\tan x}$ , then $u^2 = \tan x$ and $2 u du \; = \sec^2 x dx$ $\; = (1 + \tan^2 x) dx$ $\; = (1 + u^4) dx$ $\; = \int \; \frac{u^2 + 1}{u} \cdot \; \frac{2u}{1+u^4} du$ $\; = \int \; \frac{2 (u^2+1)}{1+u^4} du = \int \; \frac{2 \left(1 + \frac{1}{u^2}\right)}{\frac{1}{u^2} + u^2} du$ $\; = \int \; \frac{2 \left(1 + \frac{1}{u^2}\right)}{\left(u - \frac{1}{u}\right)^2 + 2} du$ Again, Let $v = u - \frac{1}{u}$ $\Rightarrow \; \; dv \; = \left(1 + \; \frac{1}{u^2}\right) du$ $\; = \int \; \frac{2}{2 \left( \frac{v^2}{2} + 1 \right)} dv = \int \; \frac{1}{\left( \frac{v^2}{2} + 1 \right)} dv$ $\; = \int \; \frac{1}{\left( \frac{v}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^2 + 1} dv$ $\; = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{v}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \cdot \sqrt{2} + C$ where $c =$ constant $\; = \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{u - \frac{1}{u}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + C$ $\; = \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{ \sqrt{\tan x} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tan x}} }{\sqrt{2}} \right) + C$ $\; = \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\tan x - 1}{\sqrt{2 \tan x}} \right) + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\;\; \text{ Let } \; I = \int \frac{\sqrt{x-2}}{2x+4} dx$ $\;\; \text{ and } \; u = \sqrt{x-2}$ $\; \Rightarrow u^2 = x-2 \; \text{ and } \; x = u^2+2$ Differentiate $x$ w.r.t $u$ , we get $\; \frac{dx}{du} \; = 2u \Rightarrow dx = 2u \, du$ $I\; = \int \frac{\sqrt{x-2}}{2x+4} dx = \int \frac{2u \cdot u}{2(u^2+2)+4} du$ $\; = \int \frac{2u^2}{2u^2+8} du = \int \frac{u^2}{u^2+4} du$ $\; = \int \frac{u^2+4-4}{u^2+4} du = \int \left(1 - \frac{4}{u^2+4}\right) du$ $\; = u - 4 \cdot \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{u}{2} \right) + C$ where, $C=$ constant $\; = u - 2 \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{u}{2} \right) + C$ $\; = \sqrt{x-2} - 2 \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{\sqrt{x-2}}{2} \right) + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $I = \int x^{49} \left[ \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) + \frac{x^{50}}{1+x^{100}} \right] dx$ $= \frac{x^n}{k} f(x) + c$ Let $u = x^{50}$ , then $du = 50 x^{49} dx$ $\text{so}, I = \int x^{49} \left[ \tan^{-1} x^{50} + \frac{x^{50}}{1+x^{100}} \right] dx$ $= \int x^{49} \left[ \tan^{-1}(u) + \frac{u}{1+u^2} \right] \cdot \frac{du}{50 x^{49}}$ $= \frac{1}{50} \int \left( \tan^{-1}(u) + \frac{u}{1+u^2} \right) du$ $= \frac{1}{50} \left[ \int \tan^{-1}(u) du + \int \frac{u}{1+u^2} du \right]$ $= \frac{1}{50} \left[ u \tan^{-1}(u) - \int \frac{u}{1+u^2} du + \int \frac{u}{1+u^2} du \right]$ [using product rule] $= \frac{1}{50} \left[ u \tan^{-1}(u) \right] + c$ $= \frac{1}{50} \cdot x^{50} \cdot \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) + c$ Comparing to original equation, we get $n = 50, k = 50, f(x) = \tan^{-1}(x^{50})$ Now, $f(x) - f(\sqrt[k]{x^n})$ $= f(x) - f\left(x^{\frac{n}{k}}\right)$ $= \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) - f\left(x^{\frac{50}{50}}\right)$ $= \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) - f(x)$ $= \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) - \tan^{-1}(x^{50}) = 0$ $\therefore f(x) - f(\sqrt[k]{x^n}) = 0$ Now, $k - n = 50 - 50 = 0$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $f(x) - f(\sqrt[k]{x^n}) = k - n$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $\text{ Let } I = \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 - 2x + 5}} dx$ $= \int \frac{x - 1 + 1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 2x + 5}} dx$ $= \int \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x^2-2x+5}} + \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+5}} dx$ Let $u = x^2 - 2x + 5$ , then $du = (2x - 2) dx$ $= 2(x-1) dx$ $= \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} + \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x-1)^2 + 4}} dx$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left(2 u^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) + \sinh^{-1} \frac{x-1}{2} + C$ $\left[ \because \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} dx = \sinh^{-1} \frac{x}{a} \right]$ Where, $C =$ constant $= \sqrt{u} + \sinh^{-1} \left( \frac{x-1}{2} \right) + C$ $= \sqrt{x^2 - 2x + 5} + \sinh^{-1} \left( \frac{x-1}{2} \right) + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: For $0 < x < 1$ , $I = \int [\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2) + \tan^{-1}(1-x)] \, dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left[ \frac{(1-x+x^2)+(1-x)}{1-(1-x+x^2)(1-x)} \right] dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2-2x+x^2}{x(2-2x+x^2)} \right) dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) dx$ $= \int \cot^{-1}(x) \, dx = \int \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} x \right) dx$ $= \int \frac{\pi}{2} \, dx - \int \tan^{-1} x \, dx$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} x - \left[ x \tan^{-1} x - \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C \right]$ [Using product rule] $= \frac{\pi}{2} x - x \tan^{-1} x + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ where $C =$ constant of integration $= x \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} x \right) + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ $= x \cot^{-1} x + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ $= x \cot^{-1} x + \log \sqrt{1+x^2} + C$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $I=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(2x) \cos^6(2x) dx$ Let $u=2x$ , then $du=2dx$ , so $dx=\frac{1}{2} du$ When $x=-2\pi, u=2(-2\pi)=-4\pi$ when $x=2\pi, u=2(2\pi)=4\pi$ $I=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(2x) \cos^6(2x) dx$ $=\frac{1}{2} \int\limits_{-4\pi}^{4\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ Since, $\sin(u)$ and $\cos(u)$ are periodic with a period of $2\pi$ , So, $\sin^4(u)$ and $\cos^6(u)$ are also periodic with a period of $2\pi$ $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=2 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ Since, the function, $f(u)=\sin^4(u) \cos^6(u)$ is an even function. $\therefore 2 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=2 \cdot 2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=4 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=4 \cdot 2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=8 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ We know that, $\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^m(u) \cos^n(u) du$ $=\frac{(m-1)(m-3)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)(n-1)(n-3)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)}{(m+n)(m+n-2)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)} \times \alpha$ where, $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}$ if both $m$ and $n$ are even, and $\alpha=1$ otherness. Here, $m=4, n=6$ both are even. So, $\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(4) \cos^6(4) du$ $=\frac{(4-1)(4-3)(6-1)(6-3)(6-5)}{(4+6)(4+6-2)(4+6-4)} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}$ $(4+6-6)(4+6-8)$ $=\frac{3 \cdot 1 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 1}{10 \cdot 8 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cdot 2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{45}{3840} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3}{256} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}$ $=\frac{3\pi}{512}$ $\therefore 8 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=8 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{512} = \frac{24\pi}{512} = \frac{3\pi}{64}$ $\therefore 8 \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du = \frac{3\pi}{64}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $f(t)=\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx, n\in$ So, $f(t+\pi)=\int\limits_{0}^{t+\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx$ $=\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx+\int\limits_{t}^{t+\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx$ Let $u=x-\pi$ $\Rightarrow du=dx$ Limit, when $x=t, u=t-\pi$ and $x=t+\pi, u=t$ So, $f(t+\pi)=f(t)+\int\limits_{t}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u+\pi)\,du$ Since, $\tan(u+\pi)=\tan u$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{t-\pi}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1}(u)\,du$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{t-\pi}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ Let $v=-u$ , the $dv=-du$ When $u=t-\pi, v=\pi-t$ , when $u=0, v=0$ , so we get $\;=f(t)-\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(-v)\,dv+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ $\;\;\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+f(t)$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi-t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ Let $w=v-\pi$ , then $dw=dv$ When $v=\pi-t, w=-t$ , when $v=\pi$ $w=0$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(w+\pi)\,dw$ $\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(w)\,dw$ Let $z=-w$ , then $dz=-dw$ when $w=-t, z=t$ and $w=0, z=0$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+\int\limits_{t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(-z)\,dz$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(z)\,dz$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-f(t)$ $=\;f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ $=\;f(t)+0 \left[ \because \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv=0 \right]$ $\;=f(t)+f(\pi) \;\; [ \because f(\pi)=0 ]$ $\therefore \;f(t+\pi)=f(t)+f(\pi)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: $I = \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4-x^2}{x^2} \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \cdot \frac{(4-x^2)^{5/2}}{x^5} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^3 (4-x^2)^{5/2} dx$ Let $u = 4 - x^2$ Then, $du = -2x \, dx$ , so $x \, dx = -\frac{1}{2} du \quad x^2 = 4 - u$ and $x^3 = x \cdot x^2 = x(4-u)$ when $x = 0, \quad u = 4$ and when $x = 2, \quad u = 0$ $\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^3 (4-x^2)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{4}^{0(4-u)} \cdot u^{5/2} \cdot \left( -\frac{1}{2} \right) du$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ 4 \cdot \frac{u^{7/2}}{7/2} - \frac{u^{9/2}}{9/2} \right]_{0}^{4}$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} u^{7/2} - \frac{2}{9} u^{9/2} \right]_{0}^{4}$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} (u)^{7/2} - \frac{2}{9} (4)^{9/2} - 0 \right]$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} (128) - \frac{2}{9} (512) \right]$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{1024}{7} - \frac{1024}{9} \right]$ $= \frac{1024}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{63} = \frac{1024}{63}$ $\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx = \frac{1024}{63} = \frac{2^{10}}{63}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, curves are $y=x^2$ and $y=8-x^2$ Equating these two equations, we get $\;x^2=8-x^2 \Rightarrow 2 x^2=8$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; x^2=4 \Rightarrow x= \pm 2$ $\;\;\text{ Thus, area }\;=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} [ (8-x^2) -x^2] dx$ $\; \;\;\;\;  \;=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} (8-x^2-x^2) dx=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} (8-2 x^2) dx$ $\;= \left[8 x-\;\frac{2}{3} x^3\right]_{-2}^2$ $\;= \{8(2)-\;\frac{2}{3}(2)^3\} - \{8(-2)-\;\frac{2}{3}(-2)^3\}$ $\;= \left(16-\;\frac{16}{3}\right) - \left(-16+\;\frac{16}{3}\right)$ $\;=16-\;\frac{16}{3}+16-\;\frac{16}{3}$ $\;=32-\;\frac{32}{3}=\;\frac{96-32}{3}=\;\frac{64}{3}$ ∴ The area of the region bounded by the curves is $\;\frac{64}{3}$ sq. units. © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, differential equation is $x^2(y+1) \frac{dy}{dx} + y^2(x+1)^2 = 0, y(1)=2$ $\Rightarrow x^2(y+1) \frac{dy}{dx} = -y^2(x+1)^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y+1}{y^2} dy = -\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2} dx$ Integrating to both sides, we get $\int \frac{y+1}{y^2} dy = -\int \frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2} dx$ $\Rightarrow \int \left( \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{y^2} \right) dy$ $= -\int \left( 1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{1}{x^2} \right) dx$ $\Rightarrow \ln|y| - \frac{1}{y} = -\left( x + 2\ln|x| - \frac{1}{x} \right) + C,$ where $C=$ constant $\Rightarrow \ln|y| + 2\ln|x| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + C$ $\Rightarrow \ln|x^2 y| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + C \cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot \text{(i)}$ Given, $y(1)=2$ , so we get $\Rightarrow \ln|1^2 \cdot 2| = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{1} - 1 + C$ $\Rightarrow \ln|2| = \frac{1}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = \ln|2| - \frac{1}{2}$ From, Eq. (i), we get $\ln|x^2 y| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + \ln|2| - \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \ln|x^2 y| - \ln|2| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x - \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \ln\left|\frac{1}{2} x^2 y\right| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x - \frac{1}{2}$ which matches option (2). © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, differential equation $\;\frac{dy}{dx}=\;\frac{2x+y-3}{2y-x+3}$ Let $x=X+h, y=Y+k$ , then $\;\frac{dY}{dX}\;=\;\frac{2(X+h)+(Y+k)-3}{2(Y+k)-(X+h)+3}$ $\;=\;\frac{2X+Y+2h+k-3}{2Y-X+2k-h+3}$ Let $2h+k-3=0$ and $-h+2k+3=0$ Solving these two equations, we get $h=\;\frac{9}{5}$ and $k=\;\frac{-3}{5}$ So, Eq. (i) becomes, $\;\frac{dY}{dX}=\;\frac{2X+Y}{2Y-X}$ Let $Y=vX$ $\Rightarrow \;\frac{dY}{dX}=v+X \;\frac{dv}{dX'}$ Substituting this into Eq. (ii), we get $\Rightarrow \;\;  x \;\frac{dv}{dx}\;=\;\frac{2+v}{2v-1}-v$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\frac{2+v-2v^2+v}{2v-1}$ $\;=\;\frac{2v-2v^2+2}{2v-1}$ $\Rightarrow \;\frac{2v-1}{-2v^2+2v+2} dv=\;\frac{2+v}{2v-1}$ Integrating both sides, we get $\int\;\frac{2v-1}{-2v^2+2v+2} dv=\int\;\frac{dX}{X}$ Let $u=-2v^2+2v+2$ Then $du=(-4v+2)dv$ $\therefore \;\frac{-1}{2} \int\;\frac{du}{u}=\int\;\frac{dX}{X} \Rightarrow \;\frac{-1}{2} \ln \lvert u \rvert = \ln \lvert X \rvert + c_1,$ where $c_1=$ constant $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \;\frac{-1}{2} \ln \lvert -2v^2+2v+2 \rvert =\ln \lvert X \rvert +c_1$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \ln \lvert -2v^2+2v+2 \rvert =-2 \ln \lvert X \rvert +c_2$ where $c_2=-2c_1$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \ln \lvert X^2 (-2v^2+2v+2) \rvert =c_2$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  X^2 (-2v^2+2v+2) =c, \;\text{ where }\; c=e^{c_2}$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  X^2 \left( \;\frac{-2Y^2}{X^2}+\;\frac{2Y}{X}+2 \right) =c$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  (-2Y^2+2XY+2X^2) =c$ Substitute $X$ and $Y$ , we get $\;-2\left(y+\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^2+2\left(x-\;\frac{9}{5}\right)\left(y+\;\frac{3}{5}\right)+2\left(x-\;\frac{9}{5}\right)^2=c$ $\;\Rightarrow-2\left(y^2+\;\frac{6}{5}y+\;\frac{9}{25}\right)+2\left(xy+\;\frac{3}{5}x-\;\frac{9}{5}y-\;\frac{27}{25}\right)+2\left(x^2-\;\frac{18}{5}x+\;\frac{81}{25}\right)=c$ $\; \;\;  \Rightarrow  \;\; -2y^2-\;\frac{12}{5}y-\;\frac{18}{25}+2xy+\;\frac{6}{5}x-\;\frac{18}{5}y$ $\; \;\; -\;\frac{54}{25}+2x^2-\;\frac{36}{5}x+\;\frac{162}{25}=c$ $\;\Rightarrow-2y^2+2xy+2x^2-\;\frac{30}{5}y-\;\frac{30}{5}x+\;\frac{90}{25}=c$ $\;\Rightarrow 2x^2+2xy-2y^2-6x-6y=c$ $\;\Rightarrow x^2+xy-y^2-3x-3y=c$ Thus, the general solution is $x^2+xy-y^2-3x-3y+c=0$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Given, $x \log x \;\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\log x^2$ $y(e)=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x \log x}y=\frac{\log x^2}{x \log x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x \log x}y=\frac{2 \log x}{x \log x}=\frac{2}{x}$ This is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ , Where $P(x)=\frac{1}{x \log x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ Now, $IF = e^{\int \frac{1}{x \log x} dx}$ Let $u=\log x$ . Then $du = \frac{1}{x} dx$ So, $IF = e^{\int \frac{1}{u} du} = e^{\log u} = u = \log x$ So, the solution is given by $y \cdot IF = \int Q(x) \cdot IF dx + c$ $y \log x = \int \frac{2}{x} \log x dx + c$ Let $v=\log x$ Then, $dv = \frac{1}{x} dx$ $\text{So,}\; y \log x = \int 2v dv + c = v^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow y \log x = v^2 + c = (\log x)^2 + c$ Given, $y(e)=0$ So, $y \log x = (\log x)^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow 0 \cdot \log(e) = (\log e)^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow 0 = 1 + c \Rightarrow c = -1$ ∴ The particular solution is $y \log x = (\log x)^2 - 1$ $\Rightarrow y = \frac{(\log x)^2 - 1}{\log x}$ So, $y(e^2) = \frac{(\log e^2)^2 - 1}{\log(e^2)}$ $= \frac{(2 \log e)^2 - 1}{2 \log(e)} \quad [\because \log e = 1]$ $= \frac{2^2 - 1}{2} = \frac{4 - 1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore y(e^2) = \frac{3}{2}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Error in surface area $S=1.2\%$ We need to find the percentage error in volume $V$ of a sphere. Relations: For a sphere of radius $r$ : $\;S=4\pi r^2$ $\;V=\;\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ Step 1: Express relative errors For small errors, $\;\;\frac{dS}{S}=2\;\frac{dr}{r}$ $\;\;\frac{dV}{V}=3\;\frac{dr}{r}$ Step 2: Connect the two From the first equation: $\;\frac{dr}{r}=\;\frac{1}{2}\;\frac{dS}{S}$ Substitute into the second: $\;\frac{dV}{V}=3\times\;\frac{1}{2}\;\frac{dS}{S}=\;\frac{3}{2}\;\frac{dS}{S}$ Step 3: Substitute given error Error in $V=\;\frac{3}{2}\times1.2\%=1.8\%$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Find acceleration $a$ . We use the formula for velocity with uniform acceleration: $v=u+at$ . Here, $u=0$ (because the body starts from rest), and after $n$ seconds, the velocity is $v$ . So: $v=an \Rightarrow a = \; \frac{v}{n}$ Step 2: Find displacement in the $n$ th second $(S_n)$ . The formula for how far an object moves during the $n$ th second is: $S_n = u + \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ Since $u=0$ : $S_n = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ Step 3: Find displacement in the $(n-1)$ th second $(S_{n-1})$ . Plug ( $n-1$ ) instead of $n$ into the formula: $S_{n-1} \; = \; \frac{a}{2} (2(n-1)-1)$ $\; = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-3)$ Step 4: Add the displacements for the $n$ th and $(n-1)$ th seconds. $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1) + \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-3)$ Combine the numbers in the brackets: $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{a}{2} [(2n-1)+(2n-3)] = \; \frac{a}{2} (4n-4)$ Step 5: Substitute $a = \; \frac{v}{n}$ from Step 1. $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot \; \frac{v}{n} \cdot (4n-4) = \; \frac{v}{2n} (4n-4)$ Simplify: $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{v}{2n} \cdot 4(n-1) = \; \frac{2v}{n} (n-1)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Write the formula for range The formula to find the range $R$ when a body is projected is: $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ Step 2: Put in the given values Here, $R = 180\sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m},\ u = 60\ \mathrm{m/s}$ , and $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ . Step 3: Arrange the formula to find $\sin 2\theta$ $\sin 2\theta = \frac{R g}{u^2}$ Step 4: Substitute the values $\sin 2\theta = \frac{180\sqrt{3} \times 10}{60 \times 60}$ $\sin 2\theta = \frac{1800\sqrt{3}}{3600} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ Step 5: Identify the angle for $\sin 2\theta$ We know that $\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . So, $2\theta = 60^{\circ}$ $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ Step 6: Check for other possible angles The range at angle $\theta$ is the same as at $90^{\circ} - \theta$ . So, the angle of projection can be $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Considering vertical motion, $u_y=u \sin \theta,\, S_y=60\,\text{m}$ $a_y=-10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2},\, t=2\,\text{s}$ Using $S_y=u_y t+\frac{1}{2} a_y t^2$ we get, $60=u \sin \theta \times 2-\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 2^2$ $\Rightarrow u \sin \theta =40$ Now, time of flight is $T=\frac{2 n \sin \theta}{g}=\frac{2 \times 40}{10}=8\,\text{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As disc is floating in air without falling, force by bullets balances gravitational force. $\Rightarrow \; \left( \frac{N \Delta p}{\Delta t} \right) = m_d g$ Here, $N=$ number of bullets fired $\; \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} =$ Rate of change of one bullet $m_d=$ mass of disc Hence, bullets rebound with same speed, momentum change for each bullet $=m(v-(-v))=2 m v$ $\therefore \; \frac{N}{t} \cdot 2 m_b v = m_d g$ Substituting given values, $10 \times 2 \times 0.05 \times v = 0.2 \times 10$ $\therefore \; v = \frac{0.2 \times 10}{10 \times 2 \times 0.05} = 2\ \text{m/s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $S=$ displacement of body beforce coming to rest Then using, $v^2-u^2=2 a S$ we get, $-u^2=2 \left(\; \frac{-F}{m}\right) S$ or $S=\; \frac{u^2 m}{2 F}$ or $S \propto u^2 m$ (for same retarding force $F$ ) $\therefore\;\; \frac{S_A}{S_B}= \; \frac{u_A^2 m_A}{u_B^2 m_B}= \; \frac{400 \times 1.5}{225 \times 3}= \; \frac{8}{9}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Displacement vector of the body is $\vec{S} = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j}$ $= (2-1)\hat{i} + (0-2)\hat{j}$ $= \hat{i} - 2\hat{j}\ \text{m}$ Force acting on the body is $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\ \text{N}$ Work done, $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{S}$ $= (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) \cdot (\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})$ $= (3)(1) + (-2)(-2)$ $= 3 + 4 = 7\ \text{J}$ Hence, the work done by the force is $7\ \text{J}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Let initial velocities are $u$ and $\; \frac{u}{2}$ and final velocities are $v_A$ and $v_B$ . Then, momentum is conserved, $m u + \frac{m u}{2} = m v_A + m v_B$ or $v_A + v_B = \frac{3 u}{2}$ Coefficient of restitution is 0.5 , $\Rightarrow e = \frac{v_B - v_A}{u_A - u_B} = \frac{v_B - v_A}{u - \left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}$ $\Rightarrow v_B - v_A = \frac{u}{4} \ldots (ii)$ From (i) and (ii) $v_B = \frac{7}{8} \cdot u$ And from (i) and (iii) $v_A = \frac{5}{8} u$ Hence, ratio $\frac{v_A}{v_B} = \frac{\frac{5}{8}}{\frac{7}{8}} = \frac{5}{7}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As sphere is in pure rolling, $v=R\omega$ Rotational KE of sphere $=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ $=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{5}mR^2\omega^2=\frac{1}{5}mv^2$ Kinetic energy of translation $=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ Total $KE = \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{5}\right)mv^2=\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ Required ratio $=\frac{1}{5}\times\frac{10}{7}=\frac{2}{7}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Moment of inertia of disc $B$ about given axis, $I_B=\;\frac{1}{2} M r^2$ Moment of inertia of disc $A$ about given axis using parallel axes theorem is, $I_A=\;\frac{1}{2} M r^2+M \cdot (2 r)^2=\;\frac{9}{2} M r^2$ $\therefore M \cdot I$ of system about given axis is, $I=I_A+I_B= \left(\;\frac{9}{2}+\;\frac{1}{2}\right) M r^2=5 M r^2$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Time period of a simple pendulum on the surface of the earth is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ At a height $h = \frac{R}{2}$ above the earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is $g_h = g \left( \frac{R}{R+h} \right)^2 = g \left( \frac{R}{R + \frac{R}{2}} \right)^2 = g \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^2 = \frac{4}{9} g$ So the time period at that height becomes $T' = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g_h}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\frac{4}{9} g}} = \frac{3}{2} \left( 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \right)$ $\therefore T' = \frac{3}{2} T$ Hence the correct option is $\frac{3T}{2}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: For particle in SHM, $T = 1.5\ \mathrm{sso}$ $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{4\pi}{3}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ Let oscillations starts from $t = 0$ and $x = A \sin \omega t$ is displacement equation Then, KE at time $t$ is, $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m \left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{2} m \cdot A^{2} \omega^{2} \cos^{2} \omega t \cdots (i)$ And total energy of particle is, $E = \frac{1}{2} k A^{2}$ Here, $k = m \omega^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} \cdots (ii)$ Given, ratio, $\frac{K}{E} = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} \cos^{2} \omega t }{ \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} } = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{2} \omega t = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \cos \omega t = \sqrt{ \frac{3}{2} }$ $\Rightarrow \omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}$ $\Rightarrow t = \frac{\pi}{6\omega} = \frac{\pi \times 3}{6 \times 4\pi} = \frac{1}{8}\ \mathrm{s}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Escape velocity from the Earth's surface $v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = 11.2\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Here $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of the Earth and $R$ is the radius of the Earth. Step 2: Orbital velocity of a satellite at height $h = R$ The orbital velocity at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ . For a height $h = R$ , the orbital radius is $r = R + R = 2R$ . So $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}}$ . Step 3: Compare the two velocities $\frac{v_{\text{orbit}}}{v_{\text{escape}}} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}}}{\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}\cdot\frac{R}{2GM}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$ Hence the orbital velocity is half the escape velocity. Step 4: Substitute the given value $v_{\text{orbit}} = \frac{v_{\text{escape}}}{2} = \frac{11.2}{2} = 5.6\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Therefore the correct option is $5.6\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Formula for Elongation The amount a wire stretches depends on Young's modulus formula: $Y=\;\frac{F l}{\Delta l A}=\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l \pi d^2}$ Step 2: What stays the same? Both wires are made of the same material, have the same length, and the same stretching force. This means their Young's modulus $(Y)$ , original length $(l)$ , and force $(F)$ are the same. Step 3: Setting up the equation for both wires Since Young's modulus is the same for both wires, we set the formulas equal for each wire: $Y_1=Y_2$ $\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l_1 \pi d_1^2}=\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l_2 \pi d_2^2}$ Step 4: Rearranging to compare elongations We can simplify to find how the elongation ( $\Delta l$ ) relates to diameter ( $d$ ): $\Delta l_1 \cdot d_1^2 = \Delta l_2 \cdot d_2^2$ So, $\Delta l_2 = \Delta l_1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{d_1}{d_2} \right)^2$ Step 5: Substitute values We are told $\Delta l_1 = 1\,\text{mm}$ (the first wire stretches 1 mm ) and $d_2 = 4 d_1$ (the second wire's diameter is 4 times bigger). $\Delta l_2 = 1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{d_1}{4 d_1} \right)^2 = 1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{1}{4} \right)^2 = \;\frac{1}{16} \text{mm}$ Final Answer The second, thicker wire stretches only $\;\frac{1}{16} \text{mm}$ when the same force is applied. © examsnet.com

Solution: As temperature is constant, for air in bubble, $p_1 V_1=p_2 V_2$ Given, $\;p_1=10 \times \rho_w \times g$ $\;p_2=(10+7.28) \rho_w \times g$ $\;V_1=\;\frac{4}{3} \pi r_1^3 \;\text{ and }\; V_2=\;\frac{4}{3} \pi r_2^3$ Now by $p_1 V_1=p_2 V_2$ $\Rightarrow  \;\;  \;\frac{V_2}{V_1}\;= \left(\;\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right) ^3=\;\frac{p_1}{p_2}$ $\Rightarrow  \;\;  \;\frac{r_2}{r_1}\;= \left(\;\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right) ^{\;\frac{1}{3}}= \left(\;\frac{10}{17.28}\right) ^{\;\frac{1}{3}}$ $\;= \left(\;\frac{1000}{1728}\right) ^{\;\frac{1}{3}}= \left(\;\frac{125}{216}\right) ^{\;\frac{1}{3}}=\;\frac{5}{6}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: As contraction in wire is prevented by extending it with a load, Thermal contraction $=$ Extension due to load $\;\Rightarrow\;\; \alpha l \Delta T = \;\frac{F l}{Y A} \Rightarrow \alpha l \Delta T = \;\frac{m g l}{Y A}$ $\;\Rightarrow\;\; m = \;\frac{\alpha \Delta T \cdot Y A}{g} = \;\frac{\alpha \Delta T Y A}{g}$ Substituting given values, $m \; = \; \frac{10^{-5} \times 100 \times 10^{11} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{10}$ $\; = 4 \times 10 = 40 \mathrm{kg}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Let $m=$ mass of steam condensed. Then, $m$ grams of steam forms $m$ grams of water at $100^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$ which further losses heat and comes at $90^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$ . Final mixture is water at $90^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$ Now using Heat lost = Heat gained, we gel Heat lost by steam in condensation + Heat lost by water formed at $100^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$ $=$ Heat gained by water at $24^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$ $\; \Rightarrow m L + m c(100-90) = 100(c)(90-24)$ $\; \Rightarrow m(540 + 1 \times 10) = 100 \times 1 \times 66$ $\; \Rightarrow m = \; \frac{100 \times 66}{550} = \; \frac{10 \times 6}{5} = 12\,\mathrm{g}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Heat supplied at constant pressure is used to do work and to raise temperature of the gas. $\therefore \;\Delta Q\;=\Delta W+\Delta U$ $\Rightarrow\;80\;=20+\Delta U$ $\Rightarrow\;\Delta U\;=60\,\mathrm{J}$ Now, $\Delta Q=n C_p \Delta T$ and $\Delta U=n C_V \Delta T$ ∴ Ratio $\;\frac{C_p}{C_V}=\;\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U}=\;\frac{80}{60}=\;\frac{4}{3}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: For a refrigerator, the coefficient of performance is defined as the heat extracted from the cold compartment divided by the work input per cycle: $COP = \frac{Q_C}{W}$ Step 2: Here $COP = 5$ and $Q_C = 250 \, \text{J}$ , so the work done per cycle is: $W = \frac{Q_C}{COP} = \frac{250}{5} = 50 \, \text{J}$ Step 3: By conservation of energy (first law) for one cycle, the heat rejected to the room equals the heat absorbed from the cooling compartment plus the work input: $Q_H = Q_C + W$ Step 4: Substitute the values: $Q_H = 250 \, \text{J} + 50 \, \text{J} = 300 \, \text{J}$ Step 5: Hence the heat released per cycle to the room is $300 \, \text{J}$ , which matches the option $300 \, \text{J}$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: Standard equation of a travelling wave is, $y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)$ Given, $y=0.5\sin(70.1x-10\pi t)$ $\therefore \omega=$ angular frequency $=10\pi$ But $\omega=2\pi f$ , where $f=$ frequency $\Rightarrow f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{10\pi}{2\pi}=5\text{ Hz}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: By Lens maker's formula, For a equviconvex lens, $\; \frac{1}{f} = \left( \frac{n_2}{n_1} - 1 \right) \left( \frac{2}{R} \right)$ In air, $n_1 = 1, n_2 = \; \frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore \;\; \frac{1}{f_{\;\text{air }\;}} = \left( \frac{3}{2} - 1 \right) \left( \frac{2}{R} \right)$ $\; \frac{1}{f_{\;\text{air }\;}} \; = \; \frac{1}{R}$ In liquid, $n_1 = x, n_2 = \; \frac{3}{2}$ $\; \frac{1}{f_l} = \left( \; \frac{3}{2x} - 1 \right) \left( \; \frac{2}{R} \right)$ Given, $\; \frac{f_{\;\text{air }\;}}{f_{\;\text{liquid }\;}} = \; \frac{1}{2}$ So, from Eq. (i) and (ii) $\; \frac{f_{\;\text{air }\;}}{f_{\;\text{liquid }\;}} = \frac{R \times 2 \left( \frac{3}{2x} - 1 \right)}{R \times 1} = \; \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow 2 \left( \; \frac{3}{2x} - 1 \right) = \; \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{3}{2x} - 1 = \; \frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{3}{2x} = \; \frac{5}{4} \; \text{ or } \; x = \; \frac{6}{5} = 1:20$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Phase difference between waves is $\varphi_1 - \varphi_2\; = \left( \omega t - \frac{2\pi x}{\lambda} + \varphi \right) - \left( \omega t - \frac{2\pi x}{\lambda} \right)$ $\; = \varphi$ As, relation of phase and path difference is, $\; \frac{\Delta \varphi}{2\pi} = \frac{\Delta L}{\lambda}$ ⇒ Path difference, $\Delta L = \frac{\lambda \varphi}{2\pi}$ . © examsnet.com

Using KVL in loop $A B C D E F G A$ ; we have; $\;-6 I-1 \;\frac{I}{2}-\;\frac{3I}{2}-I+9=0$ $\Rightarrow \;\; 9 I = 9 \; \text{ or } \; I = 1 A$ Now, potential difference between $B$ and $D$ (using KVL); $\; V_B - 6 \times 1 - 1 \times \; \frac{1}{2} = V_D$ $\Rightarrow V_B - V_D = 6 + \; \frac{1}{2} = \; \frac{13}{2} = 6.5 V$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We know the electron mobility $(\mu)$ and want to find the drift velocity $(v_d)$ . The formula is: $\mu = \frac{v_d}{E}$ Here, $E$ stands for the electric field. For a wire, $E = \frac{V}{l}$ , where $V$ is the voltage and $l$ is the length of the wire. So, the drift velocity can be found as: $v_d = E \mu = \frac{V}{l} \cdot \mu$ Plug in the values: $V = 30\,\mathrm{V},\ l = 20\,\mathrm{cm} = 20 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$ , and $\mu = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{m}^2 \, \mathrm{V}^{-1} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . $v_d = \frac{30 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{20 \times 10^{-2}}$ Do the calculation step by step: $30 \times 2 = 60,\ 20 \times 10^{-2} = 0.2$ . $v_d = \frac{60 \times 10^{-6}}{0.2} = 300 \times 10^{-6} = 3 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Here, $I_g=0.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$ $G=15\ \Omega$ and the required voltmeter range is $V_{AB}=10\ \mathrm{V}$ For a voltmeter, a resistance $R_s$ is connected in series with the galvanometer, so $V_{AB}=I_g\,(G+R_s)$ $\Rightarrow\;10=0.5 \times 10^{-3}\,(15+R_s)$ $\Rightarrow\;15+R_s=\frac{10}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}}=20000$ $\Rightarrow\;R_s=20000-15=19985\ \Omega$ Hence, the correct option is $19985\ \Omega$ . © examsnet.com

Solution: For a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, the radius of the circular path is $r=\frac{mv}{Bq}$ Since kinetic energy is $K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ , we have $mv=\sqrt{2mK}$ , so $r=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{Bq}$ Writing charge in terms of the specific charge $s=\frac{q}{m}$ (so $q=ms$ ), $r=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{B\,m\,s}=\frac{\sqrt{2K}}{B\,s\sqrt{m}}$ Thus $r\propto \frac{1}{s\sqrt{m}}$ for the same $K$ and $B$ . Given $s_1:s_2=2:1$ and $m_1:m_2=1:4$ , $\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{s_2}{s_1}\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^2\left(\frac{m_2}{m_1}\right)}$ $\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)}=\sqrt{1}=1$ Hence $r_1:r_2=1:1$ . Correct option: $1:1$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We use Curie's law to understand how the magnetism of a paramagnetic material changes with temperature and magnetic field. According to Curie's law, the magnetisation $(M)$ is directly proportional to the magnetic field $(B_0)$ and inversely proportional to the temperature $(T)$ : $M \propto \frac{B_0}{T}$ or, $M = C \cdot \frac{B_0}{T}$ where $C$ (Curie's constant) stays the same for the same substance. Curie's constant can be written as: $C = \frac{M T}{B_0}$ where: $T =$ temperature in Kelvin $B_0 =$ external magnetic field $M =$ magnetisation (total dipole moment) Since $C$ (Curie's constant) is the same for all measurements of the same sample, we can relate two cases as: $\frac{M_1 T_1}{B_{0_1}} = \frac{M_2 T_2}{B_{0_2}}$ So, $M_2 = M_1 \cdot \frac{T_1}{T_2} \cdot \frac{B_{0_2}}{B_{0_1}}$ Now, let's fill in the given values: Number of dipoles $= 2 \times 10^{24}$ Dipole moment per dipole $= 15 \times 10^{-23} \text{JT}^{-1}$ Step 1: Find Initial Total Dipole Moment Total dipole moment possible (if $100\%$ aligned): $2 \times 10^{24} \times 15 \times 10^{-23} = 3 \times 10^2 \text{JT}^{-1}$ But, at first, only $20\%$ saturation is achieved: $M_1 = 0.2 \times 3 \times 10^2 = 60 \text{JT}^{-1}$ Step 2: Use Curie's Law for New Conditions Magnetic field changes from $B_{0_1} = 0.6 \text{T}$ to $B_{0_2} = 0.9 \text{T}$ and temperature from $T_1 = 4.2 \text{K}$ to $T_2 = 2.8 \text{K}$ . Now, use the formula: $M_2 = M_1 \times \frac{T_1}{T_2} \times \frac{B_{0_2}}{B_{0_1}}$ Substitute the numbers in: $M_2 = 60 \times \frac{4.2}{2.8} \times \frac{0.9}{0.6}$ Calculate step by step: $\frac{4.2}{2.8} = 1.5$ $\frac{0.9}{0.6} = 1.5$ So, $M_2 = 60 \times 1.5 \times 1.5 = 135 \text{JT}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: We need to find the current in the coil at $t=2$ seconds. Step 1: Find the induced EMF. The magnetic flux is given by $\phi=50 t^2+4$ . To find the EMF ( $E$ ), we take the derivative of $\phi$ with respect to $t$ : $E=\;\frac{d\phi}{dt}$ Now, differentiate $\phi$ : $\;\frac{d}{dt} (50 t^2+4) =100 t$ (because the derivative of $t^2$ is $2t$ , and 50 times $2t$ is $100t$ ; the derivative of a constant is 0 ). Step 2: Calculate EMF at $t=2$ seconds. Plug in $t=2$ : $E=100 \times 2=200\;\text{ volts }\;$ Step 3: Find the current using Ohm's Law. Ohm's Law: $I=\;\frac{E}{R}$ Here, $E=200$ volts and $R=200 \Omega$ . $I=\;\frac{200}{200}=1\ \mathrm{A}$ So, the current induced in the coil at $t=2$ seconds is 1 ampere. © examsnet.com

Solution: Concept: Average AC power depends on the phase difference between voltage and current. Formula: $P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi=\frac{V_0 I_0}{2}\cos\phi$ Solution: $V_0=50\,\mathrm{V},\ I_0=50\,\mathrm{mA}=0.05\,\mathrm{A},\ \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}$ . $P=\frac{50 \times 0.05}{2}\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$ $P=1.25 \times 0.707\approx 0.884\,\mathrm{W}$ Answer: $0.884\,\mathrm{W}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Step 1: Understanding Power Power is how much energy is used or given out each second. So: Power $= \frac{\text{ Energy }}{\text{ Time }}$ Step 2: Energy of One Photon The energy in one photon of light is found using: $E = h f$ where $h$ is Planck's constant and $f$ is the frequency. Step 3: Total Energy from Many Photons If $N$ photons come out in time $t$ , the total energy is $N \times h f$ . Step 4: Linking Power and Number of Photons So, Power $= \frac{\text{ Total Energy }}{\text{ Time }} = \frac{N \times h f}{t}$ Step 5: Average Number of Photons per Second The number of photons per second is $n = \frac{N}{t} = \frac{P}{h f}$ Plug in the numbers: $n = \frac{33 \times 10^{-3}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 5 \times 10^{14}}$ Step 6: Final Calculation This works out to: $n = 10 \times 10^{16}$ So, the laser gives off $10 \times 10^{16}$ photons every second. © examsnet.com

Solution: Using, $E_n=\;\frac{-13.6}{n^2}\ \mathrm{eV}$ ; Energy of photon in transition $n=2$ to $n=1$ $\;=\Delta E_1=E_2-E_1$ $\;=(-3.4)-(-13.6)=10.2\ \mathrm{eV}$ Energy of photon in transition $n=5$ to $n=2$ $=\Delta E_2=E_5-E_2=\;-0.544-(-3.4)$ $\;=2.856\ \mathrm{eV}$ Ratio $\;\frac{\Delta E_1}{\Delta E_2}=\;\frac{10.2}{2.8}=\;\frac{102}{28}=\;\frac{25.5}{7}\approx\;\frac{25}{7}$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Using the Rydberg formula $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R z^2 \left[ \frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2} \right]$ For $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ , $z=2$ , and for the Balmer series, $n_f=2$ . The initial level is $n_i=n$ where $n>2$ . $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R(2)^2 \left[ \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{n^2} \right]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\lambda}=4R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{n^2} \right)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\lambda}=R \left( 1 - \frac{4}{n^2} \right)= \frac{R(n^2-4)}{n^2}$ Taking the reciprocal, $\lambda=\frac{n^2}{R(n^2-4)}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{n^2}{R(n-2)(n+2)}$ This matches option (0), so the marked answer is correct. © examsnet.com

Solution: Statement I If thermal energy is stronger than intermolecular forces, the substance prefers to be in gaseous state. When thermal (kinetic) energy of molecules exceeds the intermolecular attractive forces, the molecules move freely, far apart - this is the gaseous state. Statement I is correct. Statement II At constant temperature, the density of an ideal gas is proportional to its pressure. From the ideal gas law: $P V=n R T$ or $P=\;\frac{n}{V} R T$ Now, $\;\frac{n}{V} = \;\frac{\rho}{M}$ , where $\rho$ is density and $M$ is molar mass. Thus, $P=\;\frac{\rho}{M} R T \Rightarrow \rho=\;\frac{P M}{R T}$ At constant $T$ and $M$ : $\rho \propto P$ Statement II is also correct. © examsnet.com

Solution: Calculating the partial pressure of $\mathrm{H}_2$ in 10 L flask $\; p_{\mathrm{H}_2 \; \text{ initial }} \; \; V_{\mathrm{H}_2 \; \text{ initial }} = p_{\mathrm{H}_2 \; \text{ final }} \; \; V_{\text{ total }}$ $\; p_{\mathrm{H}_2 \; \text{ final }} = \; \frac{1 \times 1}{10} = 0.1 \text{ bar}$ Using Boyle's law for partial pressure of $\mathrm{O}_2$ $p_{\mathrm{O}_2 \; \text{ final }} \; = \; \frac{p_{\mathrm{O}_2 \; \text{ initial }} \times V_{\mathrm{O}_2 \; \text{ initial }}}{V_{\text{ total }}}$ $\; = \; \frac{2 \times 2}{10} = 0.4 \text{ bar}$ Use Dalton's law of partial pressure. $p_{\text{ total }} \; = p_{\mathrm{H}_2 \; \text{ final }} \; \; + p_{\mathrm{O}_2 \; \text{ final }}$ $\; = 0.1+0.4=0.5 \text{ bar}$ Since $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ do not react at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in the absence of a spark or catalyst, the total pressure is simply the sum of the partial pressures of the two gases. Hence the pressure exerted by the gaseous mixture is $0.5 \text{ bar}$ , i.e. option (3). © examsnet.com

Solution: Normality of $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3=$ molarity $\times n$ -factor $=0.5\ \mathrm{M}\times 2=1\ \mathrm{N}$ Normality of acid $A$ , $\;N_{\;\text{acid }\;} A \times V_{\;\text{acid }\;A}=N_{\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3} \times V_{\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3}$ $\;N_{\;\text{acid }\;} A=\;\frac{1\times 25}{10}=2.5\ \mathrm{N}$ Similarly normality of acid $B$ $N_{\;\text{acid }\;B}=0.625\ \mathrm{N}$ Volume of acid $A$ needed for 1 L of 1 N solution $\;N_{\;\text{acid }\;A} \times V_{A\;\text{final }\;}=N_{\;\text{final }\;} \times V_{\;\text{final }\;}$ $\;V_{A\;\text{final }\;}=\;\frac{1\times 1}{2.5}=0.4\ \mathrm{L}\;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(i)$ Volume of acid $B$ needed for 1 L of 1 N solution, $V_{B\;\text{final }\;}=\;\frac{1\times 1}{0.625}=1.6\ \mathrm{L}\;\;\;\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot(ii)$ © examsnet.com

Solution: Analysis of Statement-I: Both $\mathrm{BeSO}_4$ and $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ are readily soluble in water. The solubility of sulfates of alkaline earth metals generally decreases down the group. $\mathrm{BeSO}_4$ (Beryllium sulfate) is readily soluble in water. This is due to the very small size of the $\mathrm{Be}^{2+}$ ion, which leads to very high hydration energy. This high hydration energy more than compensates for the relatively high lattice energy, making it highly soluble. $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ (Magnesium sulfate, commonly known as Epsom salt) is also readily soluble in water. Similar to beryllium, the $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ ion is relatively small, leading to significant hydration energy. In contrast, $\mathrm{CaSO}_4$ (Calcium sulfate) is sparingly soluble, and $\mathrm{SrSO}_4$ (Strontium sulfate) and $\mathrm{BaSO}_4$ (Barium sulfate) are practically insoluble. Therefore, Statement - I is correct. Analysis of Statement - II: Among the nitrates of alkaline earth metals, only $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ on strong heating gives its oxide, $\mathrm{NO}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ . Alkaline earth metal nitrates decompose on strong heating to give the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide ( $\mathrm{NO}_2$ ), and oxygen $(\mathrm{O}_2)$ . The general reaction is: $2 \mathrm{M}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} 2 \mathrm{MO}(s) + 4 \mathrm{NO}_2(g) + \mathrm{O}_2(g)$ This decomposition pattern is observed for all alkaline earth metal nitrates. $\; \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{BeO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ $\; \mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{MgO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ $\; \mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{CaO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ And similarly for $\mathrm{Sr}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ and $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ . The thermal stability of these nitrates generally increases down the group $(\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2.$ is the least stable, and $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ is the most stable), meaning they decompose at different temperatures, but the decomposition products are the same for all of them. The statement claims that "only $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ " decomposes in this manner, which is incorrect as all alkaline earth metal nitrates follow this decomposition pathway. Therefore, Statement - II is not correct. Conclusion: Statement - I is correct. Statement - II is not correct. This matches option B. © examsnet.com

Solution: Photochemical smog: Formed when sunlight acts on nitrogen oxides (NOx) and hydrocarbons (unburnt fuel), producing secondary pollutants like ozone $(\mathrm{O}_3)$ , peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), formaldehyde, etc. It is also called Los Angeles smog or summer smog. It mainly occurs in warm, dry, and sunny climates. Option A: It is controlled by the use of catalytic converters in automobiles. Correct. Catalytic converters reduce emissions of NOx and hydrocarbons, which are precursors of photochemical smog. Option B: It causes corrosion of metals. Correct. Ozone and other oxidants in photochemical smog can corrode metals. Option C: It is a mixture of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ , smoke, and fog. Not correct. This describes classical smog (also called London smog or reducing smog), which occurs in cool, humid conditions and is a mixture of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ and particulates with fog. Photochemical smog, on the other hand, contains NOx, hydrocarbons, and oxidants such as ozone-not SO2-based smoke and fog. Option D: It causes extensive damage to plant life. Correct. Ozone and PAN damage leaves and affect photosynthesis. © examsnet.com
